topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Step-by-Step Instructions
topics.description: Step-by-step instructions for everyday tasks (making a sandwich, brushing teeth); that if instructions are wrong or missing, things go wrong; computers follow instructions exactly
evidence: Write or describe step-by-step instructions for a simple everyday task
Predict what goes wrong if a step is missing or in the wrong order
Explain that a computer follows instructions exactly — it cannot guess what you meant

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Decisions and repeats in algorithms
topics.description: Follow and describe algorithms that include a sequence of steps, branching (a decision such as 'if it is raining, take an umbrella') and iteration (repeating steps, such as 'hop 3 times')
evidence: Follow movement instructions that include a repeat (e.g. 'repeat 3 times: step forward, clap') and describe which part was repeated
Follow an algorithm with a decision (e.g. 'If the card is red, put it in the box; otherwise put it on the table') and explain what the decision did
Describe the steps, decision and repeat in a familiar routine, such as getting ready for school

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: My first visual program
topics.description: Implement a simple algorithm as a visual (block-based) program — a start event, a sequence of blocks, run and observe — in an environment such as Scratch, ScratchJr or a programmable robot app, including short sequences that act out a maths situation (e.g. jumps along a number line)
evidence: Drag blocks into a sequence so a character moves, speaks and changes costume when the green flag is clicked, then run it and check it does what the planned algorithm said
Write and run a sequence that shows a maths situation (e.g. move a robot or sprite along a number line in 3 jumps of 2 and check it stops on 6)
Swap two blocks and explain how the order of blocks changes what the program does

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Testing and debugging programs
topics.description: Test visual programs by predicting what should happen, running them, finding where the behaviour differs (bugs) and fixing them one change at a time
evidence: Predict what a short program should do for given inputs, including unusual ones (e.g. a wrong or blank answer), run it and record whether each result matched
Find and fix a bug in a given program (e.g. a character that turns the wrong way or a loop that repeats too many times)
Explain how they tracked down the bug (e.g. running one part at a time, checking each block against the algorithm)

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Concurrent events in code
topics.description: Write, read, run and alter block-based code in which two or more scripts or characters run at the same time (concurrent events, e.g. started by the same event), predicting and testing the combined outcome and distinguishing it from steps that run one after another
evidence: Write two scripts that start on the same event so two characters move at the same time, run the program and check that both happen together

Read a program with two scripts that run at the same time and predict what is on the screen at a given moment, explaining how this differs from putting the same blocks one after another in a single script
Alter one of two concurrent scripts (e.g. change a wait or the number of steps) and explain and test how the change affects what happens together

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Decisions and input in programs
topics.description: Use input (key presses, mouse clicks, sensors or typed answers) and branching blocks (if ... then, if ... then ... else) with comparison operators to make a visual program respond to the user
evidence: Program a character to move left and right when the arrow keys are pressed
Write a quiz question that asks for an answer and uses 'if answer = 12 then say Correct, else say Try again'
Use a comparison such as 'if score > 5' or 'if touching colour red' to change what the program does and explain the condition

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Loops in programs
topics.description: Use loop blocks in a visual program to repeat actions a set number of times, forever, or until a condition is true, and identify where a loop makes a program shorter
evidence: Rewrite a program that repeats 'move 10 steps' four times so that it uses one repeat block
Use a 'repeat until' block so a quiz keeps asking until the correct answer is given, or a sprite moves until it touches the edge
Explain the difference between 'repeat 10', 'forever' and 'repeat until' blocks with an example of when to use each

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Nested loops in code
topics.description: Write, run, read and alter code (block-based or text-based) that places one loop inside another (for example a loop that draws a square, repeated with a turn after each square to make a rotating pattern), predict how many times the inner steps run altogether (outer repeats × inner repeats), and describe how changing the inner or the outer loop changes the outcome
evidence: Write and run code with a loop inside a loop (e.g. repeat a 'draw a square' loop 6 times with a turn after each square) and check that the result matches the plan
Read a program with nested loops and predict how many times the inner action happens altogether (e.g. repeat 3 [repeat 4 [clap]] claps 12 times), then run it to check
Change either the inner or the outer repeat count in nested-loop code, then explain and test how the change affects what happens

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Variables in programs
topics.description: Create and use variables in visual programs to store and change values — such as a score, a timer, a counter or a user's answer — and use them in conditions
evidence: Create a 'score' variable in a game that starts at 0 and increases by 1 each time the player catches an object
Store a user's typed name in a variable and use it in a message (e.g. 'Hello Sam!')
Use a variable in a condition (e.g. 'if lives = 0 then game over') and explain what the variable holds at each stage

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: AI in Daily Life
topics.description: Recognise AI-enabled features in everyday life, such as face recognition, video recommendations, predictive text, speech recognition and translation, using information about the particular system rather than assuming that every automatic response uses AI.
evidence: Identify at least five examples of AI in their daily life
Explain that these technologies use patterns and data, not magic or real thinking
Describe one way AI makes their life easier and one time it might not work perfectly

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Real-World Robots
topics.description: What a robot really is — not the sci-fi version; robots in factories, robot vacuum cleaners, robot arms in surgery; that robots follow instructions given by people
evidence: Describe what a robot is (a machine that follows instructions to do a task)
Name at least three real robots and what they do
Explain that robots are not alive and do not have feelings — they follow instructions people wrote

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Smart Versus Not-Smart Devices
topics.description: Sorting objects into 'smart' (can sense and respond) and 'not smart' (just sits there); a toaster vs a smart speaker; introduction to the idea that some machines can sense and respond to the world
evidence: Sort a set of objects into 'smart' (responds to input) and 'not smart' (does the same thing every time)
Explain what makes a smart speaker different from a regular radio
Give an example of a machine that senses something and responds (automatic door, motion-sensor light)

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Voice Assistants and How They Work
topics.description: What happens when you talk to Alexa, Siri, or Google Assistant; they listen, try to understand, look up answers; sometimes they get it wrong; they are tools, not alive
evidence: Describe the steps that happen when you ask a voice assistant a question (it listens, processes words, finds an answer, speaks back)
Give an example of a time a voice assistant might get something wrong
Explain that a voice assistant is a computer program, not a person — it doesn't understand or feel

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Recommendation Systems and Filter Bubbles
topics.description: How recommendation systems work: YouTube, Netflix, and shop websites track what you click and find patterns; filter bubbles; the difference between helpful suggestions and manipulation
evidence: Explain how YouTube or Netflix decides what to suggest next
Describe what a 'filter bubble' is (only seeing things similar to what you already like)
Give one benefit and one risk of recommendation systems

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: AI in Computer Games
topics.description: How computer game characters 'decide' what to do; simple rule-based AI vs learning AI; NPCs, difficulty adjustment; AI as the opponent in chess or board games
evidence: Explain how a computer opponent in a game decides its moves
Describe the difference between a game character that follows fixed rules and one that learns from the player
Give an example of AI making a game more fun (adjusting difficulty, generating levels)

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: AI Mistakes and Limitations
topics.description: Machines make mistakes; they only know what they've been shown; bad training data leads to bad results; AI is not magic — just maths on data; showing edge cases and failures
evidence: Give an example of AI making a mistake (voice assistant mishearing, auto-correct error, wrong recommendation)
Explain that AI mistakes happen because of gaps or errors in training data
Describe why AI is not magic — it follows mathematical rules applied to data

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Humans Versus Machines
topics.description: Comparing human and machine capabilities: creativity, empathy, common sense vs speed, memory, repetition; the Turing Test (simplified); what makes humans unique
evidence: Name at least three things humans are better at than computers (creativity, empathy, common sense)
Name at least three things computers are better at than humans (speed, memory, repetitive tasks)
Describe the Turing Test in simple terms (can a computer fool a person into thinking it's human?)

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Machine Learning Basics
topics.description: How machine learning works at a conceptual level: show the computer many examples, it finds patterns, then it makes predictions about new things; hands-on experience with Teachable Machine or similar tool
evidence: Describe the three steps of machine learning in simple terms (give examples, find patterns, make predictions)
Train a simple model using a tool like Teachable Machine and describe what happened
Explain why showing more and better examples makes the model more accurate

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Patterns and Classification
topics.description: Humans are great at spotting patterns; computers can learn to spot patterns too, but they need lots of examples; sorting and classification activities as the basis of machine learning
evidence: Sort a set of items into categories and explain the rules they used
Explain that computers learn patterns by looking at many examples
Describe why a computer needs more examples than a human to learn the same pattern

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: AI Data Collection and Privacy
topics.description: What data AI systems collect about you; who has it and why it matters; cookies, tracking, smart speakers always listening; your data is valuable
evidence: Name at least three types of personal data that AI systems collect
Explain why personal data is valuable to companies
Describe one step they can take to protect their privacy online

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Deepfakes and AI-Generated Content
topics.description: Deepfakes, AI-generated images and text; how to spot them and why they matter; the importance of checking sources; not everything online is real
evidence: Explain what a deepfake is and give an example of AI-generated content
Describe at least two clues that might reveal an image or text was AI-generated
Explain why it matters that AI can create realistic fake content

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: AI and Fairness in Decisions
topics.description: Whether AI should make important decisions about people: jobs, loans, justice; who is responsible when AI makes unfair decisions; introduction to algorithmic fairness
evidence: Give an example of an important decision that AI might help make (hiring, medical diagnosis, loan approval)
Explain why letting AI make decisions about people can be risky if the system is biased
Suggest who should be responsible if an AI system makes an unfair decision

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: AI and the Environment
topics.description: AI needs huge amounts of energy and water to train; data centres and their environmental cost; but AI can also help — predicting weather, monitoring deforestation, optimising energy; trade-offs
evidence: Explain that training AI models uses a lot of electricity and water
Give at least two examples of AI being used to help the environment
Describe the trade-off between AI's environmental cost and its environmental benefits

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: AI and the Future of Work
topics.description: How AI is changing the world of work: some jobs disappear, new ones are created, many change; jobs AI can't do (yet); what skills matter in an AI world
evidence: Name at least two jobs that AI is changing or replacing and two new jobs AI has created
Explain why creativity, empathy, and problem-solving are skills that matter more in an AI world
Describe how AI might change a specific job they know about (teacher, doctor, farmer) without replacing it

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Bias in AI Systems
topics.description: If training data is biased, AI will be biased; examples: facial recognition working better for some skin tones, translation assuming gender; where bias comes from and whether we can fix it
evidence: Explain what bias in AI means using a real-world example
Describe how biased training data leads to biased AI results
Suggest one way to reduce bias in an AI system (use more diverse data, test with different groups)

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Designing Fair AI Rules
topics.description: Design thinking applied to AI ethics: if you were designing an AI system, what rules would you give it? Who should it help? What should it not be allowed to do?
evidence: Propose at least three rules for a hypothetical AI system they are designing
Explain why AI designers need to think about who might be harmed, not just who benefits
Describe one real example of AI being used responsibly and one where it was not

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: The Future of AI
topics.description: What AI might do in 10 years; what we want it to do and what we're worried about; children as future designers and decision-makers about AI; hopeful, empowered framing
evidence: Describe at least two ways AI might be used in the future that don't exist yet
Explain one thing they would want AI to do and one thing they would want it not to do
Describe why it matters that young people understand AI — because they will shape how it is used

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Data and Information for Computers
topics.description: What data is: information that computers use — numbers, words, pictures, sounds; everything a computer knows comes from data that people give it
evidence: Define data as information stored in a computer (numbers, text, images, sounds)
Give at least three examples of data they create every day (photos, messages, search queries)
Explain that a computer only knows what it has been given — it has no knowledge of its own

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: All data as numbers
topics.description: Explain how digital systems represent all data — text, images and sound — using numbers: each pixel's colour is stored as numbers, each letter has a number code and sound is stored as a series of number samples
evidence: Colour a pixel grid from a list of numbers (e.g. 0 = white, 1 = black) to reveal a hidden picture
Encode a short word using a number code for letters (e.g. A = 65, B = 66 in ASCII) and decode a partner's word
Explain how a photo, a text message and a song are all stored as numbers in a device

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Binary on and off
topics.description: Explore how digital systems represent data using two states — on and off, written as 1 and 0 — called bits, and use binary numbers to represent whole numbers and letters
evidence: Show every number from 0 to 31 using five binary cards (16, 8, 4, 2, 1) turned face up for 1 and face down for 0
Convert binary numbers such as 1010 and 10011 to ordinary numbers and back
Explain why computers use two states (a switch, light or current is either on or off) and show a letter as a string of bits using a given code

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Checking solutions against criteria
topics.description: Check how existing digital solutions and their own solutions satisfy users' needs, design criteria and user stories, using evidence from trying them out, and identify an unmet need or criterion and suggest an improvement
evidence: Explore an existing app or device with a known user's needs in mind (e.g. a younger sibling needs big buttons and sounds) and point out which features meet each need
Test their own program or digital product with a classmate against a checklist of design criteria and user stories and record which are met
Identify one need, criterion or user story that is not yet met and suggest a change to the solution

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Storyboarding a digital solution
topics.description: Represent a digital solution's design in a storyboard — each screen, what the user does (inputs), what the system shows or does (outputs) and the resulting behaviour — communicate it, and revise it in response to feedback
evidence: Sketch a storyboard for a simple game, app or animation showing each screen, what the user does and what happens
Present the storyboard to a partner or user, explaining its inputs, outputs and steps, and collect feedback
Revise the storyboard in response to feedback or testing and explain what changed and why

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Writing user stories
topics.description: Write user stories in the form 'As a ..., I want ..., so that ...' that state who the user is, what they need and why, for one or more users of a digital solution (with a group, with a real user or independently)
evidence: Write at least two user stories for a planned digital solution (e.g. 'As a Year 1 student, I want to hear each word read aloud, so that I can check I said it correctly')
Check that each user story names the user, what they want and why, and fix any that miss a part
Write user stories for two different users of the same solution (e.g. after asking or surveying them) and explain how their needs differ

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Community impact of digital solutions
topics.description: Evaluate the broader community impact of digital solutions: who benefits, who might be excluded, and effects on privacy, safety, wellbeing and the environment, suggesting improvements that reduce harm
evidence: Explain who benefits from a digital solution (e.g. a school app or community website) and who might be left out (e.g. families without internet, users with low vision)
Identify a privacy, safety or wellbeing effect of the solution (e.g. personal data collected, contact with strangers, screen time)
Describe an environmental effect (e.g. energy use or e-waste) or another harm and suggest an improvement that reduces it

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Designing a user interface
topics.description: Design a user interface for a digital system — the layout of screens, buttons, menus and navigation — applying principles such as consistency, readability and accessibility for the intended users
evidence: Draw wireframes for at least three connected screens of an app or game, showing buttons, menus and how the user moves between screens
Apply interface principles such as consistent button positions, readable text, clear icons and colour contrast, and explain each choice
Test a paper or digital prototype of the interface with a user and note where they got stuck

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Computers in Everyday Life
topics.description: Identifying computers in everyday life — not just laptops but phones, tablets, smart speakers, traffic lights, washing machines; what makes something a computer
evidence: Point out at least five everyday objects that contain computers
Explain what all computers have in common (they follow instructions and process information)
Sort a set of objects into 'contains a computer' and 'does not contain a computer'

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Hardware and software
topics.description: Recognise that digital systems are made of hardware (the parts you can touch, such as the screen, buttons and camera) and software (the apps and programs that tell the hardware what to do), and explore a device or app to achieve a simple purpose
evidence: Point to two hardware parts of a tablet or computer (e.g. the screen and the camera) and name an app on it as software
Use a tablet app with adult guidance for a purpose, such as taking a photo of a class pet or playing a counting game
Say what the device helped them do and which part or app they used

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Parts of a computer
topics.description: Identify the components and peripherals of digital systems — screen, keyboard, mouse, touchscreen, speakers, microphone, camera, printers, scanners, headphones and storage devices — sort them into input, output and storage, and choose components for a purpose
evidence: Label the screen, keyboard, mouse or trackpad, speaker, microphone and camera on a picture of a laptop or tablet
Sort components and peripherals (e.g. microphone, printer, headphones, scanner, USB drive) into input, output and storage devices and justify each choice
Choose the components or peripherals for a task (e.g. the camera for a photo of a plant, a microphone and headphones for a class podcast) and explain why

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Computer networks
topics.description: Examine how digital systems connect and transmit data — text, images, sound and video sent by cable or wirelessly (e.g. USB, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, mobile networks) through home or school networks with routers and servers — so they can share data and resources, noticing that larger files take longer to send
evidence: Send a photo from a tablet to a printer or another device (by cable or wirelessly) and describe the path the data took
Draw a diagram of the school or home network showing devices, the router and wired and wireless links, and explain how it lets devices share data and resources
Compare sending a text message, a photo and a short video and explain which takes longest and why, and compare a wired and a wireless connection

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: How the internet sends data
topics.description: Explain that the internet is a network of networks and that data is broken into small packets, addressed, sent along different routes and reassembled at its destination
evidence: Explain that the internet connects millions of smaller networks around the world
Act out sending a message as packets: split a sentence into numbered cards, pass them by different routes and reassemble them in order
Describe what happens when a packet is lost or arrives late (e.g. a video call freezes) and how numbering helps rebuild the message

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Inside a computer
topics.description: Investigate the main internal components of common digital systems — processor (CPU), memory (RAM), storage, circuit board, battery or power supply and wireless adaptor — and explain the function of each
evidence: Identify the processor, memory, storage and battery in a photo or teardown of a computer, tablet or phone
Explain the job of each part using an analogy (e.g. the processor does the work, memory is the desk for things in use, storage is the cupboard for files)
Compare two devices' specifications (e.g. storage size and memory) and explain how they affect what each device can do

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Collaborating in shared documents
topics.description: Use the core features of common digital tools to share content, plan tasks and collaborate — adding to a shared class book, co-editing documents or slideshows, using comments, suggestions and version history, and planning with shared task lists or boards — following agreed online behaviours
evidence: Add their own page or section to a shared class book, document or slideshow without changing anyone else's work
Use comments, suggestions or version history to give feedback or resolve changes instead of deleting a classmate's work
Plan a group task in a shared checklist or task board showing who does what and by when, and update progress as work is done

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Saving and organising files
topics.description: Save, name and organise digital files in folders following agreed conventions, so that work can be found, shared and reopened
evidence: Save a piece of work with a meaningful file name following the class convention (e.g. 'Mia_Y4_Frogs_Report')
Create a folder for a topic, move related files into it and find a file again in a later lesson
Follow other agreed conventions for digital work, such as giving image sources, using a consistent heading style and saving a new version instead of overwriting

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Choosing the right digital tool
topics.description: Select and use appropriate digital tools effectively to create, locate and communicate content — choosing between word processing, presentation, spreadsheet, graphics, video and search tools for a task, using their digital-specific features and applying common conventions
evidence: Choose the best tool for three tasks (e.g. a budget, a poster, a how-to video) and justify each choice
Use digital-specific features effectively, such as styles and templates, image cropping, spreadsheet formulas or search filters
Apply common conventions such as consistent formatting, file naming, alt text for images and acknowledging sources

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Data that is about me
topics.description: Identify some data that is personal and belongs to them — their name, age, birthday, address, photos and videos of themselves, voice recordings and drawings — and know to ask a trusted adult before sharing it
evidence: Sort picture cards into 'about me' (name, birthday, address, a photo of me) and 'not about me' (the weather, a picture of a tree)
Name two things they made that belong to them (e.g. a drawing or a voice recording on a tablet)
Say who they ask before sharing their name or photo on a device (a trusted adult)

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Apps store my data online
topics.description: Discuss that some websites and apps store their personal data online — names, photos, voice recordings, game scores and location — so the information stays there and may be seen by others
evidence: Name personal data a familiar app or game asks for or keeps (e.g. a username, a photo, a score, a location)
Explain that this data is stored on computers far away (online), not just on their own device
Discuss with a trusted adult whether an app really needs the data it asks for before agreeing

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Logging in to my account
topics.description: Access their school or learning accounts using their username and password (from a login card or from memory), log out when finished, and keep the password private except from trusted adults
evidence: Log in to their school or learning account using a login card or from memory, including when they have more than one account
Log out at the end of a session and explain why (so no-one else can use their account)
Explain that a password is like a key and is only shared with a trusted adult such as a parent or teacher

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Strong, memorable passwords
topics.description: Create passwords or passphrases that are easy for them to remember but hard for others to guess — long, made of random words, avoiding names, birthdays and simple patterns — and explain why
evidence: Sort example passwords into weak (e.g. 'password', 'ben2015', '1234') and strong (e.g. 'purple-kangaroo-jumps') and explain what makes each easy or hard to guess
Create a passphrase from three or four random words (e.g. 'violin-cactus-ocean-ladder') and explain why its length makes it hard to guess
Explain why a password must be easy for them to remember but hard for others to guess

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: What my accounts store
topics.description: Identify what personal data is stored and shared in their own online accounts (e.g. a school learning account or a game) — profile name, photo, age, location, contacts and work — who can see it, and discuss the associated risks
evidence: Explore the profile and settings of a school or game account with a teacher and list the personal data it stores
Identify who can see each item (only me, my teacher, my class, anyone) and change one privacy setting with adult support
Discuss a risk of sharing data such as a location or full name in a public profile and how to reduce it

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: A different password per account
topics.description: Use a different password or passphrase for each personal account and explain the risk of reusing passwords: if one account is breached, every account with the same password is exposed
evidence: Set up or use at least two different accounts (e.g. a school account and a learning app), each with its own password
Explain what could happen if they used the same password for every account and one website was hacked
Decide what to do after hearing that a website they use was hacked (e.g. change that password and any account that shared it, with a trusted adult's help)

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: My digital footprint
topics.description: Explain how their digital footprint is created — posts, photos, comments, searches and data collected by apps — and why it can be permanent, because content can be copied, shared and stored even after it is deleted
evidence: List the parts of their digital footprint from one day (e.g. a search, a game score, a comment, a photo a family member uploaded)
Explain why deleting a post does not guarantee it is gone (others may have copied or shared it, and services keep backups)
Decide whether to post a given photo or comment by thinking about who might see it in five years and justify the choice

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Privacy when collecting data
topics.description: Consider privacy when collecting data from users: collect only the data needed, tell people why it is collected, ask permission, avoid identifying details where possible, and store and share results safely
evidence: Review a draft class survey and remove questions that collect unnecessary personal data (e.g. full name, address)
Write a short privacy note for a survey explaining what data is collected, why and who will see it, and ask for permission
Explain how to keep survey results private (e.g. share only totals, store them in a protected folder)

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Reading for Meaning
topics.description: Understand that reading is about making meaning, not just saying words correctly — a text that can be decoded but not understood has not been read
evidence: Simple View of Reading (Gough & Tunmer)
reading comprehension research on comprehension-decoding separation

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Author's word choices
topics.description: Recognise how an author's deliberate choices — of words, structure, tone, and perspective — create particular effects on you as a reader
evidence: authorial awareness research
Understanding Author's Purpose (Firkins)
collaborative multilayered text interpretation in 5-8 year olds

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Monitoring Comprehension
topics.description: Notice the difference between decoding words and actually understanding them — recognise when you've read the words but not grasped the meaning, and do something about it
evidence: comprehension monitoring research
Metacognitive Monitoring in Reading Comprehension (MDPI 2024)

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Inference vs Explicit Meaning
topics.description: Distinguish between what a text explicitly says and what you have inferred, assumed, or read in — knowing which is which is fundamental to honest comprehension
evidence: inference vs literal comprehension development research
online inference making and comprehension monitoring (PMC 2021)

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Knowing What You Don't Know
topics.description: Monitor your own vocabulary gaps — notice words you half-know, distinguish confident from uncertain knowledge, and develop strategies to resolve the uncertainty
evidence: Noticing Unfamiliar Words Assessment research (grade 2+)
word consciousness and vocabulary metacognition research
Building Word Knowledge e-Book (PMC 2019)

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Reviewing Own Writing
topics.description: Evaluate whether your own writing achieves the effect you intended on a reader — go beyond checking for correctness to asking whether it actually works
evidence: writing self-evaluation research grades 3-5
metacognitive awareness of writing (Frontiers 2025)

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Reflecting on Your Language Use
topics.description: Reflect on yourself as a language user — how your reading, writing, and speaking shift across audiences, purposes, and contexts, and where you want to develop further
evidence: metalinguistic awareness development
register and audience awareness research

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Building sentences
topics.description: Understand that words combine to make sentences — a sentence expresses a complete thought; produce and expand complete sentences in speech and writing
evidence: Distinguish between complete sentences and fragments
Compose a complete sentence with a subject and verb
Expand a simple sentence by adding detail

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Spaces Between Words
topics.description: Separate words with spaces in writing; understand that spaces mark word boundaries in print
evidence: Leave clear finger-spaces between words when writing
Count the number of words in a written sentence by identifying spaces
Correct writing that has missing spaces between words

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Basic Nouns & Verbs
topics.description: Use frequently occurring nouns (people, places, things) and verbs (action words) appropriately in speech and writing
evidence: Use common nouns accurately in sentences (e.g. 'dog', 'school', 'book')
Use action verbs appropriately (e.g. 'run', 'eat', 'play')
Identify nouns and verbs in simple sentences when prompted

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Capitals for Names, Days and I
topics.description: Use capital letters for proper nouns (names of people, places) the days of the week, and the personal pronoun 'I'
evidence: Capitalise names of people and places consistently in writing
Write the pronoun 'I' as a capital letter
Capitalise days of the week (e.g. 'Monday')

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Grammar words: letter, word, sentence
topics.description: Use basic grammatical terminology when discussing reading and writing: letter, capital letter, word, singular, plural, sentence, punctuation, full stop, question mark, exclamation mark
evidence: Name punctuation marks correctly when pointed out in text
Use terms like 'capital letter' and 'full stop' when editing writing
Explain what a 'sentence' is using the correct term

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Joining Words with 'And'
topics.description: Join words and clauses using the conjunction 'and' to create longer sentences
evidence: Combine two simple sentences using 'and' (e.g. 'I like cats and dogs')
Join two related clauses with 'and' (e.g. 'We went to the park and we played')
Use 'and' in lists of items within a sentence

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Prepositions
topics.description: Understand and use the most frequently occurring prepositions of location and direction (e.g. to, from, in, out, on, off, for, by, with)
evidence: Use prepositions correctly in sentences (e.g. 'on the table', 'under the bed')
Follow instructions involving prepositions (e.g. 'Put the book on the shelf')
Describe positions using prepositional phrases

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Question Words
topics.description: Understand and use question words (who, what, where, when, why, how) to form and answer questions
evidence: Ask questions using appropriate question words
Answer who, what, where, when questions about familiar topics
Recognise that question words signal a question is being asked

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Regular Plural Nouns
topics.description: Form and use regular plural nouns orally and in writing by adding -s or -es; understand that plural means more than one
evidence: Say and write correct plural forms (e.g. 'one cat, two cats'; 'one wish, two wishes')
Choose -s or -es correctly based on the ending sound
Explain that plural nouns name more than one

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Starting and Ending Sentences
topics.description: Begin sentences with a capital letter and end them with the appropriate mark (full stop, question mark, or exclamation mark); recognise and name end punctuation
evidence: Write sentences beginning with a capital letter
Choose and use the correct end punctuation for statements, questions, and exclamations
Identify and name full stops, question marks, and exclamation marks when reading

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Adjectives vs adverbs
topics.description: Use adjectives and adverbs correctly, choosing between them depending on whether a noun or verb/adjective is being modified (e.g., 'She ran quickly' vs 'She is quick')
evidence: Choose the correct form: 'The dog is (slow/slowly)' vs 'The dog walks (slow/slowly)'
Identify whether a word is modifying a noun (adjective) or a verb (adverb) in a given sentence
Expand sentences by adding both an adjective and an adverb: 'The tall boy ran quickly'

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Apostrophes: Contraction and Possession
topics.description: Use apostrophes in writing for both contraction (marking omitted letters) and singular possession, distinguishing the two uses
evidence: Use apostrophes correctly in both 'don't' and 'Sam's bag' within the same piece of writing
Explain the difference between apostrophe for contraction and apostrophe for possession
Correct misplaced or missing apostrophes in a set of sentences

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Commas in lists
topics.description: Use commas to separate items in a list within a sentence (e.g., 'I bought apples, bananas, and oranges')
evidence: Write a sentence containing a list of 3+ items separated by commas: 'I bought apples, bananas, and oranges'
Identify where commas should go in an unpunctuated list sentence
Explain that commas separate items in a list so the reader knows each item

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Determiners and articles
topics.description: Use determiners (articles a/an/the and demonstratives this/that/these/those) correctly before nouns
evidence: Use 'a' before consonant sounds and 'an' before vowel sounds correctly: 'a ball', 'an apple'
Distinguish 'this/these' (near) from 'that/those' (far) when pointing to objects
Select the correct article (a/an/the) to complete a sentence

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Expanded noun phrases
topics.description: Use expanded noun phrases to describe and specify, adding adjectives and other modifiers before a noun (e.g., 'the blue butterfly', 'the old, creaky door')
evidence: Expand 'the cat' into 'the fluffy black cat' by adding adjectives
Use noun phrases with two or more modifiers in independent writing
Choose precise adjectives to make a noun phrase more vivid: e.g., 'a tiny, shivering kitten'

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Four Types of Sentences
topics.description: Understand and use the four sentence types — statement, question, exclamation, and command — recognising how grammatical patterns indicate sentence function
evidence: Write or identify a statement, question, exclamation, and command from a set of sentences
Match each sentence type to its correct end punctuation mark
Transform a statement into a question or command on request

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Grammar Terms: Nouns, Verbs and Tense
topics.description: Use and understand Year 2 grammatical terminology in discussion: noun, noun phrase, statement, question, exclamation, command, compound, suffix, adjective, adverb, verb, tense (past/present), apostrophe, comma
evidence: Use the term 'noun phrase' when discussing expanded noun phrases in own writing
Identify adjectives, adverbs, and verbs in sentences using correct terminology
Explain what 'tense' means and give an example of past and present tense

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Past, Present and Progressive Tense
topics.description: Use verbs to convey past and present tense correctly and consistently, including the progressive form (e.g., she is drumming, he was shouting), understanding how tense indicates time
evidence: Write a passage consistently in past tense without switching to present
Use progressive forms correctly: 'was running', 'is jumping' to show ongoing actions
Identify verbs in a sentence and change them from past to present tense or vice versa

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Pronouns
topics.description: Use personal, possessive, and indefinite pronouns correctly (e.g., I/me/my, they/them/their, anyone/everything), replacing nouns to avoid repetition
evidence: Replace a repeated noun with a pronoun: 'The dog was happy. He wagged his tail.'
Use I/me correctly in subject and object position in a sentence
Choose the correct possessive pronoun (my/his/her/their) to match the noun it replaces

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Simple Past, Present and Future
topics.description: Form and use the simple past, present, and future verb tenses consistently in writing
evidence: Rewrite 'I walk to school' in past tense ('I walked') and future tense ('I will walk')
Identify and correct inconsistent tense in 'Yesterday she walks to the shop and bought milk'
Write a three-sentence paragraph maintaining consistent future tense throughout

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Simple sentences: one idea
topics.description: Understand that a simple sentence is a single independent clause expressing one event or idea, usually built around one verb, and tell it apart from a sentence that joins two ideas
evidence: Say or write a simple sentence about one event (e.g. 'The cat slept.') and point to its verb
Sort sentences into 'one idea' (e.g. 'Sam ran.') and 'two ideas joined' (e.g. 'Sam ran and Mia jumped.')
Split 'We went to the beach and we swam' into two simple sentences

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Subject-verb agreement
topics.description: Use singular and plural nouns with matching verbs in sentences, maintaining subject-verb agreement (e.g., 'He hops' vs 'We hop')
evidence: Write 'The dog runs' (singular) and 'The dogs run' (plural) with correct verb agreement
Correct subject-verb agreement errors in sentences: fix 'The children plays' to 'The children play'
Choose the correct verb form to match a singular or plural subject in a gap-fill exercise

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Subordinate clauses
topics.description: Use subordination (when, if, that, because) and co-ordination (or, and, but) to join clauses and create compound and complex sentences
evidence: Write 'I stayed inside because it was raining' using a subordinating conjunction
Use 'but' and 'or' to join ideas: 'I wanted to play but it was raining'
Use 'when' and 'if' clauses in writing: 'If it stops raining, we can go outside'

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Abstract nouns
topics.description: Understand and use abstract nouns to name ideas, qualities, and states that cannot be perceived by the senses
evidence: Sort words like 'freedom', 'table', 'courage', 'pencil', 'childhood' into abstract and concrete noun categories
Complete sentences using appropriate abstract nouns: 'Her _____ (brave → bravery) inspired the whole team'
Write three sentences each containing a different abstract noun (e.g. 'honesty', 'friendship', 'happiness')

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Capital letters in titles
topics.description: Recognise and use capital letters in titles of books, stories, films and headings
evidence: Write the title of a favourite book starting with a capital letter and with capitals on its main words (e.g. 'Where the Wild Things Are')
Correct a class list of book titles where capital letters are missing
Write a heading for a poster with capitals on its main words (e.g. 'Our Garden Project')

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Choosing A or An
topics.description: Use the correct form of the indefinite article — 'a' before words beginning with a consonant sound and 'an' before words beginning with a vowel sound (e.g., a rock, an open box, an hour, a unicorn)
evidence: Choose 'a' or 'an' correctly before nouns beginning with consonant or vowel sounds (e.g., 'a ball', 'an egg', 'an umbrella')
Apply the rule to tricky words where spelling and sound differ (e.g., 'an hour' because /h/ is silent, 'a uniform' because /juː/ starts with a consonant sound)
Correct errors in a/an usage in given sentences (e.g., change 'a orange' to 'an orange')

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Comparatives & Superlatives
topics.description: Form and use comparative and superlative adjectives and adverbs, choosing correctly between them
evidence: Form comparatives and superlatives for 'big' (bigger/biggest), 'beautiful' (more/most beautiful), and 'good' (better/best)
Choose the correct form in 'She runs _____ (faster/more fast) than her brother' and explain the rule
Write sentences using both a comparative adverb ('more carefully') and a superlative adjective ('tallest') correctly

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Expressing Time, Place and Cause
topics.description: Use conjunctions (when, before, after, while, so, because), adverbs (then, next, soon, therefore) and prepositions (before, after, during, in, because of) to express time, place and cause within and across sentences
evidence: Use time conjunctions to connect clauses (e.g., 'We went inside because it was raining', 'After the bell rang, we lined up')
Use adverbs of time and cause within sentences (e.g., 'First, she opened the door. Then, she stepped outside. Therefore, she got wet.')
Use prepositions of time and cause in phrases (e.g., 'during the lesson', 'before lunch', 'because of the rain')

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Grammar Terms: Clauses and Conjunctions
topics.description: Use and understand Year 3 grammatical terminology accurately when discussing reading and writing: preposition, conjunction, word family, prefix, clause, subordinate clause, direct speech, consonant letter, vowel letter, inverted commas/speech marks
evidence: Use the terms 'clause' and 'subordinate clause' to identify parts of a multi-clause sentence (e.g., point to the subordinate clause in 'I stayed inside because it rained')
Use the terms 'conjunction', 'preposition', and 'prefix' correctly when explaining word/sentence choices in own writing
Distinguish between consonant letters and vowel letters and use the terms 'direct speech' and 'inverted commas' when discussing punctuation

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Irregular past tense verbs
topics.description: Form and use the past tense of frequently occurring irregular verbs correctly (e.g., sat, hid, told, went, came, ran), recognising that these do not follow the regular -ed pattern
evidence: Supply the correct past tense of common irregular verbs: go→went, see→saw, run→ran, tell→told
Correct over-regularised forms in writing (e.g. change 'goed' to 'went', 'hided' to 'hid')
Write a short recount using at least five irregular past-tense verbs accurately

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Irregular Plural Nouns
topics.description: Form and use irregular plural nouns (e.g., children, teeth, mice, geese) in addition to regular plurals, recognising that some nouns have irregular plural forms that do not follow the -s/-es pattern
evidence: Form and use irregular plural nouns correctly (e.g. child→children, tooth→teeth, mouse→mice, goose→geese)
Identify collective nouns that name a group (e.g. 'a flock of birds', 'a group of children', 'a pack of wolves')
Correct over-regularised plurals in writing (e.g. change 'mouses' to 'mice', 'foots' to 'feet')

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Leaving out words readers know
topics.description: Understand that texts are made cohesive by leaving out (omitting) words the reader can work out from earlier in the text (ellipsis)
evidence: Explain which word is left out in 'Mia ate an apple and Sam a banana' ('ate') and how the reader knows it
Answer 'Who wants an apple?' with 'I do' and explain which words 'do' saves repeating
Rewrite 'Tom played football and Tom played tennis' by leaving out the repeated words ('Tom played football and tennis')

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Pronouns for clarity
topics.description: Choose pronouns for clarity and cohesion, avoiding ambiguity and repetition; use reflexive pronouns correctly (e.g., myself, ourselves, himself)
evidence: Replace repeated nouns with pronouns to improve cohesion: rewrite 'Sam picked up Sam's bag' as 'Sam picked up his bag'
Use reflexive pronouns correctly in sentences (e.g. 'I made it myself', 'They helped themselves')
Identify and fix ambiguous pronoun references (e.g. 'Tom told Jack he was late' — who was late?)

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Punctuating Direct Speech
topics.description: Punctuate direct speech using inverted commas (speech marks), understanding that direct speech records the exact words spoken and must be enclosed in punctuation marks
evidence: Place inverted commas around the spoken words in a sentence (e.g., "Let's go!" shouted Tom.)
Write a sentence containing direct speech with correct punctuation including a reporting clause (e.g., Mum said, "Time for bed.")
Identify direct speech in a text and explain what the inverted commas show

topics.subject: English
topics.name: The Present Perfect Tense
topics.description: Use the present perfect form of verbs in contrast to the simple past tense, understanding how the present perfect indicates an action completed at an unspecified time or with ongoing relevance (e.g., 'He has gone out' vs 'He went out')
evidence: Form the present perfect using 'has/have' + past participle (e.g., 'She has eaten', 'They have finished')
Choose between simple past and present perfect to match the intended meaning (e.g., 'I ate lunch' vs 'I have eaten lunch')
Identify the present perfect form in a text and explain why the author used it instead of simple past

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Agreement in sentences
topics.description: Ensure subject-verb agreement and pronoun-antecedent agreement within and across sentences
evidence: Correct 'The group of children were laughing' to 'The group of children was laughing' and explain the singular subject
Choose the correct pronoun in 'Each student must bring ____ (his or her / their) book' and explain the antecedent link
Identify and fix three agreement errors in a short paragraph, explaining each correction

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Conjunctions, Prepositions and Interjections
topics.description: Explain the function of conjunctions, prepositions, and interjections in general and in particular sentences, understanding how each word class contributes to meaning
evidence: Identify conjunctions, prepositions, and interjections in sentences and explain their function
Explain how removing a preposition or conjunction changes the meaning of a sentence
Use interjections appropriately to convey emotion in dialogue or informal writing

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Doing, thinking and saying verbs
topics.description: Understand how verbs represent different processes: doing (action), feeling and thinking (sensing), saying, and relating (being and having)
evidence: Sort verbs from a story into doing (ran, built), feeling/thinking (loved, wondered), saying (whispered, asked) and relating (is, has, seems)
Explain how a saying verb like 'whispered' or 'shouted' tells the reader more than 'said'
Identify the relating verbs in an information report (e.g. 'Koalas are marsupials', 'They have sharp claws') and explain why reports use many of them

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Expanded noun phrases (age 8+)
topics.description: Expand noun phrases with modifying adjectives, nouns, and preposition phrases to add detail
evidence: Expand 'the teacher' to 'the strict maths teacher with curly hair' using adjective, noun, and preposition phrase
Write a sentence containing a noun phrase with at least three modifiers, e.g. 'the old stone bridge over the river'
Identify the head noun and its modifiers in 'the tiny grey kitten under the table'

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Fronted Adverbials and Commas
topics.description: Use fronted adverbials to vary sentence openings and punctuate them with commas
evidence: Write a sentence beginning with a time adverbial, e.g. 'Later that day, the children ran home'
Rewrite 'The fox crept through the garden at midnight' with the adverbial fronted and a comma placed correctly
Identify and correct a missing comma after a fronted adverbial in 'Before breakfast she packed her bag'

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Grammar Terms: Pronouns and Determiners
topics.description: Know and use Year 4 grammar terminology including determiner, pronoun, possessive pronoun, and adverbial
evidence: Label the determiner, pronoun, and adverbial in 'She quickly opened her present on the table'
Explain the difference between a possessive pronoun ('mine', 'theirs') and other pronouns ('I', 'they')
Use the terms 'determiner' and 'adverbial' accurately when discussing a classmate's writing

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Modal Verbs and Possibility
topics.description: Understand and use modal verbs (can, may, must, might, shall, will, could, should, would) and modal adverbs (perhaps, surely, certainly) to indicate degrees of possibility, necessity, and permission
evidence: Select a modal verb to express certainty, probability, or possibility in a sentence, e.g. 'It will rain' vs 'It might rain' vs 'It could rain'
Replace a modal verb with a modal adverb to achieve a similar effect, e.g. 'He might come' → 'Perhaps he will come'
Distinguish between modals expressing permission (may, can), obligation (must, should), and possibility (might, could) in context

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Plural vs Possessive in Nouns
topics.description: Distinguish between the plural -s suffix and the possessive -'s suffix in nouns
evidence: Sort words like 'dogs', 'dog's', and 'dogs'' into plural, singular possessive, and plural possessive categories
Explain why 'the cats bowl' is incorrect and supply the correct form ('the cat's bowl' or 'the cats' bowl') for a given meaning
Write two sentences using the same noun — one as a plural and one as a possessive

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Standard English Verbs
topics.description: Use Standard English verb inflections in place of non-standard local forms
evidence: Correct 'we was playing' to 'we were playing' and explain why the standard form is needed in writing
Choose the standard form in pairs such as 'I did / I done', 'she has / she have', 'they were / they was'
Rewrite a short passage replacing three non-standard verb forms with their Standard English equivalents

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Adjective Order in Sentences
topics.description: Order adjectives within sentences according to conventional English patterns (opinion-size-age-shape-colour-origin-material-purpose) to produce natural-sounding descriptions
evidence: Arrange multiple adjectives before a noun in conventional order, e.g. 'a lovely little old rectangular green French silver whittling knife' simplified to classroom examples like 'a small red bag' not 'a red small bag'
Identify when adjective order sounds unnatural and rearrange to match English conventions, e.g. correct 'the wooden big table' to 'the big wooden table'
Apply the size-before-colour-before-material pattern in descriptive writing, e.g. 'a tall grey stone castle' rather than 'a stone grey tall castle'

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Brackets and dashes for parenthesis
topics.description: Use brackets, dashes, and commas to indicate parenthesis — additional information inserted into a sentence that could be removed without changing the sentence's core meaning
evidence: Insert a parenthetical phrase using paired brackets, e.g. 'The oldest building (built in 1642) stands in the town square'
Use paired dashes to add an aside or extra detail within a sentence, e.g. 'My brother — who is older than me — lives in London'
Choose between brackets, dashes, and commas for parenthesis based on how much emphasis the aside should receive, recognising that dashes give most prominence and brackets give least

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Capitals for proper adjectives
topics.description: Use a capital letter for adjectives formed from proper nouns, as in "We waved the Canadian flag and ate Japanese food beside a Victorian house", explain which proper noun each adjective comes from, and tell proper adjectives apart from common adjectives in the same phrase.
evidence: Capitalises adjectives formed from proper nouns in own writing (e.g. "the Canadian flag", "Japanese food")
Corrects a sentence with lowercase proper adjectives and explains which proper noun each adjective comes from (e.g. Victorian from Queen Victoria)
In a phrase such as "the tall Canadian athlete", sorts the adjectives into proper and common and capitalises only the proper one

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Cohesion within paragraphs
topics.description: Use cohesive devices within a paragraph — including pronouns, adverbials (then, after that, firstly), and synonyms — to link sentences and build a coherent flow of ideas
evidence: Replace repeated nouns with pronouns or synonyms to maintain cohesion without ambiguity, e.g. 'The explorer found a cave. She examined it carefully'
Use adverbials of sequence (firstly, then, next, finally) and cause (therefore, as a result, consequently) to connect ideas within a paragraph
Identify where cohesion breaks down in a paragraph and insert appropriate linking devices to improve the flow

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Commas Before Joining Words
topics.description: Use a comma before a coordinating conjunction (and, but, or, so, yet) when joining two independent clauses in a compound sentence
evidence: Place a comma before the coordinating conjunction in a compound sentence, e.g. 'I wanted to go outside, but it was raining'
Distinguish compound sentences (two independent clauses) from simple sentences with compound predicates, e.g. 'She sang and danced' needs no comma but 'She sang a song, and he played the piano' does
Edit writing to insert missing commas before coordinating conjunctions in compound sentences

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Commas to avoid ambiguity
topics.description: Use commas to clarify meaning and avoid ambiguity in sentences where the absence of a comma could cause misreading
evidence: Insert a comma to prevent ambiguity, e.g. 'Let's eat, Grandma' vs 'Let's eat Grandma' or 'Most of the time, travellers worry about their bags'
Identify sentences where a missing comma changes the meaning and explain the two possible readings
Use commas after introductory elements (adverbial phrases, subordinate clauses) to prevent misreading of the main clause

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Commas with yes, no, and names
topics.description: Use commas to set off the words yes and no, to set off tag questions, and to indicate direct address in sentences
evidence: Write sentences using commas with yes and no at the beginning such as 'Yes, I understand'
Punctuate tag questions correctly such as 'It's cold today, isn't it?'
Use commas to set off names in direct address such as 'Sarah, please pass the salt'

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Converting Words into Verbs
topics.description: Convert nouns and adjectives into verbs by adding suffixes -ate, -ise (-ize), and -ify, understanding how word class changes affect sentence construction
evidence: Add -ate, -ise, or -ify to nouns or adjectives to form verbs, e.g. pollen → pollinate, advert → advertise, simple → simplify
Choose the correct verb-forming suffix for a given root and use the resulting verb in a sentence, e.g. 'They needed to classify the animals' from 'class'
Identify the word-class change when a suffix converts a noun or adjective into a verb and explain how this affects the sentence structure

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Expanded noun phrases (age 9+)
topics.description: Form and use prepositional phrases (preposition + noun phrase) to add detail about time, location, or direction within sentences, recognising how they function as adjective or adverb phrases
evidence: Identify the preposition and noun phrase within a prepositional phrase, e.g. in 'under the old bridge', 'under' is the preposition and 'the old bridge' is the noun phrase
Add prepositional phrases to expand sentences with detail about where, when, or how, e.g. 'The cat slept' → 'The cat slept on the warm windowsill throughout the afternoon'
Distinguish prepositional phrases functioning as adjectives (modifying nouns: 'the house on the hill') from those functioning as adverbs (modifying verbs: 'she ran across the field')

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Fixing Fragments & Run-Ons
topics.description: Recognise and correct sentence fragments (incomplete sentences lacking a subject or predicate) and run-on sentences (two or more independent clauses joined without proper punctuation or conjunctions)
evidence: Identify a sentence fragment by checking whether it has both a subject and a predicate, e.g. recognise 'Running through the park' as a fragment and correct to 'The dog was running through the park'

Identify a run-on sentence where two independent clauses are fused without punctuation or a conjunction, e.g. 'I like cats I also like dogs' and correct using a full stop, comma + conjunction, or semicolon
Edit a paragraph to fix fragments and run-ons, choosing the most effective correction strategy for each error

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Grammar Terms: Modal Verbs and Clauses
topics.description: Know and use Year 5 grammar terminology accurately when discussing reading and writing: modal verb, relative pronoun, relative clause, parenthesis, bracket, dash, cohesion, ambiguity
evidence: Label a relative clause in a sentence and identify the relative pronoun that introduces it, using correct terminology
Explain why a pair of brackets or dashes creates a parenthesis and describe its function using the term 'parenthesis'
Use the terms 'modal verb', 'cohesion', and 'ambiguity' when discussing how a writer has achieved particular effects in a text

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Linking paragraphs with adverbials
topics.description: Link ideas across paragraphs using adverbials of time (later, meanwhile, after a while), place (nearby, far away, beyond the wall), and number (secondly, finally, in addition) to guide the reader through a multi-paragraph text
evidence: Begin a new paragraph with an adverbial of time to signal a shift in time or sequence, e.g. 'Meanwhile, back at the castle...' or 'Several hours later, the storm finally passed'
Use adverbials of place to move the reader to a new location between paragraphs, e.g. 'Beyond the forest, the land was flat and dry'
Use numbering or addition adverbials to structure non-fiction across paragraphs, e.g. 'The first reason... The second reason... In addition...'

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Progressive and Continuous Tenses
topics.description: Form and use the progressive (continuous) verb tenses — past progressive (was walking), present progressive (am walking), and future progressive (will be walking) — to convey ongoing actions at different times
evidence: Write sentences using past progressive to describe an action that was ongoing at a particular time, e.g. 'She was reading when the phone rang'
Distinguish present progressive from simple present, e.g. 'I am eating lunch' (right now) vs 'I eat lunch at noon' (habitual)
Form the future progressive using 'will be' + present participle to describe an action that will be ongoing, e.g. 'Tomorrow at 3pm I will be travelling'

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Punctuating Titles of Works
topics.description: Use underlining, quotation marks, or italics to indicate titles of works, applying conventions for different types of works such as books, stories, poems, songs, and articles
evidence: Use italics or underlining for titles of books, films, and albums
Use quotation marks for titles of short works such as poems, songs, and articles
Apply title formatting conventions consistently in a piece of writing

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Quoted and reported speech
topics.description: Investigate how quoted (direct) and reported (indirect) speech are used, and change between them by adjusting pronouns, tense and punctuation
evidence: Change '"I am tired," said Mia' into reported speech ('Mia said that she was tired')
Change 'Tom said that he would bring the ball' into quoted speech with correct punctuation
Explain why a news report might use reported speech for most of an interview and quote only one key sentence

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Relative Clauses
topics.description: Form and use relative clauses beginning with relative pronouns (who, whose, whom, which, that) and relative adverbs (where, when, why) to add detail, qualify nouns, and create complex sentences
evidence: Combine a main clause with a relative clause using 'who' or 'which' to add information about a noun, e.g. 'The dog, which had a red collar, barked loudly'
Choose the correct relative pronoun (who for people, which for things, where for places, when for times) and identify the noun it refers back to
Recognise that a relative clause beginning with 'that' can often replace 'who' or 'which' in defining clauses, e.g. 'The book that I read' vs 'The book which I read'

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Verb Prefixes and Meaning
topics.description: Use verb prefixes (dis-, de-, mis-, over-, re-) to change verb meaning, understanding how each prefix modifies the action expressed by the root verb
evidence: Add verb prefixes to change meaning, e.g. dis- (disagree, disappear), de- (decompose, defrost), mis- (misunderstand, misbehave), over- (overlook, overreact), re- (redo, reconsider)
Select the appropriate verb prefix to express a specific meaning shift such as negation (dis-/mis-), reversal (de-/un-), repetition (re-), or excess (over-)
Distinguish verb prefixes from noun/adjective prefixes and explain how adding a prefix to a verb changes the action described

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Active and passive voice
topics.description: Use the passive voice to shift focus from the agent to the action or recipient, understanding how passive constructions affect the presentation of information in formal and objective writing
evidence: Convert active sentences to passive voice and explain the change in emphasis
Identify passive constructions in news reports and scientific writing
Choose between active and passive voice based on purpose and audience

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Apostrophes for shared ownership
topics.description: Use apostrophes correctly where there is multiple possession — joint possession (an apostrophe on the last owner only) and separate possession (an apostrophe on each owner)
evidence: Write 'Sam and Ali's house' for one house they share and 'Sam's and Ali's bikes' for their separate bikes
Correct possessive apostrophes in sentences about joint and separate ownership (e.g. 'Mum and Dad's car', 'the girls' and the boys' teams')
Write one sentence about something two friends own together and one about things they own separately (e.g. 'Mia and Jo's tent' and 'Mia's and Jo's sleeping bags')

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Bullet Point Punctuation
topics.description: Punctuate bullet points consistently to list information clearly, applying conventions for capitalisation, end punctuation, and parallel structure across items
evidence: Create bullet point lists with consistent capitalisation and punctuation throughout
Use full stops for bullet points that are complete sentences and no punctuation for fragments
Maintain parallel grammatical structure across all items in a bulleted list

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Choosing Tenses for Precise Meaning
topics.description: Use verb tense to convey various times, sequences, states, and conditions, selecting tenses deliberately to express the precise timing and nature of actions and events
evidence: Write a paragraph using multiple tenses to show the sequence of past, present, and future events
Choose between simple, progressive, and perfect tenses to express duration or completion
Explain why a specific tense is appropriate for expressing a condition or hypothetical situation

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Colons and Semicolons in Lists
topics.description: Use a colon to introduce a list and semi-colons to separate items within lists, particularly when list items contain internal commas or are complex phrases
evidence: Introduce a list with a colon after an independent clause such as 'You will need the following items:'
Use semi-colons to separate list items that contain commas such as locations with city and country
Punctuate complex lists in formal writing maintaining clarity and consistency

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Commas After Introductory Elements
topics.description: Use a comma to separate an introductory element from the rest of the sentence, including introductory words, phrases, and clauses
evidence: Place commas after introductory adverbs such as 'However' or 'Therefore' at the start of sentences
Use commas after introductory prepositional phrases like 'In the morning' or 'After the game'
Punctuate introductory dependent clauses correctly such as 'When the bell rang, we left'

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Consistent verb tense
topics.description: Recognise and correct inappropriate shifts in verb tense within and across sentences and paragraphs, maintaining consistency unless a shift is required by meaning
evidence: Identify and correct unnecessary tense shifts in a given paragraph
Edit own writing to ensure consistent tense use throughout a narrative
Explain when a tense shift is appropriate such as when describing a flashback

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Correlative Conjunctions
topics.description: Use correlative conjunctions correctly in sentences, pairing words such as either/or, neither/nor, both/and, not only/but also, and whether/or
evidence: Write sentences using each pair of correlative conjunctions correctly
Ensure parallel structure when using correlative conjunctions in complex sentences
Identify and correct errors in correlative conjunction usage in given sentences

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Grammar Terms: Voice and Punctuation
topics.description: Know and use Year 6 grammatical terminology accurately: subject, object, active voice, passive voice, synonym, antonym, ellipsis, hyphen, colon, semi-colon, bullet points
evidence: Define and give examples of subject and object in sentences
Explain the difference between active and passive voice using correct terminology
Use terms such as ellipsis, colon, and semi-colon accurately when discussing punctuation choices

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Hyphens in Prefixed Words
topics.description: Use hyphens to avoid ambiguity in compound modifiers and prefixed words, distinguishing between meanings that change based on hyphen placement
evidence: Distinguish between 'man eating shark' and 'man-eating shark' by adding or removing hyphens
Use hyphens with prefixes to clarify meaning such as 'recover' versus 're-cover'
Apply hyphens correctly in compound adjectives before nouns such as 'well-known author'

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Paragraph Cohesion
topics.description: Link ideas across paragraphs using a wider range of cohesive devices including word repetition, grammatical connections such as adverbials, and ellipsis to create coherent extended texts
evidence: Use adverbials such as 'on the other hand' and 'as a consequence' to connect paragraphs
Apply ellipsis to avoid repetition while maintaining clarity across sentences
Create cohesion by repeating key words or using synonyms to link ideas between paragraphs

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Punctuating Clauses
topics.description: Use semi-colons, colons, and dashes to mark boundaries between independent clauses, choosing the appropriate punctuation based on the relationship between the clauses
evidence: Join two related independent clauses using a semi-colon in place of a conjunction
Use a colon to introduce an explanation or elaboration of the first clause
Replace commas with dashes to create stronger pauses between clauses for emphasis

topics.subject: English
topics.name: The subjunctive mood
topics.description: Use the subjunctive form in formal writing and speech to express wishes, demands, suggestions, or hypothetical situations (e.g., 'If I were you', 'I suggest that he go', 'Were they to arrive')
evidence: Write sentences using 'If I were' to express hypothetical conditions
Transform informal sentences into formal equivalents using subjunctive forms such as 'I recommend that she attend'
Identify subjunctive mood in formal texts such as legal documents or formal letters

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Types of Sentences
topics.description: Choose among and construct simple, compound, complex, and compound-complex sentences to signal different relationships among ideas, varying sentence patterns deliberately for meaning, interest, and style
evidence: Combine short sentences into a complex sentence using a subordinating conjunction for effect
Rewrite a passage of monotonous simple sentences using a mix of sentence types for variety and flow
Identify the sentence type (simple, compound, complex, compound-complex) of given examples and explain the effect of each

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Varying Sentence Structure
topics.description: Expand, combine, and reduce sentences for meaning, reader interest, and style, using techniques such as embedding clauses, using appositives, and varying sentence length
evidence: Combine two simple sentences into one complex sentence using subordination
Expand a simple sentence by adding descriptive phrases and clauses
Reduce wordy sentences by removing redundant words while preserving meaning

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Advanced Punctuation for Clarity
topics.description: Use punctuation confidently and accurately for effect and clarity — including semicolons to link related clauses, colons to introduce lists or explanations, dashes and parentheses for parenthetical information, ellipsis for omission or suspense, and commas for coordinate adjectives and nonrestrictive elements
evidence: Use a semicolon to link two closely related independent clauses without a conjunction
Set off a nonrestrictive clause with commas and explain why the commas are needed
Use a colon to introduce an explanation or elaboration, and a dash for a dramatic aside

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Colons after labels
topics.description: Use a colon where a formal convention calls for one: after the salutation of a business or formal letter when that style is expected (e.g. "Dear Dr. Ruiz:"), in the opening of a memo — after its salutation line and/or header labels such as "To:", "From:", "Date:" and "Re:" — and after a speaker’s name to show a new speaker in script dialogue ("MAYA: Let’s go."); explain that the colon shows that what follows belongs to that greeting, label or speaker, and recognise contexts, such as a friendly letter, where a comma is used instead.
evidence: In a business-letter task that specifies a colon-based salutation style, punctuates the greeting with a colon; contrasts it with a friendly-letter task that specifies a comma-based style, and explains that greeting punctuation follows the stated convention rather than a universal business-versus-friendly rule
Sets out a memo opening with colons after the To, From, Date and Re labels; when a salutation line is included, follows the stated memo style for its punctuation
Writes a short script in which every new speaker’s name is followed by a colon before their words

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Gerunds as nouns
topics.description: Recognise a gerund — an -ing form of a verb that works as a noun to name an activity — whether it is the subject ("Swimming keeps me fit"), the object ("I enjoy swimming") or comes after a preposition ("She is good at swimming"); tell it apart from an -ing verb in a progressive tense ("She is swimming") and from an -ing word describing a noun ("the swimming dog"); and use this to understand and write sentences clearly.
evidence: In sentences such as "Reading calms me down", "My brother hates waiting" and "We talked about camping", picks out each -ing word that names an activity and shows it is doing a noun’s job, for example by swapping in a noun ("Music calms me down")

Sorts the -ing words in "The baby is crying", "Crying woke the neighbours" and "the crying baby" into part of a verb, a gerund naming an activity, and a word describing a noun, and explains the clue in each sentence
Writes sentences that use a gerund as the subject, as the object and after a preposition, and explains what a sentence such as "Her singing woke the baby" means

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Grammar for Effect
topics.description: Analyse the effectiveness and impact of grammatical features in texts read — understanding how authors make deliberate grammatical choices (sentence length, passive voice, fronted adverbials, listing) to create specific effects on the reader
evidence: Explain how an author's use of short, simple sentences creates tension or urgency in a passage
Analyse why an author uses a list of three (tricolon) in a persuasive text and evaluate its impact
Identify a grammatical choice in a text (e.g., present tense for immediacy) and explain the effect on the reader

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Literary and Language Terminology
topics.description: Discuss reading, writing, and spoken language with precise and confident use of linguistic and literary terminology — including terms for word classes, sentence types, clause types, literary devices, and text-level features
