evidence: Use terms like 'subordinate clause', 'relative pronoun', 'metaphor', 'alliteration' accurately in discussion
Explain the difference between a simile and a metaphor using correct terminology
Use metalanguage (e.g., 'the author employs enjambment to...') confidently when writing about texts

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Phrases & Clauses
topics.description: Understand and analyse the function of phrases (noun, verb, adjectival, adverbial, prepositional) and clauses (main, subordinate, relative) in general and in specific sentences, including recognising and correcting misplaced and dangling modifiers
evidence: Identify a prepositional phrase acting as an adverbial and explain its role in the sentence
Distinguish between a main clause and a subordinate clause and explain their relationship
Spot a dangling modifier in a sentence and rewrite it to remove the ambiguity

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Standard English
topics.description: Know and understand the differences between spoken and written language — including differences in formality, register, grammar, and vocabulary — and between Standard English and other varieties of English, using Standard English confidently in writing and speech
evidence: Explain three differences between how we speak informally and how we write formally (e.g., contractions, slang, sentence completeness)
Identify features of Standard English and explain why it is used in formal contexts
Rewrite an informal spoken passage (e.g., a text message) in formal written Standard English

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Verb Voice and Mood
topics.description: Understand and use active and passive voice deliberately, and recognise verb moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, conditional) and their effects — choosing the appropriate voice and mood for purpose and audience
evidence: Rewrite an active sentence in the passive voice and explain when the passive is more appropriate
Identify the subjunctive mood in a formal text (e.g., 'If I were...', 'It is essential that he be...')
Explain why a scientific report typically uses passive voice while a personal narrative uses active

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Sitting and holding a pencil
topics.description: Sit correctly at a table holding a pencil comfortably and correctly; form lower-case letters in the correct direction starting and finishing in the right place
evidence: Hold a pencil with a comfortable tripod or near-tripod grip
Write all 26 lowercase letters with correct starting points and direction
Maintain consistent letter size on lined paper

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Writing digits 0-9
topics.description: Form digits 0-9 correctly and legibly
evidence: Write all digits 0-9 clearly with correct starting points
Form digits the appropriate size relative to letter height
Write numbers legibly so they can be read by others

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Forming Capital Letters
topics.description: Form capital letters correctly; print many upper- and lowercase letters legibly
evidence: Write all 26 capital letters with correct formation
Distinguish between uppercase and lowercase forms in own writing
Use appropriate sizing so capitals are taller than lowercase letters

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Letter Formation Families
topics.description: Understand which letters belong to which handwriting families based on similar formation patterns and practise letters in groups
evidence: Group letters by similar strokes (e.g. c, a, d, g, o family — all start with a curve)
Explain why certain letters are practised together
Form letters within the same family consistently using the shared movement pattern

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Joining Letters
topics.description: Begin to join letters using diagonal and horizontal strokes, understanding which letter pairs are best left unjoined, forming letters of correct size relative to one another
evidence: Join 'in', 'un', 'it' with a diagonal stroke connecting the letters
Leave letters like 'b' unjoined when followed by certain letters, explaining why
Write with consistent letter sizing on lined paper, ascenders and descenders in proportion

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Writing neatly at speed
topics.description: Write words legibly and with growing fluency and automaticity (speed and ease), keeping letters correctly formed, sized and spaced in the handwriting script being learned (unjoined or joined)
evidence: Copy a familiar two-line sentence legibly within two minutes, keeping letters correctly formed
Write the lower-case alphabet or common letter strings (e.g. -ing, th) from memory, legibly and without pausing to think about letter shapes
Write a dictated sentence or a timed free-write at a steady pace with consistent letter size and spacing, so a partner can read every word

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Beginning touch typing
topics.description: Begin to type by touch: rest the fingers on the home-row keys, reach each key with the assigned finger and return to the home row, and keep the eyes on the screen or the text being copied while typing short familiar text. Check the typed text on the screen and correct errors, putting accuracy before speed.
evidence: Places the fingers on the home-row keys before typing and returns them there after each reach
Types a short familiar sentence using the assigned fingers while looking at the screen or the copy, not at the keys
Checks the typed text on the screen and corrects the errors, keeping accuracy ahead of speed

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Blending Sounds to Read Words
topics.description: Apply phonic knowledge to blend sounds in unfamiliar words containing taught grapheme-phoneme correspondences; respond speedily to graphemes for all 40+ phonemes
evidence: Sound out and blend unfamiliar phonically regular words (e.g. /sh/-/o/-/p/ → 'shop')
Read words containing taught GPCs without excessive sounding out
Distinguish between similarly spelled words by identifying differing letter sounds (e.g. 'big' vs 'bag')

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Consonant Digraphs
topics.description: Read and spell words containing consonant digraphs and less common consonant spellings (ch, sh, th, ck, tch, ng, ph, wh, k for /k/)
evidence: Read words with consonant digraphs (e.g. 'shop', 'chip', 'that')
Identify the sound made by ph (/f/) and wh (/w/) in words
Spell words ending in -ck (e.g. 'duck') and -tch (e.g. 'match')

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Knowing all letters
topics.description: Recognise and name all uppercase and lowercase letters of the alphabet; name the letters in order and use letter names to distinguish between alternative spellings
evidence: Name all 26 letters in both cases when shown in random order
Recite the alphabet from A to Z
Use letter names to explain spelling choices (e.g. 'Is it c or k in cat?')

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Onsets & Rimes
topics.description: Blend and segment onsets and rimes in single-syllable words; isolate and pronounce individual phonemes (initial, medial, final) in CVC words; add or substitute phonemes to make new words
evidence: Blend onset and rime to say a word (e.g. /c/ + /at/ → 'cat')
Identify the first, middle, or last sound in a CVC word
Change one sound to make a new word (e.g. change /c/ in 'cat' to /b/ → 'bat')

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Rhyming words
topics.description: Recognise and produce rhyming words; join in with predictable phrases and rhymes in stories and poems; learn to appreciate and recite poems by heart
evidence: Identify which words rhyme from a set (e.g. cat, bat, dog)
Generate a word that rhymes with a given target
Join in with repeated refrains and rhyming patterns during shared reading

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Single Letter Sounds
topics.description: Know the primary sound for each consonant and the short and long sounds for the five major vowels; respond speedily to single-letter graphemes
evidence: Say the most common sound for each consonant when shown the letter
Distinguish short vowel sounds in CVC words (e.g. /a/ in 'cat' vs /e/ in 'bed')
Associate long and short vowel sounds with common single-letter spellings

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Understanding print
topics.description: Demonstrate understanding that print carries meaning, follows left-to-right top-to-bottom directionality, and is organised page by page in books
evidence: Track words with a finger moving left to right across the page
Turn pages in the correct sequence when handling a book
Point to where reading starts on a page

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Vowel Digraphs
topics.description: Read and spell words containing common vowel digraphs (ai, ay, ee, ea, oa, oe, oo, oi, oy) including where a digraph can represent more than one sound
evidence: Read words with vowel digraphs (e.g. 'tree', 'boat', 'rain', 'coin')
Distinguish between different sounds for the same digraph (e.g. 'oo' in 'book' vs 'moon')
Spell words using common vowel digraph patterns

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Compound Words
topics.description: Recognise and spell compound words by identifying the two component words that combine to form a single word
evidence: Identify the two words in a compound (e.g. 'sunshine' = 'sun' + 'shine')
Spell compound words by combining known words
Create compound words from given word pairs

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Counting words in spoken sentences
topics.description: Segment spoken sentences into individual words by clapping, tapping or moving a counter for each word heard (phonological awareness)
evidence: Clap once for each word in the spoken sentence 'The big dog ran' and say there are 4 words
Push a counter forward for each word heard in 'I like red apples'
Say which spoken sentence has more words, 'We go' or 'We go to the park'

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Diphthongs and complex vowels
topics.description: Read and spell words containing diphthongs and complex vowel patterns (ow, ou, ew, ue, ie, aw, au) and words ending in -y as a vowel sound
evidence: Read words with variable vowel sounds (e.g. 'ow' in 'cow' vs 'snow')
Decode words with diphthongs (e.g. 'cloud', 'blue', 'pie')
Read words ending in -y pronounced as /ee/ or /igh/ (e.g. 'happy', 'my')

topics.subject: English
topics.name: R-Controlled Vowel Sounds
topics.description: Read and spell words containing r-controlled vowels (ar, er, ir, ur, or, ore) and vowel-r patterns where 'r' modifies the vowel sound
evidence: Read words with r-controlled vowels (e.g. 'car', 'bird', 'fork', 'her')
Recognise that 'r' changes the vowel sound (e.g. 'cat' vs 'cart')
Spell words with common r-controlled patterns

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Reading Contractions
topics.description: Read and understand contractions with apostrophes, knowing the apostrophe represents omitted letters
evidence: Read common contractions in text (e.g. 'I'm', 'we'll', 'don't')
Match contractions to their expanded forms (e.g. 'I'm' = 'I am')
Explain that the apostrophe shows where letters are missing

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Reading fluently
topics.description: Read aloud books matched to phonic ability accurately and with growing fluency; reread familiar texts to build confidence, speed, and expression
evidence: Read a phonically appropriate text with 90%+ accuracy
Reread familiar texts with improved pace and expression
Read emergent-reader texts with purpose and understanding

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Reading High-Frequency Words by Sight
topics.description: Read common high-frequency and exception words automatically by sight, including words with irregular spelling patterns
evidence: Read common exception words instantly without sounding out (e.g. 'the', 'said', 'was', 'you')
Note unusual correspondences between spelling and sound in exception words
Recognise at least 20-30 high-frequency words in connected text

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Reading Inflectional Endings
topics.description: Read words containing taught GPCs with common inflectional endings (-s, -es, -ing, -ed, -er, -est) and the prefix un-; read multi-syllable words with taught patterns
evidence: Read suffixed words fluently (e.g. 'jumping', 'wanted', 'faster')
Identify the root word when a suffix is added
Read words with prefix un- (e.g. 'unhappy', 'undo')

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Split Digraphs and Magic E
topics.description: Read and spell words containing split digraphs (a-e, e-e, i-e, o-e, u-e) where a final 'e' makes the preceding vowel long
evidence: Read words with split digraphs (e.g. 'cake', 'bike', 'home', 'cube')
Compare minimal pairs showing the effect of the split digraph (e.g. 'cap' vs 'cape')
Spell words with split digraphs correctly

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Spotting and making alliteration
topics.description: Recognise and generate alliteration — words close together that start with the same sound — in spoken phrases, names and tongue twisters (phonological awareness)
evidence: Say whether all the words in 'silly Sam sat' start with the same sound
Join in a tongue twister such as 'Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers' and name the repeated sound
Make up an alliterative name like 'Bouncy Ben' or 'Dancing Daisy'

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Syllables
topics.description: Count, blend, and segment syllables in spoken words; divide written words into syllables as an aid to reading and spelling
evidence: Clap out syllables in spoken words (e.g. 'butterfly' = 3 claps)
Blend syllables to form words (e.g. 'rain' + 'bow' → 'rainbow')
Segment a word into its syllable parts orally

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Trigraphs
topics.description: Read and spell words containing trigraphs — three-letter graphemes representing a single sound (igh, air, ear, are)
evidence: Read words with trigraphs (e.g. 'night', 'chair', 'near')
Distinguish between different sounds for 'ear' (e.g. 'hear' vs 'bear')
Identify the single phoneme represented by three letters in a word

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Adding, deleting and swapping sounds
topics.description: Orally manipulate phonemes in spoken words by adding, deleting and substituting initial, medial and final phonemes to make new words (phonological awareness)
evidence: Add a sound at the start or end of a word: /s/ + 'top' makes 'stop'; 'ten' + /t/ makes 'tent'
Delete initial, medial and final sounds, including from inside a cluster: 'slip' without /s/ is 'lip', 'black' without /l/ is 'back', 'tent' without the last /t/ is 'ten'
Substitute initial, medial and final sounds: change 'pin' to 'tin', 'pin' to 'pan', 'pin' to 'pig' and 'chip' to 'ship'

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Alternative Spellings for Known Sounds
topics.description: Recognise alternative grapheme-phoneme correspondences for known phonemes (e.g., /dʒ/ as ge/dge/g, /s/ as c, /n/ as kn/gn, /r/ as wr, /ʒ/ as s), reading words with less common spellings for familiar sounds
evidence: Read words with less common spellings for familiar sounds: 'badge', 'giraffe', 'city', 'knock', 'gnaw', 'write', 'treasure'
Identify that the same phoneme can be represented by different graphemes (e.g., /dʒ/ spelled g, ge, dge)
Select the correct alternative GPC to decode an unfamiliar word in context

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Blending spoken sounds
topics.description: Listen to a word spoken as separate speech sounds (phonemes) — with no printed word, letters, letter names or answer pictures — and combine them to say the whole word, from two sounds (“sh–e” → “she”) to longer sequences, including consonant clusters at the start or end (“f–r–o–g” → “frog”, “j–u–m–p” → “jump”). An adult says each sound clearly with brief, natural pauses and without adding “uh”; the child says the word naturally in their own accent. The examples show the kind of words used; they are not levels, a list or a limit.
evidence: When an adult says a word as separate sounds face to face, with nothing written or pictured (e.g. “m–a–p”), say the whole word “map” rather than repeating the sounds
Blend words with different numbers of sounds, including ones with consonant clusters at the start or end (e.g. “s–n–a–ck” → “snack”, “h–a–n–d” → “hand”)
Blend two sound sequences that differ by one sound into the two different words (e.g. “p–i–n” → “pin” but “p–i–g” → “pig”)

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Reading and spelling consonant blends
topics.description: Use consonant blends (clusters) together with short vowels, common long vowels and digraphs to write words, and blend them to read one- and two-syllable words
evidence: Read words with initial blends (e.g. 'clap', 'frog', 'step', 'string') and final blends (e.g. 'hand', 'milk', 'jump')
Spell dictated blend words such as 'stop', 'tent', 'crisp' and 'split', writing a letter for every consonant sound
Read two-syllable and compound words containing blends (e.g. 'blanket', 'sandwich', 'trumpet', 'playground')

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Reading with Expression and Accuracy
topics.description: Read aloud with accuracy, appropriate rate, and expression (prosody), re-reading familiar texts to build fluency and confidence, and using context to self-correct
evidence: Read a grade-level passage aloud with expression and appropriate pacing
Self-correct miscues during oral reading by re-reading or using context cues
Re-read a familiar book demonstrating increased fluency and confidence

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Segmenting consonant clusters
topics.description: Orally segment spoken words into separate phonemes, including consonant blends (clusters) at the beginnings and ends of words, saying each consonant sound in the cluster separately (phonological awareness)
evidence: Segment 'stop' into four sounds /s/-/t/-/o/-/p/ using fingers or sound buttons
Segment words with final clusters such as 'jump' into /j/-/u/-/m/-/p/ and 'milk' into /m/-/i/-/l/-/k/
Say how many sounds are in 'frog', 'tent' and 'stamp' (4, 4 and 5)

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Syllables (age 6+)
topics.description: Decode words of two or more syllables by breaking them into syllable chunks, applying knowledge that every syllable must contain a vowel sound, and blending the parts together
evidence: Read 'rabbit', 'thunder', 'fantastic' by breaking into syllable chunks and blending
Clap or tap syllables in a multi-syllable word, then read each chunk before blending
Identify that every syllable must contain a vowel sound

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Decoding unfamiliar words
topics.description: Read Y3-4 exception words with unusual spelling-sound correspondences, applying growing knowledge of morphology and etymology to decode unfamiliar exception words
evidence: Read exception words from the Y3-4 statutory word list accurately (e.g. 'business', 'caught', 'knowledge', 'different')
Identify unusual letter-sound correspondences in exception words and explain why the word does not follow common GPC rules
Use growing knowledge of morphology and etymology to attempt unfamiliar exception words (e.g. recognise the root 'know' in 'knowledge')

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Prefixes and suffixes
topics.description: Read words containing common prefixes and suffixes from the Y3-4 programme, applying knowledge of root words, prefixes and suffixes (morphology and etymology) to read aloud and understand new words
evidence: Read words with common prefixes (dis-, mis-, re-, pre-) and suffixes (-ation, -ous, -ly) by identifying the root word first
Apply morphological knowledge to attempt unfamiliar words (e.g. recognise 'happy' inside 'unhappiness')
Explain how a prefix or suffix changes the meaning or word class of a root word (e.g. 'care' → 'careless' → 'carelessly')

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Predicting what happens next
topics.description: Predict what might happen next in a story based on what has been read so far; discuss the significance of titles and events
evidence: Make a prediction before turning the page and explain reasoning
Discuss why a title fits or hints at the story content
Revise predictions as new information is encountered in the text

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Rhythm in rhymes and songs
topics.description: Explore and replicate the rhythms and sound patterns of nursery rhymes, chants and songs by clapping or tapping the beat and joining in with repeated sound patterns
evidence: Clap the steady beat while saying a nursery rhyme such as 'Hickory Dickory Dock'
Repeat a chant line keeping the same rhythm the teacher used
Join in a song's repeated sound pattern (e.g. 'splish, splash') at the right moment

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Book Features and Author's Reasons
topics.description: Identify front cover, back cover, and title page of a book; identify the reasons an author gives to support points in informational text
evidence: Point to and name parts of a book (front cover, back cover, title page)
Use the title page to find the title, author, and illustrator
Identify a reason the author gives for a claim in a simple non-fiction text

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Characters, settings, and events
topics.description: Identify characters, settings, and major events in stories; become familiar with key stories, fairy tales, and traditional tales and retell them with key details in sequence
evidence: Name the main characters in a story
Describe where and when a story takes place
Retell a familiar story including beginning, middle, and end events

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Comparing Characters Across Stories
topics.description: Compare and contrast the adventures and experiences of characters in familiar stories; identify similarities and differences between two texts on the same topic
evidence: Identify what two stories have in common (e.g. 'Both have a bear character')
Compare information from two books about the same topic
Discuss how characters' experiences are similar or different across stories

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Connecting reading to experience
topics.description: Link what is read or heard to own experiences; draw on background knowledge and vocabulary to support understanding of texts
evidence: Make text-to-self connections (e.g. 'This reminds me of when I...')
Use personal experience to understand a character's feelings
Relate events in a story to own life to deepen comprehension

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Different Types of Texts
topics.description: Recognise common types of texts (storybooks, poems, non-fiction); name the author and illustrator and define the role of each in telling or presenting a text
evidence: Distinguish between a story, a poem, and a non-fiction book
Point to and name the author and illustrator on the cover
Explain that the author writes the words and the illustrator makes the pictures

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Discussing Texts as a Group
topics.description: Participate in discussions about what is read, taking turns and listening to others; explain understanding clearly; actively engage in group reading activities
evidence: Share ideas about a book in a group discussion
Listen to and respond to others' opinions about a text
Take turns speaking and build on what classmates have said about a book

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Listening to Texts Read Aloud
topics.description: Listen to and discuss poems, stories, and non-fiction at a level beyond independent reading; confirm understanding of texts read aloud by asking and answering questions about key details
evidence: Answer questions about a story or non-fiction text read aloud by the teacher
Discuss events, characters, or ideas from chapter books read to the class
Ask for clarification when something in a read-aloud is not understood

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Main Topic of Informational Texts
topics.description: Identify the main topic and retell key details of informational texts; describe connections between individuals, events, ideas, or pieces of information
evidence: State what a non-fiction text is mostly about in one sentence
List two or three important facts learned from an informational text
Explain how two events or ideas in a text are connected

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Making pictures in your head
topics.description: Use visualising as a comprehension strategy when listening, viewing and reading: building and revising a mental picture from descriptive words to support literal and inferred meaning
evidence: Sketch the picture they formed from a descriptive passage without illustrations, or from a process described in an information text (e.g. the water cycle), and label it with words from the text
Describe what they see, hear and feel in their mind while listening to or reading a scene, and use the picture to infer a character's mood
Compare their mental picture with a film, illustrated or other version of the same text, and revise what they infer (e.g. 'Now I see her crying, so she is upset')

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Navigating print and screen texts
topics.description: Navigate print and screen texts to find information: use contents pages and indexes in print, and on screens swipe or scroll, tap icons, links and menus, use home, back and search, reading screen text in the same direction as print
evidence: Swipe or tap to move through a digital picture book, scroll a screen text and use the home or back icon to return to the start
Use a side-bar or drop-down menu or a link on a children's website to reach the page about a chosen animal, then return to the home page or search with a keyword
Find the same fact once with a book's index or contents page and once by following links on a website, and say which was quicker

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Pictures and Text Working Together
topics.description: Describe the relationship between illustrations and the text in which they appear; use pictures to support and extend comprehension
evidence: Use pictures to predict or confirm story events
Describe what is happening in an illustration and how it relates to the text
Explain how an illustration, photograph or labelled diagram adds information not stated in the words

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Reading between the lines
topics.description: Ask and answer questions about key details in literary and informational texts; make simple inferences based on what characters say and do
evidence: Answer 'who', 'what', 'where' questions about a text using evidence
Infer a character's feelings from their actions (e.g. 'She's sad because she's crying')
Make logical guesses about unstated information using text clues

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Retelling Stories with Structure
topics.description: Retell stories including key details in sequence, describe characters, settings, and major events using evidence from the text, and describe the overall structure of a story (beginning, middle, ending)
evidence: Retell a familiar story in order, including at least three key details from beginning, middle, and end
Describe a character's appearance, actions, or personality using details from the text
Explain how the beginning of a story introduces the characters and setting, and how the ending concludes the action

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Self-Correcting While Reading
topics.description: Check that text makes sense while reading and self-correct inaccurate reading by re-reading or using context
evidence: Notice when reading does not make sense and stop to re-read
Self-correct errors mid-sentence (e.g. 'Wait, that doesn't sound right')
Use meaning, sentence structure, and visual cues together to monitor reading

topics.subject: English
topics.name: What is this text for?
topics.description: Identify the purpose of familiar texts — to entertain (imaginative), to give information, to persuade, or to tell us what to do — and describe how imaginative, informative and persuasive texts differ
evidence: Say that a storybook is for enjoying a story, an animal fact book is for finding out facts, and a recipe or shopping list tells us what to do
Sort a storybook, a fact book and a poster saying 'Come to our school fair!' into texts that entertain, inform or persuade, and point to words in the poster that try to convince the reader
Choose which book to use to find out what koalas eat and explain why

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Characters' Viewpoints and Responses
topics.description: Identify and compare characters' points of view, recognise who is narrating a story, describe how characters respond to events and challenges, and compare characters' experiences across different stories or versions of the same story
evidence: Identify who is telling a story and explain how you know (e.g. 'The wolf is telling the story because he says I')
Describe how a character responds to a problem or challenge using evidence from the text (e.g. 'When the bridge broke, she decided to swim across')
Compare how two characters from different stories react to a similar situation (e.g. how two heroes show bravery in different ways)

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Expressive and Sensory Language
topics.description: Recognise recurring literary language in stories and poetry, identify words and phrases that suggest feelings or appeal to the senses, and discuss favourite words and phrases
evidence: Spot recurring story language such as 'Once upon a time' and 'happily ever after'
Identify sensory words and phrases in a poem: 'the icy wind howled'
Share a favourite word or phrase from a story and explain why it appeals

topics.subject: English
topics.name: How texts in subjects differ
topics.description: Identify and describe how texts across the curriculum — such as science procedures, maths word problems, history recounts and health posters — are organised differently and use language features suited to their purposes
evidence: Point out the stages of a familiar text type and their language features, e.g. a recount's orientation, events in order and closing comment, or a science procedure's goal, materials and numbered steps with command verbs
Compare a history recount's time words (first, in 1900, later) with an information report's headings and present-tense facts
Explain why a maths word problem ends with a question, a health poster uses short commands and pictures, or a persuasive speech states, argues and restates its position

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Identifying a text’s intended audience
topics.description: Identify who a text is intended for using textual and visual clues such as its topic, words, language features, pictures, layout and where the text appears
evidence: Say who a text is mainly for (e.g. a toddler's board book, a school newsletter for parents, a cereal ad for children) and point to a word, picture or layout clue
Identify the intended audience of a poster or web page from where it appears and the language it uses (e.g. 'you' and exclamations for children, technical terms for experts)
Sort a set of texts on one topic (e.g. a picture book, a science magazine article, a council notice) by intended audience and justify each choice with a clue

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Main Topic & Key Details
topics.description: Identify the main topic of a multi-paragraph informational text, determine the focus of specific paragraphs, and explain how key details support the main idea
evidence: Identify the main topic of a multi-paragraph informational text and state the focus of individual paragraphs
Describe how specific details and facts in the text support the main idea
Explain how events, ideas, or steps in a text are connected (e.g. cause-effect, sequence, comparison)

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Non-Fiction Text Features
topics.description: Recognise different non-fiction text structures and features (headings, contents, glossary, index), understanding how texts are organised to present information
evidence: Use a contents page to find information on a specific topic in a non-fiction book
Identify the purpose of headings, glossary, and index in an information text
Recognise that non-fiction books can be structured as lists, time order, or question-and-answer

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Sound and meaning in poems
topics.description: Explain the way authors use sound devices (alliteration, assonance, rhythm, rhyme, onomatopoeia) together with imagery to create meaning and effect in poetry and prose
evidence: Explain how the rhythm and rhyme of a poem (e.g. Banjo Paterson's ballad 'The Man from Snowy River') create a feeling such as galloping speed
Explain how alliteration, assonance or onomatopoeia (e.g. 'crash', 'sizzle') combine with imagery in a poem or story to create a particular mood
Read a poem aloud twice — once flatly and once stressing its sound devices — and explain how the meaning and effect change

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Story Sequence and Central Message
topics.description: Discuss the sequence of events in narrative texts and how items of information are related in non-fiction, retelling stories including key details and demonstrating understanding of central message or lesson
evidence: Retell a story in correct sequence with beginning, middle, and end
Identify the central message or lesson of a story
Explain how two pieces of information in a non-fiction text are connected

topics.subject: English
topics.name: What holds a poem together
topics.description: Explore how repeated lines, rhyming words and a steady rhythm link the parts of simple poems, chants and songs so that they hang together (cohesion) and are easy to remember
evidence: Point to the line that repeats in a chant (e.g. 'We're going on a bear hunt') and say how it ties the verses together
Find the rhyming words at the ends of lines in a short poem and explain how they connect the lines
Clap the rhythm of two verses of a song and notice that the beat stays the same in each verse

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Forms of Poetry and Performance
topics.description: Recognise different forms of poetry (free verse, narrative poetry, haiku) and discuss their features; prepare poems and play scripts to read aloud and perform with understanding through intonation, tone, volume and action
evidence: Name at least two different forms of poetry and describe a feature of each (e.g., 'narrative poetry tells a story', 'free verse does not have a regular rhyme or rhythm')
Recognise the form of a given poem and explain how you identified it (e.g., 'This is a narrative poem because it has characters and a plot')
Prepare and perform a poem or play script extract showing understanding through changes in intonation, volume, and expression

topics.subject: English
topics.name: How characters and places connect
topics.description: Discuss how characters and settings are connected in literature by First Nations Australian, other Australian and world authors and illustrators — how a place shapes what characters do and feel, and how characters belong to or change a place
evidence: Explain how Country and the characters are connected in a First Nations Australian picture book (e.g. 'Somebody's Land' by Adam Goodes, Ellie Laing and David Hardy)
Describe how the setting affects what a character does in an Australian story (e.g. the rainforest in Jeannie Baker's 'Where the Forest Meets the Sea')
Predict how a character from a world story would act if moved to a different setting, and give a reason

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Inferring Characters' Feelings and Motives
topics.description: Draw inferences from independently-read texts, such as inferring characters' feelings, thoughts and motives from their actions, and justifying inferences with evidence from the text
evidence: Infer a character's feelings or motives from their actions and dialogue (e.g. 'She slammed the door — how is she feeling?')
Justify an inference by quoting or pointing to specific evidence in the text
Distinguish between what is explicitly stated and what must be inferred from clues in the text

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Main Ideas & Note-Taking
topics.description: Identify main ideas drawn from more than one paragraph and summarise them; retrieve and record information from non-fiction texts using notes, tables or other methods
evidence: Read a multi-paragraph non-fiction text and state the main idea of each paragraph in one sentence
Summarise a text of 3+ paragraphs in 2-3 sentences capturing the key points
Retrieve specific information from a non-fiction text and record it using a simple table or notes (e.g., 'Name: hedgehog, Habitat: woodland, Diet: insects')

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Same topic, different texts
topics.description: Identify how similar topics and information are presented in different types of texts, such as a poem, an information report, a website and a picture book about the same subject
evidence: Compare a poem about the ocean with an information report about the ocean and say what each tells and how
Find the same fact about frogs on a website and in a book and describe how each presents it (e.g. video, photo, heading)
Explain why a picture book and a fact sheet about bees might be written differently

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Story Lessons and Morals
topics.description: Determine the central message, lesson, or moral of a story, fable, or folktale, explaining what the story teaches the reader and supporting the interpretation with key details from the text
evidence: State the lesson or moral of a fable in one sentence (e.g. 'The Tortoise and the Hare teaches that slow and steady wins the race')
Explain what a story's central message is using at least two details from the text as support
Distinguish the central message from a summary of events — explain what the story means, not just what happens

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Text Features & Presentation
topics.description: Identify how language choices, text structure and presentational features (illustrations, diagrams, bold print, layout) contribute to the overall meaning and effect of a text
evidence: Explain how an author's word choices create a particular effect (e.g., 'The author uses "crept" instead of "walked" to make it feel sneaky and tense')
Identify how a text's structure helps the reader (e.g., 'The headings help you find information quickly', 'The story builds suspense before the ending')
Explain how a presentational feature contributes to meaning (e.g., 'The bold words are important vocabulary', 'The diagram shows how the water cycle works')

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Themes and messages
topics.description: Identify recurring themes (good vs evil, friendship, bravery) and conventions (once upon a time, moral at the end, hero's journey) across a wide range of books including fairy stories, myths, legends and traditional tales
evidence: Identify a common theme across two different stories (e.g., 'Both "Jack and the Beanstalk" and "The Three Billy Goats Gruff" are about bravery overcoming a threat')
Name literary conventions found in fairy tales and myths (e.g., 'once upon a time', magical numbers like three, a quest or journey, good triumphing over evil)
Explain how the same theme can appear in different genres (e.g., friendship in a realistic story vs a myth)

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Why the author wrote it
topics.description: Distinguish one's own point of view from that of the author of an informational text and identify the author's purpose
evidence: Read an opinion article and state the author's point of view, then state one's own and explain how they differ
Identify whether an author's purpose is to inform, persuade, or entertain, citing evidence from the text
Explain how word choices in an informational text reveal the author's attitude toward the topic

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Words that show characters
topics.description: Discuss characters and settings across a range of texts and identify how language — adjectives, verbs, dialogue and descriptive phrases — presents them in different ways
evidence: Find the words that show a character is grumpy in one story and cheerful in another (e.g. 'stomped', 'grumbled' vs 'skipped', 'giggled')
Compare how two texts describe a beach setting and list the descriptive words each uses
Explain how what a character says (dialogue) tells the reader what they are like

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Character Traits and Motivation
topics.description: Analyse character traits, motivations, and feelings using text evidence, and distinguish one's own point of view from that of the narrator or characters
evidence: Identify two character traits from a story and cite the specific actions or dialogue that reveal each trait
Explain why a character made a particular decision by linking their motivation to events in the text
Describe where one's own opinion about a character differs from the narrator's portrayal and explain why

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Combining information from texts
topics.description: Integrate information from two texts on the same topic in order to write or speak about the subject knowledgeably, combining and comparing what each source contributes
evidence: Read two informational texts on the same topic and identify information that appears in both, information unique to each, and any contradictions between them
Combine key details from two sources into a coherent summary or short report that draws on both texts
Explain how reading a second text on the same topic added to, confirmed, or challenged understanding gained from the first text

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Connecting Ideas in Texts
topics.description: Describe connections between events, ideas, or concepts in informational text using time, sequence, cause-and-effect, and comparison language, and identify logical connections between sentences and paragraphs
evidence: Read a science text and identify three cause-and-effect relationships using signal words like 'because', 'as a result'
Explain the sequence of steps in a technical procedure using time-order language ('first', 'next', 'finally')
Describe how two paragraphs in a text are connected (e.g. comparison, cause/effect, or sequence)

topics.subject: English
topics.name: In-Depth Character and Setting Analysis
topics.description: Describe in depth a character, setting, or event in a story or drama, drawing on specific details from the text such as a character's thoughts, words, actions, and interactions
evidence: Write a detailed character description drawing on evidence from multiple points in the text, including what the character says, does, thinks, and how others respond to them
Describe a setting in depth by citing specific sensory details, figurative language, and mood clues the author provides
Explain how a key event affects the characters and plot development, citing specific textual details about actions, reactions, and consequences

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Interpreting visual information in texts
topics.description: Interpret information presented visually, orally, or quantitatively in informational texts (e.g., charts, graphs, diagrams, timelines, animations) and explain how it contributes to understanding the text
evidence: Read and interpret data from a chart, graph, or table included in an informational text and explain how it supports or extends the written information
Explain how a diagram, map, or timeline in an informational text helps the reader understand the topic in ways that words alone might not
Synthesise information from both the written text and a visual element (graph, illustration, infographic) to draw a conclusion that neither source provides independently

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Morals in Fables, Folktales and Myths
topics.description: Explain how the central message, lesson, or moral of a story is conveyed through key details across diverse text types including fables, folktales, and myths
evidence: Retell a fable and identify the moral, citing three key details that convey it
Compare how two myths from different cultures convey a similar central message through different events
Explain the difference between the topic of a story and its central message or lesson

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Quoting Accurately from Texts
topics.description: Quote accurately from literary and informational texts when explaining what the text says explicitly and when drawing inferences, using quotation marks and citations correctly
evidence: Select and copy exact words from a text to support an inference about character motivation
Use quotation marks correctly when incorporating textual evidence into written responses
Introduce quotes with signal phrases such as 'The author states' or 'According to the text'

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Same purpose, different audience
topics.description: Recognise how texts with similar purposes are created differently for different audiences, by comparing word choice, sentence length, images and layout
evidence: Compare two information texts about volcanoes, one for young children and one for adults, and list the differences in words and pictures
Explain how an invitation to a friend's party differs from an invitation to a school assembly for parents
Identify who each of two ads for the same product is aimed at and point to the features that show it

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Stories from other places, times
topics.description: Discuss characters, events and settings in different contexts (places, times, cultures) in literature by First Nations Australian, other Australian and world authors and illustrators
evidence: Discuss how the setting and events of a First Nations Australian story (e.g. 'Shake a Leg' by Boori Monty Pryor and Jan Ormerod) connect to culture and Country

Compare the setting and events of an Australian story set in the bush (e.g. Jackie French's 'Diary of a Wombat') with those of a story set in a city, noting details of daily life, customs or social rules each shows
Explain how a character's actions make sense in their story's context (e.g. a different place or time) using details from the text

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Structural terminology
topics.description: Use structural terminology (chapter, scene, stanza) to refer to parts of literary texts and describe how each successive part builds on earlier sections
evidence: Identify chapters, scenes, or stanzas in a given text and use the correct term for each
Explain how the second stanza of a poem builds on the mood established in the first
Describe how a specific chapter advances the plot by referring to events in earlier chapters

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Structure of information texts
topics.description: Describe the overall structure of an informational text (chronology, comparison, cause/effect, problem/solution) and explain how the author's chosen structure helps convey information and ideas
evidence: Identify which organisational structure an informational text uses (chronological order, compare/contrast, cause/effect, or problem/solution) and cite textual features that signal it
Explain how signal words (first, then, finally for chronology; however, similarly for comparison; because, as a result for cause/effect; the solution was for problem/solution) reveal text structure
Compare two informational texts on the same topic that use different structures and explain how each structure affects the way information is presented to the reader

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Themes Across Cultures and Traditions
topics.description: Compare and contrast the treatment of similar themes, topics, and story patterns (e.g., good vs evil, quest narratives, trickster tales) in stories, myths, and traditional literature from different cultures
evidence: Compare how two myths or folk tales from different cultures treat a similar theme (e.g., creation, heroism, the importance of honesty) and explain both similarities and differences
Identify recurring story patterns across cultures such as the trickster figure, the quest, or the transformation, providing specific examples from texts read
Explain how cultural context shapes the way a universal theme is expressed differently in stories from various traditions

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Cultural Allusions and Word Meaning
topics.description: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as used in literary texts, including understanding references to mythology and cultural allusions (e.g., Herculean, Achilles' heel)
evidence: Explain the meaning of an allusion drawn from mythology when encountered in a text, e.g. identify that 'Herculean task' means an extremely difficult task, referencing Hercules' legendary labours
Use context and knowledge of word parts to determine the meaning of unfamiliar words in a poem or story, explaining how the word contributes to tone or meaning
Identify when an author is using a word figuratively rather than literally and explain the intended meaning in context

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Explaining Events & Ideas
topics.description: Explain events, procedures, ideas, or concepts in an informational text, including what happened and why, by citing specific textual evidence about causes, effects, and steps in a process
evidence: Explain a historical event described in an informational text by identifying both what happened and the causes leading to it, using specific details from the text
Describe the steps in a procedure or process presented in an informational text, explaining why each step is necessary based on information in the text
Identify cause-and-effect relationships between ideas or events in an informational passage and explain them using evidence from the text

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Fact vs opinion
topics.description: Distinguish between statements of fact and statements of opinion in texts, recognising how authors blend factual information with subjective viewpoints
evidence: Identify and label statements as fact or opinion in a newspaper article
Explain why a statement is a fact by citing verifiable evidence or why it is an opinion
Recognise persuasive techniques that present opinions as if they were facts

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Finding Theme and Summarising
topics.description: Determine the theme of a story, drama, or poem from details in the text, and provide an objective summary that captures the key events without personal opinions
evidence: Identify the theme of a story (e.g. courage, friendship, overcoming adversity) by examining what characters learn, how they change, and what the author emphasises across the whole text
Distinguish theme from topic: explain that a topic might be 'war' while the theme is 'the cost of conflict on families'
Summarise a story, chapter, or poem objectively, including only key events and details without inserting personal opinions or minor details

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Firsthand and Secondhand Accounts
topics.description: Compare and contrast a firsthand account (autobiography, diary, letter) with a secondhand account (biography, textbook, news report) of the same event or topic, identifying differences in focus and information provided
evidence: Explain the difference between a firsthand account (written by someone who experienced the event) and a secondhand account (written by someone who researched it), using specific examples
Compare a diary entry and a textbook passage about the same historical event, identifying what each account includes, omits, and emphasises
Analyse how the perspective of the writer (participant vs observer/researcher) affects the information provided, the language used, and the overall tone

topics.subject: English
topics.name: How authors support their points
topics.description: Explain how an author of an informational text uses reasons and evidence to support particular points, evaluating whether the reasoning is sound and the evidence is relevant and sufficient
evidence: Identify the key points an author makes in an informational text and list the specific reasons and evidence provided to support each point
Evaluate whether the evidence an author uses (facts, statistics, examples, expert opinions) is relevant to the point being made and sufficient to be convincing
Distinguish between well-supported claims backed by evidence and unsupported opinions or assertions in an informational text

topics.subject: English
topics.name: How images are framed
topics.description: Explore the effect of choices in framing (close-up, mid shot, long shot), placement of elements and salience (what stands out through size, colour, light or position) on the composition of still and moving images in texts
evidence: Compare a close-up and a long shot of the same character in a picture book or film and explain how each makes the viewer feel
Identify the most salient element in an illustration or poster (e.g. the brightest or largest object) and explain why the creator made it stand out
Rearrange the elements of a simple photo or drawing on a tablet (e.g. move the main subject from the centre to the edge) and describe how the meaning changes

topics.subject: English
topics.name: How Language Choices Affect the Reader
topics.description: Evaluate how authors use language including figurative language, considering the impact of word choices, imagery, and literary devices on the reader
evidence: Explain how a specific metaphor or simile affects the reader's understanding or emotions
Evaluate an author's choice of descriptive language and its impact on atmosphere
Compare how different authors use figurative language to achieve similar effects

topics.subject: English
topics.name: How Parts Build a Whole Text
topics.description: Explain how a series of chapters, scenes, or stanzas fits together to provide the overall structure of a story, drama, or poem, analysing how each part contributes to the whole
evidence: Map the structure of a novel showing how each chapter advances plot or character development
Explain how individual stanzas in a poem build toward a central theme or message
Analyse how scenes in a play work together to develop conflict and resolution

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Human qualities in stories
topics.description: Recognise and explain BOTH ways writers give human qualities to things that are not human: personification, where a thing or idea is described as if it were a person ("the old stairs groaned"), AND anthropomorphism, where animals or objects are characters who think, talk and behave like people. For each, explain how it shapes meaning and why it suits the purpose and the intended readers, recognising that the two forms overlap because both give human qualities to something non-human.
evidence: In a poem or description, finds a personification, names the non-human thing and the human quality it is given, and explains the image or feeling it creates
In a story, identifies an anthropomorphic character, names the human behaviours it shows, and explains why the author chose it for the intended readers
From a paired example of each, explains how a personified description differs from a human-like character and how both give human qualities to something non-human

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Justifying Views About Texts
topics.description: Provide reasoned justifications for views about texts, supporting interpretations and opinions with evidence and logical arguments
evidence: State an opinion about a character's motivations and support it with three pieces of textual evidence
Construct a reasoned argument about an author's message using quotes from the text
Respond to an alternative interpretation by providing counter-evidence from the text

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Multiple Accounts of Events
topics.description: Analyse multiple accounts of the same event or topic, noting important similarities and differences in the point of view they represent
evidence: Compare two news articles about the same event and identify differences in perspective
Explain how the author's background or purpose affects their account of an event
Identify which facts are consistent across accounts and which details differ based on viewpoint

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Narrator's Point of View
topics.description: Compare and contrast the point of view from which different stories are narrated, including distinguishing between first-person and third-person narration and explaining how the narrator's perspective shapes the reader's understanding
evidence: Identify whether a story is told in first person (I/we) or third person (he/she/they) and explain how this affects what the reader knows about characters' thoughts and feelings
Compare two versions of a story or event told from different points of view and explain how each narrator's perspective changes what is emphasised, omitted, or revealed
Explain why an author might choose first-person narration (immediacy, personal voice) versus third-person narration (broader view, objectivity) for a particular story

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Poems, Drama & Prose
topics.description: Explain major differences between poems, drama, and prose, identifying structural elements unique to each form: verse, rhythm, and meter in poetry; cast of characters, dialogue, and stage directions in drama; chapters and paragraphs in prose
evidence: Compare a poem, a play script, and a prose passage on a similar theme, identifying the structural features unique to each form (e.g. stanzas vs scenes vs chapters)
Identify and explain the function of structural elements in drama: cast list, stage directions (in italics or brackets), dialogue format, and scene divisions
Describe how structural elements of poetry such as verse, rhythm, meter, and line breaks affect how a poem is read aloud and how meaning is conveyed

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Puns and playing with words
topics.description: Examine the use of literary devices and deliberate word play in literary texts, including poetry, to shape meaning: puns, invented words, double meanings and nonsense verse
evidence: Explain the double meaning in a pun (e.g. 'The bicycle couldn't stand up because it was two-tired')
Find invented words in a nonsense poem (e.g. C. J. Dennis's 'The Triantiwontigongolope' or Lewis Carroll's 'Jabberwocky') and work out what they might mean
Explain how an author uses word play in a humorous book (e.g. Andy Griffiths' 'The 13-Storey Treehouse') to make the reader laugh

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Recommending Books
topics.description: Recommend books to peers, giving reasons for choices based on knowledge of a wide range of genres, authors, and themes, and making comparisons within and across books
evidence: Recommend a book to a peer by explaining its genre, theme, and what makes it engaging, comparing it to other books the peer has enjoyed
Justify a book recommendation by referring to specific features such as the author's style, the plot structure, or how a theme is developed
Maintain a reading log or book review collection that captures key responses to books read and serves as a reference for future recommendations

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Skimming, scanning and checking
topics.description: Navigate and read texts for specific purposes, monitoring meaning using the strategies of skimming (for gist), scanning (for specific details) and confirming (re-reading to check information)
evidence: Skim an article for 30 seconds using its headings and first sentences, then state its main idea
Scan a timetable, index or web page for a specific date, name or keyword and locate it quickly
Confirm an answer by returning to the relevant section, re-reading it closely and correcting the answer if needed

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Text & Media Connections
topics.description: Make connections between the text of a story or drama and a visual or oral presentation of the text, identifying where each version reflects specific descriptions and directions from the text
evidence: Compare a passage from a book with a film or audio adaptation, identifying specific moments where the visual or oral version matches or departs from the written text
Explain how a film, illustration, or dramatic performance interprets a scene from a story, citing specific textual descriptions the adaptation reflects
Identify details in the written text (descriptions of setting, character appearance, dialogue) that a visual or oral presentation brings to life, and note any differences

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Texts as clues to time
topics.description: Describe the ways in which a text reflects the time and place in which it was created, through its language, values, references, technology and images
evidence: Identify words, references and attitudes in an older Australian story or poem (e.g. a Banjo Paterson ballad) that show when and where it was written
Compare an older and a recent text with the same purpose (e.g. a 1980s and a recent advertisement or news report) and explain what each reveals about its time and audience
Explain how a modern text or media piece (e.g. a picture book or documentary) reflects present-day concerns, values or assumptions about its audience

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Using Multiple Sources
topics.description: Draw on information from multiple print or digital sources, demonstrating the ability to locate an answer to a question quickly or solve a problem efficiently
evidence: Use search features, indexes, and headings to locate specific information across sources
Synthesise information from two or more sources to answer a research question
Evaluate which source provides the most relevant information for a given question

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Comparing Books
topics.description: Make comparisons within and across books, identifying similarities and differences in themes, characters, settings, and authorial choices across multiple texts
evidence: Compare how two authors develop similar themes using different narrative techniques
Identify similarities and differences between characters across books by the same author
Analyse how settings function differently in two texts from the same genre

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Comparing Characters, Settings and Events
topics.description: Compare and contrast two or more characters, settings, or events in a story or drama, drawing on specific details about how characters interact, settings influence action, or events connect
evidence: Create a Venn diagram comparing two characters' traits using textual evidence
Explain how a change in setting affects the mood and characters' actions in a story
Analyse how two events in a narrative are connected through cause and effect

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Comparing Structure in Information Texts
topics.description: Compare and contrast the overall structure of events, ideas, concepts, or information in two or more informational texts, identifying patterns such as chronology, comparison, cause/effect, or problem/solution
evidence: Identify the organisational structure of two texts on the same topic
Explain how one text uses cause/effect while another uses problem/solution to present information
Analyse why an author chose a particular structure for their informational text

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Different viewpoints in texts
topics.description: Describe how a narrator's or speaker's point of view influences how events are described, recognising the difference between limited and omniscient narration and how perspective shapes storytelling
evidence: Identify whether a story uses first-person or third-person narration and explain the effect
Explain how events would be described differently if told from another character's perspective
Analyse how the narrator's knowledge or bias affects what information the reader receives

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Explaining Relationships in Texts
topics.description: Explain the relationships or interactions between two or more individuals, events, ideas, or concepts in historical, scientific, or technical texts based on specific information
evidence: Explain the cause-and-effect relationship between events in a historical text
Describe how a scientific process involves sequential steps that depend on each other
Identify how key individuals in a text influenced events or other people

topics.subject: English
topics.name: How Authors Treat Similar Themes
topics.description: Compare and contrast stories in the same genre on their approaches to similar themes and topics, identifying how different authors treat common ideas
evidence: Compare how two mystery stories create suspense using different techniques
Identify common themes in adventure stories and explain how each author develops them differently
Analyse how two authors from the same genre approach the theme of friendship or courage

topics.subject: English
topics.name: How image order shapes meaning
topics.description: Explain how the sequence of images in print, digital and film texts (picture-book spreads, comic panels, slideshow images, film shots) affects meaning, pacing and the reader's or viewer's response
evidence: Rearrange the panels of a short comic strip and explain how the new order changes the story or joke
Explain how a sequence of shots in a film scene (e.g. a long shot followed by a close-up) builds tension or reveals information
Explain how the order of images in a wordless or nearly wordless book (e.g. Shaun Tan's 'The Arrival') leads the viewer to an idea

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Multimedia elements in texts
topics.description: Analyse how visual and multimedia elements contribute to the meaning, tone, or beauty of a text such as graphic novels, multimedia presentations, or illustrated editions of fiction and poetry
evidence: Explain how illustrations in a graphic novel convey emotion or advance the story
Analyse how visual elements such as colour and layout affect the tone of a multimedia text
Compare how the same scene is portrayed in text versus in visual or audio format

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Summarising Non-Fiction Main Ideas
topics.description: Determine two or more main ideas of an informational text and explain how they are supported by key details, then summarise the text without personal opinions
evidence: Identify the main ideas in each section of an informational article
List key details that support each main idea in a multi-paragraph text
Write an objective summary capturing the main ideas without adding personal opinions

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Supporting ideas with evidence
topics.description: Explain how an author uses reasons and evidence to support particular points in a text, identifying which reasons and evidence support which specific points
evidence: Match each of an author's main points with the evidence used to support it
Evaluate whether the evidence provided adequately supports the author's argument
Identify points in a text that lack sufficient evidence or reasoning

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Synthesising across multiple texts
topics.description: Integrate information from several texts on the same topic in order to write or speak about the subject knowledgeably, combining information without plagiarising
evidence: Combine information from three sources into a coherent paragraph using own words
Create a fact sheet that synthesises key information from multiple texts on one topic
Present information orally that draws on multiple sources while crediting the sources

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Analysing Text Structure
topics.description: Analyse how a text's structure — including its overall organisation, use of chapters, stanzas, scenes, paragraphs, or sections — contributes to its meaning, style, and development of ideas
evidence: Explain how a non-chronological structure (e.g., flashback, frame narrative) creates suspense or surprise
Analyse the role of a specific paragraph in developing and refining a key concept in a non-fiction text
Compare how two texts use different structures (e.g., epistolary vs. linear narrative) and the effect of each

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Blended and adapted text types
topics.description: Recognise and explain how authors adapt or blend text structures and language features for a purpose (e.g. a narrative used to inform in science, or a persuasive-information campaign page)
evidence: Identify the information-report stages and narrative features blended in a science text told as a story (e.g. a day in the life of a water droplet)
Analyse a hybrid persuasive-information text (e.g. an environmental campaign web page) and explain which stages inform and which persuade
Explain why an author adapted a familiar structure for a purpose in another learning area, such as a diary used to recount a historical event

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Critical comparison across texts
topics.description: Make critical comparisons across texts — comparing themes, characters, settings, styles, or arguments in two or more works, including texts from different periods, genres, or cultures
evidence: Compare how two novels treat a shared theme (e.g., growing up) using specific evidence from both
Analyse how a modern retelling draws on and transforms elements from a traditional story or myth
Compare conflicting accounts of the same event in two non-fiction texts and evaluate which is more convincing

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Evaluating Arguments in Non-Fiction
topics.description: Evaluate arguments and claims in non-fiction texts — assess whether reasoning is sound, evidence is relevant and sufficient, distinguish between fact and opinion, and recognise bias, propaganda, and rhetorical techniques
evidence: Identify the main claim in an argument text and evaluate whether the evidence presented is sufficient
Spot logical fallacies or irrelevant evidence introduced to distract from weak reasoning
Compare two opposing arguments on the same issue and evaluate which is more convincing, with reasons

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Figurative Language and Literary Devices
topics.description: Determine the meaning of figurative and connotative language in context, analyse the impact of specific word choices on meaning and tone, and identify literary devices such as metaphor, simile, personification, allusion, and irony
evidence: Identify a metaphor or simile in a passage and explain its effect on the reader
Explain how an author's word choice creates a particular tone (e.g., menacing, humorous, melancholic)
Recognise an allusion to a myth, the Bible, or another text and explain what it adds to the meaning

topics.subject: English
topics.name: How context shapes responses
topics.description: Identify responses to characters and events in literary texts that are drawn from historical, social or cultural contexts, in literature by First Nations Australian, other Australian and world authors, including how readers' own contexts shape their responses
evidence: Explain how the historical context of colonisation shapes readers' responses to events in an allegorical Australian picture book (e.g. 'The Rabbits' by John Marsden and Shaun Tan)
Discuss how a First Nations Australian author's verse novel (e.g. Kirli Saunders' 'Bindi') invites responses to characters and events shaped by culture and Country
Compare their own response to a character with that of a reader from a different time or culture and explain the difference

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Narrative Perspective and Unreliable Narrators
topics.description: Analyse point of view and narrative perspective — including first person, third person limited and omniscient, and unreliable narrator — and how the author's or narrator's perspective shapes the reader's understanding and creates effects such as suspense, irony, or humour
evidence: Identify the narrative perspective of a text and explain how it limits or expands the reader's knowledge
Explain how dramatic irony arises when the reader knows something a character does not
Compare how the same event might be told differently from two characters' perspectives

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Plot Structure and Character Development
topics.description: Analyse how plot structure unfolds through episodes or key events, and how characters develop, respond to challenges, and change over the course of a narrative — including the relationship between character, setting, and plot
evidence: Trace how a character's attitude changes across a story and identify the turning points
Explain how a specific incident in a drama propels the action or provokes a decision
Analyse how the setting influences a character's behaviour or the mood of a scene

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Poetic forms and conventions
topics.description: Recognise and understand poetic conventions — including form (sonnet, ballad, free verse), metre, rhyme scheme, stanza structure, imagery, and sound devices (alliteration, assonance, onomatopoeia) — and analyse how poets use them for effect
evidence: Identify the form of a poem (e.g., sonnet, haiku, ballad) and explain its key structural features
Analyse how a poet uses rhythm or sound devices to reinforce meaning or mood
Explain how enjambment or a caesura affects the pace and emphasis of a line

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Recognising an author's style
topics.description: Identify and explain the characteristics that define an author's individual style — recurring themes, sentence patterns, vocabulary, humour, narrative voice, structures such as twist endings, and illustration style
evidence: Read three stories by one author (e.g. Paul Jennings' short stories) and list recurring features such as twist endings and humour
Explain with examples how an author-illustrator's visual and written style is recognisable across books (e.g. Shaun Tan's surreal images and sparse text)
Write a short paragraph in the style of a studied author and explain which style features they imitated

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Tracing Theme Across a Text
topics.description: Determine and analyse the theme or central idea of a text, trace how it develops across the text through key details and events, and provide an objective summary distinct from personal opinion
evidence: Identify a theme in a novel and explain how specific events develop it across the plot
Distinguish between the topic of a text (what it is about) and the theme (what it is saying)
Write a concise, objective summary of a chapter or article without inserting personal opinion

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Understanding drama and performance
topics.description: Understand how dramatists communicate meaning through performance — including staging, direction, set design, lighting, and actors' choices — and how different productions can interpret the same script differently
evidence: Explain how a director's staging choices (e.g., set, lighting, blocking) affect the audience's understanding
Compare two productions or adaptations of the same play and evaluate different interpretive choices
Analyse how a filmed or live production stays faithful to or departs from the original script

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Using and Evaluating Textual Evidence
topics.description: Cite specific textual evidence to support analysis of what a text says explicitly and what can be inferred, distinguishing between strong and weak evidence and explaining how the evidence supports a point
evidence: Identify a relevant quotation to support an inference about a character's feelings
Explain why one piece of evidence is stronger than another for supporting a claim
Use embedded quotations in a written response to back up an analytical point

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Wide Independent Reading Across Genres
topics.description: Read widely and independently across fiction and non-fiction — including whole novels, short stories, plays, poetry, and non-fiction from different genres, periods, and cultures — building stamina, breadth, and personal taste as a reader
evidence: Choose books independently that offer appropriate challenge and genuine interest
Read at least two Shakespeare plays and a range of pre-1914 and contemporary literature during KS3
Maintain a personal reading record and articulate preferences with reasons

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Asking Questions
topics.description: Ask relevant questions to extend understanding; ask and answer questions to seek help, get information, or clarify something not understood
evidence: Ask a question when something is unclear or more information is needed
Answer questions with relevant and specific information
Request clarification politely (e.g. 'Can you explain that again?')

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Describing Aloud
topics.description: Describe familiar people, places, things, and events with detail; speak audibly and express thoughts, feelings, and ideas clearly; give well-structured descriptions and explanations
evidence: Describe a familiar person or place using several details
Speak clearly and loudly enough for the whole group to hear
Organise ideas logically when sharing information or telling about an event

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Exploring Ideas Through Talk
topics.description: Use spoken language to develop understanding through speculating, hypothesising, imagining, and exploring ideas; use strategies to build vocabulary through talk
evidence: Wonder aloud about possibilities (e.g. 'What if...' or 'I think it might be because...')
Try out new vocabulary in conversation after hearing it in a story or lesson
Explore ideas through talk before committing them to writing

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Expressing & Justifying Opinions
topics.description: Articulate and justify answers, arguments, and opinions; participate in discussions, presentations, performances, role play, and debates
evidence: State an opinion and give a reason (e.g. 'I think ... because ...')
Participate in a class presentation or performance with confidence
Explain thinking when answering a question rather than just giving a one-word answer

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Group discussions
topics.description: Participate actively in collaborative conversations staying on topic; continue a conversation through multiple exchanges; maintain attention in discussions
evidence: Stay on topic during a conversation for multiple turns
Build on what another speaker has said (e.g. 'I agree because...')
Maintain focus and contribute meaningfully in group discussions

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Listening and responding
topics.description: Listen and respond appropriately to adults and peers; follow agreed-upon rules for discussion such as listening to others and taking turns speaking
evidence: Demonstrate attentive listening by making eye contact and responding relevantly
Follow classroom discussion rules (e.g. raise hand, wait for turn)
Show understanding of what was said by paraphrasing or responding appropriately

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Language for different roles
topics.description: Investigate how interpersonal language choices change with the context and the role taken in an interaction, such as leader, helper, host, guest, customer or shopkeeper
evidence: Role-play being the group leader and then a helper in the same task and say how their words changed (e.g. 'Let's start with...' vs 'What would you like me to do?')
