Greet a family member at home and a teacher or visitor at school, or use host and guest language in a role-play, and say how the words change with the relationship
Explain why a shopkeeper says 'How can I help you?' while a customer says 'Could I please have...?'

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Asking, offering and requesting
topics.description: Understand how language, facial expressions and gestures work together when asking for and giving information, making offers, exclaiming, requesting and giving commands
evidence: Make a polite request with matching words and gesture (e.g. 'May I please have the glue?' with an open hand)
Make an offer to a classmate (e.g. 'Would you like a turn?') and respond to one with 'Yes, please' or 'No, thank you'
Show with face and voice the difference between an exclamation ('Wow!'), a question and a command ('Sit down, please') in role-play

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Reciting Poetry
topics.description: Learn poems by heart and recite with appropriate intonation, adding visual displays to descriptions when appropriate, and producing complete sentences in spoken presentations
evidence: Recite a poem from memory with expression and clear enunciation
Add a drawing or visual display to support an oral description or presentation
Present information to the class using complete sentences and audible voice

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Engaging Listeners and Valuing Viewpoints
topics.description: Gain, maintain and monitor the interest of listeners when speaking; consider and evaluate different viewpoints, attending to and building on others' contributions; begin to select appropriate language for different situations
evidence: Use strategies to engage listeners during a presentation (e.g., make eye contact, vary tone and pace, ask the audience a question)
Listen to a peer's viewpoint and respond by agreeing, disagreeing, or extending their idea with a reason (e.g., 'I agree with Priya because… but I also think…')
Choose more formal language for a class presentation and more informal language for a group discussion, explaining the difference

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Giving and following instructions
topics.description: Use interaction skills to receive and give spoken instructions: listening for each step, asking to clarify, and giving clear, ordered instructions to others
evidence: Follow four spoken instructions in order (e.g. to make a paper aeroplane) and ask a question if a step is unclear
Give a partner clear step-by-step instructions using order words (first, next, then, finally) to draw a simple picture
Check a partner's result and explain which instruction needs changing to be clearer

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Reporting & Recounting
topics.description: Report on a topic or recount an experience with organised facts and descriptive details, speaking clearly at an understandable pace
evidence: Deliver a one-minute oral report on a chosen topic, including at least three organised facts
Recount a personal experience using descriptive details and a clear beginning, middle, and end
Self-assess a recorded presentation for pace, clarity, and inclusion of relevant details

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Precise words in presentations
topics.description: Plan, rehearse and deliver short presentations that use topic-specific and precise vocabulary to inform, express opinions or tell stories
evidence: Plan a two-minute talk on a science topic (e.g. a frog's life cycle) that uses at least four topic words such as 'tadpole' and 'metamorphosis'
Replace vague words in a rehearsal ('thing', 'stuff', 'went') with precise ones ('gills', 'equipment', 'scurried')
Explain the meaning of a technical word to the audience during the talk

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Preparing for and Explaining in Discussions
topics.description: Come to discussions prepared, draw on preparation and known information, and explain ideas in light of the discussion
evidence: Read assigned material and prepare three discussion points or questions before a group conversation
During discussion, refer explicitly to the text or preparation notes to support a point
After a group exchange, explain how one's own thinking changed or was confirmed by others' contributions

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Building on Others in Discussions
topics.description: Pose and respond to specific questions in discussions, making comments that contribute to the discussion and elaborate on the remarks of others
evidence: Ask follow-up questions that build on another speaker's comment
Respond to a classmate's idea by adding supporting evidence or a related example
Redirect a discussion by posing a question that connects to the main topic

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Identifying Reasons Behind a Speaker's Points
topics.description: Identify the reasons and evidence a speaker provides to support particular points, evaluating whether the reasoning is logical and the evidence is relevant
evidence: Listen to a speaker's argument or presentation and list the specific reasons and evidence provided to support each main point
Evaluate whether the reasons a speaker gives are logical and whether the evidence cited is relevant to the claim being made
Ask follow-up questions that probe the strength of a speaker's reasoning, e.g. 'What evidence supports that claim?' or 'Are there other explanations?'

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Language that builds relationships
topics.description: Explore language used to develop and maintain relationships in formal and informal situations: greetings, compliments, inclusive language ('we', 'let's'), encouragement, apologies and thanks
evidence: Use inclusive and encouraging language in group work (e.g. 'Let's try your idea', 'Great thinking!') and say how it helps the group get along
Write a thank-you note to a guest speaker (formal) and a get-well message to a friend (informal) and compare the relationship-building language in each
Rephrase a blunt comment ('That's wrong') into a respectful one ('I see it differently because...')

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Multimedia Presentations
topics.description: Include multimedia components and visual displays in presentations when appropriate to enhance the development of main ideas or themes
evidence: Select graphics, images, or sound that support and clarify main ideas in a presentation
Create slides or visual aids that enhance rather than distract from the spoken content
Integrate multimedia elements smoothly into an oral presentation

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Paraphrasing What You Hear
topics.description: Paraphrase portions of a text read aloud or information presented in diverse media and formats, capturing the key ideas accurately in one's own words
evidence: Listen to a passage read aloud and restate the main idea and key details in own words without looking at the original text
Paraphrase information from a short video, podcast, or presentation, identifying the central message and supporting details
Distinguish between paraphrasing (restating in own words) and copying, demonstrating the ability to capture meaning without repeating exact wording

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Presenting an argument
topics.description: Plan, rehearse and deliver a structured spoken argument using subjective language for opinion and objective language for facts, complex sentences, visual features and deliberate control of tone, pitch, pace and volume
evidence: Plan and present a two-minute argument (e.g. 'Should our school have a longer lunch break?') with a position, two reasons with evidence, a concluding statement and a slide or chart supporting one point

Use objective language for facts ('A survey of 50 students found...'), subjective language for opinion ('I strongly believe...') and a complex sentence linking a reason to evidence, marking each in the script

Rehearse with a partner, then deliver the argument using a confident tone, enough volume for the back of the room, a slower pace and pauses for the key reason, and rising or falling pitch to stress words such as 'must', adjusting one voice feature after the partner's feedback

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Adapting Speech to Context
topics.description: Adapt speech to a variety of contexts and tasks, using formal English when appropriate to task and situation while adjusting tone, vocabulary, and style for different audiences
evidence: Present the same information formally to a panel and informally to peers
Adjust vocabulary and sentence structure when speaking to different audiences
Identify contexts that require formal English and those where informal speech is appropriate

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Drawing Conclusions from Discussion
topics.description: Review the key ideas expressed in discussions and draw conclusions in light of information and knowledge gained from the discussion
evidence: Summarise the main points made by different speakers in a group discussion
Draw a conclusion that synthesises multiple viewpoints expressed in the discussion
Explain how the discussion changed or confirmed initial understanding of a topic

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Evaluating a Speaker's Argument
topics.description: Summarise the points a speaker makes and explain how each claim is supported by reasons and evidence, evaluating the logic and relevance of the support
evidence: Identify the main claim in a spoken presentation and the evidence used to support it
Evaluate whether a speaker's reasons logically support their main argument
Explain which pieces of evidence most effectively support a speaker's points

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Summarising Spoken and Media Presentations
topics.description: Summarise a written text read aloud or information presented in diverse media and formats including visually, quantitatively, and orally
evidence: Summarise the main points of a video or audio presentation in own words
Identify key information from a graph, chart, or infographic and explain it orally
Listen to a passage read aloud and provide an accurate summary of the content

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Gestures across cultures
topics.description: Understand that the meaning of non-verbal signals — eye contact, personal space, gestures, facial expression and tone of voice — can differ between cultures, communities, families and individuals, so the same signal may be meant and understood differently; avoid reading a signal with one fixed meaning or judging a person or group from it, and use this understanding to check meaning respectfully and adjust their own signals when communicating.
evidence: Explains with general examples (how much eye contact feels polite, how close to stand, whether a gesture seems friendly) that families and communities teach different conventions for the same non-verbal signal, so it can be meant and understood differently, and that people within one community also differ by person and situation
Analyses an invented scenario in which a signal is misread, explains how the misunderstanding came from assuming one fixed meaning, and suggests a respectful way to check
In a role-play or discussion, checks meaning politely or adjusts their own signals instead of assuming rudeness or lack of interest

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Performing Scripts & Poetry
topics.description: Improvise, rehearse, and perform play scripts and poetry — using role, intonation, tone, volume, mood, silence, stillness, and action to generate language, explore meaning, and add impact to performance
evidence: Perform a scene from a play using appropriate intonation, volume, and pauses to convey character and mood
Use improvisation to explore how a character might respond in a new situation
Rehearse and perform a poem aloud, using pace and emphasis to bring out the meaning

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Presentations that build a theme
topics.description: Plan, rehearse and deliver presentations whose information, arguments and details are organised to develop a theme or idea, each section building on the last
evidence: Plan an argument that develops a theme (e.g. 'Small actions can protect our oceans') through three linked points, each supported by details or data
Organise the presentation so each section builds on the last and the conclusion returns to the theme
Rehearse for a peer, then revise the order or links between sections so the theme comes through more clearly

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Speaking Formally and Giving Presentations
topics.description: Use Standard English confidently in formal and informal spoken contexts — give short speeches and presentations expressing own ideas clearly, keeping to the point, and adapting register and vocabulary to the audience
evidence: Deliver a 2-3 minute presentation on a topic with a clear opening, organised points, and a conclusion
Adapt language between formal and informal registers depending on the context and audience
Maintain eye contact, appropriate pace, and clear articulation when speaking to a group

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Formal Debates
topics.description: Participate in formal debates and structured discussions — presenting a position with supporting evidence, responding to others’ points, summarising and building on what has been said, and following rules of discussion
evidence: Present an argument in a debate with a clear claim supported by evidence
Respond to an opposing point by summarising it fairly before offering a counterargument
Build on a previous speaker’s idea by extending, questioning, or challenging it constructively

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Phonics Vocabulary
topics.description: Know and use the vocabulary of phonics and word structure — phoneme, grapheme, GPC (grapheme-phoneme correspondence), blend, segment, digraph, CVC, vowel, consonant, syllable, root word, suffix, prefix, and homophone — and understand that these words describe the building blocks that phonics instruction is built on
evidence: Say the sounds for common graphemes (e.g. 'sh', 'ch', 'th', 'ee', 'igh') and use 'phoneme' and 'grapheme' correctly when explaining
Blend sounds together to read an unfamiliar word and explain what they are doing using the word 'blend'
Segment a word into its individual sounds for spelling and use the term 'segment' to describe the process

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Segmenting words into sounds
topics.description: Segment spoken words into phonemes and spell CVC and simple phonetically regular words by writing a letter or letters for each sound
evidence: Write CVC words from dictation (e.g. 'cat', 'bed', 'hot')
Segment words into individual sounds before choosing letters to write
Spell simple words phonetically drawing on sound-letter knowledge

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Spelling from Dictation
topics.description: Write simple sentences from memory when dictated by the teacher, applying taught GPCs, spelling rules, and common exception words
evidence: Write a dictated sentence using phonically plausible spellings
Include correct spelling of taught exception words in dictation
Apply sentence punctuation in dictated writing

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Spelling Verb Endings
topics.description: Spell words with common suffixes (-s/-es for plurals and third person verbs, -ing, -ed, -er, -est) where no change to the root word is needed
evidence: Add -s or -es correctly to make plurals (e.g. 'cats', 'boxes')
Spell words with -ing and -ed endings (e.g. 'jumping', 'helped')
Add -er and -est to adjectives (e.g. 'quicker', 'quickest')

topics.subject: English
topics.name: The Prefix un-
topics.description: Spell words using the prefix un- to change meaning; understand that un- creates opposites or reverses actions
evidence: Spell words with un- prefix correctly (e.g. 'unhappy', 'unfair', 'undo')
Explain how un- changes the meaning of a word
Create new words by adding un- to known words

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Tricky words
topics.description: Spell common exception words from memory that do not follow regular phonic patterns, including the days of the week
evidence: Correctly spell high-frequency irregular words (e.g. 'said', 'the', 'was')
Write all seven days of the week correctly
Recall and write exception words in dictated sentences

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Alternative Spellings for Sounds
topics.description: Spell words using alternative grapheme choices for known phonemes, learning new spellings for sounds already encountered (e.g., /ɔ:/ as 'a' before ll, /ʌ/ as 'o', words ending -tion), including distinguishing common homophones
evidence: Spell 'ball', 'call', 'fall' using alternative grapheme /ɔ:/ as 'a' before ll
Distinguish homophones in writing: 'there/their/they’re', 'here/hear', 'bare/bear'
Spell words ending in -tion correctly: 'station', 'fiction', 'motion'

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Apostrophes for possession
topics.description: Use the possessive apostrophe with singular nouns to show ownership (e.g., the girl's book, the dog's bone)
evidence: Write 'the cat's tail' to show the tail belongs to the cat
Distinguish plural -s ('the cats ran') from possessive 's ('the cat's bed') in writing
Add a possessive apostrophe to a singular noun in a dictated sentence

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Spelling Contracted Forms
topics.description: Spell contracted forms correctly by placing the apostrophe where letters are omitted (can't, didn't, I'll, it's, etc.)
evidence: Write 'can't' for 'cannot', 'didn't' for 'did not' with apostrophe correctly placed
Distinguish 'it's' (it is) from 'its' (possessive) in a sentence
Expand a contraction back to its full form and explain which letters are missing

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Suffixes
topics.description: Apply suffix spelling rules that require changes to the root word: dropping final -e before vowel suffixes, changing -y to -i, doubling final consonants in short-vowel words; use suffixes -ment, -ness, -ful, -less, -ly
evidence: Spell 'hoping' (drop e), 'cried' (y to i), 'running' (double consonant) applying the correct rule
Add -ful, -less, -ness, -ly correctly: 'careful', 'hopeless', 'sadness', 'slowly'
Identify which suffix rule to apply to a given root word and explain why

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Apostrophes for possession (age 7+)
topics.description: Use the possessive apostrophe accurately with both regular and irregular plural nouns (e.g., the girls' bags, the children's toys), distinguishing singular from plural possession
evidence: Place the apostrophe correctly in plural possessives: 'the dogs' kennel' vs 'the dog's kennel'
Write possessive forms of irregular plurals correctly (e.g. 'children's', 'women's', 'mice's')
Distinguish singular possession (the boy's hat) from plural possession (the boys' hats) in dictated sentences

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Homophones
topics.description: Distinguish and correctly spell common homophones and near-homophones encountered at Y3-4 level (e.g., accept/except, affect/effect, brake/break, grate/great), including using the /eɪ/ sound spelt ei, eigh, or ey
evidence: Spell pairs of homophones correctly in context (e.g., 'there/their/they're', 'brake/break', 'grate/great')
Choose the correct homophone to complete a sentence (e.g., 'The dog wagged its/it's tail')
Spell words with the /eɪ/ sound as ei, eigh, or ey (e.g., vein, eight, they, neighbour)

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Prefixes (age 7+)
topics.description: Spell words with a range of prefixes (dis-, mis-, un-, re-, pre-, anti-, auto-, super-) understanding how each prefix modifies the root word's meaning without changing its spelling
evidence: Spell words with prefixes dis-, mis-, re- correctly without altering the root (e.g., disappoint, misspell, return)
Add prefixes un-, pre-, anti-, auto-, super- to root words and use the new word in a sentence (e.g., unhappy, preview, autograph)
Explain how a prefix changes the meaning of a root word (e.g., 'dis-' means 'not' or 'opposite of')

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Spelling Word Lists (age 7+)
topics.description: Spell words from the statutory word list for Years 3 and 4, including commonly misspelt words that do not follow regular patterns
evidence: Spell at least 20 words from the Y3-4 statutory list correctly (e.g., accident, believe, different, favourite, imagine)
Identify tricky parts of statutory words and use a strategy to remember them (e.g., 'separate' has 'a rat' in the middle)
Use statutory list words accurately in own writing across subjects

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Suffixes (age 7+)
topics.description: Spell words using productive suffixes (-ation, -ly, -ous) and less common sound-spelling correspondences (/ɪ/ as y, /ʌ/ as ou, endings sounding like /ʒə/, /tʃə/, /ʒən/, /ʃən/) introduced in the Year 3-4 programme
evidence: Spell words with suffixes -ation (e.g., information, sensation), -ly (e.g., sadly, gently, happily), and -ous (e.g., famous, enormous, various)
Spell words with less common vowel patterns: /ɪ/ as y (e.g., myth, gym), /ʌ/ as ou (e.g., young, touch, double)
Spell words with endings /ʒə/ as -sure (e.g., measure, treasure), /tʃə/ as -ture (e.g., creature, furniture), /ʒən/ as -sion (e.g., division, television)

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Using a Dictionary to Check Spellings
topics.description: Use the first two or three letters of a word to check its spelling in a dictionary; consult reference materials including beginning dictionaries to verify and correct spellings
evidence: Locate a word in a dictionary using its first two or three letters (e.g., find 'beautiful' by looking up 'be-')
Check and correct a misspelling by comparing with the dictionary entry (e.g., look up 'freind' → 'friend')
Use a glossary or beginning dictionary to confirm spelling of a word used in own writing

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Spellings from Greek, French and Latin
topics.description: Spell words with etymological letter patterns from Greek (ch = /k/), French (ch = /ʃ/, -gue, -que), and Latin (sc = /s/) origins
evidence: Spell words with Greek ch such as 'scheme', 'chorus', 'chemist', 'echo' and explain the /k/ sound pattern
Spell words with French ch such as 'chef', 'chalet', 'machine' and -gue/-que endings like 'league', 'unique'
Spell words with Latin sc such as 'science', 'scene', 'discipline' and identify the silent letter pattern

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Advanced Spelling Conventions
topics.description: Spell words using assorted Y5-6 conventions: doubling after -fer when the stress remains (referring but reference), using hyphens to join prefixes to root words (co-ordinate, re-enter), the /iː/ sound spelt ei after c (receive, ceiling), and the letter string ough representing different sounds (though, through, thought, thorough, plough)
evidence: Apply the -fer doubling rule: double the r when the syllable is stressed (referring, preferred, transferred) but not when stress shifts (reference, preference)
Use hyphens correctly when a prefix ends with the same letter the root begins with (re-enter, co-own) or to avoid ambiguity (re-cover vs recover)
Read and spell words containing ough by recognising its multiple pronunciations: /oʊ/ (though), /uː/ (through), /ɔː/ (thought), /ʌf/ (rough), /aʊ/ (plough)

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Homophones (age 9+)
topics.description: Distinguish and correctly spell homophones and commonly confused words at Y5-6 level (e.g., affect/effect, practice/practise, advice/advise, complement/compliment, aisle/isle, led/lead), including confused words such as to/too/two and there/their/they're
evidence: Select the correct spelling from a pair of homophones by analysing meaning in context, e.g. 'The doctor's advice (noun) was to practise (verb) daily'
Spell commonly confused words accurately by applying word-class clues: advise/advice, practise/practice, licence/license (verb ends in -ise, noun ends in -ice)
Identify and correct homophone errors in extended writing, including to/too/two, there/their/they're, whose/who's, and its/it's

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Silent Letters in Words
topics.description: Spell words containing silent letters that are remnants of earlier pronunciation or etymology, recognising common silent-letter patterns and using word origins to remember them
evidence: Identify and spell words with silent initial consonants: knight, know, write, wrap, gnaw, psalm, applying knowledge that these letters were once pronounced
Spell words with silent internal letters: doubt (b), island (s), muscle (c), solemn (n), using etymological connections to aid memory (e.g. doubt from Latin dubitare)
Use word families and etymology to remember silent letters, e.g. sign is related to signal where the g is pronounced

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Spelling -able & -ible
topics.description: Spell words ending in -able/-ible and the corresponding adverb forms -ably/-ibly, applying patterns to determine which suffix to use based on the root word
evidence: Apply the guideline that -able is typically used with complete root words (enjoyable, comfortable) while -ible is used with incomplete roots (visible, possible), noting key exceptions
Convert -able/-ible adjectives into adverbs by changing the ending to -ably/-ibly, e.g. comfortable → comfortably, possible → possibly, terrible → terribly
Determine whether to drop or retain the final -e of the root when adding -able, e.g. adorable (drop e) vs changeable (keep e before soft g)

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Spelling Word Lists (age 9+)
topics.description: Spell words from the statutory word list for Years 5 and 6, including words with irregular or uncommon spelling patterns that must be learned individually
evidence: Spell high-frequency words from the Y5-6 list accurately in dictated sentences, e.g. accommodate, committee, correspond, exaggerate, immediately, necessary
Use look-cover-write-check and mnemonic strategies to learn words with tricky patterns such as 'separate' (a rat in separate), 'rhythm' (rhythm helps your two hips move)
Identify and self-correct misspellings of statutory list words when proof-reading extended writing

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Suffixes (age 9+)
topics.description: Spell words with Latin and French suffix patterns: endings sounding like /ʃəs/ spelt -cious or -tious (e.g., precious, cautious), /ʃəl/ spelt -cial or -tial (e.g., official, essential), and words ending in -ant/-ance/-ancy vs -ent/-ence/-ency (e.g., observant/observance, confident/confidence)
evidence: Use the root-word clue for endings that sound like /ʃəs/: when the root word ends in -ce, the ending is usually -cious (space → spacious, grace → gracious, vice → vicious, malice → malicious); learn other -cious and -tious words (such as precious, cautious and ambitious) as words to know, noting exceptions such as anxious
Choose between -cial (usually after a vowel: special, official) and -tial (usually after a consonant: essential, partial) when spelling words with the /ʃəl/ ending

Choose -ant/-ance/-ancy or -ent/-ence/-ency using clues: -ent/-ence/-ency after a soft c, soft g or qu sound (innocent/innocence, intelligent, frequent/frequency); -ant/-ance/-ancy when a related word has a clear /æ/ or /eɪ/ sound, often an -ation word (observation → observant/observance, hesitation → hesitant/hesitancy); -ent/-ence when a related word has a clear /ɛ/ sound (confidential → confident/confidence); a hard c or g sound heard just before the ending can be a possible clue for -ant (significant, elegant); and learn the many words where no clue decides

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Applying Spelling Rules to Complex Words
topics.description: Spell correctly and consistently, applying the spelling patterns and rules from KS1-2 to increasingly complex vocabulary encountered in KS3 reading and subject-specific study
evidence: Spell subject-specific vocabulary correctly when encountered in new domains (e.g., 'parliament', 'photosynthesis', 'algorithm')
Apply known spelling rules and etymological patterns to unfamiliar words
Use proofreading strategies to identify and correct spelling errors in own extended writing

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Discussing and Questioning New Words
topics.description: Ask and answer questions about unknown words in texts; discuss word meanings and link new vocabulary to words already known
evidence: Ask 'What does ___ mean?' when meeting unfamiliar words during reading
Use context and pictures to work out what a new word might mean
Explain a new word by connecting it to a known word (e.g. 'enormous means really really big')

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Shades of Meaning
topics.description: Distinguish shades of meaning among verbs describing similar actions and among adjectives differing in intensity; make real-life connections between words and their use
evidence: Compare similar verbs by acting them out (e.g. 'walk', 'march', 'strut', 'prance')
Order adjectives by intensity (e.g. big, huge, gigantic)
Connect vocabulary to personal experiences (e.g. note things at school that are 'colourful')

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Sorting & Categorising Words
topics.description: Sort common objects and words into categories to understand how concepts relate; demonstrate understanding of opposites (antonyms) for common verbs and adjectives
evidence: Group words or objects by category (e.g. animals, foods, colours)
Identify and produce opposite pairs (e.g. 'big/small', 'hot/cold', 'go/stop')
Explain why items belong together in a category

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Using New Vocabulary
topics.description: Use words and phrases acquired through conversations, being read to, and responding to texts in own speech and writing
evidence: Incorporate new vocabulary from read-alouds into conversations
Attempt to use interesting or topic-specific words in own writing
Use newly learned words appropriately in different contexts

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Word Parts as Clues
topics.description: Use knowledge of common inflections and affixes (-ed, -s, un-, -er) as clues to the meaning of unknown words; understand how the prefix un- changes meaning
evidence: Recognise that -ed signals past tense (e.g. 'jumped' = already happened)
Explain how un- makes a word mean the opposite (e.g. 'unhappy' = not happy)
Use word parts to figure out the meaning of an unfamiliar word

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Defining Words
topics.description: Define words by category and by one or more key attributes (e.g., 'a duck is a bird that swims'), making real-life connections between words and their use
evidence: Define 'tiger' as 'a large cat with stripes' — naming category and key attribute
Connect the word 'cozy' to real-life examples: places at home that feel cozy
Sort words into categories and explain why each word belongs

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Root Words & Inflections
topics.description: Identify frequently occurring root words and their inflectional forms (e.g., look/looks/looked/looking), using affixes as clues to word meaning and understanding how suffixes create nouns and adjectives
evidence: Identify 'play' as the root in 'played', 'playing', 'player'
Explain that '-ful' in 'careful' means 'full of care'
Use '-ness' and '-er' to form nouns from root words: 'sad → sadness', 'teach → teacher'

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Formal and Informal English
topics.description: Recognise and compare formal and informal uses of English, understanding that language choices vary based on audience, purpose and context
evidence: Identify whether a spoken or written example uses formal or informal language (e.g., 'Dear Sir' vs 'Hey mate')
Rewrite an informal sentence in a more formal way (e.g., change 'Can I have some?' to 'May I please have some?')
Explain why formal language might be used in one situation and informal in another (e.g., a letter to the headteacher vs a note to a friend, or a report's formal register vs an advert's direct 'you')

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Similes in texts
topics.description: Recognise a simile — a figurative comparison that uses “like” or “as” to show that two unlike things share a quality — in a story, poem or other text that is read aloud or read independently; identify the two things being compared and the quality they share; and explain the picture, feeling or meaning the simile creates in that context. Ordinary uses of “like” or “as” that do not compare unlike things (“I like pizza”, “as soon as”, “she looks like her sister”) are not similes. Interpreting metaphors (implied comparisons with no “like” or “as”) and writing new figurative language are not part of this claim. The examples are illustrations, not a word list, a limit or a level.
evidence: In a story or poem they hear or read, find a simile and name the two unlike things being compared and the quality they share (e.g. in “the puppy’s fur was as soft as a cloud”: the fur and a cloud, both soft)
Explain what picture or feeling a simile creates and how it helps the reader understand the character, setting or event in that text (e.g. “he ran like the wind” shows how fast he was going)
Tell a simile apart from ordinary uses of “like” or “as” that do not compare unlike things (e.g. “I like pizza”, “as soon as I got home”, “she looks like her sister”) and explain the difference

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Word Families and Root Words
topics.description: Explore word families based on common root words, understanding how words are related in form and meaning through shared roots, prefixes and suffixes (e.g., solve → solution, solver, dissolve, insoluble)
evidence: Generate at least 4 words in a word family from a given root (e.g., from 'play': player, playful, replay, playground)
Explain how members of a word family are connected in meaning (e.g., 'solve, solution, dissolve all relate to finding answers or breaking apart')
Use knowledge of a word family to predict the meaning of an unfamiliar member (e.g., knowing 'act' helps understand 'actor', 'action', 'react')

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Domain Vocabulary Across Subject Areas
topics.description: Acquire and use accurately academic and domain-specific vocabulary relevant to grade-level topics, including words that signal precise meaning in informational texts across subject areas
evidence: Identify and define academic vocabulary (e.g., compare, contrast, summarise, evidence, interpret) used across multiple subject areas and use these words accurately in discussion and writing
Determine the meaning of domain-specific words encountered in science, social studies, or maths texts (e.g., ecosystem, democracy, numerator) using context, glossaries, and prior knowledge
Use newly acquired academic and domain-specific vocabulary in sentences that demonstrate understanding of precise meaning and appropriate context

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Literal vs Figurative Language
topics.description: Distinguish literal from nonliteral (figurative) language in context and interpret common idioms and phrases
evidence: Identify whether 'It's raining cats and dogs' is literal or nonliteral and explain what it means
Read a passage and circle three phrases used nonliterally, restating each in literal terms
Explain the difference between 'She was on fire' (figurative — performing well) and 'The log was on fire' (literal)

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Similes & Metaphors
topics.description: Understand and identify similes (comparisons using like or as) and metaphors (direct comparisons stating something is something else) in texts, explaining how each creates imagery and conveys meaning
evidence: Identify similes in a text by locating comparisons using 'like' or 'as' and explain what two things are being compared and what quality is highlighted, e.g. 'The snow was like a white blanket'
Identify metaphors in a text and explain the implied comparison, e.g. in 'Time is a thief', explain that time is compared to a thief because it takes things away
Explain how a simile or metaphor in a poem or story creates a particular image or feeling for the reader that a literal description would not achieve

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Words with several meanings
topics.description: Know that the same word can have different meanings in different contexts and learning areas (e.g. 'table', 'volume', 'power', 'scale') and use context to choose the right meaning
evidence: Explain the meaning of 'table' at dinner and in maths, and 'volume' on a TV and in science
Use context clues to choose the right meaning of 'scale' in a sentence about fish and in one about maps
Explain how 'power' means different things in science, in maths and in everyday talk

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Antonyms & Synonyms
topics.description: Demonstrate understanding of words by relating them to their antonyms (opposites) and synonyms (words with similar meanings), using synonym and antonym relationships to refine vocabulary and improve precision in writing
evidence: Generate synonyms and antonyms for given words and explain subtle differences between synonyms, e.g. happy/joyful/ecstatic differ in intensity
Use a thesaurus to find synonyms and select the most precise word for a given context, e.g. choosing 'sprinted' rather than 'ran' to convey speed
Replace overused words in writing with more precise synonyms and explain how the substitution changes the tone or emphasis

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Greek and Latin Roots for Word Meaning
topics.description: Use knowledge of Greek and Latin affixes (prefixes and suffixes) and roots as clues to determine the meaning of unfamiliar words, building a bank of common roots and their meanings
evidence: Identify common Greek and Latin roots in unfamiliar words and use root meaning to infer word meaning, e.g. 'aqua' (water) in aquarium/aquatic, 'dict' (say) in predict/dictionary
Break a multi-morpheme word into prefix + root + suffix to determine meaning, e.g. un- (not) + believe + -able = not able to be believed
Use knowledge of Greek-origin prefixes (auto-, tele-, micro-) and Latin-origin prefixes (inter-, trans-, sub-) to decode and define unfamiliar vocabulary in context

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Idioms & Proverbs
topics.description: Recognise and interpret common idioms (break the ice, hit the nail on the head), adages (actions speak louder than words), and proverbs (a stitch in time saves nine), understanding their figurative meanings and when to use them
evidence: Explain the figurative meaning of common idioms encountered in texts, e.g. 'let the cat out of the bag' means to reveal a secret, not literally releasing a cat
Interpret the meaning and intended lesson of adages and proverbs, e.g. explain that 'the early bird catches the worm' advises that acting promptly gives an advantage
Use context clues to determine the meaning of an unfamiliar idiom or proverb encountered during reading and verify using a reference source

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Using a Thesaurus to Choose Words
topics.description: Use a thesaurus to find synonyms and extend vocabulary choices, selecting the most appropriate word based on context, connotation, and register
evidence: Use a thesaurus to find three alternatives for overused words in own writing
Select the most appropriate synonym from thesaurus options based on context and tone
Explain why one synonym is more suitable than another for a specific sentence

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Choosing Formal Vocabulary
topics.description: Distinguish between formal and informal vocabulary, selecting words appropriate for formal speech and writing such as 'discover' instead of 'find out' and 'request' instead of 'ask for'
evidence: Replace informal words with formal equivalents in a given text
Identify formal vocabulary choices in official letters and reports
Write the same message twice using formal vocabulary for a letter and informal vocabulary for a text message

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Dialects & Registers
topics.description: Compare and contrast the varieties of English used in stories, dramas, or poems, including dialects and registers, understanding how language varies by region, context, and purpose
evidence: Identify dialect features in character dialogue and explain their effect
Compare formal and informal registers in different types of texts
Explain how an author uses language variety to develop character or setting

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Academic Vocabulary
topics.description: Acquire and use accurately a broad range of general academic vocabulary and domain-specific words — drawing new vocabulary from reading and listening and deploying it consciously in writing and speech to achieve particular effects
evidence: Use academic vocabulary (e.g., analyse, evaluate, justify, convey, imply) accurately and appropriately in essay writing
Incorporate domain-specific terms from a subject studied (e.g., 'photosynthesis', 'legislature') into explanatory writing
Draw a new word or phrase from a text read and use it consciously in own writing or speech

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Advanced Figurative Language
topics.description: Understand and interpret figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meaning — including allusion, irony, pun, oxymoron, and extended metaphor — and distinguish between connotation and denotation when analysing or choosing words
evidence: Explain the connotative difference between words with similar denotations (e.g., thrifty vs. stingy vs. economical)
Identify irony or an allusion in a text and explain what it adds to the meaning
Analyse an extended metaphor across a paragraph or poem and explain how it develops an idea

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Vocabulary Strategies
topics.description: Determine the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases using a flexible range of strategies — including context clues, Greek and Latin affixes and roots, reference materials, and verification of inferred meaning
evidence: Use context clues (the overall meaning of a sentence, a word’s position or function) to infer the meaning of an unfamiliar word
Break down a word using known Greek or Latin roots and affixes to deduce its meaning (e.g., 'malevolent' = mal- (bad) + volent (wishing))
Look up a word in a dictionary to verify or refine an inferred meaning

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Changing a familiar story
topics.description: Retell and adapt a familiar story by changing a character, the setting or the ending through play, performance, drawing or simple writing
evidence: Act out 'The Three Little Pigs' with puppets but change the wolf into a different animal
Draw a new ending for a familiar story and tell it to a partner
Dictate or write a sentence that moves a familiar story to a new setting (e.g. 'The Gingerbread Man ran to the beach')

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Responding to Writing Feedback
topics.description: With teacher guidance, re-read own writing aloud to check it sounds right; listen and respond to questions and suggestions from teacher or peers to add detail, clarify meaning, and strengthen writing — this is the scaffolded beginning of writing self-evaluation, not an independent skill
evidence: Reread own writing and spot a missing word or unclear sentence
Add a detail in response to a question (e.g. 'Can you tell me more about...?')
Make at least one improvement to a piece based on feedback

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Saying Sentences Before Writing Them
topics.description: Say out loud what is going to be written; compose sentences orally before writing them down as preparation for independent writing
evidence: Say a complete sentence aloud before attempting to write it
Rehearse a sentence orally more than once to hold it in memory
Practise sentences with a partner before writing independently

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Shared Research Projects
topics.description: Participate in shared research and writing projects; recall information from experiences or gather information from sources to answer a question
evidence: Contribute ideas and information to a class writing project
Draw or write facts learned from personal experience about a topic
Help gather information from books or adults for a group research task

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Sharing and Publishing Your Writing
topics.description: Read own writing aloud clearly enough to be heard by peers and the teacher; use digital tools to produce and publish writing
evidence: Read own sentences aloud with clear voice and appropriate expression
Share a piece of writing by reading it to the class
Type simple words or sentences using a computer or tablet

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Simple Stories with Beginning and Ending
topics.description: Write simple narratives by sequencing sentences to describe events in order; narrate a single event or linked events with a beginning, middle, and ending or reaction
evidence: Write a short story with at least three sequenced sentences
Use time words like 'first', 'then', 'next' to order events
Include a reaction or ending to a narrative (e.g. 'I felt happy')

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Writing opinions
topics.description: Compose opinion pieces using drawing, dictating, or writing that name a topic or book and state a preference or opinion about it
evidence: State an opinion clearly (e.g. 'My favourite animal is a dog because...')
Give at least one reason for an opinion
Draw, dictate, or write to express a preference about a book or topic

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Writing Process Vocabulary
topics.description: Know and use the vocabulary of the writing process — compose, plan, draft, revise, edit, proofread, genre, audience, purpose, narrative, recount, instruction, paragraph, sequence, and detail — and understand that these words describe distinct steps and decisions that all writers make, not just tasks to tick off
evidence: Use 'compose', 'revise', and 'edit' correctly when describing the stages of writing
Explain who the 'audience' is for a piece of writing and how that changes what they write
Describe the purpose of a piece of writing (to persuade, inform, entertain, or instruct) and match their language to it

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Writing to inform
topics.description: Compose informative or explanatory texts using drawing, dictating, or writing that name a topic and supply some information about it
evidence: Write or dictate two or three facts about a familiar topic
Label diagrams or drawings with informative details
Name a topic and provide relevant details about it

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Basic Informational Writing
topics.description: Compose informative or explanatory texts that introduce a topic, use facts and definitions to develop points, and provide a concluding statement or section
evidence: Write an informative text that introduces a topic clearly and groups related information together
Use facts, definitions, and concrete details to develop and explain points about the topic
Provide a concluding statement or section that wraps up the information presented

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Building Writing Stamina
topics.description: Write about real events and for different purposes, developing stamina for sustained writing across genres beyond narrative (e.g., recounts, letters, instructions)
evidence: Write a recount of a school trip using temporal connectives (first, then, after that)
Write a simple set of instructions with numbered steps
Sustain writing for an extended period across a full page without stopping

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Planning Ideas Before Writing
topics.description: Plan before writing by saying aloud or noting down what will be written, writing down ideas and key words, and encapsulating ideas sentence by sentence before composing
evidence: Verbally rehearse sentences before writing them down
Jot key words or ideas in a planning format (e.g., story map) before drafting
Write a simple plan with beginning, middle, and end for a story

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Revising and editing
topics.description: Proof-read own writing to check for errors in spelling, grammar, and punctuation; evaluate and revise writing with teacher/peer support, re-reading to ensure meaning is clear and tense is consistent
evidence: Re-read own writing and spot a missing full stop or capital letter
Identify and correct a tense inconsistency in a piece of writing
Discuss improvements with a partner and make at least one revision to strengthen the writing

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Structured Opinion Writing
topics.description: Compose opinion pieces that introduce a topic, state a clear point of view, provide organised reasons linked with connecting words, and include a concluding statement or section
evidence: Write an opinion piece that introduces the topic, states a clear opinion, and provides at least two reasons
Use linking words (because, and, also, for example) to connect the opinion to supporting reasons
End an opinion piece with a concluding statement that restates or reinforces the opinion

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Writing Poetry
topics.description: Write poetry, exploring patterns of language, rhyme and rhythm, and learning poems by heart for recitation with appropriate intonation
evidence: Write a simple poem or new verse using rhyming couplets, a repeated pattern or alliteration (e.g. 'Wiggly worms wriggle')
Recite a poem from memory with expression and appropriate intonation
Identify rhyme and rhythm patterns in poems read aloud

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Borrowing from books you've read
topics.description: Create and edit imaginative texts by deliberately using or adapting language features, characters, settings, plot structures and ideas encountered in literary texts read
evidence: Write a new version of a familiar story that follows its plot or repeated pattern (e.g. a problem–attempts–resolution plot, or the repeated lines of 'Brown Bear, Brown Bear') but with new characters
Borrow a language feature from a mentor text (e.g. a repeated line or a strong opening sentence) and use it in their own story
Annotate their draft to show which character, setting or idea was adapted from which book, then edit to improve it

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Narrative Writing
topics.description: Write narratives with developed settings, characters and plot, using dialogue and description to develop experiences and show character responses to situations
evidence: Write a narrative that includes a described setting, at least one developed character, and a clear plot with a problem and resolution
Use dialogue to show what characters say and reveal their personality or feelings
Use descriptive details and temporal words to organise events into a clear sequence with a satisfying ending

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Organising Writing into Paragraphs
topics.description: Organise writing into paragraphs, grouping related material around a theme, and use simple organisational devices such as headings and sub-headings in non-narrative writing
evidence: Divide a piece of writing into paragraphs, each focused on one main idea or aspect of the topic
Use headings and sub-headings to organise a non-fiction text (e.g., a report about animals with sections 'Habitat', 'Diet', 'Appearance')
Identify where a new paragraph should begin in a given text and explain why (e.g., 'A new paragraph starts here because the topic changes from appearance to diet')

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Rehearsing and Varying Sentences
topics.description: Compose and rehearse sentences orally before writing, progressively building varied and rich vocabulary and an increasing range of sentence structures including dialogue
evidence: Rehearse a sentence containing dialogue aloud before writing it (e.g. 'Let's go!' shouted Tom)
Orally compose sentences with varied openers (e.g. time adverbials, subordinate clauses) before writing
Try out two or three different ways to express the same idea orally and choose the most effective version to write

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Revising and editing (age 7+)
topics.description: Evaluate and edit writing by assessing effectiveness, proposing changes to grammar and vocabulary for consistency, and proof-reading for spelling, grammar and punctuation errors at Y3-4 level
evidence: Read own or a peer's writing aloud and suggest specific improvements to vocabulary or sentence structure
Propose changes to grammar and word choice to improve clarity and consistency across a piece of writing
Proof-read writing at Y3-4 level for spelling, punctuation, and grammatical errors and correct them independently

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Choosing Form and Tone for Your Audience
topics.description: Identify the audience for and purpose of writing before beginning, selecting the appropriate form, tone, and register to match the intended reader and communicative goal
evidence: Determine the audience (e.g., peers, teacher, younger children, a public audience) and purpose (to persuade, inform, entertain, or explain) before drafting and explain how these choices affect language and structure
Select an appropriate form for the writing task (letter, report, story, instructions, review) based on audience and purpose
Adjust vocabulary, sentence length, and level of formality to suit the identified audience, e.g. using simpler language for younger readers and more formal language for an official letter

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Making multimodal texts
topics.description: Plan, create, edit and publish multimodal texts that combine writing with visual features — images, labelled diagrams, captions, headings and layout — using digital or print tools, choosing visual features to suit the purpose and audience
evidence: Create a digital slide, poster or e-book page that combines a short informative paragraph with a labelled diagram and a caption
Choose images, font sizes and layout in a digital tool to suit a persuasive purpose (e.g. a poster for the school fete) and explain the choices
Publish a picture-book page where the illustration adds meaning not stated in the text, then edit both text and image after feedback

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Revising and editing (age 8+)
topics.description: Read back your own writing critically and independently — notice where meaning is unclear, where a word could be stronger, or where the reader might be confused; make revisions without needing teacher prompts, using your own judgment about what is and isn't working
evidence: Reread a paragraph silently and independently identify at least one place where meaning could be clearer or a word choice improved
Make a revision that goes beyond spelling/punctuation — changing a sentence for clarity or effect
Explain in their own words why they changed something ('I thought the reader wouldn't understand what I meant')

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Short Research Projects
topics.description: Conduct short research projects that build knowledge about a topic, gather information from print and digital sources, and take brief organised notes
evidence: Generate three research questions about an assigned topic and identify two sources for each
Take brief notes from a print source, sorting key facts into provided categories
Write a short summary paragraph synthesising information gathered from two different sources

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Vivid Word Choices
topics.description: Choose precise and vivid words and phrases to create specific effects in writing
evidence: Replace vague words in 'The nice man went to the big house' with more precise alternatives and explain the effect
Write two versions of the same scene — one with plain language and one with carefully chosen words for suspense or humour
Select from a word bank the most effective verb and adjective for a given sentence, justifying each choice

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Writing Craft Vocabulary
topics.description: Know and use the vocabulary of writing craft and effect — form, structure, register, tone, voice, coherence, cohesion, argument, evidence, perspective, rhetoric, technique, formal, informal, and style — and understand that these words describe choices writers make intentionally to achieve a particular effect on the reader
evidence: Explain the difference between 'formal register' and 'informal register' and give an example of when each is appropriate
Use terms like 'coherence', 'cohesion', and 'paragraph structure' accurately when discussing or improving their own writing
Identify the 'purpose', 'audience', and 'form' of a piece of writing and explain how these shape the language choices

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Writing for an audience
topics.description: Produce clear and coherent writing in which the development and organisation are appropriate to the task, purpose, and audience, maintaining a consistent style and structure throughout
evidence: Identify the task, purpose, and audience before writing and make deliberate choices about structure, tone, and vocabulary to suit them
Organise ideas logically so that the writing flows from introduction through development to conclusion, with each section serving a clear purpose
Review a draft to check that the organisation, style, and level of formality are consistent and appropriate for the intended reader

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Evidence-Based Writing
topics.description: Draw evidence from informational texts to support analysis, reflection, and research in writing, applying grade-level reading standards to non-fiction
evidence: Write a research-based paragraph or short report that cites specific facts, details, and evidence from informational texts to support key points
Synthesise information from two informational sources into a written summary that accurately represents both, noting areas of agreement and difference
Paraphrase information from informational texts accurately and cite sources appropriately, avoiding plagiarism

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Literary Evidence in Writing
topics.description: Draw evidence from literary texts to support analysis, reflection, and research in writing, applying grade-level reading standards to literature
evidence: Write a response to a literary text that includes direct quotations and specific details from the text as evidence to support a claim or observation
Explain how a character's actions or dialogue reveal their traits or motivations, citing specific passages from the story as evidence
Compare how two literary texts treat a similar theme, using textual evidence from both to support the comparison

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Research & Note-Taking
topics.description: Gather relevant information from print and digital sources, summarise or paraphrase information in notes and finished work, and provide a basic bibliography or list of sources
evidence: Take organised notes from multiple sources using own words rather than copying
Create a bibliography listing sources used in a research project
Paraphrase key information from a source without changing the meaning

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Layout and Formatting in Informational Writing
topics.description: Use layout devices including headings, sub-headings, columns, bullets, and tables to structure text and guide the reader through informational and explanatory writing
evidence: Organise an informational text using headings and sub-headings to separate sections
Present comparative information using a table with clear row and column headers
Use columns and bullet points to display information in a scannable format

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Planning Narratives
topics.description: Plan narrative writing by considering how authors have developed characters and settings, drawing on techniques observed in texts read, heard, or performed
evidence: Identify specific authorial techniques for character development from a mentor text
Plan a character using techniques such as showing through action borrowed from a studied author
Analyse how an author builds setting and apply similar techniques in planning own narrative

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Trying figurative language in writing
topics.description: Create and edit literary texts, experimenting with figurative language (simile, metaphor, personification) and choosing the most effective figurative wording
evidence: Write a setting description that uses at least one simile, one metaphor and one personification (e.g. 'The old house groaned in the wind')
Rewrite a plain sentence from their draft in two figurative ways and choose the more effective one, explaining why
Edit a draft to replace a tired comparison (e.g. 'as cold as ice') with a fresh simile or metaphor and explain its effect

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Writing a Précis
topics.description: Precis longer passages by summarising the main ideas and key information concisely while maintaining the essential meaning and removing non-essential detail
evidence: Reduce a three-paragraph text to a single paragraph capturing all main points
Identify and remove redundant information while preserving essential meaning
Write a precis that is no more than one-third the length of the original text

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Cohesion and Transitions Across Writing
topics.description: Use varied transitions, cohesive devices, and paragraph-linking strategies to create coherence across a whole piece of writing — including temporal transitions, causal connectives, and techniques for signalling shifts in argument, time, or setting
evidence: Use a range of causal and logical connectives (consequently, nevertheless, as a result) appropriately across a discursive essay
Signal a shift in time or setting within a narrative using a transitional phrase or paragraph break
Link paragraphs using a cohesive device such as a topic sentence that refers back to the previous paragraph

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Developed Informational and Explanatory Writing
topics.description: Write informative and explanatory texts that examine a topic and convey ideas clearly — organising information logically with headings and formatting, developing the topic with relevant facts, definitions, details, and quotations, and using precise vocabulary
evidence: Organise an explanatory essay with a clear introduction, logical body paragraphs, and a conclusion
Develop a topic using well-chosen facts, definitions, concrete details, and quotations from sources
Use domain-specific vocabulary and formatting (headings, graphics) to aid the reader's comprehension

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Flashback, foreshadowing and more
topics.description: Create and edit literary texts that use narrative devices such as flashback, foreshadowing and symbolism to shape the reader's understanding and build suspense
evidence: Write a narrative that includes a flashback that reveals a character's past
Add foreshadowing to a draft (e.g. an early hint about a coming storm) and explain how it builds suspense
Edit a draft to strengthen one narrative device and annotate the change and its intended effect on the reader

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Persuasive Writing
topics.description: Write arguments to support claims with clear reasons and relevant evidence — including introducing claims, acknowledging counterclaims, organising reasons logically, maintaining a formal style, and providing a concluding statement
evidence: Write an argument essay with a clear claim supported by at least three pieces of evidence
Acknowledge and respond to a counterclaim rather than ignoring opposing views
Use linking words and phrases (however, furthermore, consequently) to connect claims, reasons, and evidence

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Planning, Revising and Editing Writing
topics.description: Plan, revise, and edit writing to improve coherence and effectiveness — considering how the writing reflects its intended audience and purpose, amending vocabulary, grammar, and structure, and proofreading for accurate spelling, punctuation, and grammar
evidence: Revise a draft to improve paragraph structure, adding or removing material for coherence
Edit sentence-level issues including word choice, grammar, and punctuation before finalising
Reflect on whether the writing achieves its intended effect on the target audience and adjust accordingly

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Research & Source Evaluation
topics.description: Summarise and organise material from reading and research — gathering relevant information from multiple sources, assessing credibility, integrating evidence without plagiarising, and supporting ideas with factual detail
evidence: Take notes from multiple sources on a topic and organise them under logical headings
Paraphrase information from a source accurately without copying word-for-word
Assess whether a source is credible and relevant before including it in research writing

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Writing Across Genres
topics.description: Write for a range of purposes and audiences beyond narrative — including scripts, poetry, personal and formal letters, notes for talks, and other forms — selecting the appropriate form, register, and conventions for each
evidence: Write a formal letter using appropriate layout, salutation, register, and sign-off conventions
Compose a script with stage directions, character names, and realistic dialogue
Adapt writing style (vocabulary, sentence structure, tone) to suit different audiences and purposes

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Writing Character & Dialogue
topics.description: Write narratives that develop real or imagined experiences using effective technique — including establishing context and point of view, developing characters through dialogue, pacing, and description, using varied transitions, and providing a reflective conclusion
evidence: Open a narrative by establishing setting, point of view, and a hook that engages the reader
Use dialogue, pacing, and descriptive detail to develop characters and advance the plot
Craft a conclusion that reflects on the narrated events rather than simply ending the action

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Writing Techniques for Effect
topics.description: Apply growing knowledge of vocabulary, grammar, and text structure to writing — drawing on literary and rhetorical devices from reading (e.g., rhetorical questions, tricolon, anaphora, contrast) to enhance impact
evidence: Use a rhetorical question or tricolon deliberately in a persuasive piece and explain the intended effect
Employ varied sentence openings and structures to maintain reader interest across a whole piece
Draw on a literary device encountered in reading and apply it consciously in own writing

topics.subject: Geography
topics.name: Finding places on a plan
topics.description: Locate positions on a two-dimensional representation (simple map or plan) of a familiar space such as the classroom or playground, and move positions by following directions and pathways
evidence: Point to or place picture markers for the teacher's desk and the door on a pictorial map, plan or block model of the classroom
Follow 'forward 3 squares, turn left, forward 2 squares' on a playground plan and say where you end up
Draw a path on a school plan from the library to the canteen and describe it using left and right

topics.subject: Geography
topics.name: Local, regional and state scales
topics.description: Represent places at different geographical scales (local, regional and state, territory or national) on maps, and describe how people and places are interconnected across those scales (e.g. through food, jobs, services and transport)
evidence: Locate their suburb or town, its region and their state or territory on a set of maps at different scales
Label the state or territory capital and one regional centre on a map of their state or territory
Trace an interconnection across scales (e.g. milk from a regional dairy farm to a local shop, or travelling to a city hospital) and draw it as a flow map

topics.subject: Geography
topics.name: Reading and drawing maps
topics.description: Interpret and create two-dimensional representations (maps and plans) of familiar environments with a key and labels, locating key landmarks and objects relative to each other
evidence: Draw a labelled map of the classroom from above with a key for desks, door and windows
Use a school map to describe where the library is relative to the hall and the oval
Mark and label three landmarks on a local park map and describe a route between them

topics.subject: Geography
topics.name: Locating neighbouring countries
topics.description: Locate the countries and regions neighbouring their own country on maps and globes and describe their direction and relative distance (e.g. Australia's neighbours New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, Indonesia, Timor-Leste and the Pacific Islands)
evidence: Locate their own country's neighbouring countries and regions on a world map or globe (e.g. for Australia: New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, Indonesia, Timor-Leste and the Pacific Islands)
Describe the direction of each neighbour from their own country using compass points (e.g. 'Papua New Guinea is north of Australia')
Use a map scale or distance tool to compare which neighbouring country is closest

topics.subject: Geography
topics.name: Grid references and directions
topics.description: Create and interpret grid reference systems that name cells or regions (e.g. B3), using grid references and directions (left/right, north/south/east/west) to locate and describe positions and pathways
evidence: Name the grid square that contains the playground on a map as C4
Describe a path from A1 to D3 using grid references and compass directions
Draw a 5 x 5 grid over a park plan, label rows and columns, and list the grid references of three features

topics.subject: Geography
topics.name: Our school's Country
topics.description: Recognise that the school is on the Country/Place of a particular First Nations Australian people, name that people using information the school has confirmed, and explain in simple terms why Country/Place is important to First Nations Australians
evidence: Name the First Nations Australian people on whose Country/Place the school stands, using information the school has confirmed (e.g. from its Acknowledgement of Country)
Join in an Acknowledgement of Country and explain that it shows respect for the Traditional Owners and Custodians
Explain that Country/Place is important to First Nations Australians because it is connected to their family, culture and identity, and that people care for it

topics.subject: Geography
topics.name: Special places I belong to
topics.description: Describe the features of familiar places they belong to (home, school, park, place of worship), explain why some places are special to them and others, and suggest how places can be looked after
evidence: Draw a familiar place they belong to and label two features (e.g. the swings, the big tree, the front door)
Explain why a place is special to them or their family (e.g. 'Grandpa's garden is where we have picnics')
Suggest one way to look after a special place (e.g. putting rubbish in the bin at the park)

topics.subject: Geography
topics.name: Changing and caring for places
topics.description: Describe how places change (seasons, growth, new buildings, events) and how they can be cared for by different groups, including First Nations Australians caring for Country/Place, council workers, volunteers and students
evidence: Compare an old and a recent photo of a local place and describe two changes
Describe how different groups care for places (e.g. council workers, Landcare volunteers, First Nations rangers caring for Country, students in a school garden)
Explain that First Nations Australians have cared for Country/Place for many thousands of years, using a story, picture book or local resource shared in class

topics.subject: Geography
topics.name: Natural, managed and built features
topics.description: Identify the natural, managed and constructed features of local places and describe their location
evidence: Sort photos of local features into natural (creek, hill), managed (park, farm, garden) and constructed (road, school, shops)
Locate local places on a simple map of the neighbourhood and describe where they are with position words (e.g. 'the park is next to the library')
Explain why a park is a managed feature (people plant and look after it) even though it contains natural plants

topics.subject: Geography
topics.name: Raising farm animals
topics.description: Explore how farm animals are raised for food, clothing and other products — how farmers feed, house and care for them — and what comes from them (milk, eggs, meat, wool, leather)
evidence: Describe how a farmer looks after an animal such as a chicken, cow or sheep (food, water, shelter, health checks)
Match animals to the products they provide (e.g. sheep → wool → jumper; cow → milk → cheese)
Order pictures of how wool gets from a sheep to a jumper (shearing, washing, spinning, knitting)

topics.subject: Geography
topics.name: First Nations and local Country
topics.description: Describe the interconnections of First Nations Australians with Country/Place — the local Country and Countries in other environments (e.g. desert, rainforest, saltwater and island peoples) — through culture, language, seasonal knowledge, stories and caring for Country, using local or approved First Nations sources
evidence: Name the First Nations people of the local area and, where the school has confirmed it, a local-language name for a place, river or animal
Describe from a local First Nations source or a regional First Nations seasonal calendar how Country provides food, water and materials and how seasons, plants and animals are linked

Compare how the local First Nations people and a group from a different environment (e.g. Torres Strait saltwater peoples) are connected with Country/Place, explaining that these connections are spiritual and cultural as well as practical and continue today

topics.subject: Geography
topics.name: Food and fibre production
topics.description: Describe the main ways of producing food and fibre — cropping, livestock grazing, horticulture (fruit and vegetables), aquaculture, forestry, and wool and cotton production — including First Nations peoples' food production and land and sea management
evidence: Match plants and animals to the products they give and the production system they come from (e.g. wheat → bread → cropping, cotton → T-shirt, pine trees → timber, wool → livestock, farmed salmon → aquaculture)

Describe the main steps in producing one food or fibre and who does each step (e.g. bread: the farmer grows wheat, the miller makes flour, the baker bakes; cotton: planting, irrigating, picking, ginning, spinning)
Describe one First Nations food production practice (e.g. stone fish traps or managing plants with fire) using a school-approved source

topics.subject: Geography
topics.name: Australia's states and territories
topics.description: Identify how contemporary Australia is represented as six states and two self-governing territories (the Australian Capital Territory and the Northern Territory), locating each and its capital city, and recognise that Australia also has other territories
evidence: Label Australia's six states and its two self-governing territories, the Australian Capital Territory and the Northern Territory, with their capital cities on a map
Identify their own state or territory, name the states or territories that border it, and describe where one is using compass directions (e.g. 'Queensland is north of New South Wales')

Recognise that Australia also has other territories besides the ACT and the Northern Territory, such as Jervis Bay Territory and external territories like Norfolk Island and the Australian Antarctic Territory

topics.subject: Geography
topics.name: Comparing places in different countries
topics.description: Compare the natural, managed and constructed features of places in their own country and in neighbouring or other countries (e.g. Australia and its neighbours)
evidence: Compare photos of an Australian place and a place in a neighbouring country (e.g. a Queensland coastal town and a village in Papua New Guinea) and list the natural, managed and constructed features of each
Record similarities and differences in a table or Venn diagram
Explain one reason for a difference (e.g. climate, landforms or how people use the land)

topics.subject: Geography
topics.name: First Nations Countries of Australia
topics.description: Use an indicative map to recognise that Australia is made up of the many Countries/Places of First Nations Australians, which existed before colonisation and continue today, each with its own people and languages
evidence: Use an indicative map of First Nations Australia (e.g. the AIATSIS Map of Indigenous Australia) to explain that there were hundreds of First Nations Countries/Places before colonisation, that they and people's connections to them continue today, and that the map shows general areas rather than exact, fixed boundaries
Find the general area of the Country/Place the school is on and name its people, using information the school has confirmed
Compare the indicative map with a map of states and territories and explain that they represent Australia in different ways, with boundaries that do not match

topics.subject: Geography
topics.name: Caring for Country
topics.description: Describe the custodial responsibility First Nations Australians have for Country/Place and how it supports the sustainable use of resources (e.g. cultural burning, sustainable harvesting, seasonal knowledge and Indigenous ranger programs)
evidence: Explain what custodial responsibility for Country/Place means and give an example of how First Nations Australians practise it (e.g. cultural burning or harvesting only what is needed)
Describe the work of an Indigenous ranger group caring for land or sea Country, using a source
Explain how seasonal knowledge guides when and what is harvested so that plants and animals are not used up

topics.subject: Geography
topics.name: Why environments matter
topics.description: Explain the importance of environments, including natural vegetation and water sources, to people and animals, comparing an environment in their own country (e.g. Australia) with one on another continent
evidence: Explain how a native vegetation type (e.g. eucalypt forest, mangroves or grasslands) provides food, shelter and other needs for animals and people
Describe the importance of an Australian water source (e.g. the Murray–Darling Basin, a billabong or the Great Artesian Basin) to farming, towns and wildlife
Compare the importance of an Australian environment with one on another continent (e.g. the Amazon rainforest) for people and animals

topics.subject: Geography
topics.name: Managed environments for food
topics.description: Explain how and why food and fibre are produced in managed environments — greenhouses, irrigated fields, orchards, feedlots, aquaculture ponds and plantations — to control conditions, increase yield, protect crops and animals, and manage sustainability
