evidence: Describe how a managed environment controls conditions (e.g. a greenhouse controls temperature and water; irrigation supplies water in dry areas)
Explain why producers manage environments (e.g. year-round supply, protection from pests and weather, higher yield)
Evaluate one sustainability impact of a managed environment (e.g. water use from irrigation, waste from aquaculture) and a way producers reduce it

topics.subject: Geography
topics.name: Managing natural hazards
topics.description: Describe how environments and communities are managed to reduce the impacts of natural hazards and severe weather events such as bushfires, floods, droughts and cyclones, and the consequences of these events (e.g. in Australia)
evidence: Explain how bushfire risk is managed (e.g. hazard reduction burns, cultural burning, fire danger ratings and bushfire plans) and the consequences of a major bushfire
Describe how a community manages flood or cyclone risk (e.g. levees, flood maps, cyclone-rated buildings after Cyclone Tracy in 1974)
Explain how farmers and communities manage drought (e.g. water storage and restrictions) and its consequences

topics.subject: Geography
topics.name: People shaping places
topics.description: Describe the influence of people, including First Nations Australians and people in other countries, on the characteristics of a place
evidence: Explain how First Nations Australians shaped places through practices such as cultural burning and building fish or eel traps (e.g. Budj Bim in Victoria or the Brewarrina fish traps in New South Wales)
Describe how people in another country influence an Australian place (e.g. overseas demand for minerals creating mining towns, or migrant communities shaping a suburb's shops and food)
Compare how a place's characteristics changed through human influence, using two maps or photos

topics.subject: Geography
topics.name: How countries are interconnected
topics.description: Describe a country's interconnections with other countries through migration, aid, tourism and culture (e.g. Australia's), and how these interconnections change people and places
evidence: Describe a migration interconnection (e.g. families moving from another country to Australia) and one effect on the places involved
Describe an interconnection through aid, tourism or culture (e.g. Australian aid to Pacific neighbours, international students or sport)
Explain how one interconnection changes a place or people's lives in Australia or another country

topics.subject: Geography
topics.name: Places in the Asia region
topics.description: Describe the geographical diversity and location of places in the Asia region and its location in relation to their own country (e.g. Australia)
evidence: Locate countries of the Asia region (e.g. China, India, Japan, Indonesia and Vietnam) on a map and describe their direction and distance from Australia
Describe the diversity of environments in the Asia region (e.g. the Himalayas, monsoon rainforests, deserts, islands and megacities)
Compare a place in Asia with a place in Australia using climate data or photos

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Discovering Tutankhamun's Tomb
topics.description: Understand that we know about ancient Egypt because archaeologists have dug up and studied objects buried in the sand for thousands of years — and that one of the most exciting discoveries ever was when Howard Carter found the hidden tomb of Tutankhamun in 1922, filled with golden treasures
evidence: Explain that archaeologists find and study old objects to learn about people who lived long ago
Retell the story of Howard Carter discovering Tutankhamun's tomb
Understand that discoveries like this help us learn about how ancient Egyptians lived and what they believed

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Egyptian Gods and the Afterlife
topics.description: Understand that the ancient Egyptians believed in many gods and goddesses and believed that life continued after death in a wonderful afterlife — which is why they took great care to prepare bodies and fill tombs with food, jewellery, and precious objects for the dead person to use
evidence: Explain that ancient Egyptians worshipped many different gods and goddesses
Describe the basic belief that Egyptians thought life continued after death
Give a reason why tombs were filled with treasures and everyday objects

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Egypt, the Nile, and the Desert
topics.description: Locate Egypt on a map of Africa and understand that it is a country in a very hot, dry desert, but the River Nile — the longest river in the world — flows through it, bringing water and rich soil that allowed people to grow food and build one of the earliest great civilisations
evidence: Point to Egypt on a map and identify the River Nile running through it
Explain why the Nile was so important to the ancient Egyptians (water, food, transport)
Describe how the desert and the river created two very different environments side by side

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Everyday Life in Ancient Egypt
topics.description: Describe what everyday life was like for ordinary people in ancient Egypt: farmers grew wheat and barley near the Nile, families lived in mud-brick houses, children played games and had pets, and people ate bread, fish, fruit, and vegetables
evidence: Describe at least two things ordinary Egyptian families did in their daily lives
Name foods that ancient Egyptians ate or crops they grew
Identify at least one similarity and one difference between life in ancient Egypt and life today

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Hieroglyphs and Papyrus
topics.description: Know that the ancient Egyptians used a special writing system called hieroglyphs — pictures and symbols that stood for sounds and words — and that they wrote on a paper-like material called papyrus, which was made from a plant that grew along the Nile
evidence: Describe hieroglyphs as a writing system that uses pictures and symbols
Explain that papyrus was a material like paper made from a river plant
Understand that only specially trained people called scribes could read and write hieroglyphs

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Pharaohs and Tutankhamun
topics.description: Know that ancient Egypt was ruled by powerful kings and queens called pharaohs, who lived in grand palaces and made the laws — and that one of the most famous pharaohs is Tutankhamun, a boy who became pharaoh as a child and whose golden tomb was discovered thousands of years later
evidence: Explain that a pharaoh was the ruler of ancient Egypt, like a king or queen
Name Tutankhamun as a famous pharaoh and describe at least one fact about him
Understand that pharaohs were very powerful and made important decisions for everyone in Egypt

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Pyramids and the Great Sphinx
topics.description: Know that the ancient Egyptians built enormous stone pyramids as tombs for the pharaohs, that the Great Pyramid at Giza was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World and is still standing today, and that the Great Sphinx — a statue with a lion's body and a human head — guards the pyramids
evidence: Explain that pyramids were built as tombs to protect the pharaoh's body for the afterlife
Describe the Great Pyramid as very large, very old, and still standing at Giza
Describe the Sphinx as a stone statue with a lion's body and a human head

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Vocabulary: ancient egypt
topics.description: Know and use the key vocabulary of ancient Egypt — pharaoh, pyramid, tomb, mummy/mummification, hieroglyphs, papyrus, sarcophagus, canopic jar, natron, archaeologist, artefact, Nile, delta, irrigation, shaduf, scribe, vizier, obelisk, sphinx, cartouche — and apply these terms accurately when describing Egyptian society, religion, and material culture
evidence: Use 'pharaoh', 'pyramid', and 'hieroglyphs' correctly and naturally in a spoken or written account of ancient Egypt
Explain what mummification is and why the Egyptians did it, using 'sarcophagus', 'canopic jar', and 'natron'
Use 'archaeologist' and 'artefact' correctly when discussing how we know about ancient Egypt

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Ancient Egypt on the Timeline
topics.description: Place ancient Egypt on a timeline spanning over 3,000 years — from around 3100 BCE (unification under the first pharaoh) to 30 BCE (Roman conquest) — understanding that this civilisation lasted longer than the time between the Romans and today, and was divided into major periods: the Old Kingdom (pyramid age), Middle Kingdom, and New Kingdom (empire age)
evidence: Place ancient Egypt on a timeline showing it lasted over 3,000 years
Name the three main periods (Old, Middle, New Kingdom) and associate one fact with each
Compare the length of ancient Egyptian civilisation with another time period the child knows

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Building the Pyramids
topics.description: Understand how the pyramids were built: thousands of workers moved enormous stone blocks using ramps, rollers, and sledges, the work was organised by the pharaoh's officials, and the design evolved from flat-topped mastabas to step pyramids (like Djoser's) to the smooth-sided Great Pyramid — and know that later pharaohs were buried in hidden rock-cut tombs in the Valley of the Kings
evidence: Describe at least two methods used to move and raise heavy stone blocks
Explain that pyramid design changed over time from simple tombs to the Great Pyramid
Explain why later pharaohs chose hidden tombs in the Valley of the Kings instead of pyramids

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Egyptian Gods and Goddesses
topics.description: Name and describe key Egyptian gods and goddesses: Ra the sun god who sailed across the sky each day, Osiris the ruler of the afterlife, Isis the goddess of magic and motherhood, Anubis the jackal-headed god of mummification, Horus the falcon-headed sky god, Thoth the ibis-headed god of writing, and Bastet the cat goddess of protection
evidence: Name at least four Egyptian gods/goddesses and describe their roles
Explain why many gods were shown with animal heads and what the animals represented
Understand that Egyptians built temples as homes for the gods and performed daily rituals there

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Egyptian Social Hierarchy
topics.description: Describe a simplified model of ancient Egyptian social hierarchy: the pharaoh at the top, then priests and nobles, followed by scribes and soldiers, then craftworkers and merchants, with farmers and labourers at the base. Family background and status often shaped people’s work, resources and opportunities, while some people could move to a different position.
evidence: Draw or describe the social pyramid with at least four levels correctly ordered
Explain that most people were farmers and had very different lives from the pharaoh

Give a supported example of how social position affected daily work or access to resources, such as scribes keeping administrative records while farmers grew crops; do not assume that only professional scribes could read.

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Egyptian Tomb Paintings and Artefacts
topics.description: Use tomb paintings, artefacts, and objects from ancient Egypt as evidence to find out about daily life: Nebamun's tomb paintings show hunting and feasting, jewellery and furniture reveal craftsmanship, and everyday objects like pots and tools tell us what ordinary people used — understanding that these sources are how we piece together information about a civilisation that ended thousands of years ago
evidence: Describe what can be learned about Egyptian life by studying a tomb painting or artefact
Explain that objects found in tombs and ruins are evidence that helps archaeologists understand the past
Give an example of something specific a painting or object reveals (e.g., what food they ate, what games they played)

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Mummification Step by Step
topics.description: Describe the step-by-step process of mummification: the body was washed, internal organs were removed and placed in canopic jars, the body was dried with natron salt for 40 days, then wrapped in linen bandages with amulets tucked between the layers, and finally placed in a decorated coffin (sarcophagus)
evidence: List the main steps of mummification in the correct order
Explain the purpose of canopic jars and what was stored in them
Describe why mummification was performed (to preserve the body for the afterlife)

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Scribes and the Rosetta Stone
topics.description: Know that scribes were specially trained people who could read and write hieroglyphs, that the Rosetta Stone — a slab with the same text in three scripts — was the key to cracking the hieroglyphic code, and that Jean-François Champollion used it to decipher hieroglyphs in 1822 after centuries of mystery
evidence: Explain the importance of scribes as the only people who could read and write
Describe the Rosetta Stone as having the same message in three different scripts
Name Champollion as the person who decoded hieroglyphs using the Rosetta Stone

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Upper and Lower Egypt
topics.description: Understand that ancient Egypt was divided into Upper Egypt (the narrow river valley in the south) and Lower Egypt (the wide delta in the north), that the two lands were united under one pharaoh, and that Egyptians managed the Nile's water through irrigation canals and shadufs to grow crops year-round
evidence: Identify Upper and Lower Egypt on a map and explain why they had different landscapes
Describe how irrigation tools like shadufs and canals helped farmers water their fields
Explain that uniting the two lands was an important achievement of the early pharaohs

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Ancient Egypt's Lasting Legacy
topics.description: Evaluate ancient Egypt's lasting legacy: the Egyptians developed early forms of medicine, mathematics (used to build pyramids and survey land after floods), astronomy (calendar based on star observations), and engineering that influenced later civilisations including Greece and Rome — and compare ancient Egypt with other early civilisations (Mesopotamia, Indus Valley, Shang Dynasty) to identify shared features like writing, agriculture, cities, and organised religion
evidence: Name at least two Egyptian achievements that influenced later civilisations
Identify at least two features that ancient Egypt shared with other early civilisations
Explain why studying ancient Egypt helps us understand how human civilisation developed

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Cleopatra and the End of Egypt
topics.description: Know that ancient Egypt eventually came to an end: the last pharaoh was Cleopatra VII, who allied with Rome but was defeated by Octavian (later Augustus) in 31 BCE, after which Egypt became a province of the Roman Empire — ending over 3,000 years of pharaonic rule and beginning a new chapter in Egypt's history
evidence: Name Cleopatra VII as the last pharaoh of ancient Egypt
Explain that Egypt was conquered by Rome and became part of the Roman Empire
Understand that the end of pharaonic rule did not mean the end of Egyptian culture

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Egyptian Art and Architecture
topics.description: Analyse Egyptian art and architecture: understand that Egyptian paintings followed strict conventions (people shown from the side with eyes from the front, size indicating importance), that tomb and temple design evolved from mastabas to step pyramids to smooth pyramids to rock-cut temples like Abu Simbel, and that obelisks, colossal statues, and temples like Karnak demonstrated the pharaoh's power and devotion to the gods
evidence: Identify at least two conventions used in Egyptian painting and explain their purpose
Describe how monument design changed over the course of Egyptian history
Explain why pharaohs built such enormous structures (power, religion, afterlife)

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Egyptian Trade and Economy
topics.description: Understand that ancient Egypt had a thriving economy based on farming surplus, trade, and specialised labour: the Nile's fertile soil produced enough food to support craftworkers, priests, and officials, and Egypt traded along the Nile and across the Mediterranean — exchanging gold, papyrus, and grain for cedarwood from Lebanon, lapis lazuli from Afghanistan, and incense from Punt
evidence: Explain how agricultural surplus along the Nile allowed people to specialise in non-farming jobs
Name at least two goods Egypt exported and two it imported, and where they came from
Describe how the barter system worked and why trade routes were important to Egypt's wealth

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Judgement of the Dead
topics.description: Describe the Egyptian belief in the judgement of the dead: after death, the heart was weighed against the feather of Ma'at in the Hall of Judgement, with Anubis overseeing the scales and Thoth recording the result — a pure heart meant entry to the Field of Reeds (paradise), while a heavy heart was devoured by the monster Ammit, and know that the Book of the Dead contained spells to help the deceased pass this test
evidence: Describe the weighing of the heart ceremony and name the gods involved
Explain the role of the Book of the Dead as a guide through the underworld
Connect the concept of the ka (life force) and ba (personality) to why Egyptians preserved the body

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Maps of ancient Egypt
topics.description: Interpret maps of ancient Egypt showing the Nile, the Nile delta, trade routes and the location of key sites such as Memphis, Thebes and the Valley of the Kings
evidence: Read a map of ancient Egypt and identify the Nile, Memphis, Thebes and the Valley of the Kings
Locate the Nile delta on a map and use the map to tell which sites lie along the river valley and which lie in the delta
Trace an ancient Egyptian trade route on a map (e.g. along the Nile or across the Mediterranean) and name a place it connected

topics.subject: History
topics.name: The Pharaoh as Living God
topics.description: Understand that the pharaoh was not just a ruler but was believed to be a living god — the intermediary between the gods and the people — and that the concept of Ma'at (truth, justice, and cosmic order) guided Egyptian law and government, with viziers and officials administering the kingdom on the pharaoh's behalf
evidence: Explain the pharaoh's dual role as both political ruler and divine figure
Describe Ma'at as the principle of truth, justice, and order that governed Egyptian society
Identify the role of viziers and officials in running the government day to day

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Modern Archaeology and Egyptian Ethics
topics.description: Understand that modern Egyptologists use advanced technologies — CT scanning of mummies, satellite imagery to find buried structures, DNA analysis — alongside traditional excavation, and think critically about the ethics of archaeology: whether mummies should be displayed in museums, who owns ancient artefacts, and how colonial-era collecting affects how we study and present ancient Egypt today
evidence: Name at least two modern technologies used in Egyptology and explain what they reveal
Discuss at least one ethical question about how ancient Egyptian artefacts are treated today
Understand that how we study ancient Egypt reflects our own values and biases, not just facts about the past

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Egyptian Maths and Engineering
topics.description: Describe the Egyptian achievement in mathematics and engineering: the Rhind Mathematical Papyrus shows calculations of area, volume, and fractions; the precision of pyramid alignment (within 0.05° of true north) required sophisticated surveying; and Egyptian medical papyri describe detailed anatomical knowledge and pharmacological remedies — placing Egypt as a major contributor to the early history of science and technology
evidence: Describes the Rhind Mathematical Papyrus as containing worked examples of arithmetic, geometry, and unit fractions
Explains one specific engineering achievement: pyramid alignment, ramp logistics, or the accuracy of the Great Pyramid's dimensions
Names at least one medical papyrus (e.g. Ebers Papyrus) and describes the type of medical knowledge it contains

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Historical Sources on Ancient Egypt
topics.description: Explain how knowledge of ancient Egypt is built from multiple source types — inscriptions, papyri, artefacts, and physical remains — and critically evaluate each: what biases, gaps, and distortions exist? Explore how Champollion’s decipherment of hieroglyphs transformed the field, and why the same artefact can be interpreted differently by different scholars
evidence: Identifies at least four types of historical source (inscriptions, papyri, tomb art, physical artefacts) and explains what each type can and cannot tell us
Explains that hieroglyphic sources were created by the literate elite and therefore tend to record official versions of events, not ordinary people's experiences
Describes at least one example where the same artefact or text has been interpreted in significantly different ways by scholars, and explains why this happens

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Egypt and Its Neighbours
topics.description: Examine Egypt's relationships with neighbouring civilisations: trade networks reaching Nubia, the Levant, and Punt; the Hyksos invasion and the introduction of the chariot; and the New Kingdom empire and its conflict with the Hittites, culminating in the Battle of Kadesh and the world's earliest surviving peace treaty — understanding Egypt not as isolated but as part of a connected ancient world
evidence: Describes the trade relationship with Nubia and Punt, naming at least two goods exchanged in each direction
Explains how the Hyksos invasion introduced new military technologies to Egypt, including the horse-drawn war chariot
Describes the Battle of Kadesh (Ramesses II vs. the Hittites) and the resulting Egypto-Hittite peace treaty as a landmark in diplomatic history

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Who Really Built the Pyramids
topics.description: Analyse who built the pyramids and why, evaluating the evidence against the alien-builder myth and the slave-labour myth: archaeological evidence from worker villages at Giza shows a paid, skilled, well-fed workforce; discuss the social functions of monument building as a form of state organisation, religious duty, and employment; and assess the current controversy over newly discovered construction ramps and logistics
evidence: Cites at least three pieces of archaeological evidence from Giza that point to an organised, skilled, fed workforce rather than slaves or aliens (e.g. worker villages, bakery remains, graffiti tags, medical care)
Explains why the alien hypothesis fails to meet the standards of historical evidence and what the burden of proof in history requires
Evaluates at least two proposed explanations for ramp logistics and describes which is currently supported by the most evidence

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Fall of Ancient Egyptian Civilisation
topics.description: Trace the end of ancient Egyptian civilisation through its successive conquests — Assyrian, Persian, Macedonian (Alexander the Great), and finally Roman — and explain how each conqueror was simultaneously shaped by Egyptian culture; examine Cleopatra VII as the last pharaoh and as a multilingual political strategist; and consider what survives of ancient Egypt in modern culture, religion, and language
evidence: Names the main conquerors of Egypt in chronological order (Assyrians, Persians, Macedonians under Alexander, Romans) and gives approximate dates
Describes Cleopatra VII accurately: not as a romantic icon but as a politically sophisticated ruler who spoke multiple languages and tried to preserve Egyptian independence

Identifies at least two enduring legacies of ancient Egypt in the modern world (e.g. the Coptic language as a descendant of ancient Egyptian, obelisks in Rome and Paris, Egyptian motifs in Western art and architecture)

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Ancient Greece and Rome on the Map
topics.description: Locate Greece and Italy on a map and know they are countries around the Mediterranean Sea where two great ancient civilisations — Ancient Greece and Ancient Rome — grew up thousands of years ago, long after the ancient Egyptians but long before our time
evidence: Point to Greece and Italy on a world map or globe
Say that Ancient Greece and Ancient Rome were around the Mediterranean Sea
Place Greece and Rome on a simple timeline after Ancient Egypt and before today

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Ancient life vs today
topics.description: Compare how children in ancient Greece or Rome lived with how children live today — including differences in school (writing on wax tablets, learning to fight in Sparta), food (olives, bread, grapes), games, and clothing (tunics and sandals) — and understand these civilisations existed thousands of years ago
evidence: Name two ways a child's life in ancient Greece or Rome was different from today
Describe what ancient Greek or Roman children might have eaten or worn
Say that these civilisations existed thousands of years ago — long before grandparents were born

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Greek gods & Mount Olympus
topics.description: Know that the ancient Greeks believed in many gods and goddesses who lived on Mount Olympus — including Zeus (king of the gods, thunder), Athena (wisdom), Poseidon (the sea), Hermes (messages), and Aphrodite (love) — and that each god had special powers and a role in the world
evidence: Name at least three Greek gods and say what each one was god of
Say that the Greek gods were believed to live on Mount Olympus
Explain that the ancient Greeks prayed to different gods for different things

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Greek Myths and Heroes
topics.description: Retell at least one Greek myth involving a hero and a monster — such as Theseus and the Minotaur in the labyrinth, Heracles (Hercules) and the lion, or Perseus and Medusa — and understand that these were stories ancient Greeks told to explain the world and teach lessons
evidence: Retell a Greek myth naming the hero, the monster, and what happened
Explain that myths were stories the ancient Greeks told to make sense of the world
Describe what made a Greek hero brave or clever in the story

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Roman soldiers & builders
topics.description: Know that Roman soldiers marched across a huge empire building straight roads and strong walls, and that some Roman roads, walls, and buildings can still be seen today — showing that the Romans were powerful builders whose work has lasted thousands of years
evidence: Describe Roman soldiers as part of a powerful army that marched across an empire
Name something the Romans built that we can still see today such as roads or walls
Explain that Roman buildings and roads lasted because the Romans were skilled builders

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Romulus & Remus
topics.description: Know the Roman founding myth of Romulus and Remus — twin brothers abandoned as babies, raised by a she-wolf, who grew up to found the city of Rome — and understand that this is a legend the Romans told about how their city began
evidence: Retell the story of Romulus and Remus being raised by a wolf
Say that Romulus founded the city of Rome
Explain that this is a legend — a story people told, not necessarily true

topics.subject: History
topics.name: The first Olympics
topics.description: Know that the Olympic Games began in ancient Greece at a place called Olympia as athletic competitions held in honour of Zeus, and that the modern Olympic Games we watch today were inspired by those ancient games
evidence: Say that the Olympic Games started in ancient Greece at Olympia
Name at least one sport or event from the ancient Olympics such as running or wrestling
Explain that today's Olympic Games got the idea from the ancient Greek ones

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Athenian Democracy
topics.description: Understand that Athens invented democracy — a system where free male citizens gathered in an Assembly to debate and vote on important decisions for the city — but that women, enslaved people, and foreigners were not allowed to vote
evidence: Explain what democracy meant in Athens: citizens voted on decisions together
Identify who could vote in Athenian democracy (free men born in Athens) and who could not
Say that the idea of people voting on decisions started in Athens and still influences us today

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Athens Versus Sparta
topics.description: Compare Athens and Sparta as two very different Greek city-states: Athens focused on learning, arts, debate, and democracy, while Sparta focused on military training, discipline, and obedience — and understand that a city-state was a city that ruled itself like a small country
evidence: Name at least two differences between life in Athens and life in Sparta
Explain what a city-state was and why Greek city-states were independent from each other
Describe what was valued most in Athens (learning, arts) versus Sparta (military strength)

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Boudicca's Revolt Against Rome
topics.description: Tell the story of Boudicca, queen of the Iceni tribe, who led a fierce revolt against Roman rule in Britain — burning Colchester, London, and St Albans — before her army was defeated, and understand her significance as a symbol of resistance against a powerful empire
evidence: Retell the story of Boudicca: who she was, why she revolted, what happened
Name at least one town Boudicca's army destroyed during the revolt
Explain why Boudicca is remembered as a symbol of resistance against the Romans

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Daily Life in a Roman Town
topics.description: Describe daily life in a Roman town — the forum (marketplace and meeting place), public baths, amphitheatre, and villas — and explain that the Romans were brilliant engineers who built straight roads, aqueducts to carry water, underfloor heating (hypocaust), and Hadrian's Wall to mark the empire's northern frontier in Britain
evidence: Describe at least three features of a Roman town such as forum, baths, or amphitheatre
Explain what an aqueduct was and why the Romans built them
Describe Hadrian's Wall and say why it was built

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Gladiators & Pompeii
topics.description: Know that Romans watched gladiators fight in huge arenas like the Colosseum in Rome, that gladiators were usually enslaved people or prisoners trained to fight, and that the city of Pompeii was buried by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD 79, preserving an extraordinary snapshot of Roman daily life
evidence: Describe what gladiators were and where they fought
Explain that the Colosseum in Rome was a giant arena for public entertainment
Retell what happened to Pompeii and why it is important for understanding Roman life

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Gods & the Parthenon
topics.description: Name the major Greek gods and their roles — Zeus (king, thunder), Hera (queen, marriage), Athena (wisdom, warfare), Poseidon (sea), Apollo (sun, music), Artemis (hunting, moon), Ares (war), Aphrodite (love), Hermes (messengers), Hephaestus (fire, crafts), Hades (underworld) — and know that the Parthenon in Athens was a grand temple built to honour Athena
evidence: Name at least five Greek gods and say what each was responsible for
Describe the Parthenon as a temple to Athena built on the acropolis in Athens
Explain that Greeks built temples to honour their gods and held festivals and sacrifices

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Greek Gods with Roman Names
topics.description: Understand that the Romans adopted the Greek gods but gave them new names — Zeus became Jupiter, Hera became Juno, Ares became Mars, Athena became Minerva, Poseidon became Neptune, Aphrodite became Venus — and that this shows how deeply Rome was influenced by Greek culture
evidence: Match at least four Greek gods to their Roman names
Explain that the Romans took Greek gods and gave them Latin names
Say that this borrowing shows Rome was strongly influenced by Greek culture

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Greek theatre
topics.description: Know that the ancient Greeks invented theatre, performing tragedies and comedies in large open-air amphitheatres with actors wearing masks — and that plays were performed as part of religious festivals honouring the god Dionysus, with audiences of thousands
evidence: Explain that the Greeks invented theatre with two types of plays: tragedies and comedies
Describe how Greek actors wore masks and performed in open-air amphitheatres
Say that plays were part of festivals honouring the god Dionysus

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Marathon and Thermopylae
topics.description: Describe the battles of Marathon and Thermopylae as moments when Greek city-states united against the invading Persian Empire — the runner Pheidippides bringing news of victory at Marathon (origin of the marathon race), and the heroic stand of 300 Spartans at Thermopylae — and understand these wars were fought to defend Greek independence
evidence: Retell the story of the Battle of Marathon and the runner Pheidippides
Describe the Spartan stand at Thermopylae against a much larger Persian army
Explain that the Persian Wars were about Greek city-states defending their freedom

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Roman Army and Conquest of Britain
topics.description: Describe how the Roman army was organised into legions of highly trained soldiers, how Julius Caesar first raided Britain in 55 BC and Emperor Claudius later conquered it in AD 43, and explain why the Romans wanted to expand their empire — for land, resources, taxes, and glory
evidence: Describe a Roman legion as a large unit of highly trained, disciplined soldiers
Explain that Julius Caesar raided Britain first and Claudius conquered it later
Give at least one reason why the Romans invaded Britain

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Alexander the Great's Empire
topics.description: Describe how Alexander the Great of Macedon conquered a vast empire stretching from Greece to Egypt to India, spreading Greek language, culture, and ideas across the ancient world — creating a period known as the Hellenistic Age where Greek and Eastern cultures blended
evidence: Describe the extent of Alexander's empire on a map (Greece to Egypt to India)
Explain that Alexander spread Greek culture and language across the lands he conquered
Say what the Hellenistic Age was — a blending of Greek and Eastern cultures

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Evidence for Greek and Roman Life
topics.description: Understand that historians and archaeologists piece together ancient Greek and Roman life from evidence — pottery paintings, coins, inscriptions, ruins like Pompeii, and written texts by authors such as Homer and Pliny — and that the same evidence can be interpreted in different ways by different historians
evidence: Name at least three types of evidence historians use to learn about ancient Greece and Rome
Explain why Pompeii is especially valuable as a source of evidence about Roman life
Give an example of how the same piece of evidence could be interpreted in more than one way

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Fall of the Western Roman Empire
topics.description: Describe how the Western Roman Empire gradually declined due to a combination of factors — military pressure from invading peoples, political instability, economic problems, and an overstretched empire — and finally fell in AD 476, while the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire continued for nearly a thousand more years
evidence: Name at least two reasons why the Western Roman Empire declined and fell
State the date AD 476 as when the last Western Roman emperor was removed
Explain that the Eastern (Byzantine) Empire survived for nearly 1,000 years after the West fell

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Greek and Roman Architecture
topics.description: Identify Greek column styles — Doric (plain and sturdy), Ionic (scroll-shaped capitals), and Corinthian (ornate leafy capitals) — and Roman architectural innovations — the arch, the dome, and concrete — and spot their influence in modern public buildings such as courthouses, museums, government buildings, and monuments
evidence: Identify the three Greek column orders (Doric, Ionic, Corinthian) from pictures
Name Roman architectural innovations: the arch, the dome, and concrete
Point out Greek or Roman architectural features in a modern public building

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Greek and Roman Legacy Today
topics.description: Evaluate the lasting contributions of Greek and Roman civilisations to modern life — democracy, law, language (Latin roots), architecture (columns, arches, domes), sport (Olympics), philosophy, literature, and theatre — and understand that Greek ideas reached us through Rome, and then through later European civilisations, in a chain of cultural transmission
evidence: List at least five ways ancient Greece and Rome still influence modern life
Explain how Greek culture spread to Rome and then from Rome across Europe
Give a specific modern example of a Greek or Roman legacy such as democratic voting or architectural columns

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Greek Philosophers and Medicine
topics.description: Know that Greek thinkers called philosophers developed ways of understanding the world that still influence us today — Socrates asked challenging questions to test ideas (the Socratic method), Plato imagined the ideal society, Aristotle observed and classified the natural world — and that Hippocrates is called the father of medicine for insisting on natural causes of illness rather than blaming the gods
evidence: Describe what Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle each contributed to thinking and learning
Explain the Socratic method as learning by asking questions rather than just being told answers
Say why Hippocrates is called the father of medicine

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Roman Law, Latin, and Christianity
topics.description: Understand that Roman law became the basis for legal systems across Europe and beyond, that Latin is the root of French, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese, and Romanian and gave English hundreds of words (e.g. exit, video, annual, education), and that Christianity spread throughout the Roman Empire, eventually becoming its official religion under Emperor Constantine
evidence: Give examples of English words that come from Latin
Explain that Roman law influenced modern legal systems in Europe and beyond
Describe how Christianity spread through the Roman Empire and became its official religion

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Roman Republic and Empire
topics.description: Explain how Rome was first governed as a republic — with elected consuls, a powerful Senate, and a distinction between patricians and plebeians — before becoming an empire ruled by emperors like Augustus (who brought peace, the Pax Romana) and Nero, and compare republican government with Athenian direct democracy
evidence: Describe the Roman Republic's structure: consuls, Senate, patricians, and plebeians
Explain how Rome changed from a republic to an empire under Augustus
Compare Athenian direct democracy (citizens vote on decisions) with Roman republican government (citizens elect representatives)

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Hidden Voices of Greece and Rome
topics.description: Examine the lives of people usually left out of the Greek and Roman story — enslaved people who made up roughly 30% of Athens and powered Rome's economy, women whose lives varied dramatically between Athens (largely confined to the home) and Sparta (physical training, property ownership), and conquered peoples across both empires — and evaluate whose voices are missing from the historical record and why
evidence: Describe the daily life of an enslaved person in Athens or Rome using available evidence
Compare the lives of women in Athens and Sparta, explaining key differences
Explain why the historical record favours elite men and what this means for our understanding

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Inclusion and Exclusion in Athens
topics.description: Analyse who was included and excluded from Athenian democracy — only free adult male citizens (roughly 30% of adults) could participate, while women, enslaved people (who may have made up a third of the population), and foreign residents (metics) were excluded — and evaluate whether Athens truly deserves the title 'birthplace of democracy' by comparing it with modern representative democracies
evidence: Calculate approximately what fraction of the Athenian population could participate in democracy
List the groups excluded from Athenian democracy and explain why each was excluded
Construct an argument for or against calling Athens a true democracy, using evidence

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Troy: Myth or History?
topics.description: Explore how Heinrich Schliemann's excavation at Hisarlik in modern Turkey raised questions about whether the Trojan War described in Homer's Iliad was historical, partly historical, or entirely mythical — understanding that archaeology and literary sources can support or contradict each other, and that the line between myth and history in the ancient world is often blurred
evidence: Describe Schliemann's excavation at Hisarlik and what he claimed to have found
Explain how archaeological evidence at Troy both supports and complicates Homer's story
Discuss why the boundary between myth and history is difficult to draw for the ancient world

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Fall of the Roman Republic
topics.description: Trace how Roman political violence — the murder of the Gracchi brothers, civil wars between Marius and Sulla, Caesar's crossing of the Rubicon and assassination on the Ides of March, and the final war between Octavian and Antony — destroyed the Republic and led to one-man rule under Augustus, and debate whether the fall of the Republic was inevitable or a series of choices
evidence: Describe at least three key events in the collapse of the Roman Republic in chronological order
Explain what 'crossing the Rubicon' meant and why it was a point of no return
Construct an argument about whether the Republic's fall was inevitable or could have been prevented

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Celebrations we share
topics.description: Describe the celebrations and commemorations of significant events that they share with their families and others, and how they are marked
evidence: Describe how their family celebrates a special event (e.g. a birthday, Christmas, Diwali, Eid or Lunar New Year) using a photo or object from home
Compare one way their celebration is the same as a classmate's and one way it is different
Recognise that some days are commemorations when people remember something important (e.g. Anzac Day) and say how people mark them

topics.subject: History
topics.name: My family and where we're from
topics.description: Identify the people in their family, where family members were born and raised, and how they are related to each other
evidence: Name the people in their family and say how each is related to them (e.g. 'Nan is Mum's mum')
Draw or complete a simple family picture or tree with photos or drawings of family members
Share where they and one older family member were born or grew up, using a photo, map or story from home

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Childhood then and now
topics.description: Identify continuity and change between aspects of their daily lives and their parents' and grandparents' childhoods, such as school, play, toys, chores, food and technology
evidence: Interview a parent or grandparent with prepared questions about school, toys or chores when they were young
Sort pictures into 'same then and now' and 'changed' (e.g. playing ball games vs video games, walking vs being driven to school)
Explain one continuity and one change between their life and a grandparent's childhood, using information from the interview

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Important local people and places
topics.description: Investigate a local individual, group, place or building and the reasons for its importance, including social, cultural or spiritual significance
evidence: Find out about a local place or building (e.g. a war memorial, place of worship, old school or community hall) using photos, a plaque or a visit and record two facts
Explain why it is important to the community, saying whether the reason is social (people meet there), cultural or spiritual
Describe a local individual or group that contributed to the community (e.g. a founding family, a volunteer group or a local Elder) and why they are remembered

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Technology changes how we live
topics.description: Describe how technological developments changed people's lives at home and the ways they worked, travelled and communicated
evidence: Compare how a household job was done in the past and today (e.g. washing clothes with a copper and washboard vs a washing machine) and describe the effect on people's lives
Order pictures of transport (horse and cart, steam train, car, plane) and explain how each changed travel
Explain how communication changed from letters and telegrams to telephones, email and video calls, using one source as evidence

topics.subject: History
topics.name: How our community changed
topics.description: Identify causes and effects of changes to the local community (e.g. a new railway, new housing, migration, a factory closing) and how people from diverse backgrounds, including First Nations Australians and migrants, have contributed to these changes
evidence: Identify one change in the local community and explain a cause and an effect (e.g. a new train line led to more houses being built)
Use photos, maps or a local history website to compare the community at two different times
Describe the contribution of a person or group from a diverse background (e.g. a migrant family business, a First Nations community organisation or a refugee support group)

topics.subject: History
topics.name: National days and commemorations
topics.description: Identify significant days that are important to Australia's identity and diversity and how they are commemorated or recognised, including Australia Day, Anzac Day, NAIDOC Week and National Sorry Day
evidence: Explain what is commemorated on Anzac Day (25 April) and on National Sorry Day (26 May), and how people mark each

Explain that Australia Day (26 January) commemorates the First Fleet's arrival at Sydney Cove in 1788 (the fleet had reached Botany Bay earlier in January) and that many First Nations Australians mark it as a day of mourning or survival, and describe what NAIDOC Week celebrates
Describe how one of these days is marked in their school or community (e.g. a dawn service or a NAIDOC Week assembly) and why

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Timelines of past events
topics.description: Collect, sort and record information about past events on unscaled timelines, placing pictures or labelled events in order from earliest to latest
evidence: Place photos or drawings of themselves as a baby, a toddler and now, or labels for five events from their own life, in order on an unscaled timeline
Place events from a family or local history story on an unscaled timeline using words such as 'before', 'after' and 'long ago'
Use information from a provided source (a photo or interview) to add one event to a class timeline in the correct place and explain why it goes there

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Different perspectives and accounts
topics.description: Recognise that different people can have different perspectives on, and give different accounts of, the same object, place or event — and that both can be genuine while still disagreeing
evidence: Explain how a child and a grandparent might feel differently about the same old toy, photo or place
Describe how different people (e.g. a child, a driver and a shop owner) might view a change to a local place, such as a park becoming a car park
Explain why two honest people's accounts of the same event can differ (e.g. where they stood or what mattered to them) without either of them lying

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Evidence from the Past
topics.description: Understand that everything we know about the past comes from evidence that has survived — objects, buildings, pictures, documents and stories — and use clues in that evidence to work out how people lived
evidence: Explain that we know about the past from evidence that has survived, such as objects, photos, buildings, documents and stories
Use clues from an old object or photo to infer how it was used and who might have used it
Explain why we know less about times or people that left fewer surviving objects or records

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Questions about the past
topics.description: Develop questions about objects, people, places and events in the past and present, such as who used an object, what a place was like long ago or how an event was celebrated
evidence: Write or say three questions to ask a grandparent about their childhood (e.g. 'What games did you play?')
Ask who, what, when, where and why questions about an old object or photo (e.g. 'Who used this? When was it made?')
Pose a question comparing a place in the past and present (e.g. 'What was here before the shops?')

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Vocabulary: historical thinking
topics.description: Know and use the vocabulary of historical thinking — source, evidence, primary source, secondary source, artefact, chronology, chronological order, BC/BCE, AD/CE, century, decade, era, period, timeline, excavation, archaeologist, interpretation, corroborate, bias, perspective — and apply these terms when discussing how we know about the past and how reliable our knowledge is
evidence: Correctly use BC/BCE and AD/CE to place events in time and explain what the letters stand for
Distinguish between a primary source and a secondary source with an example of each
Use 'evidence', 'interpretation', and 'bias' correctly in a sentence about a historical source

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Checking Sources Against Each Other
topics.description: Corroborate: check whether multiple sources agree on the same facts — and investigate why they might not
evidence: Compare two accounts of the same event (e.g. two family members' stories or two short sources) and list the facts on which they agree and disagree
Suggest a reason two sources disagree (e.g. one writer was not there, or remembered it years later)
Decide which facts are best supported because more than one source agrees, and explain why

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Dated timelines with notes
topics.description: Locate, collect and record information from a range of sources on annotated timelines with dates, an appropriate scale and a brief note and source for each event
evidence: Create a timeline of local community history with dates and a scale (e.g. one centimetre for every ten years), placing at least five events, and calculate the number of years between two of them
Annotate each event with a short note and the source it came from (e.g. a council website or an old newspaper)
Use the completed timeline to identify a period of rapid change and explain it using the annotations

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Questioning Historical Sources
topics.description: Before trusting a historical source, ask: who made this, when, and why? — the answers shape how much weight the source should carry
evidence: Wineburg sourcing heuristic
Teaching Historical Thinking Using Primary Sources (Library of Congress)

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Understanding People in Their Own Time
topics.description: Understand that people in the past saw the world very differently from us — judge their actions by the context they lived in, not only by today's values
evidence: Historical Empathy: A Cognitive-Affective Theory (ERIC)
Year 4-6 historical empathy research

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Evidence Versus Interpretation
topics.description: Distinguish between historical evidence and historical interpretation — evidence is what survived, interpretation is the argument a historian builds from it, and the same evidence can support different arguments
evidence: Development of historical understanding among 9-14 year olds
Ways of Seeing: Evidence and Learning in the History Classroom (RRCHNM)

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Kings & Queens
topics.description: What medieval kings and queens did: ruling the land, making laws, collecting taxes; the crown and throne as symbols of power; the Tower of London
evidence: Explain what a medieval king or queen did (ruled, made laws, led armies, collected taxes)
Describe at least one symbol of royal power (crown, throne, sceptre)
Name one famous medieval monarch or describe the Tower of London's role

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Knights & Armour
topics.description: What knights were: trained warriors who served a lord; armour, shields, swords, and lances; the code of chivalry as rules for how knights should behave
evidence: Describe what a knight wore and carried (armour, helmet, shield, sword, lance)
Explain that knights trained from a young age and served a lord
Name one rule of the code of chivalry (be brave, be honest, protect the weak)

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Medieval Clothing
topics.description: What people wore in medieval times: peasant clothes (wool, linen) vs noble clothes (silk, fur, bright colours); no zippers or buttons; how clothes showed your place in society
evidence: Describe what a medieval peasant would typically wear
Explain how noble clothing was different from peasant clothing
Give one way that what you wore showed your place in society

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Medieval Food & Feasts
topics.description: What people ate in medieval times: bread and pottage for ordinary people, grand feasts for the rich; no forks, eating with hands; the great hall as the centre of castle life
evidence: Describe what ordinary people ate most days (bread, pottage, vegetables, ale)
Explain how a feast in a great hall was different from everyday meals
Name one surprising table manner from medieval times (no forks, shared cups, food thrown on the floor)

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Robin Hood & King Arthur
topics.description: The legends of Robin Hood (Sherwood Forest, stealing from the rich, Merry Men) and King Arthur (Round Table, Excalibur, Camelot); that these are stories, not proven history, but reflect medieval values
evidence: Retell the basic story of Robin Hood or King Arthur
Name at least two characters from one of these legends
Explain that these are legends (stories) rather than proven facts

topics.subject: History
topics.name: The Vikings
topics.description: Who the Vikings were: seafaring warriors and traders from Scandinavia; longships; Viking raids on Britain; that Vikings also settled and farmed
evidence: Describe who the Vikings were and where they came from
Explain what made longships special (fast, could sail in shallow water, dragon prows)
State that Vikings were not just raiders but also farmers, traders, and settlers

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Village Life
topics.description: Daily life for ordinary people in a medieval village: thatched houses, farming, baking bread, fetching water; how different life was from today
evidence: Describe what a typical medieval village looked like (thatched cottages, fields, church)
Name at least three daily tasks a medieval villager would do
Give two differences between life in a medieval village and life today

topics.subject: History
topics.name: What Is a Castle?
topics.description: What a castle is: a fortified building used as both a home and a defence; key parts including towers, moat, drawbridge, and thick walls; why castles were built
evidence: Name at least four parts of a castle (tower, moat, drawbridge, walls, gatehouse)
Explain that castles were both homes and defences
Describe why someone in medieval times would need a castle

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Anglo-Saxon Britain
topics.description: Who the Anglo-Saxons were: Germanic peoples who settled in Britain after the Romans left; their kingdoms, villages, place names, art, and eventual conversion to Christianity
evidence: Explain who the Anglo-Saxons were and when they came to Britain (after the Romans left)
Name at least two Anglo-Saxon kingdoms (e.g. Wessex, Mercia, Northumbria)
Give an example of Anglo-Saxon influence still visible today (place names ending in -ton, -ham, -bury)

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Battle of Hastings and 1066
topics.description: The events of 1066: the death of Edward the Confessor, three claimants to the throne, the Battle of Hastings, William the Conqueror, and the Bayeux Tapestry as a historical source
evidence: Explain why there was a crisis when Edward the Confessor died in 1066
Describe the Battle of Hastings and its outcome
Explain what the Bayeux Tapestry is and why it is important as a historical source

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Castle Design Through the Ages
topics.description: How castles were built and evolved: from wooden motte-and-bailey to stone keeps to concentric castles; rooms and their uses; how castle design responded to new attack methods
evidence: Describe the difference between an early motte-and-bailey castle and a later stone castle
Name at least three rooms or areas in a medieval castle and their purpose
Explain one way castle design changed to resist new attack methods

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Medieval Pyramid of Power
topics.description: How medieval society was organised: king at the top, then lords, then knights, then peasants/serfs; who owed what to whom; the pyramid of power and mutual obligations
evidence: Draw or describe the feudal pyramid showing king, lords, knights, and peasants
Explain what each level owed to the level above (loyalty, military service, labour)
Describe what a serf's life was like and why they couldn't easily leave

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Siege Warfare
topics.description: How castles were attacked and defended: siege weapons (trebuchets, battering rams, siege towers), boiling liquids, arrow slits, murder holes; the drama of a medieval siege
evidence: Name at least three siege weapons or attack methods
Describe at least two ways a castle was designed to resist attack
Explain what a siege was and why it could last weeks or months

topics.subject: History
topics.name: The Black Death
topics.description: The Black Death of 1348-49: what the plague was, how it spread, its devastating death toll; how it changed society by giving surviving workers more power and higher wages
evidence: Describe what the Black Death was and at least two symptoms
Explain how the plague spread (fleas on rats, person to person)
Describe one major way the Black Death changed society (fewer workers led to higher wages, peasants gained power)

topics.subject: History
topics.name: The Crusades
topics.description: A simplified account of the Crusades: why Europeans travelled to the Holy Land, what they found there, the cultural exchange between Christian Europe and the Islamic world
evidence: Explain in simple terms why European armies travelled to the Holy Land
Describe at least one thing Europeans learned from the Islamic world during the Crusades
Acknowledge that the Crusades involved violence and suffering on both sides

topics.subject: History
topics.name: The Medieval Church
topics.description: The enormous power of the medieval Church: monasteries and the daily life of monks and nuns; building great cathedrals; pilgrimage as a religious journey; the Church's influence over everyday life
evidence: Explain why the Church was so powerful in medieval times (owned land, controlled education, people feared God's punishment)
Describe what daily life was like for a monk or nun
Explain what a pilgrimage was and give one reason people went on them

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Vikings vs Anglo-Saxons
topics.description: The conflict between Vikings and Anglo-Saxons for control of England: Viking raids, Alfred the Great's resistance, the Danelaw, Athelstan as first king of all England, Edward the Confessor
evidence: Describe the Viking raids on Anglo-Saxon England and their impact
Explain who Alfred the Great was and why he was important
Describe what the Danelaw was (the area of England under Viking control)

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Art & Architecture
topics.description: Medieval cultural achievements: illuminated manuscripts, Gothic cathedrals (flying buttresses, stained glass), Gregorian chant, the Bayeux Tapestry; art and architecture as expressions of faith and power
evidence: Describe what an illuminated manuscript is and who made them
Name at least two features of Gothic cathedral architecture (pointed arches, flying buttresses, stained glass)
Explain how medieval art and buildings were connected to the Church and religious belief

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Crime & Punishment
topics.description: How justice worked in medieval times: trial by ordeal, trial by combat, the role of the sheriff; punishments including stocks, pillory, and dungeons; how different it was from modern justice
evidence: Describe at least two medieval methods of deciding guilt (trial by ordeal, trial by combat)
Name at least two medieval punishments and explain what they involved
Compare one aspect of medieval justice to how justice works today

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Magna Carta and Limiting Royal Power
topics.description: King John, the barons' revolt, and the sealing of the Magna Carta in 1215; what the Magna Carta said about limiting the king's power; its lasting importance for democracy and rights
evidence: Explain why the barons rebelled against King John
Describe what the Magna Carta said (the king must follow the law too, fair trial rights)
Explain why the Magna Carta still matters today (foundation of democracy and human rights)

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Medieval Legacy in Modern Life
topics.description: What the Middle Ages gave us: Parliament, universities, common law, Gothic architecture, the English language (Anglo-Saxon + Norman French), place names, surnames; why we are still fascinated by the medieval world
evidence: Name at least three things from the Middle Ages that still affect our lives today
Explain how the English language was shaped by Anglo-Saxon and Norman French
Give a reason why people today are still fascinated by the medieval period (castles, knights, fantasy literature, games)

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Medieval Worlds Beyond Europe
topics.description: The medieval world beyond Europe: the Islamic Golden Age (maths, medicine, architecture), the Mali Empire and Mansa Musa, Song Dynasty China; how the medieval world was connected through trade routes like the Silk Road
evidence: Name at least two achievements of the Islamic Golden Age (algebra, hospitals, architecture)
Describe who Mansa Musa was and why he is remembered
Explain how the Silk Road connected distant parts of the medieval world through trade

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Printing Press & Renaissance
topics.description: The invention of the printing press by Gutenberg and its arrival in England with William Caxton; how printed books changed everything; the transition from the Middle Ages to the Renaissance
evidence: Explain what the printing press was and why it was revolutionary
Describe William Caxton's role in bringing printing to England
Give at least one way printed books changed society (more people could read, ideas spread faster)

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Towns & Trade
topics.description: The growth of medieval towns: markets, guilds, the merchant class; how towns won charters of self-governance; the shift from purely rural to partly urban life
evidence: Describe how medieval towns were different from villages (markets, walls, guilds, more people)
Explain what a guild was and why it mattered for tradespeople
Describe one way towns changed medieval society (new merchant class, more freedom for townspeople)

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Women in the Middle Ages
topics.description: The lives of medieval women: noblewomen managing estates, peasant women's hard daily work, nuns and abbesses, notable figures like Eleanor of Aquitaine and Joan of Arc
evidence: Describe the different lives of noblewomen, peasant women, and nuns
Name at least one notable medieval woman and explain what she did
Explain one way women's lives in medieval times were more restricted than today

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Contact and invasion
topics.description: Explain the effects of contact with the British on First Nations Australians and their Countries/Places following the arrival of the First Fleet, and why this was viewed by First Nations Australians as an invasion
evidence: Describe effects of contact on the Eora and neighbouring peoples, such as loss of land and food sources and the smallpox epidemic of 1789
Explain why First Nations Australians viewed the arrival of the British as an invasion of their Country/Place, using a First Nations source or perspective
Describe the actions of a First Nations person in the early colony (e.g. Pemulwuy's resistance or Bennelong's role between his people and the colonists) using evidence

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Life in the first colony
topics.description: Describe the experiences of individuals and groups involved in establishing the first British colony at Sydney Cove, including Governor Arthur Phillip and other officials, marines, and male and female convicts
evidence: Describe the First Fleet's voyage (11 ships, reaching Botany Bay in January 1788 and then moving to Sydney Cove, where the colony was established on 26 January) from the point of view of a convict, a marine or an official
Use a primary source extract (e.g. from the journals of marine officer Watkin Tench) to describe hardships such as food shortages in the early years
Compare the experiences of a female convict and a marine officer in the colony

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Why Britain colonised in 1788
topics.description: Explain the causes of the establishment of the first British colony in Australia in 1788, such as overcrowded British prisons and prison hulks, the loss of the American colonies as a destination for convicts, and strategic and trade interests following James Cook's 1770 voyage
evidence: Explain why British prisons and prison hulks were overcrowded in the 1780s and why transportation was used as a punishment
Explain how the American War of Independence ended the transportation of convicts to America
Describe other reasons Britain chose New South Wales, such as Cook's 1770 claim, a base in the Pacific and resources such as timber and flax, using a source as evidence

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Impact of the colonies
topics.description: Describe the impact of the development of British colonies in Australia on the lives of First Nations Australians, colonists and convicts, and on the natural environment
evidence: Describe impacts on First Nations Australians, such as loss of land, frontier conflict, massacres and disease, using an appropriate source (e.g. on the Myall Creek massacre of 1838)
Compare the life of a free settler, a convict and a First Nations person in one colony
Explain how colonial development changed the environment (e.g. land clearing and introduced animals such as rabbits and sheep)

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Significant people in a colony
topics.description: Investigate the role of a significant individual or group, including First Nations Australians and people who migrated to Australia, in the development of events in an Australian colony
evidence: Research the role of a significant person or group in a colony (e.g. Yagan in the Swan River Colony, Caroline Chisholm in New South Wales or Chinese miners on the Victorian goldfields)
Explain how their actions shaped events in that colony, using at least two sources
Present a profile of the person or group, including different perspectives on their significance

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Why new colonies began
topics.description: Explain the economic, political and social causes of the establishment of British colonies and settlements in Australia after 1800 (e.g. Van Diemen's Land 1803, Moreton Bay 1824, the Swan River Colony 1829, Port Phillip 1835, South Australia 1836)
evidence: Place the founding of colonies and settlements after 1800 on an annotated timeline with dates
Classify causes as economic (e.g. land for wool), political (e.g. keeping out the French) or social (e.g. separating convicts, free settlement)
Explain the causes of one colony's founding (e.g. the free-settler plan for South Australia) using a primary or secondary source

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Changing rights in the 1900s
topics.description: Describe changes to Australia's political system and citizenship after Federation and throughout the 20th century that affected First Nations Australians, migrants, women and children
evidence: Place key changes on an annotated timeline: federal voting rights for most women (1902), the creation of Australian citizenship (from 1949), the right of all First Nations Australians to vote in federal elections (1962) and the 1967 referendum

Explain that the 1967 referendum changed the Constitution so the Commonwealth Parliament could make laws for Aboriginal people and so Aboriginal people would be counted in the national population, and that it did not itself grant citizenship or voting rights

Explain how the Immigration Restriction Act 1901 (the basis of the White Australia policy) affected migrants, and how policies of forcibly removing First Nations children (the Stolen Generations) affected children, using appropriate sources

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Federation and the Constitution
topics.description: Describe the significant individuals, events and ideas that led to Australia's Federation in 1901, the Constitution and the democratic system of government
evidence: Explain reasons for Federation such as defence, trade between the colonies, immigration and a shared national identity

Describe the roles of significant individuals (e.g. Henry Parkes and his 1889 Tenterfield Oration, Edmund Barton as first Prime Minister, and Catherine Helen Spence, who stood for the 1897 Federal Convention)
Explain that the Constitution was approved by voters in colonial referendums and came into effect on 1 January 1901, and name one thing it does (e.g. sets up the Commonwealth Parliament)

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Migration stories since 1901
topics.description: Explain the causes of people migrating to Australia since Federation and throughout the 20th century, their stories and the effects on Australian society, including migrants from the Asia region
evidence: Explain push and pull factors for migration after World War II (e.g. the 'populate or perish' program, the Snowy Mountains Scheme and displaced persons)
Retell a migrant's story using an oral history or primary source (e.g. a Vietnamese refugee arriving after 1975)
Describe effects of migration on Australian society, such as new foods, languages, businesses and festivals

topics.subject: Learning to Learn
topics.name: Asking for Help
topics.description: Ask for help when you've had a go yourself and are still stuck — knowing when to ask is a skill in itself
evidence: Hattie visible learning
self-regulated learning research

topics.subject: Learning to Learn
topics.name: Checking Your Own Work
topics.description: After finishing a task, look back at what you did and ask yourself: does this seem right?
evidence: After finishing a piece of work, re-read or review it without being asked to
Spot and correct at least one error in their own work by checking back through it
Describe what they checked for — e.g. 'I re-read each line to make sure my answers matched the question'

topics.subject: Learning to Learn
topics.name: Persisting When It's Hard
topics.description: Keep trying when something feels hard — making mistakes and trying again is how learning happens
evidence: Keep working on a difficult task for a sustained period without giving up or asking someone else to do it
After making a mistake, try again with a different approach rather than saying 'I can't do it'
Talk about difficulty positively — e.g. 'This is hard but I'm getting better' rather than 'I'm no good at this'

topics.subject: Learning to Learn
topics.name: Feeling of not understanding
topics.description: Notice the feeling of not understanding — recognise when something is confusing rather than reading or listening past it
evidence: comprehension monitoring research
Flavell metacognitive monitoring

topics.subject: Learning to Learn
topics.name: Planning a Task
topics.description: Make a simple plan before starting a task: what do I need to do, and what should I do first?
evidence: Before starting a task, describe what they need to do and what order to do it in
Break a larger task into smaller steps without being prompted — e.g. 'First I'll read the question, then I'll draw a diagram'
Gather the materials or information they need before beginning, rather than starting and then stopping to find things

topics.subject: Learning to Learn
topics.name: Reflecting After Learning
topics.description: After completing a piece of learning, reflect on the process: what helped most, what was confusing, and what would you do differently next time?
evidence: After finishing a project or piece of learning, say what helped most and what was confusing, giving a specific example
Compare what they planned with what actually happened in the process (e.g. the order of making steps, how testing went or how the team worked) and explain one difference
Name one change to how they will work next time (the process, not just the finished product) and explain why it would help

topics.subject: Learning to Learn
topics.name: Thinking Before Starting
topics.description: Before starting something new, stop and think: what do I already know about this topic?
evidence: prior knowledge activation research
Ausubel meaningful learning

topics.subject: Learning to Learn
topics.name: Trying a New Approach
topics.description: When your first approach isn't working, try a different one — being flexible about strategies is part of being a good learner
evidence: When stuck on a problem, try a completely different approach rather than repeating the same method — e.g. drawing a picture instead of writing equations
Describe a time they changed strategy mid-task and explain why the new approach worked better
Accept that their first idea might not work and show willingness to start over with a fresh plan

topics.subject: Learning to Learn
topics.name: Connecting New & Old Ideas
topics.description: Look for connections between new ideas and things you already know — how does this fit with what I've learned before?
evidence: elaborative encoding
schema theory (Bartlett, Rumelhart)

topics.subject: Learning to Learn
topics.name: Spotting Patterns
topics.description: Spot patterns and recurring structures — in numbers, words, nature, sounds, or events — and use them to make sense of new information
evidence: Spot a pattern in a set of numbers, shapes, or facts without being told to look for one
Use a pattern they noticed to make a prediction — e.g. 'The next one should be 16 because it's doubling each time'
Explain the pattern they found and why they think it works

topics.subject: Learning to Learn
topics.name: Teaching It Back
topics.description: After learning something new, explain it in your own words — to yourself, a family member, or even a toy
evidence: Explain a concept they've learned to someone else in their own words, not just repeating what the teacher said
After teaching something to a friend or sibling, identify a gap in their own understanding that they only noticed through explaining
Summarise a lesson by pretending to teach it back, using examples they made up themselves

topics.subject: Learning to Learn
topics.name: Describing Rules & Patterns
topics.description: When you notice a pattern repeating, describe it as a rule that works every time — then test whether the rule holds in new cases
evidence: Describe a pattern or rule they've noticed in their own words — e.g. 'Every time you add 0 to a number, it stays the same'
Test whether a rule they've described holds for new examples they haven't seen before
Explain the difference between noticing a pattern and proving it always works

topics.subject: Learning to Learn
topics.name: Learning from Mistakes
topics.description: When you get something wrong, investigate why — what did you misunderstand or overlook? Analysing errors is one of the most powerful ways to learn
evidence: error analysis research
Hattie feedback effect size

topics.subject: Learning to Learn
topics.name: Transferring Skills
topics.description: Recognise when a skill or strategy learned in one subject or situation can be applied in a completely different one
evidence: transfer of learning research
Perkins & Salomon transfer taxonomy

topics.subject: Learning to Learn
topics.name: Understanding Why
topics.description: Go beyond knowing *that* something is true — ask *why* it is true and *how* it works
evidence: Ask 'why?' or 'how does that work?' about something they've been told, rather than just accepting it
Explain the reason behind a rule or method — e.g. 'We carry the ten because 13 ones is the same as 1 ten and 3 ones'
Show deeper understanding by connecting a new idea to something they already know — e.g. 'Oh, that's like when we...'

topics.subject: Learning to Learn
topics.name: Choosing a Strategy
topics.description: Before starting a study task, choose a deliberate strategy; after finishing, evaluate honestly whether that strategy actually helped
evidence: Before starting a task, name the strategy they plan to use and explain why — e.g. 'I'll make a mind map first because there's a lot to organise'
After finishing, honestly evaluate whether their chosen strategy helped or whether a different one would have been better
Describe at least three different learning strategies and explain when each works best

topics.subject: Learning to Learn
topics.name: Finding Knowledge Gaps
topics.description: Survey your own understanding of a whole topic — identify where your knowledge is solid, where it is shaky, and what still needs work
evidence: metacognitive monitoring research
Flavell metacognition framework

topics.subject: Learning to Learn
topics.name: Setting Learning Goals
topics.description: Set a specific learning goal, work towards it with a deliberate plan, then honestly assess whether you achieved it and what you would change
evidence: Set a specific, achievable learning goal for themselves — e.g. 'By Friday I want to know all my 7-times tables' rather than just 'get better at maths'
