Make a simple plan for how to reach their goal and follow through on it over several days
After the deadline, honestly assess whether they achieved the goal and describe what they would do differently next time

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Buyers & Sellers
topics.description: When someone makes or has something, they can sell it; when someone wants something, they can buy it; introduction to the concept of exchange and transactions
evidence: Explain what a buyer does and what a seller does
Act out a simple buying and selling transaction with a partner
Describe a time they or a family member bought something from a person (market stall, car boot sale, bake sale)

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Goods & Services
topics.description: Some people make things (goods) and some people do things for others (services); recognising both in everyday life and understanding that both have value
evidence: Sort a set of pictures into goods (things you can touch) and services (things people do for you)
Give three examples of goods and three examples of services from their everyday life
Explain that both making things and helping people are valuable kinds of work

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Making Something to Sell
topics.description: The experience of creating a product to sell — a craft, a drawing, baked goods; what makes something worth buying; pride in making something others want
evidence: Create a simple product (craft, drawing, baked item) that could be sold
Explain what makes their product good enough for someone to want to buy it
Suggest a fair price for their product and give a reason

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Who Is a Customer?
topics.description: Understanding that a customer is someone who buys what you make or do; thinking about what customers want and need; the idea that businesses serve people
evidence: Define what a customer is in their own words
Suggest what a customer might look for when deciding whether to buy something (quality, price, looks nice)
Explain why it matters to think about what the customer wants, not just what you want to make

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Being a Good Seller
topics.description: Customer service, fairness, and honesty in business; keeping promises to customers; why being trustworthy matters for repeat business and reputation
evidence: Explain why being honest about what you're selling matters
Describe what good customer service looks like (being polite, helpful, keeping promises)
Give an example of how being unfair or dishonest could hurt a business

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Costs & Revenue
topics.description: It costs money to make things (costs/expenses); you earn money by selling them (revenue); if revenue is more than costs, that's profit; if costs are more, that's a loss
evidence: Explain what costs, revenue, and profit mean using a simple example
Calculate profit from a given scenario (e.g. spent £3 on ingredients, sold cakes for £8, profit = £5)
Explain what happens if costs are higher than revenue (you make a loss)

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Having a Business Idea
topics.description: Where business ideas come from; spotting everyday problems and thinking of solutions; the difference between inventing something new and improving something that exists
evidence: Identify a simple everyday problem and suggest a product or service that could solve it
Explain the difference between an invention (something new) and an innovation (making something better)
Describe where one real entrepreneur got their business idea from

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Learning from Failure
topics.description: Not every business idea works; entrepreneurs try, fail, learn, and try again; iteration and resilience as core entrepreneurial skills; famous failure-to-success stories
evidence: Give an example of a famous entrepreneur who failed before succeeding
Explain what they would do differently if a business idea didn't work the first time
Describe why failing and trying again is better than giving up

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Making a Simple Plan
topics.description: Before starting a business, making a simple plan: what will I make or do, who will buy it, what do I need, how much will it cost, and what price will I charge?
evidence: Write or draw a simple business plan covering: product, customer, materials needed, and price
Identify at least three things they would need before they could start selling
Explain why planning ahead is better than just starting without thinking

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Marketing Basics
topics.description: How people find out about what you're selling; signs, posters, social media, word of mouth; being persuasive; the basics of advertising and promotion
evidence: Design a simple poster or advert for a product or service
Name at least three ways to let people know about something you're selling
Explain why a catchy name or eye-catching design helps sell more

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Teamwork in Business
topics.description: Most businesses need more than one person; working together, dividing tasks, and using different people's strengths; the value of teamwork in business
evidence: Describe how they would divide tasks in a team business project (one person makes, one sells, one designs)
Explain why using people's different strengths makes a business better
Give an example of a problem that could happen if a team doesn't work well together

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Social Enterprise
topics.description: Using business skills to help others or solve social and environmental problems; making money AND making a difference; examples of social enterprises
evidence: Explain what a social enterprise is in their own words (a business that helps people or the planet)
Give an example of a real social enterprise or charity shop
Suggest a social enterprise idea that could help their school or community

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Ethics in Business
topics.description: Being honest, being fair, treating workers well, not harming the environment; what makes a 'good' business; whether businesses should care about more than profit
evidence: Name at least two things that make a business ethical (fair wages, honest advertising, environmentally responsible)
Explain why a business that only cares about profit might cause problems
Describe a situation where a business owner faces an ethical choice and suggest what they should do

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Pitching an Idea
topics.description: Presenting a business idea to others convincingly; explaining what makes it good and why people should support it; building confidence in public speaking about ideas
evidence: Deliver a 1-2 minute pitch for a business idea covering: what it is, who it helps, and why it's good
Answer at least two questions about their idea from an audience
Explain why being able to explain your idea clearly matters for getting support

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Real Entrepreneurs
topics.description: Stories of real entrepreneurs who started young: Mikaila Ulmer (Me & the Bees), Moziah Bridges (Mo's Bows), Cory Nieves (Mr. Cory's Cookies); what makes someone an entrepreneur
evidence: Retell the story of at least one real entrepreneur who started as a child
Identify three qualities that helped that entrepreneur succeed (creativity, persistence, passion)
Explain what the word 'entrepreneur' means in their own words

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Scaling Up
topics.description: What happens when a small business grows; making more products, hiring people, reaching more customers; the challenges and opportunities of scaling
evidence: Describe what 'scaling up' means for a business
Identify at least two challenges of growing a business (need more money, more people, more materials)
Explain how a lemonade stand could grow into a bigger business step by step

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Supply Chains
topics.description: Where products come from before they reach the customer; raw materials, making, transporting, and selling; the journey of a product from start to finish
evidence: Trace the journey of a familiar product (e.g. chocolate bar) from raw material to shop shelf
Identify at least three stages in a supply chain
Explain why a long supply chain can make a product more expensive

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Natural, human and capital resources
topics.description: Classify the resources used to make a product as natural, human or capital, and explain why resources are limited and the choices this forces
evidence: Sort the resources used to make a product (e.g. bread) into natural (wheat, water), human (bakers' skills) and capital (ovens, delivery trucks)
Identify which type of resource a business would need more of to make more of its product and explain why
Explain why resources are limited and what choices a business or family makes as a result

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Keeping food safe and clean
topics.description: Follow food hygiene and safety practices when handling and preparing food: washing hands, cleaning surfaces and equipment, washing fruit and vegetables, keeping cold food cold and checking for allergies
evidence: Wash hands with soap, tie back long hair and wipe down the bench before preparing food
Wash fruit and vegetables and use clean equipment and separate boards for different foods
Explain why some foods are kept in the fridge and why to check for allergies before sharing food

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Preparing simple healthy snacks
topics.description: Select and prepare simple healthy foods by washing, tearing, peeling, spreading, cutting soft foods with a child-safe knife and combining ingredients
evidence: Choose healthy ingredients for a snack (e.g. a fruit kebab or a salad wrap) and explain why they are healthy
Prepare the snack by washing, peeling, spreading and cutting soft foods with a child-safe knife under supervision
Follow simple picture steps to combine the ingredients and serve the snack

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Cutting food with bridge and claw grips
topics.description: Cut fruit and vegetables safely with an appropriate knife under adult supervision, holding the food with the bridge grip (hand arched over the food) or claw grip (fingertips tucked in), keeping the board stable and making controlled cuts
evidence: Set up a stable chopping board (e.g. on a damp cloth) and choose an appropriate knife for the food with an adult
Hold a round vegetable or fruit with the bridge grip and cut it in half with a controlled downward cut
Use the claw grip with fingertips tucked in to slice a vegetable (e.g. a cucumber or carrot) into even pieces, keeping fingers clear of the blade

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Following a measured recipe
topics.description: Prepare a simple recipe by reading the steps, gathering the correct ingredients, measuring them with appropriate cups, spoons or scales, following the steps in order and checking the result
evidence: Read a simple recipe (e.g. fruit smoothie, overnight oats or a no-cook dip) and gather the correct ingredients and equipment
Measure ingredients accurately with measuring cups, spoons or kitchen scales as the recipe states
Follow the recipe steps in order and check the result against the recipe (e.g. right amount, right texture)

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Food characteristics and preparation
topics.description: Explain how the characteristics of foods — nutritional (vitamins, fibre, fat), sensory (taste, texture, colour) and functional (eggs bind, yeast makes dough rise, cut apples brown) — influence how they are selected and prepared for healthy eating, and how a preparation method can change texture, colour and nutrient retention (effects depend on the food, the nutrient and the method)
evidence: Explain how a functional property affects preparation (e.g. eggs bind a burger mix; lemon juice stops cut apple browning)

Compare two preparation methods for the same vegetable (e.g. steaming and boiling broccoli for the same time), record changes in colour, texture and taste, and use the comparison and a reliable source to explain how each method can affect nutrient retention, without assuming one method is always healthier
Run a simple sensory test of a healthy recipe (taste, texture, appearance) and adjust the preparation using the results

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Buying Things
topics.description: How buying and selling works: prices, paying for items, receiving change; the basic transaction process in shops and markets
evidence: Explain what happens when you buy something in a shop (choose, pay, get change)
Read a price label and say whether they have enough money to buy the item
Act out a simple buying scenario using real or play coins

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Coins & Notes
topics.description: Recognise the common coins and notes of the local currency by their features (size, shape, colour, image, texture), know their values, understand that physical size alone does not rank monetary value and that different designs can share one value, and know that different combinations can make the same amount (in Canada, for example: nickel 5¢, dime 10¢, quarter 25¢, loonie $1, toonie $2, and $5, $10, $20 and $50 bills; a play-money penny can stand for 1¢)
evidence: Sort a handful of mixed local coins into groups by value and state the value of common coins and notes when shown them, recognising each by its features (in Canada, for example: nickel 5¢, dime 10¢, quarter 25¢, toonie $2; in Australia: 5c, 10c, 20c, 50c, $1 and $2 coins and $5 to $100 notes)

Order coins and notes by value and explain that a bigger coin is not always worth more (e.g. the Canadian dime is smaller than the nickel but worth more; the Australian $2 coin is smaller than the 50c coin) and that two different designs can have the same value
Find two different ways to make the same amount using different coins and notes, real or virtual

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Jobs People Do
topics.description: Different kinds of work people do; that people earn money by working; how jobs help the community; linking personal interests to possible jobs
evidence: Name at least five different jobs and describe what each person does
Explain that people get paid money for the work they do
Connect a personal interest to a job (e.g. 'I like animals so I could be a vet')

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Looking After Money
topics.description: Keeping money safe; not losing coins or notes; understanding that money has real value and should be treated carefully; basic money responsibility
evidence: Describe at least two ways to keep money safe (purse, wallet, money box, giving to a grown-up)
Explain why it matters if you lose money
Show that they treat real coins and notes carefully rather than leaving them lying around

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Needs & Wants
topics.description: The difference between things we need (food, shelter, clothing) and things we want (toys, treats); that we sometimes have to choose because money is limited
evidence: Sort a set of pictures into 'need' and 'want' categories and explain their choices
Give an example of something everyone needs and something that is a want
Explain why a family might choose to buy a need before a want

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Saving Money
topics.description: Why people save money; piggy banks and saving jars; setting a savings goal; the idea that not spending now means having more later
evidence: Explain why someone might save money instead of spending it straight away
Describe a savings goal they could set and how they would work towards it
Tell you what delayed gratification means in their own words (waiting to get something better)

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: What Money Is
topics.description: What money is and why we use it; that money is exchanged for goods and services; brief history from barter to coins to digital payments
evidence: Explain that people use money to pay for things they need or want
Give an example of how buying worked before money existed (swapping or bartering)
Name at least two forms money can take (coins, notes, card, phone payment)

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Making Change
topics.description: Calculating totals and change from a purchase in the local currency, working with its main and smaller units together (for example pounds and pence, or dollars and cents); solving practical money problems involving addition and subtraction
evidence: Calculate the change from a note when buying items, e.g. from £5 for a £2.75 comic, or from $20 for a $4 drink and a $7 sandwich
Add two or three prices together to find a total cost and say whether a given note is enough
Check whether they have been given the correct change in a role-play scenario (in Australia, cash totals are rounded to the nearest 5 cents)

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Advertising & Spending
topics.description: How advertising tries to influence what we buy; being a critical consumer; understanding 'value for money'; the difference between emotional and rational spending
evidence: Spot at least two persuasion techniques in a real advert (bright colours, celebrity, special offer)
Explain what 'value for money' means and compare two similar products at different prices
Describe a time when advertising made them want something they didn't really need

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Banks & Saving
topics.description: What banks do and why people use them; bank accounts as safe places for money; that savings in a bank can earn interest; children's savings accounts
evidence: Explain what a bank does in simple terms (keeps money safe, lets you save)
Describe what interest means (the bank pays you a little extra for keeping money there)
Name one reason a bank account is safer than keeping all your money at home

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Budgeting Pocket Money
topics.description: What a budget is; planning how to spend a fixed amount of pocket money or allowance; making trade-offs between different things you want to buy
evidence: Create a simple spending plan for £10 showing what they would buy and how much is left
Explain what a budget is and why it helps to plan spending
Identify a trade-off (choosing one thing means not having enough for another)

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Earning Money
topics.description: Ways that children and adults earn money; the connection between work, skills and pay; that harder or more skilled work often pays more
evidence: Name at least three different ways people can earn money
Explain why a doctor might earn more than a shop assistant (training, skills, responsibility)
Describe a way a child could earn money (chores, car wash, selling crafts)

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Fair Trade & Ethics
topics.description: Where products come from and who makes them; that people around the world produce what we buy; fair pay for workers; making ethical choices as consumers
evidence: Explain that the things we buy are made by real people, sometimes in other countries
Describe what 'fair trade' means in simple terms (workers get paid fairly)
Give an example of a kind choice a shopper could make (buying fair trade chocolate, choosing less packaging)

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Ways to Pay
topics.description: Different ways to pay: cash, debit cards, contactless, online payments, mobile payments; that digital payments still use real money; keeping payment details safe
evidence: Name at least four different ways people can pay for things

Explain that an ordinary debit-card or linked-account phone payment spends money from the account, while a credit-card payment creates borrowing that must be repaid; the stated payment arrangement matters
Give one reason why you should keep card numbers and passwords private

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Scams & Online Safety
topics.description: Recognising financial scams and tricks; phishing emails and fake websites; protecting personal and financial information online; 'if it seems too good to be true, it probably is'
evidence: Identify at least two warning signs of a scam (asking for personal details, too-good-to-be-true offers, urgency)
Explain why you should never share passwords or bank details online
Describe what to do if they receive a suspicious message or email (don't click, tell an adult)

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Borrowing & Debt
topics.description: What borrowing money means; that borrowed money must be repaid and interest or fees may be charged under the agreement; what credit is; why too much debt can be risky; responsible borrowing
evidence: Explain what a loan is, that borrowed money must be repaid, and that any interest or fees depend on the agreement
Give an example of when borrowing might be sensible (buying a house) versus risky (buying luxuries you can't afford)
Describe what happens if someone borrows too much money and can't repay it

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Financial Planning
topics.description: Setting longer-term financial goals; planning and prioritising spending; how saving regularly adds up over time; the value of thinking ahead with money
evidence: Set a realistic savings goal and calculate how long it would take saving a fixed amount each week
Create a simple financial plan for a specific purpose (birthday party, school trip, gift)
Explain why planning ahead with money is better than spending everything as it comes in

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Global Trade
topics.description: Why countries trade with each other; imports and exports; how goods travel around the world; that different countries use different currencies
evidence: Explain why countries buy goods from other countries (they can't make everything themselves)
Give examples of imported and exported products from their own country
Explain that different countries use different currencies and you need to exchange money when travelling

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: How the Economy Works
topics.description: What an economy is; producers and consumers; supply and demand; why prices change; the basics of how markets work
evidence: Explain what 'supply and demand' means using a simple example (ice cream on a hot day)
Describe the difference between a producer and a consumer
Give a reason why the price of something might go up or down

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Taxes & Public Services
topics.description: What taxes are and why people pay them; how taxes fund schools, hospitals, roads, and emergency services; that governments decide how to spend tax money
evidence: Explain what tax is and that most working adults pay it
Name at least three things that taxes pay for (schools, hospitals, roads, police, fire service)
Describe why taxes are needed (everyone chips in so everyone benefits)

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Types of taxes and who collects them
topics.description: Describe common kinds of taxes by what is taxed — income, purchases (consumption) and property — and identify which government or governments collect each kind where the learner lives (in some places, including Canada, more than one level of government can collect the same kind of tax), and recognise that collected taxes are pooled to pay for public facilities, services and programs, which can have more than one source of funding
evidence: Sort examples of taxes — money taken from a pay cheque, money added when buying something, and money charged on a home — into taxes on income, purchases and property

Using reliable local information, name which government or governments collect a given kind of tax where they live, giving a local example of more than one level collecting the same kind of tax where that applies (e.g. in Canada, income tax goes to both the federal and the provincial government)
Explain, using one local facility or service (e.g. a library, road repair or school), that tax money is pooled and that the service can be paid for by more than one government or source

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Comparing ways to pay
topics.description: Describe advantages and disadvantages of different ways of paying for goods and services — for example cash, debit card, credit card, prepaid or gift card, or mobile and online payment — using criteria such as convenience, where the method is accepted, what happens if it is lost or stolen, how easily spending can be tracked, and any charges stated in the given situation, and use given information about a purchase to choose a suitable method and explain the choice
evidence: For at least two payment methods, give an advantage and a disadvantage of each (for example, cash needs no card reader but is hard to get back if lost)

Using a given fictional scenario, explain how two chosen methods differ in keeping a record of spending and in any stated charges or where the money comes from (for example, an ordinary debit payment draws from the payer's account, though account terms matter; credit is borrowing that must be repaid, if credit is one of the methods compared)
Given a purchase scenario (such as a bus fare, a present bought online, or lunch at a market stall), choose a payment method and justify the choice using at least two criteria

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Interest rates and bank fees
topics.description: Explain interest as money earned or charged for the use of money, based on the balance, the interest rate (a percent) and the stated period it applies to (for example, per year), and distinguish interest earned on savings from interest charged on loans and credit; explain fees as charges for an account, a service or an event, which may be a flat amount (such as a monthly account fee) or depend on the amount or the number of transactions; and identify the interest rates and fees on given fictional account and loan information, recognising that rates, fees and product types vary between banks and other financial institutions
evidence: Read a fictional savings-account card and a fictional loan card and identify each interest rate, the period it applies to, and each fee and what it is charged for

For a given balance, rate and period (for example, $200 at 3% per year with a $2 monthly fee), explain whether the account holder earns or pays the interest, why a larger balance changes the interest but not a flat monthly fee, and why keeping the account for more months adds more monthly fees

Compare two fictional accounts or loans over the same given period and explain which features (rate, flat fee, transaction-based fee) matter most for a described use, without calculating compound interest

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Addition and subtraction word problems
topics.description: Solve addition and subtraction word problems within 10 using objects or drawings
evidence: Solve 'There are 6 apples, 2 are eaten, how many left?' using counters
Solve 'add to' and 'take from' result-unknown problems
Solve 'put together/take apart' problems with total unknown

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Addition as combining or putting together two

topics.subject: Mathematics

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Adding within 100

Relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Addition and subtraction strategies

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Addition and subtraction within 20

Use a known fact (8 + 4 = 12) to derive 12 − 8 = 4

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Addition in any order

evidence: Explain that 3 + 8 gives the same answer as 8 + 3
Use commutativity to choose the larger number to count on from
Demonstrate that subtraction is not commutative (5 − 3 ≠ 3 − 5)

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Estimating by rounding
topics.description: Estimate the answer to a calculation and use inverse operations to check answers; apply to increasingly large numbers using rounding and inverse reasoning
evidence: Round numbers to the nearest 10 or 100 (or money amounts to the nearest dollar or pound) to estimate a sum or difference before calculating, e.g. $4.95 + $2.10 + $7.85 is about $15
Use addition to check a subtraction answer, or vice versa
Identify when a calculated answer, such as an amount of change, is unreasonable based on the estimate

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Finding a missing number in addition

evidence: Solve 10 − 8 by thinking 'what do I add to 8 to make 10?'

Use known addition facts to solve related subtraction problems

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fluent adding and subtracting within 10
topics.description: Fluently add and subtract within 10
evidence: Answer any addition fact within 10 quickly from memory
Answer any subtraction fact within 10 quickly from memory
Complete a timed set of within-10 facts with high accuracy

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fluent addition and subtraction
topics.description: Recall and use addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently, and derive and use related facts up to 100
evidence: Rapidly recall 7 + 8 = 15 and 15 − 8 = 7
Use 6 + 4 = 10 to derive 60 + 40 = 100
Derive 35 + 5 = 40 from knowledge that 5 + 5 = 10

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Grouping numbers to add
topics.description: Understand and apply the associative property of addition: when adding three numbers, any two can be added first
evidence: Solve 2 + 6 + 4 by first adding 6 + 4 = 10, then 2 + 10 = 12
Explain that grouping addends differently gives the same total
Choose which two numbers to add first to make the calculation easier

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Inverse: addition undoes subtraction
topics.description: Recognise and use the inverse relationship between addition and subtraction to check calculations and solve missing-number problems

Explain that addition and subtraction 'undo' each other

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Mental addition and subtraction (age 6+)

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Mental and written addition and subtraction

evidence: Solve a two-step problem: 'I had 35p, spent 12p, then found 5p. How much now?'
Choose an appropriate method (mental or written) for a given problem
Solve problems involving measures, e.g. 'a ribbon is 45cm, I cut off 18cm'

topics.subject: Mathematics

evidence: Calculate 70 − 30 = 40
Use base-ten blocks to show 80 − 50 = 30

topics.subject: Mathematics

evidence: Solve 'Sam has 4 red, 7 blue and 6 green pencils. How many pencils does he have?' with counters or a drawing, writing 4 + 7 + 6 = ☐ and answering 'Sam has 17 pencils'

topics.subject: Mathematics

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: What the equals sign means

evidence: Explain that 6 = 6 is true because both sides are the same

topics.subject: Mathematics

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fluent adding and subtracting within 20

evidence: Answer any single-digit addition fact within 3 seconds

topics.subject: Mathematics

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Solving Linear Equations
topics.description: Use algebraic methods to solve linear equations in one variable, including equations that require rearrangement, expanding brackets, and collecting terms on both sides; solve equations with rational number coefficients
evidence: Solve one-step and two-step linear equations in one variable
Solve equations requiring expansion of brackets and collection of like terms
Solve equations with the unknown on both sides and with fractional or negative coefficients

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Substituting into Formulae
topics.description: Substitute numerical values into formulae and expressions including scientific formulae; evaluate expressions by replacing variables with given values and computing the result using correct order of operations
evidence: Substitute positive and negative values into algebraic expressions and evaluate
Substitute values into formulae involving multiple operations and powers
Use correct order of operations when evaluating expressions after substitution

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Factorising Expressions
topics.description: Factorise algebraic expressions by taking out common factors — identify the highest common factor of all terms and write the expression as a product, e.g., 6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3)
evidence: Identify the highest common factor of all terms in an expression
Write the factorised form as a product of the HCF and a bracket
Check factorisation by expanding the brackets back out

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Linear Function Graphs
topics.description: Recognise that a linear function produces a straight-line graph, understand the relationship between an equation of the form y = mx + c and its graphical representation, and interpret gradient and y-intercept in context
evidence: Explain that changing m in y = mx + c alters the steepness and direction of the line
Identify the y-intercept of a line from its equation and from its graph
Determine whether a given equation will produce a straight line or a curve

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Plotting Linear Graphs
topics.description: Plot linear graphs by generating a table of values, reduce a two-variable linear equation to the form y = mx + c, and calculate gradients from two points on a line
evidence: Generate a table of (x, y) values for a linear equation and plot the points accurately
Rearrange an equation such as 2x + 3y = 12 into the form y = mx + c
Calculate the gradient between two coordinate points using rise over run

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Simple formulae
topics.description: Understand and use standard mathematical formulae; rearrange formulae to change the subject, performing inverse operations to isolate a different variable
evidence: Identify the subject of a given formula
Use inverse operations to rearrange a formula to make a different variable the subject
Rearrange formulae involving multiple steps including fractions and powers

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Estimating answers (age 13+)
topics.description: Use graphs of linear and quadratic functions to estimate output values for given inputs, find approximate solutions to equations, and interpret graphical information in real-world contexts
evidence: Read off an approximate y-value for a given x from a plotted curve
Find approximate solutions to an equation by identifying where a graph crosses the x-axis or another line
Interpret a real-world graph (e.g., distance–time) to answer contextual questions

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Expanding Double Brackets
topics.description: Expand products of two or more binomials, e.g., (x + 3)(x - 2) = x² + x - 6, using the grid method or FOIL; simplify the result by collecting like terms
evidence: Expand the product of two binomials using a systematic method (grid or FOIL)
Collect like terms after expansion to simplify the result
Expand products involving negative terms correctly

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Quadratic Graphs
topics.description: Recognise that quadratic functions produce curved (parabolic) graphs, distinguish them from linear graphs, and use plotted quadratic graphs to estimate values and find approximate solutions
evidence: Explain why x² produces a U-shaped curve rather than a straight line
Plot a simple quadratic such as y = x² − 4 from a table of values
Read approximate solutions from a quadratic graph (e.g., where y = 0)

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Simultaneous Equations
topics.description: Understand that two linear equations can be solved simultaneously by finding the point where their graphs intersect, and interpret this graphically and algebraically as the pair of values satisfying both equations
evidence: Explain that the intersection of two lines represents values satisfying both equations
Find the approximate solution to a pair of simultaneous equations by reading a graph
Verify a proposed solution by substituting into both equations

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing groups: more or fewer
topics.description: Compare two groups of objects to determine which has more, fewer, or whether they are equal, using matching and counting strategies
evidence: Use one-to-one matching to compare two groups
State which group has more/fewer after counting both
Use the language 'equal to', 'more than', 'less than', 'fewer', 'most', 'least'

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: How Many in Total?
topics.description: Cardinality principle: the last number said when counting a set tells how many objects are in the set, regardless of arrangement or order counted
evidence: After counting a set, answer 'how many?' with the last number stated
Understand that rearranging objects does not change the count
Understand that counting in a different order gives the same total

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: One More Each Time
topics.description: Each successive counting number represents a quantity that is one larger than the previous number
evidence: Given a set of 5, know that adding one object makes 6
Explain that 8 is one more than 7
Given a number, identify one more and one less

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: One-to-one counting
topics.description: One-to-one correspondence when counting objects: each object is paired with exactly one number name
evidence: Point to or touch each object exactly once while saying number names
Do not skip objects or double-count when counting a set
Recognise an error when someone counts an object twice

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Representing numbers with objects
topics.description: Represent numbers using objects, pictorial representations, and the number line
evidence: Show a given number using counters, cubes, or fingers
Draw a pictorial representation of a quantity (e.g. tally marks, dots)
Locate a number on a number line

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Two written numerals between 1 and 10
topics.description: Compare two written numerals between 1 and 10 to determine which is greater or less
evidence: Given two written numerals (e.g. 4 and 7), identify which is greater
Correctly use > and < or 'greater than' / 'less than' to compare single-digit numerals

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Counting in 2s
topics.description: Count in multiples of 2, 5, and 10 (skip counting)
evidence: Count 2, 4, 6, 8 … up to at least 20
Count 5, 10, 15, 20 … up to at least 50
Count 10, 20, 30 … up to 100

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Counting objects to 20
topics.description: Count a set of objects to answer 'how many?' for sets up to 20 (arranged in lines, arrays, circles, or scattered)
evidence: Accurately count up to 20 objects in a line
Count up to 10 scattered objects without losing track
Given a number 1–20, count out that many objects from a larger set

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Rote counting to 100
topics.description: Rote count forwards and backwards from 0 to 100, beginning from 0, 1, or any given number, by ones
evidence: Recite the number sequence 1–100 without skipping or repeating
Count backward from 20 to 0
Count forward starting from a number other than 1 (e.g. 'start at 23')

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Seeing parts within 10
topics.description: Use subitising to recognise and name the parts of a collection up to 10 and combine them — e.g. seeing 7 on a ten frame as 5 and 2, or a domino as 3 and 3 — connecting part-part-whole thinking to quick recognition
evidence: Look at a ten frame showing 7 and say 'five and two more makes seven' without counting every dot
Name the two parts on a domino showing 4 and 2 and say the total is 6
Show 8 as two groups (e.g. 4 and 4, or 5 and 3) and name the parts quickly

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Subitising to 5
topics.description: Recognise and name the number of objects in a collection of up to 5 instantly, without counting one by one (subitising), using dot patterns, dice faces, fingers and small groups of objects
evidence: Say how many dots are on a dice face showing 4 after a one-second glimpse, without counting
Show 3 fingers quickly without counting them up one at a time
Name the number in a flashed group of 2 or 5 counters arranged in different layouts

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Counting big collections in groups
topics.description: Quantify collections of up to 120 objects by partitioning them into equal groups (twos, fives or tens) and skip counting, explaining why grouping makes counting faster and more reliable
evidence: Count 85 pegs by sorting them into groups of ten and counting on 10, 20, ... 80, 85
Count 46 shoes by pairing them and skip counting by twos
Explain why counting 120 straws in bundles of ten is easier than counting one by one

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Counting forwards and backwards
topics.description: Count forwards and backwards in steps of 3 from 0
evidence: Count 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 … up to at least 30
Count backwards in 3s from 30
Identify the next number in a sequence of multiples of 3

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Counting forwards and backwards (age 6+)
topics.description: Count forwards and backwards in tens from any number (not just multiples of 10)
evidence: Count 7, 17, 27, 37 … from a non-multiple starting point
Count backwards in tens from 83
Explain the pattern of adding/subtracting 10

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Counting Within 1,000
topics.description: Count within 1000, including skip-counting by 5s, 10s, and 100s
evidence: Count forwards and backwards within 1000 from any starting number
Skip-count by 5s from any multiple of 5 to 1000
Skip-count by 100s from any number (e.g. 150, 250, 350 …)

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Skip Counting (4s, 8s, 50s, 100s)
topics.description: Count from 0 in multiples of 4, 8, 50, and 100
evidence: Recite the multiples of 4 from 0 to at least 48
Recite the multiples of 8 from 0 to at least 96
Count in steps of 50 and 100 from 0 to 1000

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Counting in 6s
topics.description: Count in multiples of 6, 7, 9, 25, and 1000
evidence: Recite the multiples of 6 from 0 to at least 72
Recite the multiples of 7 from 0 to at least 84
Count in steps of 25 from 0 to 1000 and in steps of 1000 up to 10,000

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Pictograms and tally charts
topics.description: Interpret and construct simple pictograms, tally charts, block diagrams, and simple tables, including giving displays a title, labels and the source of the data
evidence: Read a pictogram where each symbol represents one item
Construct a tally chart from collected data
Draw a block diagram, or build a concrete graph with one real object per data value, and give it a title, category labels and the data source (e.g. 'Our class survey, Monday')

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Sorting into categories
topics.description: Classify objects into given categories, count the number in each category, and sort the categories by count
evidence: Sort a set of shapes by colour and count how many in each group
Sort objects by size (big/small) and state how many in each category
Identify which category has the most/fewest after sorting and counting

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Carrying out a statistical investigation
topics.description: Carry out a statistical investigation for a given question of interest: collect categorical or discrete numerical data (for example by observation or survey), record and represent it in a suitable display (by hand or with digital tools) and interpret the results in terms of the question
evidence: Investigate 'Which playground equipment is used most at lunch?' by tallying observations over three days or by collecting survey responses
Represent the results in a bar graph with a title and labelled axes, by hand or with a digital tool
Write two sentences answering the investigation question using the data

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Collecting data for a question
topics.description: Acquire categorical and discrete numerical data to address a question of interest by observing, collecting or accessing a data set, and record it using appropriate methods including frequency tables and spreadsheets
evidence: Collect data on how students travel to school to answer 'What is the most common way to get to school?', e.g. by observation, a class survey or an online form
Record the number of siblings each classmate has in a frequency table with tallies and totals
Enter the same data into a spreadsheet with one column for the category and one for the count

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing results from two groups
topics.description: Predict whether the category counts from one group (e.g. a class tally of favourite fruit) will be the same in a different group of the same size, collect or check the second group's counts, compare the two tallies or pictographs category by category, and explain why equal-size groups can still give different counts
evidence: Predict before collecting whether another class of the same size will choose favourite fruits in the same numbers as their own class, and give a reason
Collect or check the second group's tallies and compare them with the first group's category by category (e.g. 'apples: 8 in ours, 5 in theirs')
Say whether their prediction was right and explain that groups of the same size can like different things, so their counts need not match

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Pictograms and tally charts (age 6+)
topics.description: Read, write, and use the vocabulary of data collection and display — data, tally, tally chart, frequency, frequency table, survey, pictogram, bar chart, axis/axes, scale, label, category, discrete data, continuous data, line graph, pie chart — and apply these terms when collecting, organising, and presenting data
evidence: Correctly label the axes of a bar chart including a title, axis labels, and scale
Distinguish between discrete data (counted) and continuous data (measured) with an example of each
Use 'tally', 'frequency', and 'pictogram' correctly when describing how to record and display data

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Picture & Bar Graphs
topics.description: Draw a picture graph and a bar graph (with single-unit scale) to represent a data set with up to four categories; solve put-together, take-apart, and compare problems using information presented in a bar graph
evidence: Draw a picture graph with a symbol representing one unit for each data point
Draw a bar graph with labelled axes and a single-unit scale
Use a bar graph to answer comparison questions (e.g. 'How many more votes did cats get than dogs?')

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Sorting Data into Categories
topics.description: Organise and represent data with up to three categories by counting objects in each category and sorting categories by quantity
evidence: Sort a set of objects into 2-3 given categories and count each group
Create a simple table or list showing category names and counts
Order categories from most to fewest or fewest to most

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Sorting into categories (age 6+)
topics.description: Interpret categorical data by asking and answering questions about totals, how many in each category, and how many more or less one category has than another
evidence: Answer 'how many?' for each category in a data set
Calculate the total number of data points across all categories
Compare two categories using 'how many more/fewer' language

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Choosing displays for a purpose
topics.description: Compare different displays of the same data set (for example a tally chart and a picture graph, or a table and a bar graph), describe what is common and what each display makes easy to see, and choose the display that best suits a question or purpose
evidence: Show the same pet survey as a tally chart and as a picture graph and say what is the same in both and what each makes easier to see
Answer the same question (e.g. 'How many chose dogs?') from two different displays of the same data and say which display made it quicker
Choose a table to read an exact count and a bar graph to compare categories at a glance for a given purpose, and explain the choice

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Finding the mode
topics.description: Identify the mode of a data set shown in a tally, pictograph, concrete graph, bar graph, line plot or table: every value or category that occurs most often, so a data set can have one mode or several tied modes; use the convention that there is no mode when every value occurs exactly once; explain what the mode tells about the data; and compare the modes of two data sets
evidence: Point to the mode on a pictograph or bar graph of favourite fruits and on a line plot of shoe sizes, and say it is the most common response
Name every mode when two or more categories tie for the most (e.g. apples, bananas and grapes each chosen 6 times), and say there is no mode when every value occurs exactly once
Find the modes of two classes' favourite-fruit tallies and say whether the modes are the same, even when the counts in each category are different

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Sorting data by two attributes
topics.description: Sort and organise data about people or things according to two attributes at the same time using a Venn diagram (with an overlap), a Carroll diagram or two-way table, or a two-way tally table, and read and answer questions from these logic diagrams and tables
evidence: Sort a set of pictures or shapes into a Venn diagram for two attributes (e.g. 'has stripes' and 'has four legs'), placing items with both in the overlap and items with neither outside
Record a class survey with two pieces of information (e.g. pet type and whether they walk to school) in a two-way tally table or Carroll diagram and give the total in each cell
Answer questions from a Venn diagram, Carroll diagram or two-way table (e.g. 'How many have stripes but not four legs?') and draw a simple conclusion

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Bar graphs
topics.description: Interpret and present discrete and continuous data using appropriate graphical methods, including bar charts and time graphs
evidence: Read a time graph showing temperature changes over a day
Present data about plant growth over weeks as a time graph
Explain the difference between a bar chart (discrete) and a time graph (continuous)

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Calculating the Mean
topics.description: Calculate and interpret the mean as an average of a data set
evidence: Calculate the mean of five test scores: 72, 85, 90, 68, 95
Explain what the mean represents and how it differs from individual data values
Find a missing data value given the mean and all other values

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Reading tables
topics.description: Complete, read, and interpret information in tables, including timetables
evidence: Read a bus timetable to find the departure time for a particular stop
Complete a two-way table from given data about favourite sports by gender
Calculate how long a train journey takes using a timetable

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Scaled picture and bar graphs
topics.description: Draw a scaled picture graph and a scaled bar graph to represent a data set; solve one- and two-step comparison, sum, and difference problems using bar charts, pictograms, and tables
evidence: Draw a bar graph where each square represents 5 pets
From a scaled pictogram, answer: how many more children chose football than tennis?
Solve a two-step problem: how many votes in total for the top two choices?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing displays and distributions
topics.description: Analyse how effectively different displays or visualisations show and compare data distributions, and describe the shape of a distribution and the variation in the data
evidence: Compare a column graph and a pictograph of the same data and explain which shows the differences between categories more clearly
Describe a dot plot of hand spans as 'most values cluster around 16 cm with a few much larger'
Explain which display best compares the heights of two classes and why

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Finding the median
topics.description: Find the median of a data set by putting the values in order and taking the middle value when there is an odd number of values, or the value halfway between the two middle values when there is an even number (so the median need not be one of the data values and need not be a whole number), and explain that the median is a central value of the ordered data: at least half of the values are at or below it and at least half are at or above it
evidence: Put five values such as 12, 7, 15, 9 and 10 in order and state that the median is 10, the middle value
Find the median of an even number of values such as 4, 6, 7, 8, 10, 12 by finding the value halfway between the two middle values 7 and 8 (7.5, or 7½)
Find the median of a data set with repeated values, such as 1, 2, 2, 2, 9 (median 2), and explain that at least half of the values are at or below 2 and at least half are at or above 2

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Line graph problems
topics.description: Solve comparison, sum, and difference problems using information presented in a line graph
evidence: Read a line graph of temperature over a week and identify the warmest day
Find the difference in rainfall between two months from a line graph
Explain what a rising/falling line means on a time-series graph

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Multiple-bar graphs
topics.description: Construct and read a multiple-bar (grouped) bar graph that shows two or more data sets side by side for the same categories, using a key that maps each colour or pattern to its data set, a title, axis labels and an appropriate scale; compare the data sets within each category and across categories, recognising that bar heights show counts, so when the groups are different sizes a taller bar does not by itself mean a larger share of that group
evidence: Draw a multiple-bar graph of favourite sports for two classes, with each class's bar beside the other for every sport, a key, a title, labelled axes and a suitable scale
Read a given multiple-bar graph, using the key, to compare the data sets for one category and to find the category where they differ most
Explain, using the group sizes, why the group with more votes for a sport is not necessarily the group in which that sport is more popular when the groups are different sizes

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Statistical Analysis Vocabulary
topics.description: Read, write, and use the vocabulary of statistical analysis — mean, median, mode, range, frequency, data, sample, average, chart, table, graph, pie chart, scatter graph, correlation — with understanding of what each term describes
evidence: Correctly define and calculate the mean, median, mode, and range of a small data set
Use 'outlier' correctly to identify a value that doesn't fit the pattern, and explain its effect on the mean
Use 'correlation' correctly when describing the relationship shown in a scatter graph

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Stem-and-leaf plots
topics.description: Organise a data set into a stem-and-leaf plot by splitting each value by place value into a stem (e.g. the tens, or the hundreds and tens for larger values) and a leaf (the next digit), listing the stems in order and every leaf in order on its row, including repeated values, with a key that states the place value (e.g. 4 | 7 = 47); read a stem-and-leaf plot to find values, the least and greatest values, how many values there are, and where values cluster or leave gaps; and compare two data sets shown in separate plots that use the same key
evidence: Make a stem-and-leaf plot of scores such as 38, 41, 47, 47, 52, 59, 63 with the stems in order, the leaves in order on each row (writing a repeated value such as 47 twice) and a key such as 4 | 7 = 47
Read a given stem-and-leaf plot to state the smallest and largest values, how many values there are, and where the values cluster or leave gaps
Compare two data sets shown in separate stem-and-leaf plots with the same key (e.g. the jump distances of two groups) and say, using the plots, which set has more high values

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Critiquing statistics in the media
topics.description: Identify statistically informed arguments in traditional and digital media and critique their methods, data representations (e.g. truncated axes, distorted pictographs, selective data) and conclusions
evidence: Explain how a bar graph whose vertical axis starts at 90 exaggerates a small difference
Identify the sample size and who was surveyed in a news claim such as '9 out of 10 kids prefer Brand X' and judge whether the conclusion is justified
Rewrite a misleading online headline so that it matches what the data actually show

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Line graphs
topics.description: Construct and interpret line graphs for continuous data (e.g. temperature over time, plant growth); read intermediate values, identify trends, and solve comparison and difference problems
evidence: Read values from a line graph showing temperature over a day, including estimating between plotted points
Construct a line graph from a table of continuous data, choosing an appropriate scale and labelling axes correctly
Use a line graph to solve a two-step problem, such as finding the time period with the greatest rate of change

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Line plots with fractions
topics.description: Make a line plot to display a data set of measurements in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8); use operations on fractions to solve problems involving data in line plots (e.g. redistribute total equally)
evidence: Create a line plot showing lengths measured to the nearest 1/8 inch
Use the line plot to find the total of all measurements by adding fractions
Solve: 'If the total liquid were redistributed equally among all beakers, how much would each have?'

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Pie charts
topics.description: Interpret and construct pie charts: calculate sector angles from data, draw sectors accurately, and read values from pie charts to solve problems
evidence: Read a pie chart and determine what fraction or percentage of the total each sector represents
Construct a pie chart from given data by calculating sector angles
Use a pie chart to determine the actual quantity represented by each sector given the total

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Planning a statistical investigation
topics.description: Plan and conduct a statistical investigation by posing a question or identifying a problem, collecting relevant data, choosing appropriate displays, interpreting the data and communicating findings in context
evidence: Pose an investigation question such as 'Do Year 5 students sleep less on school nights?', refining a vague question (e.g. 'Do kids like sport?') into one that data can answer, and plan how to collect the data
Choose and justify a display (column graph, dot plot or table) for the collected data
Write a short report that answers the question and states one limitation of the data

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Populations, samples and fair sampling
topics.description: Distinguish a population from a sample drawn from it; explain why a convenient or biased sample (choosing whoever is easiest to reach, volunteers, or a group linked to the answer) can misrepresent the population; explain that random selection gives every member of the population an equal chance of being chosen, which tends to produce representative samples — while recognising that any single random sample can still, by chance, be unrepresentative
evidence: In a described survey (e.g. a school asks 40 of its 800 pupils about the lunch menu), identify the population and the sample, and explain why a sample is used instead of asking everyone

Identify the selection bias in a sampling method (e.g. asking people leaving a gym how often they exercise, or surveying only the lunch queue on pizza day), explain the direction in which it would likely distort the result, and propose a better method using random selection from the whole population (e.g. drawing names from the full school register)

Explain the difference between random selection and simply choosing whoever is easiest to reach, and explain — with an example such as a random sample of 10 pupils that happens to contain mostly Year 7s — why random sampling makes a representative sample likely but does not guarantee it

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Stacked-bar graphs
topics.description: Construct and read stacked-bar graphs (vertical or horizontal) in which each bar is divided into segments for the categories of a data set, building each bar by placing every segment on top of the previous one and using a key, title, labels, source and an appropriate scale; read a segment's size as the difference between its top and bottom edges (not the value at its top) and read each bar's total; and compare the make-up of different groups, using bars that show each part as a share of its group's total (a relative-frequency or 100% scale) when the groups are different sizes
evidence: Build a stacked-bar graph from given counts (e.g. how students in three classes travel to school: walk, bus, car), stacking the segments in the same order in every bar, with a key, title, labels, source and a suitable scale
Read a stacked bar to find one segment's value by subtracting the value at its bottom edge from the value at its top edge, and read the total for the whole bar

Explain why a stacked bar that shows each segment as a share of its group's total is better for comparing two groups of different sizes than counts alone, and use such bars to compare the groups' make-up

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Validating and describing categorical data
topics.description: Acquire, validate and represent nominal and ordinal categorical and discrete numerical data using software including spreadsheets, process it (totals, differences), and report on the distribution by its mode and shape in context
evidence: Check a spreadsheet of survey responses for missing or impossible entries and correct or remove them
Classify 'favourite colour' as nominal and 'rating from 1 to 5' as ordinal and explain the difference
Use spreadsheet formulas to total each category, then report the mode and describe the shape of the column graph

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Average distance from the mean
topics.description: Calculate the mean absolute deviation (MAD) of a small numerical data set — find the mean, find each value's distance from the mean (a non-negative number: a value equal to the mean has distance 0), then find the mean of those distances; interpret the MAD as the average distance of the values from the mean, stated in the original units of the data (e.g. minutes, cm, points); and use MADs to compare the spread or consistency of two data sets, recognising that a larger MAD means values typically sit further from the mean and that the MAD is 0 only when every value equals the mean
evidence: Calculate the MAD of 4, 6, 8, 9, 13 (mean 8; distances 4, 2, 0, 1, 5; MAD 2.4), counting the value equal to the mean as a distance of 0
Explain that a MAD of 3 cm for a set of plant heights means the heights are, on average, 3 cm away from the mean height
Decide which of two bowlers, both with a mean score of 120, is more consistent when their MADs are 8 and 21 points, and justify the choice

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Averages and range
topics.description: Describe, interpret, and compare observed distributions of a single variable using measures of central tendency (mean, median, mode) and spread (range), including choosing a suitable average and the effect of outliers; comparisons describe the observed data sets themselves and do not yet scale the difference in centres by a measure of variability or generalise from samples to wider populations
evidence: Find the mean, median and mode of 3, 5, 5, 6, 11 (6, 5 and 5) and say which average best represents a typical value
Find the range of 12, 14, 15, 15, 48 and explain why the outlier 48 pulls the mean (20.8) well above the median (15)
Compare two classes' spelling scores using their medians and ranges and write one conclusion about which class did better and one about which was more consistent

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Box plots
topics.description: Construct and interpret a box plot on a numerical scale from a five-number summary (minimum, lower quartile, median, upper quartile, maximum), using the stated convention that the whiskers extend to the minimum and maximum values; interpret the median, quartiles, IQR and range, recognising that each whisker and each half of the box represents roughly a quarter of the data however long or short it is drawn; explain what a box plot does not show (individual values, clusters, gaps, the number of values, or the mean); and compare two distributions using their box plots
evidence: Draw a box plot for the five-number summary 3, 6, 9, 14, 21 on a labelled scale, stating that the whiskers run from the minimum to the maximum, and read the median, quartiles, IQR (8) and range (18) back from a given box plot

Explain that the longer upper whisker (from 14 to 21) shows the top quarter of values is more spread out — not that it contains more values — and reject claims a box plot cannot support, such as 'the mean is 9', 'most values are close to 9' or the exact number of data values

Explain with an example how two data sets can have the same box plot but different shapes (e.g. one with values spread evenly, the other with two clusters separated by a gap), and compare two classes' box plots using their medians and IQRs in context

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing data sets digitally
topics.description: Interpret and compare data sets for nominal and ordinal categorical and discrete and continuous numerical variables using comparative displays (side-by-side column graphs with ordinal categories in a common order, back-to-back dot plots) made with digital tools, processing the data (percentages, ranges) and comparing distributions by mode, range and shape
evidence: Make a side-by-side column graph in a spreadsheet comparing the favourite sports (nominal) of Year 3 and Year 6 students and state the mode for each group

Compare two classes' ratings of 'How much do you enjoy reading?' (never, sometimes, often, always) as percentages on side-by-side graphs with the categories in the same order, and say which class's ratings sit higher on the scale
Compare two classes' jump distances by mode, range and shape using back-to-back dot plots made with a digital tool

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Describing distributions
topics.description: Describe the distribution of a numerical data set by its centre, spread and overall shape — recognising clusters, gaps, peaks, symmetry or skew (a longer tail on one side) and unusual values — and interpret each feature in the context in which the data were collected, recognising that distributions with similar centres can differ greatly in spread and shape
evidence: Describe a dot plot of 25 pupils' reaction times by its centre (a typical value), its spread (where most values lie and how far they extend) and its shape — naming any cluster, gap, symmetry or skew and unusual value — and link each feature to the context (e.g. a gap between two groups of times might reflect pupils who had practised and pupils who had not)

Compare two distributions with the same mean — e.g. two classes both averaging 60% on a test, one with scores clustered between 52% and 68%, the other spread from 20% to 95% in two separate clusters — and explain what the shared mean hides and why the difference matters in context

Use the context to judge whether an unusual value is more likely a recording error or a genuine extreme (e.g. a reaction time of 4.2 s among times near 0.3 s), and identify claims the display alone cannot support, such as the reason for a skew or that the same pattern would hold for a different group

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Dot plots
topics.description: Construct and interpret dot plots for numerical data sets of any kind (counts, scores, times or measurements), extending earlier measurement line plots: draw a number-line scale with equal intervals that runs from at least the minimum to the maximum value, including values nobody recorded so that gaps stay visible; place one dot per observation, stacking repeated values in evenly spaced columns; label the scale with the attribute and its units; and read the plot to find how often a value occurs, the minimum, maximum and most common values, and the total number of observations, recognising that the height of a stack is a count of observations, not a data value
evidence: Draw a dot plot of 20 pupils' numbers of books read last month (values 0 to 12) on a scale marked 0, 1, 2, …, 12, leaving the empty value 7 visible as a gap and stacking the four 3s evenly
Read from a dot plot that the value 5 occurs 6 times, the minimum is 0, the maximum is 12 and the most common value is 5
Explain that a stack of 6 dots above 5 means six pupils each read 5 books, not that someone read 6 books, and count all the dots to give the number of pupils

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Histograms
topics.description: Construct and interpret histograms for continuous or numerical data grouped into equal-width class intervals on a continuous number-line scale, with no gaps between bars; state the interval-boundary convention used (e.g. 140 ≤ h < 150, so a value of exactly 150 belongs to the next interval); read frequencies from bar heights; describe the distribution shown; and explain how a histogram differs from a bar chart of categories. Unequal-width intervals and frequency density are not included.
evidence: Group 30 pupils' heights into equal-width 10 cm intervals (130 ≤ h < 140, 140 ≤ h < 150, …), stating that a height of exactly 150 cm is counted in the 150 ≤ h < 160 interval, and draw the histogram with a continuous horizontal scale, touching bars and labelled axes

Read frequencies accurately from a histogram (e.g. how many pupils are at least 150 cm but less than 160 cm, and how many are shorter than 150 cm in total) and describe the distribution's centre, spread and shape in context

Explain why a histogram's bars touch and sit on a numerical scale while a bar chart of categories (e.g. favourite sport) has gaps and an order that could be rearranged — and identify claims the histogram cannot support, such as the exact height of the tallest pupil or how many pupils are exactly 145 cm tall

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Pictograms and tally charts (age 11+)
topics.description: Construct and interpret frequency tables, bar charts, pie charts, pictograms, and vertical line charts for both categorical and grouped numerical data, choosing appropriate representations for the data type
evidence: Construct a grouped frequency table from raw continuous data, choosing appropriate class intervals
Draw a pie chart by calculating the angle for each category
Interpret a bar chart comparing two data sets and draw a conclusion about the difference

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Quartiles and interquartile range
topics.description: Find the median, lower quartile and upper quartile of a data set using one explicit convention — order the data, find the median, split the data into a lower and an upper half (leaving out the median itself when there is an odd number of values), and take the median of each half as the lower and upper quartile — while recognising that other textbooks, calculators and software may use slightly different conventions; calculate the interquartile range (IQR = upper quartile − lower quartile) and interpret it as the spread of the middle half of the data; and compare what the range and the IQR reveal, including their different sensitivity to extreme values
evidence: Using the stated convention, find the median (9), lower quartile (6, the median of 3, 5, 6, 7, 8) and upper quartile (14, the median of 11, 12, 14, 15, 21) of the 11 values 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12, 14, 15, 21, giving IQR = 8; and for the 10 values 2, 4, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 15, find median 7.5, lower quartile 4 and upper quartile 10, giving IQR = 6

Interpret an IQR in context (e.g. 'the middle half of the puzzle times lie between 6 and 14 minutes, a spread of 8 minutes') and explain that about half of the values lie between the quartiles, with about a quarter below the lower quartile and about a quarter above the upper quartile

Show that changing the largest value from 21 to 40 increases the range from 18 to 37 but leaves the IQR at 8, and use this to decide — and justify — whether the range or the IQR gives the better summary of spread for a data set with an extreme value or a long tail

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Statistical questions
topics.description: Distinguish a statistical question — one that anticipates variability in the data collected to answer it, so its answer must account for that variability (even when it is reported as a single summary value such as a mean or median) — from a question answered by a single fixed fact; for a statistical question, identify the population (who or what is being asked about), the attribute being investigated, and the variation expected in the answers
evidence: Sort questions such as 'How tall am I?', 'How tall are the pupils in my class?', 'How many days are in March?' and 'How many hours of sleep do 12-year-olds usually get?' into statistical and non-statistical, explaining each choice by whether the answers are expected to vary

For a given statistical question, name the population and the attribute being measured, describe the variation they expect (e.g. 'sleep times will differ from person to person, perhaps from 7 to 11 hours'), and explain that a good answer must account for that variability in the data — even a single-number summary such as 'a typical 12-year-old sleeps about 9 hours' stands for many differing values, unlike the one fixed answer to 'How many days are in March?'

Explain why a question about a group can still be non-statistical (e.g. 'How many pupils are in my class?' has one fixed answer), and rewrite a non-statistical question as a statistical one (e.g. 'How long is my journey to school?' becomes 'How long are journeys to school for pupils in my year?')

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: What was measured, and how
topics.description: Before summarising a numerical data set, state its context precisely: report the number of observations (n) by counting the values in a list or the dots on a dot plot, or by adding the frequencies in a table or histogram (not by counting rows or bars); describe the attribute investigated (what was measured or counted, and for whom or what), how it was measured (the instrument or method and the precision or rounding used, e.g. measured with a tape to the nearest cm versus self-reported) and its units; and use these details to give every summary value with its units and to judge what the data can show, for example recognising when values bunch at round numbers because of how they were recorded
evidence: Report that a frequency table with frequencies 3, 7, 6 and 4 records 20 observations, not 4 (the number of rows) or 7 (the largest frequency)
Write a context statement such as 'hand spans of 28 pupils, measured with a ruler from thumb tip to little-finger tip, to the nearest 0.5 cm'
Explain that a pile-up of self-reported bedtimes at exactly 9:00 and 9:30 may come from people rounding their answers rather than from real bedtimes

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Writing a data summary
topics.description: Write a complete summary of a numerical data set in relation to its context, bringing together: the number of observations; the attribute, how it was measured and its units; a measure of centre with a matching measure of variability, each with units, chosen between median with IQR and mean with MAD; the overall pattern and any striking deviations, interpreted in context; and a justification of that choice by the shape of the distribution and the context (e.g. median and IQR for skewed data or data with extreme values, mean and MAD for roughly symmetric data without extreme values)
evidence: Write a summary of 25 pupils' reaction times that states n, the attribute, how it was measured and the units, a centre and a matching measure of spread with units, and any unusual value
Choose the median and IQR rather than the mean and MAD for a set of journey times with a long tail of slow journeys, and justify the choice by that tail
Rewrite the summary 'the average is 14' as 'the 30 pupils' median journey time is 14 minutes, with the middle half of times between 9 and 22 minutes'

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing two populations
topics.description: Use measures of centre and variability calculated from random samples of two populations to make informal comparative inferences about those populations (e.g. whether words in a Grade 7 science book are generally longer than words in a Grade 4 science book): check that each sample was randomly drawn from the population it is meant to describe and is reasonably representative; weigh the difference between the sample centres against the variability within the samples and against how much centres vary from one random sample to another; and state qualified conclusions ('generally', 'on average', 'probably') rather than claiming every member of one population exceeds every member of the other — recognising that a small difference between two samples may be due to chance alone
evidence: Compare random samples of 20 word lengths from two books (means 6.2 and 4.4 letters, both MADs about 0.9) and conclude that the first book probably uses longer words on average
Explain why surveying volunteers at one school's sports club cannot support a conclusion that all pupils at that school are fitter than pupils at another school
Judge that a 1-point difference between two sample medians is not convincing when repeated random samples from one population give medians that vary by about 3 points

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Estimating from a sample
topics.description: Use data from a random sample to estimate a characteristic of the population, such as a proportion, total count, or mean; present the result as an estimate rather than an exact population measurement; state the assumptions the inference relies on (the sample was randomly drawn from the population being described and is reasonably representative) and explain how the conclusion is limited or invalid when those assumptions fail
evidence: Use a sample proportion to estimate a population count — e.g. 18 of a random sample of 60 pupils walk to school, so estimate about 270 of the school's 900 pupils walk — and state the answer as an approximate estimate rather than an exact count
