topics.description: Move between a real-world situation and a mathematical representation using concrete objects, drawings, diagrams, tables, number sentences, or bar models
evidence: Given a story about combining groups, represent it with counters or cubes and find the total
Given a set of objects, tell a simple addition or subtraction story to match
Connect a physical action (putting together, taking away) to the matching operation

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Spotting mathematical patterns
topics.description: Notice simple patterns and structures: spot that changing order doesn't change the total, and recognise how numbers relate to each other
evidence: Notice that 3 + 2 gives the same answer as 2 + 3 (early commutativity)
Recognise that teen numbers are 'ten and some more' (e.g. 14 is 10 and 4)
Spot a pattern in a sequence of objects or numbers and predict what comes next

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Using objects to model real problems
topics.description: Use objects, drawings, or simple number sentences to represent a real-world situation (early mathematical modelling)
evidence: Draw a picture or use objects to represent a simple real-world situation involving counting or comparing
Write or dictate a number sentence to describe a real-world situation (e.g. 'I had 5 apples and ate 2')
Use the model to answer a question about the situation

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Connecting maths to real life
topics.description: Represent real-world problems with number sentences, bar models, or diagrams, and interpret the mathematical result back in context; use the model to make a prediction, check it against the real situation and revise the model if it does not fit (early modelling cycle)
evidence: Choose and write a number sentence, bar model or diagram for a measurement, money, two-step or comparison word problem
Interpret the numerical answer in context (e.g. '15 cm means the ribbon is 15 centimetres long')
Use the model to predict something about the situation (e.g. how many cups the class needs), check against what really happens and change the model if it does not fit

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Connecting Representations
topics.description: Move between real-world situations, drawings, and number sentences, explaining how each representation connects to the others (quantitative reasoning)
evidence: Write a number sentence (e.g. 14 + 5 = 19) to match a word problem and explain the connection
Draw a bar model or part-whole diagram to represent a problem, then solve using the diagram
Translate between a concrete model and a symbolic equation, describing what each number represents

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Explaining Mathematical Reasoning
topics.description: With teacher prompting, explain and justify mathematical reasoning using drawings, number sentences, or words
evidence: Explain a solution strategy using a drawing or number sentence (e.g. 'I made ten first, then added the rest')
Justify why an answer is correct by showing an alternative method that gives the same result
Identify and explain an error in a worked example or a peer's solution

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Generalising Patterns
topics.description: Recognise and use repeated reasoning to generalise: spot calculation patterns, describe rules for sequences, and predict results using known mathematical facts
evidence: Use a known doubles fact to derive a near-doubles answer (e.g. 6 + 7 = 6 + 6 + 1 = 13)
Notice that subtracting 10 from any two-digit number always reduces the tens digit by 1
Describe a rule for a pattern and use it to extend or predict (e.g. 'each time we add 5, the ones digit alternates between 0 and 5')

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Guided Multi-Step Problem Solving
topics.description: With teacher guidance, make sense of multi-step and more complex problems by planning a pathway to the solution, identifying relevant information, and choosing appropriate operations
evidence: When given a word problem within 20 or 100, identify the known information and what needs to be found
Try a strategy (drawing, number line, known fact) and switch approach if the first attempt stalls
Check the reasonableness of an answer using estimation or a different method

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Numbers on a number line
topics.description: Select and use appropriate tools and representations (number lines, hundred squares, rulers, part-whole models) to support problem-solving
evidence: Choose a number line or hundred square to support adding or subtracting two-digit numbers
Select a ruler when a problem requires measuring length
Explain why one representation (e.g. a number line vs cubes) is more helpful for a particular problem

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Precise Maths Communication
topics.description: Communicate with mathematical precision: use correct vocabulary, specify units, and use symbols accurately
evidence: Use the = sign correctly to mean 'is the same as' rather than 'the answer is'
Include units when giving a measurement answer (e.g. '12 cm' not just '12')
Use precise terms such as 'edge', 'vertex', 'face' when describing 3-D shapes, and 'greater than', 'less than' when comparing numbers

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Shape patterns
topics.description: Look for and use mathematical structure: apply properties of operations, place-value patterns, and relationships between shapes to solve problems efficiently
evidence: Use the commutative property deliberately (e.g. reorder 3 + 9 as 9 + 3 to count on from the larger number)
Use place-value structure to add or subtract tens (e.g. 47 + 10 = 57 because only the tens digit changes)
Recognise structural similarities between shapes (e.g. rectangles and squares both have 4 sides and 4 right angles)

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Working with money
topics.description: Model real-world problems involving measurement, money, and time by choosing appropriate representations and interpreting results in context
evidence: Choose whether to use a bar model, number line, or equation for a measurement problem
Model a multi-step money problem with equations and interpret the final answer as change or total cost
Create a line plot from measurement data and use it to answer questions about the real-world situation

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Choosing the right strategy
topics.description: Select and use appropriate tools and representations strategically, including choosing between mental methods, jottings, formal algorithms, and calculators for arithmetic with multi-digit numbers, decimals, and fractions
evidence: Choose a mental method for 345 + 200 but a written method for 345 + 278
Select a ruler vs a metre stick based on the object being measured
Decide when a number line is more useful than base-ten blocks for a given problem

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Extending Table Patterns
topics.description: Recognise and use repeated reasoning to generalise: extend multiplication table patterns, derive unknown facts from known ones, and describe rules for sequences
evidence: Notice that all multiples of 4 are even and use this to check answers
Derive 8 × 7 from 8 × 5 + 8 × 2 by spotting the pattern
Describe a rule for a growing pattern (e.g. 'add 50 each time') and use it to predict the next terms

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Justifying mathematical reasoning
topics.description: Construct and follow multi-step mathematical arguments; identify errors in reasoning and explain why a method works or does not work
evidence: Explain step by step why a columnar addition method gives the correct answer
Find and explain an error in a worked example (e.g. incorrect regrouping)
Construct a simple argument for why a general statement is true (e.g. 'adding two even numbers always gives an even number')

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Multi-Step Problem Solving
topics.description: With teacher support, make sense of multi-step problems involving larger numbers or mixed operations by breaking them into parts, choosing strategies, and checking answers for reasonableness — children at this stage are developing the habit with guidance; independent strategy evaluation comes later
evidence: Break a two-step word problem within 1000 into sub-problems and solve each part
Estimate an answer before calculating to set a reasonableness benchmark
Check an answer using a different method or inverse operation and revise if needed

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Shape patterns (age 7+)
topics.description: Look for and use mathematical structure: apply place-value patterns to three-digit operations, use multiplication/division relationships, and exploit shape properties to classify
evidence: Use the structure of place value to explain why adding hundreds only changes the hundreds digit
Use commutativity and the relationship between multiplication and division to derive unknown facts
Classify shapes by their structural properties (number of sides, right angles, parallel lines)

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Understanding fractions
topics.description: Move fluently between real-world situations, diagrams, and symbolic equations involving three-digit numbers and fractions, explaining what each part represents
evidence: Write an equation with three-digit numbers to match a measurement or money word problem
Draw a bar model to represent a fraction problem and use it to solve
Explain how a number line diagram relates to the quantities in a word problem

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Understanding fractions (age 7+)
topics.description: Communicate with mathematical precision: use correct place-value and fraction vocabulary, specify units in measurement answers, and use notation accurately
evidence: Consistently specify units in measurement answers (e.g. '35 cm' not '35')
Use fraction vocabulary precisely (numerator, denominator, equivalent)
Write equations with correct notation including £/p, >, <, = and fraction symbols

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Choosing mathematical tools
topics.description: Select and use appropriate tools and representations strategically: choose between mental, written, and diagrammatic methods; use calculators for checking; select fraction models suited to the task
evidence: Decide to use mental multiplication for 25×4 but a written method for 167×3
Choose fraction strips rather than a number line to compare 3/8 and 1/4
Use a ruler and squared paper to verify area by counting squares after calculating l×w

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Connecting multiplication, fraction and decimal representations
topics.description: Move fluently between real-world situations, diagrams, number lines, and symbolic equations involving multiplication, fractions, and decimals, explaining what each representation shows
evidence: Represent a sharing problem as both a fraction diagram and a division equation
Explain how a bar model for 4 × 23 connects to the area model and the written method
Translate a decimal on a number line into a fraction and explain the equivalence

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Justifying mathematical reasoning (age 8+)
topics.description: Construct and present multi-step mathematical arguments; critique the reasoning of others and explain clearly why a method works or fails
evidence: Explain why 1/3 > 1/5 using the idea that more parts means smaller pieces
Find and explain an error in a peer's column subtraction with exchanges
Present a chain of reasoning: since 6×8=48 and 6×2=12, then 6×10=60 so 6×8=60−12=48

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Mathematical Precision
topics.description: Communicate with mathematical precision: use correct fraction/decimal vocabulary, name angle types accurately, specify units in measurement and money, and use notation (=, <, >, ÷, ×) correctly
evidence: Distinguish between 'three fourths' and 'three quarters' and use both correctly
State an answer in the correct unit: '63 square centimetres' not just '63'
Write 15:45 in 24-hour notation and explain the distinction from 3:45 pm

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Modelling with multiplication and fractions
topics.description: Model real-world problems involving multiplication, area, fractions, and unit conversion by choosing appropriate representations and interpreting mathematical results in context
evidence: Model a tiling/area problem with an array and write the corresponding multiplication
Represent a recipe-scaling problem as a fraction calculation and interpret the answer in grams
Use a bar model to set up a unit conversion problem (metres to centimetres)

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Multi-Step Problem Solving
topics.description: Make sense of multi-step problems involving four operations, fractions, and area/volume by identifying sub-steps, choosing a strategy, and monitoring progress
evidence: Break a two-step word problem into parts and explain a plan before calculating
Choose between drawing a diagram or writing equations for a perimeter problem
Check a fraction-of-quantity answer by estimating: 3/5 of 20 must be more than half of 20

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Times tables (age 8+)
topics.description: Recognise and use repeated reasoning to generalise: extend patterns in times tables and equivalent fractions, derive unknown facts from known facts efficiently, describe general rules
evidence: Notice that all fractions equivalent to 1/2 have a numerator that is half the denominator
Use the pattern 3×4=12, 3×40=120, 3×400=1200 and explain the generalisation
Derive 8×7 from 8×5=40 plus 8×2=16 and describe the strategy as a general approach

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Using a calculator well
topics.description: Use a calculator efficiently and appropriately to solve multi-step addition, subtraction, multiplication and division problems, deciding when a calculator is the best tool and checking the result with an estimate
evidence: Use a calculator to total 1468 + 2975 + 813, or a shopping list such as $4.85 + $12.30 + $7.95 (reading the display as dollars and cents), and check the result against an estimate
Decide whether to use mental strategies or a calculator for 400 x 3 and for 387 x 46, and explain the choice
Spot that a calculator answer of 4 150 for 83 x 5 must be a keying error because 80 x 5 = 400

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Using Mathematical Structure
topics.description: Look for and use mathematical structure: exploit place-value patterns for ×10/×100, use the distributive property to break apart multiplications, apply fraction equivalence to compare and compute, use shape properties to classify quadrilaterals
evidence: Decompose 7×13 into 7×10 + 7×3 using the distributive property
Explain why multiplying by 10 shifts digits one place left using place-value structure
Use the fact that a square is a special rectangle to reason about quadrilateral properties

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Choosing representations strategically
topics.description: Select and use tools and representations strategically: choose between mental methods, formal written methods, protractors, fraction strips, and diagrams based on the demands of the problem
evidence: Choose mental multiplication for 25 × 40 but long multiplication for 347 × 26
Select a protractor to verify an estimated angle rather than relying on visual inspection alone
Choose a common-denominator approach vs. benchmark comparison for ordering fractions, and explain why

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Complex Multi-Step Problems
topics.description: Make sense of complex multi-step problems involving large numbers, fractions, decimals, and percentages by analysing what is known and unknown, planning multi-step strategies, and evaluating reasonableness through estimation and inverse operations
evidence: Break a three-step problem involving unit conversion and multiplication into sub-problems and solve systematically
Estimate 4,832 × 7 as roughly 5,000 × 7 = 35,000 to check a calculated answer of 33,824
Identify that a percentage answer over 100% doesn't make sense in context

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fractions, Decimals & Percentages
topics.description: Look for and use mathematical structure: exploit the relationship between fractions, decimals, and percentages; use factor pairs to simplify multiplication; apply angle facts to find unknowns; use properties of regular polygons systematically
evidence: Use the structure 25 × 16 = 25 × 4 × 4 = 100 × 4 = 400 by exploiting factor pairs
Recognise that 0.75 = 3/4 = 75% and use whichever form is most efficient for the problem
Use the fact that angles on a straight line sum to 180° as a structural tool to find missing angles

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Connecting multiplication, fraction, decimal and percentage representations
topics.description: Move fluently between real-world situations, diagrams, number lines, bar models, and symbolic equations involving multi-digit multiplication, fractions, decimals, and percentages, explaining connections between representations
evidence: Represent a scaling problem as both a bar model and a multiplication equation
Show how 0.35, 35/100, and 35% all represent the same quantity on a hundredths grid
Translate a line-graph reading into a subtraction equation to find the difference

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Precise Maths Vocabulary
topics.description: Communicate with mathematical precision: use correct vocabulary for primes, factors, multiples, angle types, and polygon regularity; specify units including cm², m³, °; use notation for squares/cubes and percentages accurately
evidence: Distinguish 'factor' from 'multiple' in a written explanation
Write an area answer as 48 cm² (not just 48) and a volume estimate as approximately 60 cm³
Use 5² notation correctly and read it as 'five squared'

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Real-World Maths Modelling
topics.description: Model real-world problems involving scaling, unit conversion, area/perimeter, and percentage by selecting appropriate mathematical representations and interpreting results in context
evidence: Model a recipe-scaling problem with multiplication and fractions, then interpret the answer in grams
Represent a room-carpet problem by drawing a scale diagram and applying the area formula
Use a percentage bar model to find a sale price and explain the answer in £

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Reasoning with Equivalences
topics.description: Recognise and use repeated reasoning to generalise: extend patterns in equivalent fractions and percentage conversions, derive unknown facts from known facts, describe general rules for sequences and predict terms
evidence: Notice that multiplying any number by 25 can be done by multiplying by 100 then dividing by 4, and explain why
Describe the general rule for a sequence and predict the 20th term
Generalise: to find 10% divide by 10, to find 5% halve 10%, and use this to find 35% of any number

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Understanding fractions (age 9+)
topics.description: Construct and present logical mathematical arguments involving multiple steps; critique others' reasoning about fractions, angles, or calculations and clearly explain errors or alternative methods
evidence: Prove that 3/4 > 2/3 using a common denominator argument and a visual model
Find and explain an error in a long multiplication where a partial product was misaligned
Present a chain of reasoning to show that angles in a triangle sum to 180° by tearing and arranging

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Advanced Maths Vocabulary
topics.description: Communicate with mathematical precision: use correct vocabulary for ratio, proportion, algebra, volume, coordinate geometry, and circle parts; specify units including cm³, m³, and miles/km; use notation for algebraic expressions and order of operations accurately
evidence: Use 'radius', 'diameter', and 'circumference' correctly when describing a circle
Distinguish between an expression, an equation, and a formula in mathematical writing
Specify units correctly when presenting volume calculations (e.g. 60 cm³ not just 60)

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Advanced Multi-Step Problems
topics.description: Make sense of complex multi-step problems involving ratio, proportion, algebra, negative numbers, and all four operations with fractions and decimals by analysing given and unknown quantities, planning solution strategies, and evaluating reasonableness using estimation and inverse operations
evidence: Break down a three-step ratio problem into sub-problems and plan a solution pathway
Identify which quantities are known/unknown in an algebraic word problem and set up equations
Use estimation to check whether a decimal division answer is reasonable before finalising

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Choosing Maths Tools
topics.description: Select and use tools and representations strategically: choose between mental methods, formal written methods, algebraic approaches, coordinate grids, and technology based on the demands of the problem
evidence: Explain why long division is more appropriate than mental methods for 4,752 ÷ 13
Choose a coordinate grid approach to verify a translation rather than computing from a description alone
Select a formula-based approach rather than counting cubes to find volume efficiently

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Constructing mathematical arguments
topics.description: Construct and present logical mathematical arguments involving multiple steps and formal reasoning; critique others' reasoning about fractions, algebra, ratio, or geometry and clearly explain errors or alternative approaches
evidence: Prove that a given angle must be 60° by chaining angle facts in a logical sequence
Find and explain the error in a peer's fraction division calculation
Construct a counter-example to disprove a false conjecture (e.g. 'multiplying always makes bigger')

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Generalising with repeated reasoning
topics.description: Recognise and use repeated reasoning to generalise: describe algebraic rules for nth terms, use properties of operations to simplify, and verify generalisations with specific cases
evidence: Explain that the interior angle sum of an n-sided polygon is (n−2) × 180° based on the pattern for triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons
Predict the 20th term of a linear sequence by identifying and applying the general rule
Generalise that dividing by n always gives a denominator of n in the fraction, for any whole numbers

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Order of operations (age 10+)
topics.description: Look for and use mathematical structure: exploit the hierarchy of 2-D shapes to deduce properties; use order of operations and algebraic structure to simplify expressions; connect fraction–decimal–percentage equivalences; use ratio structure to solve proportion problems efficiently
evidence: Use the property that all rectangles are parallelograms to deduce missing angle facts
Recognise that 3 × (n + 5) = 3n + 15 by applying distributive structure
Use the equivalence 1/8 = 0.125 = 12.5% flexibly to solve a comparison problem

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Real-World Mathematical Modelling
topics.description: Model real-world problems involving ratio, scale, volume, unit conversion, and proportional reasoning with appropriate tools, diagrams, or equations
evidence: Choose a bar model or double number line to represent a ratio problem and solve it
Model a volume problem with a labelled diagram, apply the formula, and interpret the result in context
Determine whether a measurement answer should be rounded and to what degree of accuracy

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Understanding fractions (age 10+)
topics.description: Move fluently between real-world situations, diagrams, coordinate grids, algebraic expressions, tables, and symbolic equations involving fractions, ratio, and algebra, explaining connections between representations
evidence: Translate a word problem into an algebraic equation and also represent it on a bar model
Plot data from a table onto a coordinate grid and interpret the relationship
Explain how a pie chart, a fraction, and a percentage all represent the same proportion

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing Capacity
topics.description: Compare and describe capacity and volume using language such as full, empty, more than, less than, half full
evidence: Compare two containers and say which holds more/less
Use 'half full' and 'quarter full' to describe a container
Solve practical problems like 'Which cup has more water?'

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Time comparison words
topics.description: Use comparative language for time: quicker, slower, earlier, later
evidence: Compare two events and say which was quicker/slower
Use 'earlier' and 'later' correctly to describe daily events
Solve practical problems like 'Who finished first?'

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing Lengths & Heights
topics.description: Compare two objects directly by length or height and describe the difference using language such as long, short, tall, longer, shorter, taller, double, half
evidence: Stand two children back-to-back and say who is taller/shorter
Directly compare the heights of two towers and describe one as taller
Use 'longer' and 'shorter' to compare two ribbons placed side by side

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Measurable Attributes of Objects
topics.description: Describe and identify measurable attributes of objects such as length, height, weight, and capacity; use comparative language (longer, shorter, heavier, lighter, more, less)
evidence: Identify that a pencil has length and can be measured
Describe multiple attributes of one object (e.g. a bottle has height, weight, and capacity)
Use words like 'long', 'heavy', 'full' to describe objects

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Measuring mass and weight (age 4+)
topics.description: Compare two objects directly by mass or weight and describe the difference using language such as heavy, light, heavier than, lighter than
evidence: Heft two objects and say which is heavier/lighter
Use a simple balance to compare the weight of two objects
Describe one object as 'heavier than' another

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Ordering Events in Time
topics.description: Sequence events in chronological order using language such as before, after, next, first, today, yesterday, tomorrow, morning, afternoon, evening
evidence: Order three daily events using 'first', 'next', 'last'
Use 'yesterday', 'today', 'tomorrow' correctly
Describe an event as happening in the 'morning' or 'afternoon'

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Capacity and volume
topics.description: Measure and begin to record capacity and volume using non-standard and standard units
evidence: Measure capacity by counting how many cups fill a container
Begin to use litres as a unit of capacity
Record capacity measurements with a number and unit

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Coin Values
topics.description: Recognise and know the value of different coins and notes
evidence: Identify 1p, 2p, 5p, 10p, 20p, 50p, £1 and £2 coins
Know that a £2 coin is worth more than a 50p coin
Recognise £5 and £10 notes

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Days, Weeks, Months & Years
topics.description: Recognise and use language relating to dates, including days of the week, weeks, months, and years
evidence: Name the seven days of the week in order
Name the twelve months of the year in order
Understand that a year is made up of months and weeks

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Measuring and recording durations
topics.description: Measure and begin to record time in hours, minutes, and seconds
evidence: Use a sand timer or stopwatch to time an activity
Begin to understand that 1 minute = 60 seconds
Record a duration in simple terms (e.g. 'it took about 2 minutes')
Estimate whether brushing teeth takes about 2 seconds, 2 minutes or 2 hours, then use a supplied suitable timer to measure the event and record its duration

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Measuring length and height (age 5+)
topics.description: Measure and begin to record lengths and heights using non-standard and standard units
evidence: Measure the length of a table using cubes and record the result
Begin to use a ruler to measure in centimetres
Record a measurement as a number with a unit

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Measuring mass and weight
topics.description: Measure and begin to record mass/weight using non-standard and standard units
evidence: Use a balance to compare masses of two objects
Measure mass using non-standard units (e.g. 'this book weighs 5 cubes')
Begin to read a simple scale for mass

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Telling Time: Hours and Half Hours
topics.description: Tell and write the time to the hour and half past the hour on analogue clocks and digital displays (e.g. 3 o'clock = 3:00, half past 7 = 7:30), and draw clock hands to show these times, placing the hour hand halfway between two numbers for half past
evidence: Read an analogue clock showing 3 o'clock and one showing half past 7
Write half past 7 as 7:30 and match the digital times 3:00 and 7:30 to the right analogue clocks
Draw the hands on a blank clock face for half past 2, with the minute hand on 6 and the hour hand halfway between 2 and 3

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Adding money and giving change
topics.description: Find different combinations of coins that equal the same amount of money
evidence: Show that 50p can be made with 2×20p + 1×10p, or 5×10p, or 1×50p
Systematically find multiple coin combinations for a given total
Explain why different coin sets give the same total

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Area (age 8+)
topics.description: Measure areas by counting unit squares (square cm, square m, square in, square ft)
evidence: Count unit squares to find the area of an L-shaped figure
Measure the area of a book cover using square-centimetre tiles
Compare areas of two shapes by counting their unit squares

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Choosing measurement units
topics.description: Choose and use appropriate standard units to measure length (m/cm), mass (kg/g), temperature (°C), and capacity (litres/ml) to the nearest appropriate unit
evidence: Measure the length of a table in centimetres using a ruler
Weigh an object in grams using a scale
Measure the capacity of a container in millilitres using a measuring jug

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing and ordering measurements
topics.description: Compare and order lengths, mass, and capacity and record results using >, <, and =
evidence: Measure two objects and write 45cm > 32cm
Order three containers by capacity after measuring each
Use = when two measurements are the same

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing mass and capacity indirectly
topics.description: Compare and order the mass and capacity of objects indirectly, using a balance or a third object or container as a go-between, and explain the reasoning
evidence: Use a balance to show the apple is heavier than a block and the block is heavier than the egg, so the apple is heavier than the egg
Pour water from two bottles into the same jug to find which bottle holds more
Order three containers by capacity using cups of rice and explain the order

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Estimating capacity
topics.description: Estimate the capacity of containers by comparing them with a known measure and check by filling: informal units (e.g. cups or scoops) at an early stage, and litres and millilitres (e.g. against a 1-litre bottle, as in England Key Stage 2) when standard units are known; at the standard-unit stage, distinguish a container's capacity (how much it can hold) from the volume of liquid in it. Estimating the volume of solids with 1 cm³ cubes is covered in Counting Unit Cubes
evidence: Estimate how many cups of water a jug holds by comparing it with a container they know, then fill it to check (informal units)
Estimate whether a mug holds about 30 ml, 300 ml or 3 litres, or compare a jug with a 1-litre bottle, then check with a measuring jug (standard units)
Explain that a 1-litre jug half full of water has a capacity of 1 litre but holds 500 ml of water (standard-unit stage)

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Estimating Lengths
topics.description: Estimate lengths by comparing with a known reference unit and check by measuring: informal units (e.g. paper clips, cubes, hand spans) at an early stage, and standard units (inches, feet, centimetres and metres, as in US Grade 2) when those units are known
evidence: Estimate the length of a classroom object before measuring it, using a known unit (e.g. 'about 8 paper clips long', or in standard units 'about 30 cm')
Use a known reference to make reasonable estimates (e.g. the length of one cube or paper clip, or the width of a finger ≈ 1 cm for standard units)
Check estimates by measuring (laying same-size units end to end, or with a ruler for standard units) and evaluate how close they were

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Measuring length
topics.description: Order three objects by length and compare the lengths of two objects indirectly using a third object
evidence: Put three ribbons in order from shortest to longest
Use a piece of string to compare the heights of two objects that cannot be placed side by side
Explain that if A is longer than B and B is longer than C, then A is longer than C

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Measuring length (age 6+)
topics.description: Measure the length of an object using same-size length units laid end to end with no gaps or overlaps
evidence: Measure a book by laying paper clips end to end and counting them
Understand that the length measurement is the number of units that span the object
Avoid gaps and overlaps when placing units

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Money Addition & Subtraction
topics.description: Solve simple money problems involving addition and subtraction, including giving change
evidence: Calculate the total cost of two items priced in pence
Work out change from 50p after buying an item costing 35p
Solve 'How much more money do I need?' problems

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Money notation and units
topics.description: Recognise and use the symbols and notation for the main and smaller units of the local currency (for example £ and p, or $ and c), knowing that 100 of the smaller unit make 1 of the main unit, and combine amounts to make a particular value
evidence: Write £1.50 as 150p, or $2.70 as 270c and 450c as $4.50
Combine coins to make a given total, e.g. 50p + 20p + 5p = 75p, or show $3.60 in two different ways
Read prices written with currency symbols, e.g. £3.45 or $3.45, as main units and smaller units

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Number of minutes in an hour
topics.description: Know the number of minutes in an hour and the number of hours in a day
evidence: State that there are 60 minutes in an hour
State that there are 24 hours in a day
Use these facts to solve simple time problems

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing and ordering durations
topics.description: Compare and sequence intervals of time
evidence: Order three events by how long they took
Compare the duration of two activities (e.g. 'the race took longer than the walk')
Sequence intervals on a timeline
Compare a 35-minute bus journey with a 40-minute walk and say which takes longer and by how much
Compare 1 minute 20 seconds with 75 seconds by expressing them in a common unit

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Telling time to 5 minutes
topics.description: Tell and write the time to five minutes on analogue clocks, including quarter past and quarter to the hour, write these times in digital form, and draw clock hands to show them
evidence: Read an analogue clock showing 3:25 and write the time in digital form as 3:25
Write 'quarter past 9' as 9:15 and 'twenty to four' as 3:40
Draw clock hands to show twenty to four, with the minute hand on 8 and the hour hand just before 4

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Understanding Area
topics.description: Understand that a unit square has one square unit of area and that the area of a plane figure is the number of unit squares that cover it without gaps or overlaps
evidence: Identify a unit square and state its area is 1 square unit
Explain why a figure covered by 12 unit squares has area 12 square units
Distinguish between area and perimeter as different measurements

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Using a calendar
topics.description: Read a calendar to identify today's date and the day of the week for a given date, determine the number of days between two events, and use a supplied local calendar to find the holidays and season changes it marks. On a supplied calendar, count intervals between explicitly marked whole-month boundaries, including across a year boundary.
evidence: Find 15 March on a calendar page, say which day of the week it is, and write today's date from the classroom calendar in day-month form
Count how many days from 3 June to a birthday on 17 June
Use a supplied local calendar (e.g. an Ontario school-year calendar in Canada) to name the holidays it marks and the month in which each marked season begins, and say how many weeks until one of them
On a supplied calendar with the first of March and the first of June marked, count three whole-month intervals rather than four month names, checking by the month-boundary changes

Use the marked first of December and first of February in the following year to count two whole-month intervals; explain that this does not mean every month has 30 days and that other end-of-month conventions must be supplied rather than invented

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Addition and subtraction word problems
topics.description: Solve word problems involving lengths within 100, using addition and subtraction with drawings and equations
evidence: Solve 'The rope is 45 cm long. I cut off 18 cm. How long is it now?'
Draw a diagram (e.g. a ruler drawing) to represent a length word problem
Write an equation with a symbol for the unknown to represent the problem

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: a.m. and p.m. times
topics.description: Tell and write times to five minutes on analogue and digital clocks with a.m. or p.m. (before or after midday), relating times to daily events and using the words morning, afternoon, evening, noon and midnight. Roman-numeral clock faces and the 24-hour clock are covered in Roman numeral and 24-hour clocks
evidence: Say whether school starts at 8:45 a.m. or 8:45 p.m., and whether bedtime is 7:30 a.m. or 7:30 p.m.
Write 'twenty-five past four in the afternoon' as 4:25 p.m.
Explain that 12 noon is midday, so times just after it are p.m., while times just after midnight are a.m.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Calculating with measurements
topics.description: Measure, compare, add, and subtract lengths (m/cm/mm), mass (kg/g), and volume/capacity (l/ml) using standard units
evidence: Measure a length in centimetres and millimetres
Weigh an object using grams and kilograms
Add two measurements in the same unit (e.g. 250 ml + 400 ml = 650 ml)

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing lengths by measuring
topics.description: Measure to determine how much longer one object is than another, expressing the length difference in terms of a standard length unit
evidence: Measure two objects and calculate the difference in length
Express the difference using the correct unit (e.g. '7 cm longer')
Solve a comparison problem: 'How much taller is the bookshelf than the desk?'

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Calculating elapsed duration
topics.description: Calculate the duration between a known start time and a known finish time, including across an hour boundary; distinguish the interval length from either clock reading.
evidence: Work out that a TV show from 5:17 p.m. to 5:43 p.m. lasted 26 minutes
Find that an activity from 2:50 p.m. to 4:10 p.m. lasts 1 hour 20 minutes, explaining the regrouping at 60 minutes
Solve a lesson from 10:15 to 11:00 as a duration of 45 minutes, using a number line or another valid method

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Giving Change
topics.description: Add and subtract amounts of money to give change, using both £ and p in practical contexts
evidence: Calculate the total cost of two or three items priced in pounds and pence
Work out the change from £5 or £10
Record money calculations using £ and p notation correctly (e.g. £3.47)

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Measuring length (age 7+)
topics.description: Measure the length of an object by selecting and using appropriate tools such as rulers, yardsticks, metre sticks, and measuring tapes
evidence: Choose the most appropriate tool for measuring a given object

Align the zero mark of a ruler with the end of the object and read the measurement; for an offset or broken ruler, count the unit spaces or subtract the starting reading from the ending reading (e.g. 3 cm to 10 cm is 7 cm)

Measure lengths in inches, feet, centimetres, and metres using the correct tool. For example, use the centimetre marks on a metre stick to explain that 1 m is 100 cm, or mark off and check a line of a given length with a ruler.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Measuring Perimeters
topics.description: Measure the perimeter of simple 2-D shapes
evidence: Measure each side of a rectangle and add the lengths to find the perimeter
Calculate the perimeter of a regular shape given the side length
Explain that perimeter is the total distance around a shape

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Measuring & Plotting Lengths
topics.description: Generate measurement data by measuring lengths to the nearest whole unit and display the data on a line plot
evidence: Measure the lengths of several objects and record the data
Create a line plot with a horizontal scale marked in whole-number units
Interpret a line plot to answer questions about the data

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Measuring with different units
topics.description: Measure the length of an object using two different length units and describe how the measurements relate to the size of the unit chosen
evidence: Measure a desk in both centimetres and inches and compare the two numbers
Explain that measuring with a smaller unit gives a larger number
Predict whether a measurement in centimetres will be greater or less than in inches

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Money word problems
topics.description: Solve word problems involving dollar bills, quarters, dimes, nickels, and pennies, using $ and ¢ symbols appropriately
evidence: Determine the total value of a collection of coins
Solve a word problem about making change with US currency
Use $ and ¢ symbols correctly in answers

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Quarter past and quarter to
topics.description: Recognise, read and show quarter past and quarter to the hour on an analog clock, linking each to a quarter turn of the minute hand
evidence: Read a clock showing 3:15 as 'quarter past three'
Set the hands of a clock to quarter to seven
Explain that the minute hand has turned a quarter of the way round at quarter past

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Roman-numeral clock faces
topics.description: Tell and write the time from analogue clocks with Roman-numeral faces I to XII, including IV (also shown as IIII on some clocks) and IX. Interpret the numeral positions and hands as on an ordinary numbered clock face.
evidence: Read a Roman-numeral clock with the minute hand on IX and the hour hand between IV and V as quarter to five (4:45)
Match I to XII to hour positions on a clock face, including IV or IIII, IX and XII
Read the same hand positions on Roman and ordinary numbered clock faces, explaining that changing numeral labels does not change the time

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Smaller units for accuracy
topics.description: Choose a smaller uniform informal unit when a measurement needs to be more accurate, recognising that a smaller unit gives a larger count, for length, mass and capacity
evidence: Measure a book with pencils (about 2) and then with paperclips (about 9) and explain why the paperclip count is bigger
Choose teaspoons instead of cups to measure how much a small glass holds and explain why
Explain why '3 and a bit hand spans' is less accurate than measuring the same table in counting cubes

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Time to the nearest minute
topics.description: Read and write time to the nearest minute on analogue and digital clocks. Coordinate the minute scale with the hour hand, and express equivalent minutes-past and minutes-to readings.
evidence: Read 7:43 from an analogue clock face and write it on a digital display, keeping the hour as 7 although the hour hand is near 8
Read an analogue clock showing 11:06, explaining why the hour hand is just past 11 and the minute hand is six minutes past the hour
Express 9:57 as three minutes to ten and explain the hour-hand position

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Time Units and Calendar Facts
topics.description: Know the number of seconds in a minute and the number of days in each month, year, and leap year
evidence: State that there are 60 seconds in a minute
Name the months and state the number of days in each
Explain that a leap year has 366 days; leap years usually follow a four-year pattern, with calendar exceptions, so check a calendar for a particular year

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: 12-hour and 24-hour time
topics.description: Read, write and convert time between ordinary analogue and digital 12-hour and 24-hour clocks. Morning hours 1–11 keep their hour (7:05 a.m. = 07:05); afternoon/evening hours 1–11 add 12 (3:20 p.m. = 15:20). The 12 o’clock hour has separate noon and midnight cases: 12:20 p.m. = 12:20 and 12:20 a.m. = 00:20. Convert in both directions without requiring Roman-numeral clock faces.
evidence: Convert 3:45 pm to 15:45 in 24-hour time
Read 19:30 and state the 12-hour equivalent as 7:30 pm
Match a set of 12-hour and 24-hour times
Convert 12:20 a.m. to 00:20 and 12:20 p.m. to 12:20, explaining the midnight and noon cases
Read an ordinary analogue clock with a stated afternoon context and write the equivalent 24-hour digital time; translate back to a 12-hour display

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Area and the distributive property
topics.description: Use tiling to demonstrate the distributive property: the area of a rectangle with sides a and (b+c) equals a×b + a×c; use area models to represent the distributive property
evidence: Tile a 3×(4+2) rectangle and show it decomposes into 3×4 and 3×2
Use an area model to compute 6×13 as 6×10 + 6×3
Draw an area model showing 5×(7+3) = 5×7 + 5×3

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Area by Tiling
topics.description: Find the area of a rectangle by tiling it with unit squares and show that the result equals the product of the side lengths
evidence: Tile a 4×6 rectangle and count 24 squares, then verify 4×6=24
Explain why the number of rows times the number in each row gives the area
Draw a rectangle on squared paper, tile it, and write the multiplication

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Area of compound shapes
topics.description: Recognise area as additive; find areas of rectilinear figures by decomposing into non-overlapping rectangles and summing their areas
evidence: Decompose an L-shape into two rectangles, find each area, and add them
Find the area of a floor plan shaped like a T by splitting into rectangles
Solve: A room is L-shaped (3m×5m plus 2m×4m) — what is the total area?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Area of rectangles by multiplication
topics.description: Multiply side lengths to find areas of rectangles and represent whole-number products as rectangular areas
evidence: Calculate the area of a 7 cm × 9 cm rectangle as 63 cm²
Draw a rectangle with area 36 square units and label its side lengths
Solve: A garden is 8 m by 5 m — what is its area?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Converting measurement units
topics.description: Convert between related measurement units using their unit relationship and the relative sizes of the units to choose multiplication or division. Handle whole-number and decimal measurements at the task’s specified precision, including three-decimal-place examples, compound measures and reverse conversions with remainders; explain equivalents and record them in conversion tables. Include metric length, mass and capacity, and time relationships (hours/minutes, minutes/seconds, years/months and weeks/days), distinguishing fixed rates from variable month lengths.
evidence: Convert 3.25 kg to 3250 g and 45 cm to 0.45 m, explaining why the count grows or shrinks; convert 5 g to 0.005 kg without adding or deleting zeros mechanically
Convert 2 hours 35 minutes to 155 minutes and 150 seconds to 2 minutes 30 seconds, preserving the mixed part or remainder and explaining why the rate is 60 rather than 100
Convert 8 weeks 3 days to 59 days and 2 years 3 months to 27 months; explain why an unspecified month cannot be converted to one fixed number of days
Build and interpret a two-column equivalence table for cm and mm, explain the factor, and use the same relationship to convert in either direction
Convert 2.5 hours to 9000 seconds through minutes, tracking the unit at each step and checking by reversing the conversion

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Finding start or finish times
topics.description: Find an unknown start or finish time from a given duration and the other clock time. Choose whether to move forwards or backwards, regrouping minutes at 60 when crossing an hour; a number line is one useful representation.
evidence: A film starts at 2:15 p.m. and lasts 47 minutes: find its finish time of 3:02 p.m.
A show ends at 10:05 a.m. and lasts 45 minutes: find its start time of 9:20 a.m.
Explain why a known start and duration require moving forwards, while a known finish and duration require moving backwards; check the result against the story

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Estimating, comparing and calculating measures and money
topics.description: Estimate, compare, and calculate different measures including money in pounds and pence
evidence: Estimate the length of the classroom in metres
Compare 1.5 kg and 1200 g and identify which is heavier
Calculate the total cost of 3 items at £2.45, £1.30, and £0.75

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Halves and quarters (age 8+)
topics.description: Generate measurement data by measuring lengths to the nearest half and quarter inch; display the data on a line plot with a scale marked in whole numbers, halves, and quarters
evidence: Measure five objects to the nearest 1/4 inch
Create a line plot showing the lengths of classmates' pencils in half-inches
Read a line plot and answer questions about the data

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Measuring Liquids & Masses
topics.description: Measure and estimate liquid volumes and masses of objects using grams, kilograms, and litres; solve one-step word problems involving mass or volume
evidence: Estimate the mass of a textbook in grams or kilograms
Read a scale to measure liquid volume in litres
Solve: 3 bags weigh 250 g each — what is the total mass?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Perimeters of polygons
topics.description: Solve problems involving perimeters of polygons: find perimeter from side lengths, find an unknown side length, and explore rectangles with same perimeter but different areas (or vice versa)
evidence: Calculate the perimeter of a rectangle with sides 8 cm and 5 cm
Find the missing side of a pentagon with perimeter 30 cm and four known sides
Draw two rectangles both with perimeter 24 cm but different areas

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Area and perimeter of rectangles
topics.description: Apply the area formula (l × w) and perimeter formula (2l + 2w) for rectangles including squares in real-world and mathematical problems; calculate and compare areas using standard units (cm², m²) and estimate areas of irregular shapes
evidence: Find the width of a room given area = 48 m² and length = 8 m
Calculate the area of a square with side 7.5 cm
Estimate the area of an irregular pond drawn on a cm² grid

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing best buys
topics.description: Compare the value of products sold in different quantities or prices by working out and comparing unit prices (price per item or per unit of mass or volume), using a calculator where appropriate, and explain which is the better buy
evidence: Decide whether a 2 kg bag of rice for $5.80 or a 500 g bag for $1.60 is better value and explain why
Work out the price per 100 g of two pack sizes of cereal and say which is cheaper per 100 g
Explain why the bigger pack is not always the better buy (e.g. when the unit price is higher or the food would be wasted)

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Counting Unit Cubes
topics.description: Measure and estimate the volume of solids by counting unit cubes: build cuboids from 1 cm³ cubes and count them, count the cubes in models and drawings (including hidden cubes), estimate how many cubes will fill a box and check by filling it, and record volumes in cubic units (cm³, in³, ft³ or improvised units)
evidence: Build a 3 × 2 × 2 cuboid from 1 cm³ cubes and state its volume as 12 cm³
Count the cubes in a drawing of a solid built from cubes, including the hidden ones at the back, and give the volume in cubic units
Estimate how many centimetre cubes will fill a small box, then fill it to check

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Measurement word problems with fractions and decimals
topics.description: Solve word problems involving distances, time intervals, liquid volumes, masses, and money using the four operations with fractions or decimals; represent with diagrams including number lines
evidence: A 2.5 kg bag of flour is split equally into 4 portions — what does each weigh?
A journey takes 1 hr 45 min; what time do you arrive if you leave at 09:20?
Three ribbons of 0.75 m, 1.2 m, and 0.95 m — what is the total length?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Measurement Line Plots
topics.description: Make a line plot to display measurement data in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8); solve problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions using line plot data
evidence: Create a line plot of seed growth measurements in 1/8-inch increments
Use a line plot to find the difference between the longest and shortest specimens
Calculate the total length of all items in a line plot by adding the fractional measurements

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Metric & Imperial Conversion
topics.description: Understand and use approximate equivalences between metric units and common imperial units (inches, pounds, pints)
evidence: State that 1 inch ≈ 2.5 cm and use this to estimate length in inches
Know that 1 kg ≈ 2.2 pounds and estimate a person's weight in pounds
Convert approximately between litres and pints (1 litre ≈ 1.75 pints)

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Perimeter of Compound Shapes
topics.description: Measure and calculate the perimeter of composite rectilinear shapes in centimetres and metres
evidence: Find the perimeter of an L-shaped figure by identifying all side lengths
Calculate the perimeter of a composite shape where some sides must be deduced
Draw a composite rectilinear shape with a perimeter of 40 cm

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Reading between scale marks
topics.description: Interpret unmarked and partial units on scaled instruments and read digital instruments when measuring length, mass, capacity, duration and temperature, using appropriate units
evidence: Read 500 g on kitchen scales numbered every 200 g where the pointer sits halfway between 400 g and 600 g
Read 175 ml on a jug marked every 50 ml and 23 degrees on a thermometer marked every 2 degrees
Read and record a time of 1 minute 26.4 seconds from a digital stopwatch and a length of 12.7 cm on a ruler

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: What volume means
topics.description: Recognise volume as an attribute of solid figures; understand that a unit cube (side length 1 unit) has 'one cubic unit' of volume and can be used to measure volume; a solid packed with n unit cubes has volume n cubic units
evidence: Explain what 'volume' means for a 3D shape and how it differs from area
Identify a unit cube and explain that it represents one cubic unit of volume
Determine the volume of a small solid by counting the unit cubes that fill it

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Area of Triangles & Parallelograms
topics.description: Find the area of parallelograms and triangles by relating them to rectangles: rearrange a parallelogram (cut off a triangle and move it) into a rectangle with the same base and perpendicular height; see a right triangle as half of a rectangle and any triangle as half of a parallelogram (or as two right triangles); use the resulting formulae A = b × h for parallelograms and A = ½ × b × h for triangles, always using the perpendicular height rather than a slanted side, including when the height falls outside an obtuse triangle; and recognise when an area formula can be used (rectangles, parallelograms, triangles) and when another method is needed, such as counting or estimating squares for an irregular shape
evidence: Cut a right-angled triangle off one end of a parallelogram with base 8 cm and perpendicular height 5 cm, move it to the other end to make an 8 cm × 5 cm rectangle, and state the area as 40 cm²

Show that a right triangle with legs 6 cm and 4 cm is half of a 6 cm × 4 cm rectangle (12 cm²), and that an obtuse triangle with base 12 cm and perpendicular height 7 cm, drawn outside the triangle, is half of a parallelogram (42 cm²)

Decide that a formula gives the area of a parallelogram with base 10 cm and perpendicular height 5 cm (50 cm², not the 60 cm² from its slanted 6 cm side) but not of an irregular leaf shape, whose area must be estimated by counting squares

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Solving problems with measurement conversions
topics.description: Choose and sequence unit conversion and calculation in multi-step real-world measurement problems using decimals. Decide when quantities need a common unit, carry out the operations and interpret and check the result; the conversion procedure itself is covered in Converting measurement units.
evidence: Solve: 'A recipe uses 0.75 kg of flour. How many grams are needed for 3 batches?'
Compare 2.5 litres and 2,450 ml by converting to the same unit
Solve a multi-step problem involving time, distance, and unit conversion

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Miles & Kilometres
topics.description: Convert between miles and kilometres using the approximate relationship (5 miles ≈ 8 km)
evidence: Convert 40 miles to approximately 64 km
Explain why the conversion factor between miles and km is approximately 1.6
Use the miles↔km relationship to compare a 10 km race with a 6-mile run

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Perimeter (age 10+)
topics.description: Recognise that shapes with the same area can have different perimeters and vice versa; explore this relationship systematically
evidence: Draw two rectangles with area 24 cm² but different perimeters
Find two shapes with perimeter 20 cm but different areas
Explain why a long thin rectangle and a square can have the same area but different perimeters

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Volume as additive
topics.description: Recognise volume as additive; find volumes of composite solid figures made of two or more non-overlapping right rectangular prisms
evidence: Decompose an L-shaped solid into two cuboids and calculate total volume
Solve a real-world problem requiring the volume of a composite figure (e.g. a step-shaped structure)
Explain why splitting a composite solid into rectangular prisms allows calculation of total volume

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Volume of cuboids
topics.description: Find the volume of right rectangular prisms by packing with unit cubes and show it equals l × w × h (or base area × height); apply V = l × w × h and V = B × h to solve real-world problems; calculate, estimate, and compare volumes of cubes and cuboids in standard units (cm³, m³); and recognise that the formula applies to cuboids, while an irregular solid built from cubes must be counted or split into cuboids
evidence: Use V = l × w × h to find the volume of a cuboid 4 cm × 3 cm × 5 cm = 60 cm³
Explain why packing a prism with unit cubes gives the same result as multiplying edge lengths
Compare the 60 cm³ cuboid with an irregular model built from 58 centimetre cubes, explaining that the formula works for the cuboid but the model's cubes must be counted

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Area by splitting shapes
topics.description: Find the area of polygons such as trapezoids, kites, rhombuses, irregular quadrilaterals and other rectilinear or non-rectilinear polygons by decomposition or composition: decompose the shape into rectangles and triangles and add the parts, or compose it into an enclosing rectangle and subtract the pieces outside; record the dimensions used for each piece, check that the pieces neither overlap nor leave gaps, and apply this to real-world problems such as floor plans, gardens and signs, giving answers in square units. The focus is the decomposition and composition strategy, which works for any polygon whether or not a dedicated formula is known
evidence: Find the area of a trapezoid with parallel sides 6 cm and 10 cm and height 4 cm by splitting it into a 6 cm × 4 cm rectangle and two triangles with a combined base of 4 cm (24 + 8 = 32 cm²)
Find the area of a kite with diagonals 8 cm and 6 cm by enclosing it in an 8 cm × 6 cm rectangle and subtracting the four corner triangles (48 − 24 = 24 cm²)
Work out the turf needed for a garden shaped like a 12 m × 8 m rectangle with a right triangle (legs 8 m and 3 m) attached to one end (96 + 12 = 108 m²)

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Discounts and GST
topics.description: Solve and estimate financial problems in Australian dollars involving percentage discounts and adding the 10% GST to prices given before GST (recognising that GST-inclusive prices already contain it), using a calculator or spreadsheet where appropriate
evidence: Work out the sale price of an $80 jacket with a 25% discount and estimate it first as about $60
For a $45 price given before GST, find the 10% GST of $4.50 and the GST-inclusive price of $49.50, and explain why a price already marked 'GST inclusive' does not get another 10% added
Use a spreadsheet or calculator formula to apply a 15% discount to a list of prices and check one result by estimation

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Surface area using nets
topics.description: Represent right rectangular prisms, triangular prisms and pyramids with rectangular or triangular bases using nets made of rectangles and triangles; use the solid's dimensions to label every face on the net; find the surface area as the sum of the face areas, in square units; distinguish surface area (the area covering the outside) from volume (the space inside); and apply this to real-world problems such as wrapping, painting or making boxes, including deciding which faces to include (e.g. an open-topped box)
evidence: Draw the net of a 5 cm × 4 cm × 3 cm cuboid, label each rectangle's dimensions, and find the surface area as 2 × (20 + 15 + 12) = 94 cm²
Use the net of a square-based pyramid with 6 cm base edges and triangular faces of height 5 cm to find its surface area (36 + 4 × 15 = 96 cm²)
Find the card needed for an open-topped box 30 cm × 20 cm × 10 cm, leaving out the top (600 + 2 × 300 + 2 × 200 = 1,600 cm²), and explain why the answer is in cm² rather than cm³

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Volume with fraction lengths
topics.description: Find the volume of a right rectangular prism with fractional edge lengths by packing it with cubes whose edge is a suitable unit fraction of a unit (e.g. 1/2 or 1/4), working out the volume of one such cube (a cube with 1/2-unit edges has volume 1/8 cubic unit), counting the cubes and multiplying; show that this gives the same result as multiplying the edge lengths; and apply V = l × w × h and V = B × h with fractional or mixed-number edge lengths in real-world and mathematical problems
evidence: Show that 8 cubes with 1/2 cm edges fit exactly into a 1 cm cube, so each has a volume of 1/8 cm³
Pack a 1½ cm × 1 cm × 2½ cm prism with 1/2 cm cubes (3 × 2 × 5 = 30 cubes), find its volume as 30 × 1/8 = 3¾ cm³, and check that 1½ × 1 × 2½ gives the same answer
Find how much sand fills a box 2¼ ft long, 1½ ft wide and 2/3 ft deep using V = l × w × h (2¼ ft³)

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Division as equal sharing
topics.description: Understand division as sharing equally into groups or as grouping (how many groups of a given size can be made)
evidence: Share 10 counters (real or on-screen) equally between 2 plates
Group 20 objects into sets of 5 and find there are 4 groups, e.g. by skip counting 5, 10, 15, 20, or alternatively by subtracting 5 repeatedly (20, 15, 10, 5, 0)
Use concrete objects or a drawing to solve 'How many groups of 2 in 8?'

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Arrays for multiplication
topics.description: Use arrays to represent multiplication and division situations
evidence: Build an array of 3 rows of 4 objects to show 3 × 4
Read an array and state the total
Use an array to solve a simple division problem (e.g. 12 objects in rows of 4 → 3 rows)

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Multiplication as repeated addition
topics.description: Understand multiplication as repeated addition and grouping equal sets
evidence: Explain that 3 groups of 2 is the same as 2 + 2 + 2
Use objects to make equal groups and count the total
Recognise an array as showing equal rows

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Commutative Multiplication
topics.description: Understand and apply the commutative property of multiplication and recognise that division is not commutative
evidence: Explain that 3 × 5 = 5 × 3 and show this with an array rotated
Use commutativity to choose the easier calculation
Demonstrate that 12 ÷ 3 ≠ 3 ÷ 12

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Multiplication as repeated addition (age 6+)
topics.description: Solve problems involving multiplication and division using arrays, repeated addition, mental methods, and known facts
evidence: Solve 'There are 5 bags with 2 apples in each. How many apples?' using repeated addition or known fact
Solve 'Share 15 sweets equally among 3 children' using grouping
Draw an array to solve a multiplication problem in context

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Odd and even numbers
topics.description: Recognise odd and even numbers
evidence: Identify whether a given number is odd or even
Explain that even numbers can be divided into 2 equal groups
Spot the pattern: even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Reading ×, ÷, and = Symbols
topics.description: Read, write, and interpret the symbols ×, ÷, and = in multiplication and division number sentences
evidence: Read 3 × 4 = 12 aloud as 'three times four equals twelve'
Write a multiplication sentence to match an array
Read 12 ÷ 3 = 4 aloud correctly

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Times tables
topics.description: Recall and use multiplication and division facts for the 2, 5, and 10 multiplication tables
evidence: Quickly answer 5 × 3 = 15 from memory
Quickly answer 20 ÷ 5 = 4 from memory
Recite the 2, 5, and 10 times tables fluently

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Arrays for multiplication (age 7+)
topics.description: Use addition to find the total number of objects arranged in rectangular arrays with up to 5 rows and 5 columns; write an equation to express the total as a sum of equal addends
evidence: Count objects in a 3×4 array and write 4 + 4 + 4 = 12
Explain that each row has the same number of objects so the total can be found by repeated addition
Draw a rectangular array to model a given repeated-addition equation

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Multi-Step Multiply & Divide
topics.description: Solve problems involving multiplication and division, including scaling problems and correspondence problems where n objects are connected to m objects
evidence: Solve a scaling problem (e.g. 'the ribbon is 3 times as long')
Solve a correspondence problem (e.g. '4 shirts and 3 trousers — how many outfits?')
Solve a missing-number multiplication or division problem

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Rows & Columns in Rectangles
topics.description: Partition a rectangle into rows and columns of same-size squares and count to find the total number of them
evidence: Divide a rectangle into equal rows and columns of unit squares
Count the total number of squares using repeated addition or skip counting
Relate the rows-and-columns structure to a rectangular array

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Times tables (age 7+)
topics.description: Recall and use multiplication and division facts for the 3, 4, and 8 multiplication tables
evidence: Recall 3 × 1 through 3 × 12 and corresponding division facts
Recall 4 × 1 through 4 × 12 and corresponding division facts
Recall 8 × 1 through 8 × 12 and corresponding division facts

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Written Multiplication & Division
topics.description: Write and calculate mathematical statements for multiplication and division using known tables, including two-digit × one-digit, using mental and progressing to formal written methods
evidence: Calculate 23 × 4 using partitioning (20 × 4 + 3 × 4)
Calculate 96 ÷ 8 using known table facts
Begin to use a formal written layout for short multiplication

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: All times tables to 12×12
topics.description: Recall multiplication and division facts for multiplication tables up to 12 × 12
evidence: Recall any fact from the 1–12 times tables rapidly
Recall the corresponding division fact for any multiplication fact
Use known facts to check or derive answers in calculations

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Division as Unknown Factor
topics.description: Understand division as an unknown-factor problem (e.g. find 32 ÷ 8 by finding the number that makes 32 when multiplied by 8)
evidence: Explain that 32 ÷ 8 = ? is the same as 8 × ? = 32
Use a known multiplication fact to find a division answer
Describe the relationship between multiplication and division as inverse operations

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Factor Pairs & Commutativity
topics.description: Recognise and use factor pairs and commutativity in mental calculations
evidence: List all factor pairs of a given number (e.g. 24: 1×24, 2×12, 3×8, 4×6)
Use commutativity to reorder a multiplication for easier mental calculation
Explain what a factor pair is and how commutativity helps

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fluent multiplication and division facts
topics.description: Fluently multiply and divide within 100 using strategies such as the relationship between multiplication and division
evidence: Answer any single-digit multiplication fact within 3 seconds
Answer any related division fact within 3 seconds
Use known facts to derive unknown facts (e.g. 9 × 7 from 10 × 7 − 7)

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Mental multiplication and division
topics.description: Use place value, known and derived facts to multiply and divide mentally, including multiplying by 0 and 1, dividing by 1, and multiplying together three numbers
evidence: Calculate 40 × 6 = 240 mentally using place value
Explain why any number × 0 = 0 and any number × 1 = the number itself
Multiply three numbers mentally by choosing a useful pair first (e.g. 2 × 7 × 5 = 2 × 5 × 7 = 70)

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Multiplication and Division Word Problems
topics.description: Use multiplication and division within 100 to solve word problems involving equal groups, arrays, and measurement quantities
evidence: Solve an equal-groups word problem using multiplication
Solve a measurement division problem (e.g. 'How many 4-cm pieces from a 28-cm ribbon?')
Solve an array/area word problem using multiplication

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Multiplicative Comparison
topics.description: Interpret a multiplication equation as a comparison (e.g. 35 = 5 × 7 means 35 is 5 times as many as 7); represent verbal statements of multiplicative comparisons as equations
evidence: Explain that '4 times as many' means multiply by 4
Write an equation for: Sarah has 3 times as many stickers as Tom, who has 8 stickers
Distinguish multiplicative comparison from additive comparison in word problems

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Multiply & Add Problems
topics.description: Solve problems involving multiplying and adding, including using the distributive law, integer scaling problems, and harder correspondence problems
evidence: Use the distributive law to solve 14 × 6 as 10 × 6 + 4 × 6
Solve a scaling problem (e.g. 'A tower is 3 times as tall as a 15 m building')
Solve a correspondence problem (e.g. '3 types of bread, 4 types of filling — how many different sandwiches?')

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Multiplying by Tens
topics.description: Multiply one-digit whole numbers by multiples of 10 in the range 10–90 using strategies based on place value and properties of operations
evidence: Calculate 7 × 30 = 210 by reasoning 7 × 3 tens = 21 tens = 210
Explain why multiplying by a multiple of 10 adds a zero to the product
Use this skill to estimate products of larger numbers

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Patterns in Times Tables
topics.description: Identify arithmetic patterns (including patterns in the addition table or multiplication table) and explain them using properties of operations
evidence: Notice that all products of 5 end in 0 or 5 and explain why
Observe that the sum of two even numbers is always even
Identify a pattern in the multiplication table and explain it using commutativity or the distributive property

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Properties of Operations
topics.description: Apply properties of operations (commutative, associative, distributive) as strategies to multiply and divide
evidence: Use commutativity: if 6 × 4 = 24 then 4 × 6 = 24
Use the distributive property: 8 × 7 = 8 × 5 + 8 × 2 = 40 + 16 = 56
Use associativity to multiply three numbers: 2 × 3 × 5 = 6 × 5 = 30

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Unknown in Multiplication & Division
topics.description: Determine the unknown whole number in a multiplication or division equation relating three whole numbers (e.g. 8 × ? = 48, ? × 6 = 42)
evidence: Find the missing factor in 7 × ? = 63
Find the missing dividend in ? ÷ 5 = 9
Explain the strategy used (e.g. using the related multiplication fact)

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: What Division Means
topics.description: Interpret whole-number quotients (e.g. 56 ÷ 8 as the number of objects in each share or the number of equal groups)
evidence: Explain that 56 ÷ 8 can mean sharing 56 into 8 equal groups or making groups of 8
Draw a picture to represent a division expression
Match a division expression to a word problem involving equal sharing or grouping

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: What Multiplication Means
topics.description: Interpret products of whole numbers (e.g. 5 × 7 as the total number of objects in 5 groups of 7)
evidence: Explain that 4 × 6 means 4 groups of 6 objects
Draw a picture or array to represent a multiplication expression
Match a multiplication expression to a word problem involving equal groups

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Written Multiplication
topics.description: Multiply two-digit and three-digit numbers by a one-digit number using formal written layout
evidence: Set out and solve 47 × 6 using short multiplication
Set out and solve 234 × 5 using short multiplication with carrying
Check the answer using estimation (e.g. 234 × 5 ≈ 200 × 5 = 1000)

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Division with remainders
topics.description: Solve multi-step word problems using the four operations with whole numbers, including interpreting remainders in context; represent with equations using a letter for the unknown; check with estimation
evidence: 52 children go on a trip in minibuses holding 9 each — how many minibuses are needed? (interpret the remainder, including a calculator display such as 5.777… meaning 6 minibuses)
A shop sells packs of 6 pencils for £1.50 each — how much do 5 packs cost?
Represent a two-step problem with an equation using n for the unknown

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Factors, multiples, and primes

Find all common factors of 36 and 48
Identify the first three common multiples of 6 and 8
Determine whether a given number (e.g. 97) is prime and justify the reasoning

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Factors, multiples, and primes (age 9+)
topics.description: Solve problems involving multiplication and division using knowledge of factors, multiples, squares, and cubes
evidence: Is 156 a multiple of 6? Explain how you know

Use factor pairs to simplify 24 × 25 as 6 × (4 × 25) = 6 × 100 = 600

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Long multiplication
topics.description: Multiply a whole number of up to four digits by a one-digit number, and multiply two two-digit numbers, using formal written methods including long multiplication; illustrate with area models

Draw an area model for 45 × 23 and connect to the written method

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Mental multiplication and division (age 9+)
topics.description: Multiply and divide numbers mentally drawing upon known facts, including related facts and place-value adjustments
