Derive 7 × 15 by calculating 7 × 10 + 7 × 5
Calculate 360 ÷ 9 mentally using 36 ÷ 9 = 4

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Multiplicative Comparison
topics.description: Solve word problems involving multiplicative comparison using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number
evidence: A blue ribbon is 3 times as long as a red ribbon of 7 cm — how long is the blue ribbon?
36 is 4 times a number — what is the number?
Explain why 'Sam has 5 more' is additive but 'Sam has 5 times as many' is multiplicative

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Multiplying and dividing
topics.description: Multiply and divide whole numbers and those involving decimals by 10, 100, and 1000
evidence: Calculate 3.45 × 100 = 345
Calculate 72 ÷ 1000 = 0.072
Explain that multiplying by 10 shifts each digit one place to the left

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Odd and even number rules
topics.description: Explain and use the properties of odd and even numbers when adding, subtracting and multiplying, e.g. odd + odd = even, odd + even = odd, and any whole number multiplied by an even number is even
evidence: Explain with paired counters why the sum of two odd numbers is always even
Predict without calculating whether 347 + 129 is odd or even and justify it
Explain why 6 x 37 must be even

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Prime numbers
topics.description: Know and use the vocabulary of prime numbers, prime factors, and composite numbers; establish whether a number up to 100 is prime; recall prime numbers up to 19
evidence: Explain that a prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself
Determine whether 51 is prime or composite and justify the answer
List all prime numbers up to 19 from memory

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Shape patterns
topics.description: Generate a number or shape pattern that follows a given rule; identify apparent features of the pattern not explicit in the rule and explain informally why they occur
evidence: Given 'start at 1, add 3', generate terms and notice they alternate odd/even
Given a shape pattern, predict the next three terms and describe the rule
Explain why starting at 2 and adding 4 always gives even numbers

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Short division with remainders
topics.description: Divide numbers up to four digits by a one-digit number using short division (and place-value/array strategies); interpret remainders appropriately for the context
evidence: Calculate 4,932 ÷ 6 using short division
Solve 125 ÷ 8 and interpret: 15 remainder 5 means 15 full bags with 5 left over
Use the multiplication–division relationship to check a division answer

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Square and cube numbers
topics.description: Recognise and use square numbers and cube numbers, and the notation for squared (²) and cubed (³)
evidence: Identify 49 as 7² and explain that 7 × 7 = 49
Calculate 4³ = 64 and explain it means 4 × 4 × 4
List the first ten square numbers

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Understanding fractions
topics.description: Solve problems involving scaling by simple fractions and problems involving simple rates
evidence: A recipe for 4 people needs 200 g of flour — how much for 6 people?
If 3 kg costs £12, how much does 5 kg cost?
Scale a shape by a factor of 1/2 and find the new dimensions

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Brackets in Expressions
topics.description: Use parentheses, brackets, or braces in numerical expressions and evaluate expressions containing these grouping symbols
evidence: Evaluate 3 × (4 + 5) by computing inside the parentheses first
Evaluate {2 × [3 + (7 − 1)]} with nested grouping symbols
Insert parentheses into an expression to make it equal a target value

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Multiplying decimals by whole numbers
topics.description: Multiply one-digit numbers with up to two decimal places by whole numbers (e.g. 3.47 × 6)
evidence: Correctly compute 4.56 × 7 using a written method
Use place-value reasoning to explain why 3.2 × 5 = 16.0
Model a decimal multiplication using an area diagram or expanded form

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Dividing by two-digit numbers
topics.description: Divide numbers up to 4 digits by a two-digit number using formal written short division where appropriate, interpreting remainders according to context
evidence: Use short division to compute 3,648 ÷ 16 efficiently
Explain when short division is more appropriate than long division
Interpret a remainder as a decimal or fraction in a measurement context

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Division with Decimals
topics.description: Use written division methods in cases where the answer has up to two decimal places; divide decimals to hundredths by whole numbers
evidence: Compute 14.76 ÷ 4 using a written method to get 3.69
Explain how to continue long division past the decimal point to obtain a decimal quotient
Solve a context problem that requires dividing a decimal amount equally (e.g. sharing £18.60 among 5 people)

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Division with remainders (age 10+)
topics.description: Divide numbers up to 4 digits by a two-digit divisor using formal written long division, interpreting remainders as whole numbers, fractions, or by rounding as appropriate
evidence: Compute 4,752 ÷ 13 using long division and express the remainder as a fraction
Decide whether to round up or down a division remainder in a real-life context (e.g. buses needed)
Explain each step of the long division algorithm for a 4-digit ÷ 2-digit calculation

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Estimation to check answers to calculations
topics.description: Use estimation to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, an appropriate degree of accuracy
evidence: Estimate 487 × 23 by rounding to 500 × 20 and use this to check a calculated answer
Determine whether an exact answer or an estimate is more appropriate in a given context
Spot an unreasonable answer by comparing with a quick mental estimate

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Factor algorithms and spreadsheets
topics.description: Create and use algorithms with steps and decisions, and digital tools such as spreadsheets, to experiment with factors, multiples and divisibility, and describe the patterns that emerge
evidence: Write an algorithm that tests every number from 1 to 24 and records it if 24 divided by it leaves no remainder
Use a spreadsheet column of multiples of 6 and highlight those that are also multiples of 4
Describe the pattern found when listing numbers between 1 and 50 that have exactly two factors

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Long multiplication (age 10+)
topics.description: Fluently multiply multi-digit whole numbers (up to 4 digits by 2 digits) using the formal written method of long multiplication
evidence: Correctly compute 2,463 × 37 using long multiplication
Explain each partial product in a long multiplication and why they are added
Multiply a four-digit number by a two-digit number without procedural errors

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Mental calculation strategies
topics.description: Perform mental calculations including with mixed operations and large numbers, using strategies such as partitioning, compensation, and derived facts
evidence: Mentally compute 45 × 8 by partitioning into 40 × 8 + 5 × 8
Use known facts to derive 6.5 × 4 mentally
Solve a multi-operation mental calculation such as 250 × 3 + 500 and explain the strategy used

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Multiplying and dividing by 10, 100 and 1,000
topics.description: Multiply and divide numbers by 10, 100, and 1000 giving answers up to three decimal places, understanding that digits shift position in the place-value chart
evidence: Compute 3.456 × 100 = 345.6 correctly
Compute 45 ÷ 1000 = 0.045 correctly
Explain why multiplying by 10 shifts each digit one place to the left

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Multi-step problems: choosing operations
topics.description: Solve problems involving addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division, deciding which operations and methods to use and why; solve multi-step problems in contexts
evidence: Solve a three-step word problem involving a mix of all four operations
Explain why particular operations were chosen for each step of a multi-step problem
Identify and correct an error in a multi-step solution that used the wrong operation

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Order of operations
topics.description: Understand and apply the conventional order of operations (PEMDAS/BODMAS) to carry out calculations involving the four operations
evidence: Explain why 8 + 2 × 5 = 18 (not 50) by referencing multiplication before addition
Evaluate a multi-step expression like 12 ÷ 3 + 4 × 2 correctly as 12
State the correct order: brackets, then orders/exponents, then multiplication/division (L→R), then addition/subtraction (L→R)

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Rounding Answers
topics.description: Solve problems which require answers to be rounded to specified degrees of accuracy
evidence: Compute a division and round the result to one decimal place as specified
Determine the appropriate degree of accuracy for a measurement context (e.g. round to nearest penny)
Solve a problem where an unrounded decimal answer must be interpreted in context (e.g. whole containers needed)

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Writing Number Sentences

evidence: Write an expression for 'add 8 and 7, then multiply by 2' using parentheses
Explain what 4 × (365 − 12) represents without computing it
Compare two expressions and determine which is larger without evaluating

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Divisibility rules
topics.description: Decide without dividing whether a whole number is divisible by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9 or 10 by choosing the appropriate rule — the last digit (2, 5, 10), the number formed by the last two or three digits (4, 8), the sum of the digits (3, 9), or divisibility by both 2 and 3 (6) — and explain why a rule works using place value and known multiples (for example, 100 is a multiple of 4, so only the last two digits matter for 4)
evidence: Use the appropriate rule to decide whether a number such as 4 536 is divisible by each of 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9 and 10, and check one of the answers by dividing

Explain why a number divisible by both 2 and 3 is divisible by 6, and use a counterexample such as 12 (divisible by 2 and by 4 but not by 8) to show that combining rules only works for suitable pairs

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Estimating to check decimals
topics.description: Use estimation and rounding to check the reasonableness of answers when multiplying and dividing decimals (including by multiples of powers of 10), identifying misplaced decimal points
evidence: Estimate 4.87 x 30 as about 5 x 30 = 150 before calculating 146.1
Decide whether 63.6 / 20 = 31.8 is reasonable by rounding to 60 / 20 = 3 and find the error
Round 2.46 x 400 to 2.5 x 400 = 1000 to check a calculated answer of 984

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Factors, multiples, and primes (age 11+)
topics.description: Use the concepts and vocabulary of prime numbers, factors, multiples, common factors, common multiples, highest common factor (HCF), lowest common multiple (LCM), and prime factorisation including product notation and the unique factorisation property

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Priority of operations

evidence: Evaluate expressions involving brackets, indices, and all four operations in the correct order
Explain why the order of operations is necessary to avoid ambiguity
Use the reciprocal of a number and understand that a number multiplied by its reciprocal gives 1

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Sign Rules for Multiplication
topics.description: Multiply and divide with positive and negative integers and rational numbers, understanding the rules for the sign of the product or quotient
evidence: Apply the sign rules when multiplying two integers (positive × negative, negative × negative)
Apply the sign rules when dividing two integers
Solve multi-step real-world problems involving all four operations with positive and negative rational numbers

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Using inverse operations
topics.description: Recognise and use relationships between operations including inverse operations; use these relationships to check answers and simplify calculations
evidence: Use addition and subtraction as inverse operations to check and solve problems
Use multiplication and division as inverse operations to check and solve problems
Recognise that squaring and square-rooting are inverse operations

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Number Words to Twenty

evidence: Read the word 'twelve' and identify it as 12
Write the word form of a given number 1–20
Match numeral cards to number word cards

topics.name: Ordering numbers to 20

evidence: Put the cards 14, 3, 19, 0 and 8 in order from smallest to largest

Say the number that comes just before 13 and just after 13

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Reading and writing numbers to 100
topics.description: Read and write numerals from 0 to 100, and describe the different ways numbers are used in everyday life (to count, measure, put things in order or label them)
evidence: Read two-digit numerals up to 100 correctly
Write any number 0–100 as a numeral from dictation
Find numbers around home or school (e.g. a house number, a price, a page number, a bus number) and say whether each one counts, measures, orders or labels something

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Reading and writing numbers to 20
topics.description: Read and write numerals from 0 to 20
evidence: Read any numeral 0–20 when shown it
Write numerals 0–20 legibly from dictation
Represent a number of objects with the correct written numeral

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: The teen numbers

Decompose 17 into 10 + 7 and record as an equation
Explain that 13 is 'one ten and three ones'

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: 10 More or 10 Less

Explain that adding 10 increases the tens digit by 1
Answer '10 more than 73' without using fingers or counting on

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: A Hundred Is Ten Tens
topics.description: Understand that 100 can be thought of as a bundle of ten tens — called a 'hundred'
evidence: Explain that 10 groups of 10 ones make 100
Bundle ten tens sticks into one hundred and describe what happened

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: A Ten Is Ten Ones

topics.subject: Mathematics

Order a set of numbers from smallest to largest, including numbers either side of 100 (e.g. 98, 104, 111, 120)

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Number Words to 100
topics.description: Read and write numbers to at least 100 in words

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Place value understanding and number facts
topics.description: Use place value understanding and number facts to solve problems
evidence: Use knowledge that 34 = 30 + 4 to help add 34 + 20 = 54
Solve 'I think of a number, add 10, and get 45. What was my number?'
Apply partitioning to solve a problem in an unfamiliar context

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Reading and writing numbers to 120
topics.description: Count to 120 starting at any number less than 120; read and write numerals to 120
evidence: Count from 47 to 120 without errors
Read the numeral 108 correctly, e.g. by finding it on a number chart continued past 100
Write the numeral for one hundred and fifteen

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Renaming two-digit numbers

topics.name: Representing numbers to 120

Show 63 as 6 tens and 3 ones with base-ten blocks or a drawing, and show 112 with bundles of ten straws and loose straws (real or on-screen)
Estimate 'about how many' objects are in a set of 30–50 without counting, then count to check

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: The multiples of 10

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: 10 or 100 More or Less

Given a three-digit number, state what is 100 more and 100 less

topics.subject: Mathematics

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Ordering Numbers to 1000
topics.description: Compare and order numbers up to 1000 using >, =, and < symbols, based on place-value understanding
evidence: Compare two three-digit numbers by examining hundreds first, then tens, then ones
Use >, =, and < correctly to record comparisons of three-digit numbers
Order a set of numbers up to 1000 from smallest to largest, e.g. by placing them on a paper or interactive number line

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Place Value to 1000
topics.description: Solve number problems and practical problems involving place value of numbers up to 1000
evidence: Solve a problem that requires identifying how many hundreds, tens, or ones are in a number
Apply place-value knowledge to a practical context (e.g. counting money in pounds)
Explain the strategy used to solve a place-value problem

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Reading and writing numbers to 1000
topics.description: Read and write numbers to 1000 in numerals, number names, and expanded form
evidence: Read a three-digit numeral aloud correctly
Write a three-digit number in words (e.g. 'three hundred and forty-two')
Write a number in expanded form (e.g. 600 + 30 + 7)

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Representing numbers to 1000
topics.description: Identify, represent and estimate three-digit numbers using different representations: place a number on a 0–1000 number line marked only in hundreds or unmarked, estimate the value of a marked point, and represent a number with base-ten blocks (hundreds, tens and ones), a place-value chart and a drawing, including numbers with a zero digit and non-standard partitions
evidence: Mark 346 in about the right place on a 0–1000 number line marked in hundreds (between 300 and 400, a little before halfway), and estimate that an unlabelled point three-quarters of the way along is about 750
Represent 507 with physical or on-screen base-ten blocks and on a place-value chart, showing the empty tens column as 0
Match a drawing of 3 hundreds, 14 tens and 2 ones to the numeral 442

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: The multiples of 100
topics.description: Understand that the multiples of 100 (100–900) each represent a number of hundreds with 0 tens and 0 ones
evidence: Identify that 300 means 3 hundreds, 0 tens, 0 ones
Place multiples of 100 on a number line to 1000
Read and write multiples of 100 and explain their place-value structure

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: The three digits of a three-digit number
topics.description: Understand that the three digits of a three-digit number represent amounts of hundreds, tens, and ones
evidence: State the value of each digit in a three-digit number (e.g. in 362, the 3 represents 3 hundreds)
Partition a three-digit number into hundreds, tens, and ones (e.g. 485 = 400 + 80 + 5)
Explain why 706 has 7 hundreds, 0 tens, and 6 ones

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: 1000 More or Less
topics.description: Find 1000 more or less than a given number
evidence: Given 4,562, state that 1000 more is 5,562 and 1000 less is 3,562
Explain using place value that only the thousands digit changes
Apply this skill to numbers beyond 10,000

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing Large Numbers
topics.description: Order and compare numbers beyond 1000
evidence: Compare two four-digit numbers using >, <, and = by examining digits from the highest place value
Order a set of numbers up to 10,000 from smallest to largest
Justify the ordering using place-value reasoning

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Negative Numbers
topics.description: Count backwards through zero to include negative numbers
evidence: Count backwards from 5 through zero: 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0, −1, −2 …
Place negative numbers on a number line
Understand that negative numbers are less than zero and use them in context (e.g. temperature)

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Numbers to 10,000
topics.description: Identify, represent, and estimate numbers up to 10,000 using different representations
evidence: Represent a four-digit number on a place-value chart or with base-ten materials
Estimate where a number falls on a 0–10,000 number line
Match different representations of the same number (e.g. expanded form, place-value counters, numeral)

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Place value of each digit
topics.description: Recognise the place value of each digit in a four-digit number (thousands, hundreds, tens, and ones)
evidence: State the value of each digit in a four-digit number (e.g. in 7,345 the 7 represents 7 thousands)
Partition a four-digit number into thousands, hundreds, tens, and ones
Compose a four-digit number from given place-value parts (e.g. 3000 + 400 + 50 + 2 = 3,452)

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Place Value Problem-Solving
topics.description: Solve number and practical problems involving place value with increasingly large positive numbers
evidence: Solve a problem requiring rounding, comparing, or ordering numbers beyond 1000
Apply place-value knowledge in a practical context (e.g. population figures, distances)
Explain the strategy used, referencing place-value understanding

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Reading and writing numbers (age 9+)
topics.description: Read, write, order, and compare whole numbers up to at least 1,000,000 using base-ten numerals, number names, expanded form, and place-value understanding
evidence: Write 403,072 in words and in expanded form
Compare 548,301 and 543,801 using < and explain the reasoning
Order four six-digit numbers from smallest to largest

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Roman numerals to 100
topics.description: Read Roman numerals to 100 (I to C) and understand that the numeral system changed over time to include zero and place value
evidence: Read and write Roman numerals I, V, X, L, C and combinations up to 100
Convert between Roman numerals and Hindu-Arabic numerals (e.g. XLIV = 44)
Explain that Roman numerals have no zero and no place-value system

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Rounding to 10, 100, 1000
topics.description: Round any number to the nearest 10, 100, or 1000
evidence: Explain the rounding rule using a number line (which multiple is closer)
Apply rounding to estimate calculations

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Counting forwards and backwards (age 9+)
topics.description: Count forwards and backwards in steps of powers of 10 (10, 100, 1000, 10,000, 100,000) for any given number up to 1,000,000
evidence: Count on in 10,000s from 462,000
Count back in 100,000s from 800,000
Identify the next three terms: 375,000; 475,000; 575,000; ...

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Negative numbers in context
topics.description: Interpret negative numbers in context (temperature, sea level, bank balance); count forwards and backwards with positive and negative whole numbers, including through zero
evidence: Place –3, –1, 0, 2, 5 on a number line
The temperature is –4°C and rises by 7 degrees — what is the new temperature?
Count backwards from 3 in ones: 3, 2, 1, 0, –1, –2

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Place Value × 10 Pattern
topics.description: Recognise that in a multi-digit whole number, a digit in one place represents ten times what it represents in the place to its right (e.g. 700 ÷ 70 = 10)
evidence: Explain that the 3 in 3,000 is ten times the 3 in 300
Complete: 700 ÷ 70 = __ and explain using place-value reasoning
State how many times greater the value of the 5 in 50,000 is than the 5 in 5,000

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Roman numerals to 1000
topics.description: Read Roman numerals to 1000 (M) and recognise years written in Roman numerals
evidence: Read MCMXCIX as 1999
Write 2024 in Roman numerals (MMXXIV)
Explain the subtractive principle: IV = 4 not IIII

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Rounding Large Numbers
topics.description: Round any whole number up to 1,000,000 to the nearest 10, 100, 1,000, 10,000, or 100,000 using place-value understanding
evidence: Round 456,782 to the nearest 10,000 (460,000)
Round 950,500 to the nearest 100,000 and explain the boundary case
Use rounding to estimate the sum of 387,412 + 214,560

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Working with Large Numbers
topics.description: Solve number and practical problems involving reading, writing, ordering, comparing, and rounding whole numbers up to 1,000,000
evidence: What is the largest six-digit number with digits summing to 15?
A stadium holds 67,450 people. Round to the nearest thousand for a news report
Order the populations of five cities and find the difference between the largest and smallest

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Rounding whole numbers and decimals
topics.description: Round decimals to any place using place-value understanding; round any whole number to a required degree of accuracy
evidence: Round 3.4567 to 2 decimal places (3.46)
Use rounding to estimate 4.83 × 2.17 ≈ 5 × 2 = 10

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Measuring temperature
topics.description: Use negative numbers in context (temperature, finance, sea level); calculate intervals across zero
evidence: The temperature falls from 3°C to −5°C — what is the drop? (8 degrees)
Calculate the difference between a bank balance of −£120 and £350
Order −7, −3, 0, 2, 5 on a number line and find the interval from −7 to 5

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Numbers to Ten Million
topics.description: Solve number and practical problems involving reading, writing, ordering, comparing, rounding, and negative numbers up to 10,000,000
evidence: A country's population is 8,274,500 — round to the nearest million for a headline
Order the depths of three ocean trenches given in metres including negative values
Estimate the total attendance at three events by rounding each to the nearest 100,000

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Patterns with Powers of Ten
topics.description: Explain patterns in zeros when multiplying by powers of 10 and in decimal-point placement when multiplying/dividing by a power of 10; use whole-number exponents to denote powers of 10 (e.g. 10³ = 1000)
evidence: Write 10⁴ = 10,000 and explain the exponent means four factors of 10
Explain why 3.4 × 10² = 340 by describing the decimal shift
Predict 2.56 × 10³ without calculating and explain the pattern

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Place Value × 10 and ÷ 10
topics.description: Recognise that in a multi-digit number, a digit in one place represents 10 times as much as in the place to its right and 1/10 of what it represents in the place to its left
evidence: Explain that the 4 in 0.04 is 1/10 of the 4 in 0.4
State that a digit moving one place left is ×10 and one place right is ÷10
Compare the value of the 6 in 6,000 and in 0.006

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Reading, writing and comparing decimals to thousandths
topics.description: Read, write, and compare decimals to thousandths using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form; compare using >, =, < based on place-value meaning
evidence: Compare 0.372 and 0.38 using place-value reasoning
Write 'five and sixty-two thousandths' as 5.062

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Reading and writing numbers to 10,000,000
topics.description: Read, write, order, and compare numbers up to 10,000,000 and determine the value of each digit
evidence: Write 4,302,561 in words
Order four seven-digit numbers from smallest to largest
State the value of the 7 in 7,045,200 as seven million

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Decimal place value to thousandths
topics.description: Identify the value of each digit in numbers given to three decimal places (e.g. in 4.378, the 7 represents 7 hundredths)
evidence: State the value of each digit in 2.635 (2 ones, 6 tenths, 3 hundredths, 5 thousandths)
Explain the relationship between adjacent decimal places (each place is ten times smaller)
Write a number given digit values (e.g. 4 ones, 0 tenths, 7 hundredths, 3 thousandths = 4.073)

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Absolute value as distance
topics.description: Understand the absolute value of a rational number as its distance from zero on the number line; interpret absolute value as magnitude in real-world contexts; distinguish absolute value comparisons from ordering statements
evidence: Define absolute value as distance from zero on a number line
Calculate the absolute value of positive and negative rational numbers
Distinguish between comparing absolute values and comparing signed numbers in real-world contexts

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Rounding to decimal places or significant figures
topics.description: Round numbers and measures to an appropriate degree of accuracy including to a specified number of decimal places or significant figures
evidence: Round numbers to a given number of decimal places
Round numbers to a given number of significant figures
Choose an appropriate degree of accuracy for a given context

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Place value and number-line representation
topics.description: Understand and use place value for decimals, measures, and integers of any size; extend the number system to include all positive and negative integers, decimals, and fractions on a single number line
evidence: Identify the value of any digit in numbers of any size including decimals
Place positive and negative integers, decimals, and fractions on a number line
Use place value to compare and order numbers across the full number system

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Ordering and comparing signed integers, decimals and fractions
topics.description: Order positive and negative integers, decimals, and fractions on a number line; use the symbols =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥ to compare values including negative numbers and mixed representations
evidence: Order a mixed set of positive and negative integers, decimals, and fractions
Use the symbols =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥ correctly in mathematical statements
Compare numbers presented in different forms such as 0.75 and 3/4

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Square and cube numbers
topics.description: Use integer powers and associated real roots (square, cube, and higher); recognise powers of 2, 3, 4, and 5; distinguish between exact representations of roots and their decimal approximations
evidence: Calculate squares, cubes, and higher integer powers of whole numbers
Find square roots and cube roots of perfect squares and perfect cubes
Recognise key powers (powers of 2 up to 2¹⁰, powers of 3 up to 3⁵, etc.) and distinguish exact roots from approximations

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Estimating by rounding
topics.description: Use approximation through rounding to estimate answers and calculate possible resulting errors expressed using inequality notation a < x ≤ b; understand upper and lower bounds of rounded values
evidence: Estimate the answer to a calculation by rounding all values appropriately
Calculate upper and lower bounds of a rounded measurement
Express error intervals using inequality notation

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Powers of Ten Notation
topics.description: Interpret and compare numbers in standard form A × 10ⁿ where 1 ≤ A < 10 and n is an integer; convert between ordinary numbers and standard form
evidence: Convert large and small numbers into standard form A × 10ⁿ
Convert numbers from standard form back to ordinary notation
Compare and order numbers given in standard form

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Number Sets & Infinity
topics.description: Appreciate the infinite nature of the sets of integers, real numbers, and rational numbers; position integers on a number line and distinguish between rational and irrational numbers
evidence: Explain that rational numbers can be written as a fraction of two integers and have terminating or repeating decimals
Give examples of irrational numbers and explain why their decimal expansions neither terminate nor repeat
Appreciate that between any two numbers there are infinitely many other numbers

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Likelihood Language
topics.description: Use probability language to describe and compare the likelihood of everyday events using words such as certain, likely, even chance, unlikely, impossible
evidence: Place five everyday events (e.g. 'the sun will rise tomorrow', 'it will snow in July', 'I'll flip heads'; for example an event and its opposite, such as 'it will rain today' and 'it will not rain today') on a scale from impossible to certain
Use 'likely', 'unlikely', 'certain', 'impossible', and 'even chance' correctly to describe different events
Explain why pulling a red ball from a bag of mostly red balls is 'likely' but not 'certain'

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Simple Chance Experiments
topics.description: Conduct simple probability experiments — flipping a coin, rolling a die, pulling coloured counters from a bag — record results, and compare experimental outcomes with expected theoretical outcomes
evidence: Flip a coin 20 times, record heads and tails in a tally chart, and describe what they notice about the results
Roll a die 30 times and compare how often each number came up with what they expected
Pull counters from a bag, record results, and explain whether the outcomes matched their prediction

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Equally Likely Outcomes
topics.description: Understand that 'equally likely' means every outcome has exactly the same chance of occurring; identify whether a given situation has equally likely outcomes (a fair coin, a fair die, a spinner with equal sections) or unequally likely outcomes (a bag with more of one colour, a spinner with unequal sections)
evidence: Explain that a fair coin has equally likely outcomes because heads and tails each have the same chance
Identify whether a spinner with unequal sections has equally likely outcomes or not, and explain why
Give an example of a situation with equally likely outcomes and one without, explaining the difference

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Ordering Likelihoods
topics.description: Compare the likelihood of different events and order them from least to most likely — including situations with unequal outcomes such as a bag with more of one colour than another, or a spinner with sections of different sizes — and explain reasoning using informal language
evidence: Order four or more events from least likely to most likely and justify each placement
Compare likelihoods when outcomes are not equally likely — e.g. 'Drawing red from a bag with 7 red and 3 blue is more likely than drawing blue'
Explain why some events are closer to 'even chance' and others are closer to 'certain' or 'impossible'

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Experimental vs Theoretical
topics.description: Run repeated probability experiments and compare experimental (relative frequency) results with theoretical predictions; understand and demonstrate that as the number of trials increases, the experimental probability tends towards the theoretical probability — and that short runs can give very different results
evidence: Roll a die 60 times and compare experimental frequencies with the expected 10 per number
Explain why experimental results don't exactly match theoretical predictions but get closer with more trials
Predict what would happen if the experiment were repeated 600 times instead of 60, and check the prediction with a digital simulation of many more trials

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Independent and dependent events
topics.description: Identify whether events in chance experiments and everyday situations are independent (one does not affect the other) or dependent (the first outcome changes the chances of the next)
evidence: Explain that getting heads on one coin flip does not change the chance of heads on the next flip
Explain why taking a red marble out of a bag and not putting it back changes the chance of drawing red next
Sort five described pairs of events into independent and dependent

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Probability as a Fraction
topics.description: Describe the probability of simple equally-likely outcomes using unit fractions: the probability of rolling a 6 on a fair die is 1/6, flipping heads is 1/2, picking one specific colour from three equally represented colours is 1/3; place these fractional probabilities on a 0-to-1 probability scale
evidence: State that the probability of rolling a 6 on a fair die is 1/6 and explain why
Express the probability of picking a red card from a standard deck as 26/52 or 1/2
Write the probability of a simple event as a fraction: favourable outcomes over total outcomes

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Calculating Simple Probability
topics.description: Calculate the probability of a simple event with equally likely outcomes using the formula: probability = number of favourable outcomes ÷ total number of possible outcomes; express the result as a fraction in its simplest form; apply to rolling dice, drawing from bags, and other simple chance situations
evidence: Calculate the probability of drawing a blue marble from a bag of 3 blue and 7 red as 3/10
Use the formula P(event) = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes to solve at least three different problems
Explain why increasing the number of favourable outcomes increases the probability

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Experimental probability
topics.description: Record, describe, and analyse the frequency of outcomes from probability experiments to develop an understanding of relative frequency as an estimate of probability
evidence: Conduct a coin-toss experiment, record results in a frequency table, and calculate relative frequencies
Compare experimental results with theoretical probability and explain discrepancies
Predict that relative frequency approaches theoretical probability as the number of trials increases

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Probabilities Sum to One
topics.description: Understand that when all possible outcomes of a trial are listed, their probabilities must add up to 1; use this to find the probability of an event NOT happening: P(not A) = 1 − P(A); apply this shortcut to avoid counting all unfavourable outcomes directly
evidence: List all outcomes of spinning a 4-colour spinner and verify their probabilities add up to 1
Calculate P(not rolling a 3) as 1 − 1/6 = 5/6 using the complement rule
Spot an error in a probability table where the values don't sum to 1 and explain what's wrong

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: The 0-to-1 Probability Scale
topics.description: Understand probability as a measure expressed as a number between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain); place events on the probability scale; express probabilities as fractions, decimals, and percentages
evidence: Place events on a number line from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain), expressing positions as fractions or decimals
Explain that a probability of 0.5 means 'even chance' and connect this to the informal word 'likely'
Convert between informal language ('very unlikely') and a numerical position on the 0-to-1 scale

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Complementary events
topics.description: Understand and apply the rule that probabilities of all mutually exclusive outcomes sum to one; use this to find the probability of a complementary event (P(not A) = 1 − P(A))
evidence: Verify that probabilities of all outcomes listed for a spinner sum to 1
Calculate the probability of NOT rolling a 6 as 1 − 1/6 = 5/6
Identify an error in a probability distribution where the values do not sum to 1

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: The Probability Scale
topics.description: Understand probability as a measure on a scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain); use the language of probability including likely, unlikely, certain, and impossible
evidence: Place everyday events on a 0-to-1 probability scale with justification
Explain why a fair six-sided die gives each number a probability of 1/6
Distinguish between equally likely outcomes (fair coin) and unequally likely outcomes (biased spinner)

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Probability models
topics.description: Develop a probability model (a list of all the outcomes of a chance process with a probability for each, adding to 1) and use it to find probabilities of events: a uniform model gives every outcome the same probability (e.g. selecting a student at random from a class); a non-uniform model uses probabilities estimated from the observed frequencies of a chance process (e.g. how a tossed paper cup lands); compare a model's probabilities with observed frequencies and, when they disagree, explain whether the difference is plausibly chance variation or a sign that the model does not fit (e.g. a biased die or unequal spinner sections)
evidence: Use a uniform model to find that a randomly chosen student from a class of 25 with 12 girls is Jane with probability 1/25 and is a girl with probability 12/25
Toss a paper cup 50 times (e.g. 31 on its side, 13 open end up, 6 open end down), write a model with probabilities 0.62, 0.26 and 0.12, and explain why the three outcomes are not equally likely
Compare 600 rolls of a die that showed 160 sixes with the 100 sixes a fair-die model predicts, and argue that a difference this large suggests the die is biased rather than just chance

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Sets & Venn Diagrams
topics.description: Enumerate sets and their unions and intersections systematically using tables, grids, and Venn diagrams to organise and count outcomes
evidence: List the elements in the union and intersection of two sets using a Venn diagram
Use a two-way table to enumerate all possible outcomes of two combined events
Shade regions of a Venn diagram to represent A ∪ B, A ∩ B, and A′ (complement)

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Simulating chance events
topics.description: Design and use a simulation to estimate the probability of a compound event: choose a random device (coins, dice, spinners, counters drawn with replacement, random-digit tables, or calculator or software random numbers) and a mapping whose probabilities match the situation; define one complete trial (what is generated and when the trial stops) and the event being counted; run many trials; and estimate the probability as the event's relative frequency. Explain why the model fits (each simulated outcome has the same probability as the real one, and successive outcomes are independent when the real ones are), and why different runs give different estimates that become more consistent as the number of trials grows; where a theoretical value can be found (e.g. with a tree diagram), compare it with the estimate
evidence: Map random digits 0–3 to 'type A' and 4–9 to 'not type A' to model donors who are type A with probability 40%, and explain why the mapping fits (4 of the 10 equally likely digits)

Define one trial as reading digits until the first 0–3 appears, count it as a success if at least four digits were needed, run 50 trials and report the relative frequency as the estimated probability that at least four donors are needed
Explain why two groups who each ran 50 trials estimated 0.18 and 0.26, and why pooling their trials (or running 500) gives a more reliable estimate

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Tree diagrams
topics.description: Generate theoretical sample spaces for single and combined events using listing, tables, and tree diagrams, and calculate theoretical probabilities as the number of favourable outcomes divided by the total number of equally likely outcomes
evidence: List all 36 outcomes when rolling two dice and find P(total = 7)
Draw a tree diagram for two successive events and multiply along branches for combined probabilities
Calculate the probability of a combined event using a sample space diagram and simplify the fraction

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Venn Diagrams and Counting Outcomes
topics.description: Construct and interpret Venn diagrams with two or three sets to organise and count outcomes; use systematic listing and the product rule for counting to enumerate all possible outcomes of combined events
evidence: Draw a two-circle Venn diagram to sort 30 students by whether they like football, like cricket, or like both
Shade the intersection A ∩ B and the union A ∪ B on a Venn diagram and explain what each region represents
Use a completed Venn diagram to calculate P(A), P(B), P(A ∩ B), and P(A ∪ B)

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Bar Models for Ratios
topics.description: Represent ratio and proportion problems using bar models (rectangular strips divided into equal parts labelled with quantities) and tape diagrams (segmented strips showing part-to-part and part-to-whole relationships); use these visual models to set up and solve unequal sharing, scaling, and percentage problems — drawing the diagram first, then reading off the answer
evidence: Draw a bar model to represent a ratio problem — e.g. sharing £20 in the ratio 3:2 by drawing 5 equal blocks
Use a bar model to solve a proportion problem and explain each step
Compare bar models with other representations (tables, double number lines) and explain when each is most useful

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Percentages (age 9+)
topics.description: Know and use the vocabulary of ratio and proportion — ratio, proportion, percentage, scale, equivalent, unequal, relative size, part-to-part, part-to-whole, and out of — and understand the difference between ratio (comparing parts to parts) and proportion (comparing a part to the whole)
evidence: Explain the difference between a 'ratio' and a 'proportion' using a concrete example like mixing paint
Use 'per cent' correctly and convert between fractions, decimals, and percentages in context
Define 'scale factor' and use it to describe how a shape has been enlarged or reduced

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Calculating Percentages
topics.description: Solve problems involving the calculation of percentages of amounts (e.g. 15% of 360) and the use of percentages for comparison
evidence: Calculate 15% of 360 by finding 10% and 5% and combining
Compare two discounts given as percentages of different original prices
Explain a strategy for finding any percentage of an amount using known percentage facts

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Ratio Problems
topics.description: Solve problems involving the relative sizes of two quantities where missing values can be found by using integer multiplication and division facts
evidence: If the ratio of red to blue beads is 3:5 and there are 15 blue beads, find the number of red beads
Use multiplication facts to find the missing value: 'For every 2 apples there are 5 oranges; if there are 20 oranges, how many apples?'
Explain the multiplicative relationship between two quantities in a ratio context

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Scale and similar shapes
topics.description: Solve problems involving similar shapes where the scale factor is known or can be found
evidence: Find the missing side of a similar rectangle given a scale factor of 3
Determine the scale factor between two similar triangles from given side lengths
Use a scale factor to enlarge or reduce a shape and verify that all sides are in the same ratio

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Understanding fractions
topics.description: Solve problems involving unequal sharing and grouping using knowledge of fractions and multiples
evidence: Share 40 sweets between two children in the ratio 3:5
Solve: 'Tom gets twice as many as Sam and Sam gets three times as many as Jo. If there are 30 altogether, how many does each get?'
Use fraction knowledge to explain why sharing in ratio 2:3 means one person gets 2/5 of the total

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Compound Units
topics.description: Use compound units such as speed (distance ÷ time), unit pricing (cost ÷ quantity), and density (mass ÷ volume); solve problems involving compound units
evidence: Calculate average speed given distance and time, converting between km/h and m/s if needed
Compare unit prices of two products sold in different quantities to find the better deal
Use the density formula to find mass, volume, or density given the other two values

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Dividing Quantities by Ratio
topics.description: Divide a given quantity into two parts in a given part:part or part:whole ratio, and express the division as a fraction of the whole
evidence: Share £60 between two people in the ratio 2:3 by finding the value of one part
Express the result of sharing 24 sweets as 10 and 14 in ratio form as 5:7
Solve problems involving three-part ratios (e.g. divide 180 in the ratio 1:2:3)

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: One Quantity as a Fraction
topics.description: Express one quantity as a fraction of another where the result may be less than 1 or greater than 1, and interpret the meaning in context
evidence: Express 45 minutes as a fraction of 2 hours (= 3/8)
Express a larger quantity as a fraction of a smaller one and explain why the result exceeds 1
Simplify the resulting fraction and interpret its meaning in the original context

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Percentages as Fractions
topics.description: Define percentage as 'number of parts per hundred'; interpret percentages and percentage changes as a fraction or a decimal; express one quantity as a percentage of another; compare quantities using percentages; work with percentages greater than 100%
evidence: Convert fluently between percentages, fractions, and decimals
Express one quantity as a percentage of another
Calculate percentage increases and decreases and interpret percentages greater than 100%

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Proportional Reasoning Vocabulary
topics.description: Know and use advanced vocabulary of multiplicative reasoning — direct proportion, inverse proportion, ratio, rate, unit rate, compound unit, scale factor — accurately in problem-solving contexts
evidence: Distinguish between 'direct proportion' and 'inverse proportion' with real-world examples
Use 'rate', 'speed', and 'density' correctly and explain what units they are measured in
Calculate using compound measures — e.g. work out the speed of a car that travels 120 miles in 2 hours

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Proportion Graphs
topics.description: Represent proportional relationships using double number lines (two parallel number lines aligned at 0) and ratio tables; recognise that equivalent ratios generate straight lines through the origin when graphed
evidence: Plot pairs of proportional values on a coordinate grid and draw the straight line through the origin
Explain why a directly proportional relationship always passes through (0,0)
Read a proportion graph to find an unknown value — e.g. 'If 3 kg costs £6, how much does 5 kg cost?'

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Ratio Notation
topics.description: Use ratio notation to describe the relationship between two or more quantities, simplify ratios to their simplest form, and convert between ratio and fraction representations
evidence: Write a ratio from a word problem and simplify it (e.g. 12:8 = 3:2)
Convert a ratio to equivalent fractions of a whole (e.g. 3:2 means 3/5 and 2/5)
Simplify ratios involving decimals or fractions by finding a common multiplier

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Scale drawings and maps
topics.description: Use a scale, given as a ratio (e.g. 1:50), as a statement such as '1 cm represents 2 m', or as a scale factor, to work out actual lengths from a scale drawing or map and drawing lengths from actual lengths; reproduce a scale drawing at a different scale by finding each new drawing length, either through the actual length or from the ratio of the two scales; and solve map, room-plan and design problems with consistent units, converting between mm, cm, m and km before or after scaling. Areas from scale drawings and the area factor are developed in the follow-on topic Area from scale drawings
evidence: On a 1:50 room plan, find that a 9 cm wall is 450 cm = 4.5 m long, and that a 1.2 m doorway should be drawn 2.4 cm wide
Redraw a 1:50 plan at 1:100 by halving every drawing length (the 9 cm wall becomes 4.5 cm), and check one length by converting it back to the actual 4.5 m
Find the real distance between two towns 6.5 cm apart on a 1:25,000 map and give it in kilometres (162,500 cm = 1.625 km)

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Area and volume unit conversions
topics.description: Convert between related area and volume units by deriving and applying the square or cube of the linear conversion factor, including the relationship between cubic centimetres and litres. Use decimal notation up to three decimal places where appropriate; general linear-unit and time conversions are covered in Converting measurement units.
evidence: Explain from a 100-by-100 cm square why 1 m² = 10,000 cm², and use that factor in both directions
Explain from a cube why 1 m³ = 1,000,000 cm³ rather than 100 cm³, and convert using the cubic factor
Use 1000 cm³ = 1 litre to express 2500 cm³ as 2.5 litres, tracking the kind of unit

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Area from scale drawings
topics.description: Find actual areas from a scale drawing or map, either by converting each drawing length to an actual length before multiplying or by using the area factor; explain why, when every length is multiplied by a scale factor k, areas are multiplied by k² (both dimensions are scaled), and avoid the mistake of applying the length factor to an area; convert between square units consistently (e.g. 1 m² = 10,000 cm²); and apply this to map, room-plan and design problems such as flooring, turf, paint or land area
evidence: Find the actual floor area of a room drawn 6 cm × 4 cm on a 1:50 plan by converting to 3 m × 2 m (6 m²), and check it with the area factor 50² = 2,500 (24 cm² × 2,500 = 60,000 cm² = 6 m²)
Show by drawing that enlarging a 2 cm × 1 cm rectangle by scale factor 3 gives a 6 cm × 3 cm rectangle containing 9 copies of the original, so the area factor is 3² = 9, not 3
Find the real area of a park shown as 8 cm² on a 1:10,000 map (8 × 10,000² cm² = 80,000 m²), giving the answer in square metres

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Percentages (age 12+)
topics.description: Solve problems involving percentage increase, percentage decrease, finding the original value after a percentage change, and calculating simple interest
evidence: Calculate a 15% increase on £240 using a decimal multiplier (× 1.15)
Find the original price before a 20% discount resulted in a sale price of £64
Calculate simple interest on £500 at 3% per annum for 4 years

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Proportion
topics.description: Recognise and solve problems involving direct proportion (as one quantity increases, the other increases at a constant rate) and inverse proportion (as one increases, the other decreases), including graphical and algebraic representations
evidence: Identify whether a real-world relationship is direct or inverse proportion and justify the choice
Set up and solve a direct-proportion equation (e.g. if 4 pens cost £6, find the cost of 10)
Sketch graphs showing direct proportion (straight line through origin) and inverse proportion (curve)

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Ratio Notation and Relationships
topics.description: Understand that a multiplicative relationship between two quantities can be expressed as a ratio; use ratio notation; simplify ratios
evidence: Explain why 'for every 2 red beads there are 5 blue beads' can be written as 2:5 or as 2/5 of the blue count
Identify the multiplicative relationship in a table of values (e.g. y is always 3 times x)
Connect the ratio a:b to the fraction a/b and to the linear function y = (a/b)x

topics.subject: Personal & Social Development
topics.name: Expressing Feelings with Words
topics.description: Express their own feelings appropriately using words rather than actions — saying 'I feel angry because...' instead of hitting, shouting, or withdrawing
evidence: Use an 'I feel ___ when ___' statement during a disagreement
Choose to tell an adult how they feel instead of acting out physically
Describe their feelings about a difficult situation using at least two emotion words

topics.subject: Personal & Social Development
topics.name: Feelings Change and Differ
topics.description: Understand that everyone has feelings, that feelings change throughout the day, and that the same event can make different people feel different things
evidence: Give an example of a time their feelings changed during a single day
Explain why two children might feel differently about the same event
Recognise that feelings are temporary and can change

topics.subject: Personal & Social Development
topics.name: Naming Basic Emotions
topics.description: Name and recognise basic emotions — happy, sad, angry, scared, excited, and surprised — in themselves and in others by looking at facial expressions and body language
evidence: Label at least five basic emotions from pictures or real situations
Match facial expressions to emotion words in a sorting activity
Say 'I feel ___' using a correct emotion word when asked about their own day

topics.subject: Personal & Social Development
topics.name: Triggers and Causes of Feelings
topics.description: Understand that feelings have causes — something happens (a trigger) and that makes us feel a certain way — and begin to identify what triggers their own emotions
evidence: Describe a trigger for at least three different emotions from their own experience
Complete 'I felt ___ because ___' sentences accurately
Identify what made a character in a story feel a particular way

topics.subject: Personal & Social Development
topics.name: How Emotions Feel in Your Body
topics.description: Understand the connection between emotions and the body — recognising physical signals like butterflies in the stomach (nervous), clenched fists (angry), racing heart (scared or excited), and tight shoulders (stressed)
evidence: Name at least three body sensations and match them to the emotions they signal
Notice a physical feeling in their own body and identify the emotion behind it
Explain why the body reacts physically when we have strong emotions

topics.subject: Personal & Social Development
topics.name: Emotion Vocabulary
topics.description: Use a wider vocabulary of emotion words beyond the basics — including frustrated, worried, anxious, embarrassed, jealous, proud, disappointed, grateful, and lonely — and distinguish between similar emotions
evidence: Use at least five emotion words beyond the basic six in everyday conversation
Explain the difference between two similar emotions such as angry and frustrated
Choose a precise emotion word that fits a described scenario

topics.subject: Personal & Social Development
topics.name: Hidden and Masked Feelings
topics.description: Recognise that people sometimes hide or mask their true feelings — smiling when they're actually sad, or saying 'I'm fine' when they're not — and understand why someone might do this
evidence: Give an example of a time someone might hide their feelings and explain why
Identify mismatches between someone's words and their body language
Explain that hiding feelings is common but that it's usually better to share with someone trusted

topics.subject: Personal & Social Development
topics.name: Mild to Strong Emotions
topics.description: Understand that emotions come in different intensities — from mild to strong — and that the same emotion can feel very different depending on how intense it is (e.g., annoyed → angry → furious, or nervous → anxious → panicked)
evidence: Place three related emotion words in order from mild to strong
Rate their own emotion on a simple scale (e.g., 1-5) in a real situation
Explain why recognising intensity matters for choosing how to respond

topics.subject: Personal & Social Development
topics.name: Culture and Experience Shape Emotions
topics.description: Understand that emotional responses are shaped by personal experiences, culture, and context — the same situation triggers different emotions in different people because of their backgrounds and past experiences
evidence: Explain why two people might have very different emotional reactions to the same event
Give an example of how a past experience shaped someone's emotional response
Describe how cultural background might influence what makes someone feel proud or embarrassed

topics.subject: Personal & Social Development
topics.name: Emotional Patterns Over Time
topics.description: Reflect on their own emotional patterns over time — noticing recurring triggers, understanding their typical responses, and recognising how their emotional awareness has grown
evidence: Identify a recurring emotional trigger and their typical response to it
Describe how their emotional understanding has changed compared to when they were younger
Set a personal goal related to emotional awareness, such as noticing when stress is building

topics.subject: Personal & Social Development
topics.name: Emotions and Decision-Making
topics.description: Understand how emotions influence thinking and decision-making — that strong feelings can cloud judgement, that we often make different choices when calm versus when upset, and that recognising this gives us more control
evidence: Give an example of a time a strong emotion led them or someone else to a poor decision
Explain the idea of 'cooling off' before making an important choice
Describe how the same situation looks different when you're calm versus upset

topics.subject: Personal & Social Development
topics.name: Mixed and Conflicting Emotions
topics.description: Understand that people can experience mixed or conflicting emotions at the same time — feeling excited and nervous about starting a new school, or happy for a friend who won but disappointed for yourself
evidence: Describe a personal situation where they felt two emotions simultaneously
Explain why mixed feelings are normal and not something to worry about
Identify mixed emotions in a character from a book or film

topics.subject: Personal & Social Development
topics.name: Brain Science of Emotions
topics.description: Understand how the amygdala triggers emotional responses and how the prefrontal cortex (still developing in adolescence) regulates them; explain why stress hormones (cortisol, adrenaline) affect thinking and memory; understand that the adolescent brain's dopamine system makes feelings more intense; distinguish between emotion regulation (managing feelings effectively) and emotion suppression (pushing feelings down, which is counterproductive); introduce cognitive reappraisal as a research-backed technique for changing how we interpret a situation

topics.subject: Personal & Social Development
topics.name: Identity and Belonging in Adolescence
topics.description: Understand that adolescence involves active construction of identity, leading to emotional complexity around questions of 'who am I?'; explore the emotional dynamics of belonging to multiple groups simultaneously (family, peer group, cultural or religious identity); understand social comparison and its intensification through social media; recognise that identity is not fixed and that uncertainty about identity is normal, not a sign of failure; develop language for navigating emotions tied to group membership and personal values

topics.subject: Personal & Social Development
topics.name: Emotional Intelligence
topics.description: Introduce Goleman's emotional intelligence model (self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, social skills); develop vocabulary for complex emotional states (ambivalence, ennui, schadenfreude, awe, nostalgia, cognitive dissonance); understand the evidence linking emotional intelligence to wellbeing, relationship quality, and long-term life outcomes; reflect on personal emotional growth over the secondary school years; explore the relationship between emotional literacy and mental health, and know when to seek professional support

topics.subject: Personal & Social Development
topics.name: Everyday Kindness and Care
topics.description: Show kindness and care towards others in simple everyday ways — comforting a friend who is upset, helping someone who has dropped their things, sharing without being asked, and saying kind words
evidence: Spontaneously offer comfort to someone who is visibly upset
Help another person with a practical task without being asked
Use kind words to encourage or cheer up someone who is struggling

topics.subject: Personal & Social Development
topics.name: Other People's Feelings and Thoughts
topics.description: Understand that other people have their own feelings and thoughts, and that these might be different from your own — a foundational awareness that not everyone sees or feels things the same way
evidence: State that other people can feel differently about the same thing
Give an example of a time someone felt differently from them about the same situation
Accept another child's feeling as valid even when it differs from their own

topics.subject: Personal & Social Development
topics.name: Similarities & Differences
topics.description: Notice and appreciate ways that people are similar to and different from each other — including appearance, family structures, languages spoken, foods eaten, and celebrations observed — and understand that differences make communities interesting
evidence: Name several ways people in their class or community are different from each other
Describe at least one thing they have learned from someone who is different from them
Express a positive attitude about differences rather than judging them

topics.subject: Personal & Social Development
topics.name: Vocabulary: understanding others
topics.description: Know and use the key vocabulary for understanding others — empathy, perspective, kind, fair, community, similar, different, and care — and understand that these words describe real habits of thinking and feeling
evidence: Use the word 'empathy' correctly and distinguish it from 'sympathy' — e.g. 'Empathy means I try to feel what they feel'
Explain what 'perspective' and 'point of view' mean and demonstrate by describing how two people might see the same event differently
Use words like 'community', 'belonging', and 'inclusion' accurately when talking about their school or neighbourhood

topics.subject: Personal & Social Development
topics.name: First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples
topics.description: Recognise that First Nations, Métis and Inuit are three distinct groups of Indigenous peoples in Canada who live, work, create and carry on their cultures today, each with diverse communities: First Nations are many different Nations; the Métis are a distinct people and Nation with their own culture, history and communities — not simply anyone with mixed ancestry; Inuit are a distinct people with their own communities. A story or artwork by a First Nations, Métis or Inuit creator shows particular characters, experiences and perspectives; it cannot speak for every member of a people.
evidence: Name First Nations, Métis and Inuit as three different Indigenous peoples in Canada and say that they live in cities, towns and communities today, not only long ago
Say that First Nations include many different Nations and that Métis and Inuit are each a distinct people — not all one group

After hearing a story by a First Nations, Métis or Inuit creator, say who made it using the information given with the book (e.g. “the author is Métis”) and that the story shows some characters’ experiences, not what every person of that people does

topics.subject: Personal & Social Development
topics.name: Seeing Someone Else's Point of View
topics.description: Practise perspective-taking by imagining how someone else might feel in a given situation — using prompts like 'How would you feel if that happened to you?' and applying this when reading stories or during real interactions
evidence: Describe how a character in a story feels and give reasons based on the plot
Predict how another child would feel in a described scenario
Use perspective-taking during a real disagreement to understand the other person's view

topics.subject: Personal & Social Development
topics.name: Different Lives and Experiences
topics.description: Understand that people's lives and experiences can be very different from their own — that some children face challenges like disability, poverty, family difficulties, or being new to a country — and develop compassion rather than judgement
evidence: Describe at least two ways another child's life experience might differ significantly from their own
Explain why it's important not to judge someone based on their circumstances
Suggest a kind action they could take to help someone facing a difficult situation

topics.subject: Personal & Social Development
topics.name: Fairness, Equality and Equity
topics.description: Understand what fairness means and why it matters — recognising that fair doesn't always mean equal (everyone getting the same) but can mean equitable (everyone getting what they need), and applying this understanding in group situations
evidence: Explain the difference between treating everyone the same and treating everyone fairly
Give an example of a situation where equal treatment wouldn't be fair
Apply fairness thinking when sharing resources or making group decisions

topics.subject: Personal & Social Development
topics.name: Vocabulary: social awareness
topics.description: Know and use the vocabulary of social awareness — including stereotype, prejudice, discrimination, equality, equity, bias, compassion, and fairness — and understand what distinguishes these closely related concepts
evidence: Explain what 'stereotype' and 'prejudice' mean and give an example of each from everyday life
Use words like 'equality', 'equity', and 'bias' correctly when discussing a scenario — e.g. 'That's not equity because not everyone got what they needed'
Identify an example of discrimination in a story or news article and explain why it is unfair using the correct vocabulary

topics.subject: Personal & Social Development
topics.name: Australian national symbols
topics.description: Identify symbols and emblems important to Australia's identity and diversity — the Australian flag, the Aboriginal flag, the Torres Strait Islander flag, the Commonwealth Coat of Arms, the golden wattle and the national anthem — and what they represent
evidence: Identify the Australian flag, the Aboriginal flag and the Torres Strait Islander flag, and say where they are flown together (e.g. at schools or council buildings)
Describe what is shown on the Commonwealth Coat of Arms (a shield with state badges, held by a kangaroo and an emu) and name the golden wattle as the national floral emblem
Explain what one symbol represents (e.g. the Aboriginal flag's colours: black for the Aboriginal people, red for the earth and yellow for the sun)

topics.subject: Personal & Social Development
topics.name: How stereotypes shape choices
topics.description: Describe how stereotypes can influence people's choices and actions, such as the toys, activities, sports, careers or clothes people choose or avoid
evidence: Give examples of how a stereotype might stop someone choosing an activity (e.g. 'only boys play football', 'only girls do dance')
Describe how repeated portrayals in ads, TV, books or games (e.g. toy ads aimed at boys or girls, or who is shown as a nurse or engineer) can shape what people choose or expect to do
Suggest how to make a choice based on interests and strengths rather than stereotypes

topics.subject: Personal & Social Development
topics.name: Prejudice and discrimination
topics.description: Understand the impact of prejudice and discrimination on individuals and communities — that treating people unfairly because of their identity causes real harm — and describe strategies that value diversity and challenge discrimination
evidence: Define prejudice and discrimination in their own words and describe the harm discrimination causes to the person experiencing it
Explain how a specific example of discrimination (e.g. excluding someone because of their accent or religion) affects both the person and the wider community
Describe two strategies that value diversity or challenge discrimination (e.g. including others, learning about other cultures, safely speaking up) and explain why each helps

topics.subject: Personal & Social Development
topics.name: Religious and cultural festivals
topics.description: Describe how religious and cultural festivals (e.g. Easter, Christmas, Diwali, Eid al-Fitr, Lunar New Year and Hanukkah) are celebrated in their community and country, and what each means to the people who celebrate it
evidence: Describe how one religious festival (e.g. Easter, Christmas, Eid al-Fitr or Diwali) is celebrated in their country and what it means to the people who celebrate it
Compare how two cultural or religious festivals are celebrated (e.g. food, gatherings, symbols and stories)
Explain why festivals from many cultures are celebrated in a diverse community, using a local example

topics.subject: Personal & Social Development
topics.name: Stereotypes and Individual Differences
topics.description: Recognise stereotypes — oversimplified beliefs about groups of people based on gender, race, age, or other characteristics — and understand that stereotypes are unfair because they ignore individual differences
evidence: Define what a stereotype is in their own words
Identify a common stereotype and explain why it is inaccurate
Challenge a stereotype they encounter by giving a counter-example

topics.subject: Personal & Social Development
topics.name: The world contains many cultures, traditions
topics.description: Understand that the world contains many cultures, traditions, and belief systems, and that learning about others' perspectives enriches our own understanding — developing genuine curiosity about and respect for cultural diversity
evidence: Describe a cultural practice different from their own and explain what they find interesting about it
Ask respectful questions to learn about someone else's traditions or beliefs
Explain why understanding different cultures makes communities stronger

topics.subject: Personal & Social Development
topics.name: Diverse First Nations peoples
topics.description: Describe the diversity of First Nations Australians — Aboriginal peoples and Torres Strait Islander peoples, each made up of many distinct groups — including the more than 250 languages spoken before colonisation and the languages spoken and being revived today; their social organisation (family and kinship, Elders, roles and responsibilities); and their continuous connections to Country/Place, recognising that Aboriginal peoples have lived on the Australian continent for more than 60,000 years and that Torres Strait Islander peoples have their own distinct histories and connections to their islands and seas
evidence: Explain that Aboriginal peoples and Torres Strait Islander peoples are distinct peoples, each made up of many groups, and that more than 250 languages were spoken before colonisation, with many still spoken or being revived today
Describe, from an approved source, how social organisation is based on family and kinship, with Elders holding knowledge and responsibilities

Explain evidence that Aboriginal peoples have lived on the Australian continent for more than 60,000 years (e.g. archaeological sites and rock art), recognising that different places have different histories, and describe Torres Strait Islander peoples' distinct histories and continuing connections to their islands and seas

topics.subject: Personal & Social Development
topics.name: Groups I belong to
topics.description: Describe the diversity of cultural, religious and social groups to which they and others in the community belong, and explain the importance of belonging to identity
evidence: Make an identity map showing the groups they belong to (e.g. family, cultural, religious, sporting, school and club groups)
Compare their groups with a classmate's and describe the diversity in the class
Explain how belonging to a group shapes who they are (e.g. language, traditions, friendships)

topics.subject: Personal & Social Development
topics.name: Questioning Your Own Biases
topics.description: Reflect on their own assumptions and biases — recognising that everyone carries unconscious assumptions about others, and that actively questioning these assumptions is an ongoing practice that leads to greater fairness and empathy
evidence: Describe a time they made an assumption about someone that turned out to be wrong
Explain what unconscious bias means in simple terms
Describe a strategy for checking their own assumptions, such as asking questions before judging

topics.subject: Personal & Social Development
topics.name: Systemic Inequality and Allyship
topics.description: Move beyond 'treating everyone the same' to understand that structural advantages and disadvantages exist regardless of individual effort or intention; explore concrete examples of systemic inequality (educational attainment gaps, gender pay gap, representation in leadership); distinguish between individual prejudice and structural discrimination; understand intersectionality — how multiple aspects of identity interact; develop informed compassion rooted in evidence rather than pity; explore what being a genuine ally means in practice

topics.subject: Personal & Social Development
topics.name: Taking action to include others
topics.description: Plan and carry out a strategy to value diversity and include others in their class, school or community, then reflect on its effect using how people responded and improve it
evidence: Plan an inclusion action for a real situation (e.g. inviting a left-out classmate into a game, or making a welcome sign in families' home languages), saying who it is for and why
Carry out the action and record what people said or did in response
Reflect on the effect of the action using those responses and suggest one way to improve it next time

topics.subject: Personal & Social Development
topics.name: Sympathy Versus Empathy
topics.description: Distinguish sympathy ('I feel sorry for you') from empathy ('I understand what you're experiencing'); develop active listening skills: reflecting, paraphrasing, asking open questions, resisting the urge to problem-solve too quickly; understand empathic curiosity as genuine interest in another person's inner world; practise being present for someone in distress without trying to fix or minimise their experience; understand vicarious trauma and compassion fatigue, and how empathetic people can protect their own wellbeing while staying present for others

topics.subject: Personal & Social Development
topics.name: Global Citizenship
