evidence: Measure and record shadow length and direction at different times of day
Create a graph showing how shadow length changes throughout the day
Connect shadow patterns to the sun's apparent position and Earth's rotation

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Star Brightness & Distance
topics.description: Support an argument that the apparent brightness of the sun and stars is due to their relative distances from Earth, understanding the sun is a relatively close star
evidence: Explain that the sun is a star, and it appears much brighter because it is much closer to Earth
Describe how a torch looks brighter close up and dimmer far away as an analogy
Argue that differences in apparent brightness of stars are mainly due to their different distances from Earth

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Phases of the Moon
topics.description: Explain the phases of the Moon as the changing angle of sunlight on the lunar surface as seen from Earth, and describe how solar and lunar eclipses occur
evidence: Explains that the phases of the Moon arise from the changing geometry of Sun, Earth, and Moon, not Earth's shadow
Describes the sequence of Moon phases over approximately 28 days
Distinguishes between a solar eclipse (Moon between Sun and Earth) and a lunar eclipse (Earth between Sun and Moon)

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: The solar system (age 11+)
topics.description: Describe the detailed structure of the solar system, including moons, asteroids, and comets, compare orbital periods and distances of the planets, and distinguish between planets, dwarf planets, and other bodies
evidence: Names the eight planets in order and gives one distinguishing fact about each
Describes the difference between a planet, a dwarf planet, an asteroid, and a comet
Explains the relationship between distance from the Sun and orbital period (planets further out take longer)

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Why We Have Seasons
topics.description: Explain that the seasons are caused by the tilt of Earth's axis during its orbit around the Sun, distinguishing this from the common misconception that seasons are caused by changing distance from the Sun
evidence: Explains that Earth's axis is tilted at about 23.5° relative to its orbit
Describes how the tilted axis causes one hemisphere to receive more direct sunlight in summer and less in winter
Refutes the misconception that distance from the Sun causes seasons by noting Earth is actually slightly closer to the Sun in January

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Galaxies and the universe
topics.description: Describe the scale of the universe, including the structure of galaxies, the position of the Sun in the Milky Way, and the use of light years as a unit of distance, and appreciate why space exploration requires enormous timescales
evidence: Defines a light year as the distance light travels in one year
Describes the structure of a galaxy and states that the Sun is a star in the Milky Way galaxy
Compares the distances within the solar system with the distances between stars and between galaxies, expressing them in appropriate units

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Universal Gravitation
topics.description: Describe gravity as a universal attractive force between all masses, explain that orbital motion arises because gravity provides the centripetal force keeping objects in orbit, and compare gravitational field strengths on different planets
evidence: States that gravity is a universal attractive force acting between all objects with mass
Explains that orbital motion occurs because gravity continuously deflects the path of the orbiting object
Compares gravitational field strength on different planets and explains how this affects weight

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Life Cycle of a Star
topics.description: Describe the life cycle of a star from nebula through main sequence to its end state (white dwarf, neutron star, or black hole depending on mass), and relate the life cycle to the origin of elements heavier than hydrogen
evidence: Describes the main stages in the life cycle of a star similar to the Sun: nebula → protostar → main sequence → red giant → planetary nebula → white dwarf
Explains that more massive stars end as a supernova followed by a neutron star or black hole
States that nuclear fusion inside stars produces heavier elements from hydrogen and helium

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Basic Body Needs
topics.description: Know that the body needs food for energy, water to stay hydrated, sleep to rest and grow, and exercise to keep muscles and the heart strong — and that these are basic needs every human body has
evidence: List the four basic needs: food (energy), water (hydration), sleep (rest and growth), exercise (strength)
Explain that food gives the body energy to move, think, and grow
Describe what happens if one need isn't met (e.g. feeling tired without sleep, thirsty without water)

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Bones & Muscles
topics.description: Know that the body has a skeleton made of bones inside it that gives the body its shape and protects important organs like the brain (skull) and heart (ribcage), and that muscles attached to bones allow the body to move
evidence: State that bones give the body shape, support, and protection
Name at least three bones or bone groups (e.g. skull, ribcage, spine, leg bones)
Explain that muscles pull on bones to make the body move

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: How Breathing Works
topics.description: Know that we breathe air into our lungs through the nose and mouth, that our lungs take in oxygen from the air which our body needs to stay alive, and that we breathe out carbon dioxide as waste
evidence: Trace the path of air: nose/mouth → windpipe → lungs
State that lungs take oxygen from the air, which the body needs
State that we breathe out carbon dioxide, which the body doesn't need

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: The Brain Controls the Body
topics.description: Understand that the brain is the body’s control centre: it receives messages from the senses, thinks and makes decisions, and sends messages through nerves to tell muscles what to do
evidence: State that the brain is inside the skull and controls the whole body
Describe the basic loop: senses send information to the brain, the brain decides what to do, and sends messages to muscles
Give an example (e.g. eyes see a ball coming, brain decides to catch it, nerves tell hands to move)

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: The Five Senses
topics.description: Explore the five senses in detail: sight uses eyes to detect light, hearing uses ears to detect sound, touch uses skin to feel pressure and temperature, taste uses the tongue to detect flavours, and smell uses the nose to detect odours
evidence: Name all five senses and match each to the correct body part
Describe what each sense detects (e.g. eyes detect light, ears detect sound waves)
Give an example of using each sense in everyday life (e.g. smelling food cooking, feeling hot water)

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: The Heart & Blood
topics.description: Understand that the heart is a muscle that pumps blood around the body through tubes called blood vessels, and that we can feel our heartbeat by placing a hand on our chest or fingers on our wrist
evidence: Locate their own heartbeat by touch (chest or pulse point)
State that the heart pumps blood through the body continuously
Describe blood vessels as tubes that carry blood to every part of the body

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Balanced Diet & Food Groups
topics.description: Distinguish food groups from nutrients. Food groups are the groups of foods in a healthy-eating guide; choose a variety of foods from each group in suitable proportions using the applicable local healthy-eating guide (e.g. in Australia, the five food groups of the Australian Guide to Healthy Eating). Foods supply nutrients (carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and fibre), and with water these provide energy, materials for growth and repair, and help the body work properly and resist illness
evidence: Sort everyday foods into the food groups of the local healthy-eating guide (e.g. the five groups of the Australian Guide to Healthy Eating: vegetables and legumes/beans; fruit; grain (cereal) foods; lean meats and poultry, fish, eggs, tofu, nuts and seeds, and legumes/beans; milk, yoghurt, cheese and/or alternatives)

Explain that carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and fibre are nutrients found in foods, not food groups, and say what carbohydrates (energy), proteins (growth and repair), fats (energy and warmth) and vitamins and minerals (help the body work properly and resist illness) do
Choose a day's meals with a variety of foods from every group in the local guide in proportions that match the guide (e.g. plenty of vegetables and grain foods), with water as the main drink

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Keeping clean and healthy
topics.description: Explain and practise hygiene habits that stop germs spreading and keep the body healthy: washing hands properly, brushing teeth, covering coughs and sneezes, and bathing
evidence: Demonstrate washing hands with soap for about 20 seconds and explain when to do it (after the toilet, before eating)
Describe how to brush teeth twice a day and why it helps prevent tooth decay
Explain how covering a cough or sneeze with an elbow or tissue stops germs spreading to others

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Cells, Tissues & Organs
topics.description: Understand that the body is organised in a hierarchy: tiny cells are the building blocks, groups of similar cells form tissues, tissues combine into organs (like the heart or stomach), and organs work together in organ systems (like the circulatory system)
evidence: State that cells are the smallest building blocks of the body, too small to see without a microscope
Describe the hierarchy: cells → tissues → organs → organ systems
Give an example: muscle cells form muscle tissue, which forms the heart organ, which is part of the circulatory system

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: How Muscles Move Bones
topics.description: Understand that muscles work in pairs to move bones: when one muscle contracts (gets shorter and pulls), the opposite muscle relaxes, and that some muscles are voluntary (we choose to use them) while others like the heart are involuntary (they work automatically)
evidence: Demonstrate or describe how biceps and triceps work as a pair to bend and straighten the arm
Explain the difference between voluntary muscles (we control them) and involuntary muscles (they work automatically)
Name the heart and muscles of the digestive system as examples of involuntary muscles

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: How the Eye Works
topics.description: Describe how the eye works: light enters through the pupil, the lens focuses it onto the retina at the back of the eye, and the retina sends signals along the optic nerve to the brain, which interprets the image
evidence: Name the main parts: pupil (lets light in), lens (focuses light), retina (detects light), optic nerve (sends signals to brain)
Describe the sequence: light enters → lens focuses → retina detects → nerve signals brain → brain interprets image
Explain that the pupil gets bigger in dim light and smaller in bright light to control how much light enters

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Naming Major Bones
topics.description: Identify major bones of the human skeleton by name (skull, spine/vertebrae, ribcage, pelvis, femur, humerus) and explain the skeleton’s three jobs: supporting the body’s shape, protecting organs, and enabling movement with muscles
evidence: Name and locate at least six major bones or bone groups on a diagram or their own body
Explain the three functions: support (holds us upright), protection (skull protects brain, ribs protect heart/lungs), movement (bones work with muscles)
State that not all animals have internal skeletons — some have shells or exoskeletons

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: The Digestive Journey
topics.description: Trace the journey of food through the digestive system: food enters the mouth where teeth break it down and saliva begins digestion, travels down the oesophagus to the stomach, passes through the small intestine where nutrients are absorbed, and waste moves through the large intestine
evidence: List the organs in order: mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine
Describe what happens at each stage (teeth chew, stomach churns with acid, small intestine absorbs nutrients)
State that the small intestine is where most nutrients pass into the blood, and the large intestine removes water from waste

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Types of Teeth
topics.description: Identify the four types of human teeth (incisors for cutting, canines for tearing, premolars and molars for grinding) and understand that tooth shape is linked to function, just as in other animals — herbivores have flat teeth, carnivores have sharp teeth
evidence: Name the four tooth types and describe each one's job: incisors cut, canines tear, premolars/molars grind
Compare human teeth to herbivore teeth (flat, for grinding plants) and carnivore teeth (sharp, for tearing meat)
Explain that humans have all types because we are omnivores — we eat both plants and meat

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Growing Up & Puberty
topics.description: Describe the stages of human development from birth to old age: baby, toddler, child, adolescent (puberty), young adult, middle-aged adult, elderly — understanding the physical changes that happen at each stage, especially during puberty
evidence: Name and order at least six life stages from birth to old age
Describe key physical changes during puberty (growth spurts, body shape changes, development of adult features)
Explain that puberty is triggered by hormones — chemical messengers released by glands

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Healthy Lifestyle Choices
topics.description: Understand how lifestyle choices affect the body’s health: a balanced diet, regular exercise, adequate sleep, and avoiding harmful substances (tobacco, alcohol, drugs) help body systems function well, while poor choices increase the risk of disease
evidence: Explain how regular exercise strengthens the heart, lungs, and muscles
Describe how a poor diet high in sugar and fat can lead to obesity, tooth decay, and heart problems
State at least two harmful effects of smoking (damages lungs, increases heart disease risk) or alcohol (damages liver, affects brain)

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Keeping up a healthy routine
topics.description: Apply healthy and safe behaviours in their own routines and to support others: choose a health or safety routine, plan it, track it over time, reflect on how well it went and how it supports health, and identify ways to support someone else's health or safety
evidence: Choose a health or safety routine to build (e.g. sun-safe habits, drinking water, hand-washing or screen-time limits) and plan when and how they will do it
Track the routine for a week and reflect on how well they kept it, what got in the way and how it helps their health
Choose one behaviour that would help a friend or family member stay healthy or safe and explain how they could support them

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Circulation & Breathing Together
topics.description: Understand how the circulatory and respiratory systems work together: the lungs oxygenate the blood, the heart pumps it around the body, cells use the oxygen and produce carbon dioxide waste, and the blood carries the waste back to the lungs to be breathed out
evidence: Describe the cycle: lungs add oxygen to blood → heart pumps oxygenated blood to body → cells use oxygen → blood returns CO₂ to lungs
Explain why heart rate and breathing rate increase during exercise (muscles need more oxygen)
Measure their own resting and post-exercise heart rate and explain the difference

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Heart & Blood Circulation
topics.description: Describe the circulatory system in detail: the heart has four chambers (two atria, two ventricles) that pump blood in a double loop — one to the lungs for oxygen and one to the rest of the body to deliver it — through arteries, veins, and tiny capillaries
evidence: Name the four heart chambers and describe the double-loop pathway (heart → lungs → heart → body)
Distinguish arteries (carry blood away from heart), veins (carry blood back to heart), and capillaries (tiny vessels where exchange happens)
Name the components of blood: red blood cells (carry oxygen), white blood cells (fight infection), platelets (help clotting), plasma (liquid)

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: How the Lungs Work
topics.description: Explain how the respiratory system works in detail: air travels through the nose/mouth, down the trachea, into bronchi and bronchioles, reaching tiny air sacs (alveoli) in the lungs where oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out
evidence: Trace the air pathway: nose/mouth → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli
Explain gas exchange in the alveoli: oxygen passes into blood capillaries, carbon dioxide passes out
Describe the mechanical process: the diaphragm contracts to pull air in and relaxes to push air out

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: The Immune System
topics.description: Know that the body has an immune system that protects against illness: the skin acts as a barrier, white blood cells identify and destroy germs (bacteria and viruses), and vaccines train the immune system to recognise specific diseases before they cause illness
evidence: Describe the skin as the body's first line of defence against germs
Explain that white blood cells detect and fight bacteria and viruses inside the body
Describe how vaccines work: they contain weakened or inactive germs that train the immune system to recognise the real disease

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: The Nervous System
topics.description: Understand that the nervous system has two parts — the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) and nerves that branch throughout the body — and that nerve signals travel at high speed to coordinate senses, thought, and movement
evidence: Name the two parts of the nervous system: central (brain + spinal cord) and peripheral (nerves throughout the body)
Describe the reflex arc: stimulus → sensory nerve → spinal cord/brain → motor nerve → muscle response
State that nerve signals travel extremely fast, which is why reflexes happen almost instantly

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Immunity & Vaccines
topics.description: Distinguish innate (non-specific, immediate) from adaptive (specific, memory-forming) immunity; explain how B cells produce antibodies that recognise specific antigens, how T cells destroy infected cells, and why immunological memory makes vaccines work; and describe the gut microbiome as a community of trillions of microbes that significantly influences immune function
evidence: Distinguishes innate immunity (rapid, non-specific barriers and inflammation) from adaptive immunity (slow, specific, memory-forming)
Explains how B cells produce antibodies that bind to specific antigens on pathogens, targeting them for destruction
Explains immunological memory: after first exposure, memory B and T cells remain, making subsequent response faster and stronger — the basis of vaccine protection

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Neurons & Brain Structure
topics.description: Explain how neurons transmit signals as electrochemical impulses across synapses, describe how the brain is organised (lobes and functions, limbic system for emotion), and explain neuroplasticity — why learning and practice physically change brain structure — connecting to optical illusions as evidence that the brain constructs reality rather than passively recording it
evidence: Describes the neuron-to-neuron signal pathway: electrical impulse travels along axon, neurotransmitter crosses the synapse, new impulse begins in the next neuron
Names the four lobes of the cerebral cortex (frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital) and gives one function for each
Explains neuroplasticity: repeated neural pathways become stronger and faster — this is the biological mechanism of learning and skill development

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Reading nutrition labels
topics.description: Read and compare the nutrition information on food packaging — serving size, per-100 g values for energy, sugars, salt (sodium), saturated fat and fibre, and any front-of-pack rating used locally — to choose the healthier of similar products
evidence: Find the per-100 g column on the nutrition panels of two breakfast cereals and say which has less sugar and which has more fibre
Compare the salt (sodium) and saturated fat of two snacks per 100 g, rather than per serve, and explain why per 100 g gives a fair comparison
Use the nutrition panel together with a local front-of-pack rating (e.g. the Health Star Rating in Australia) to choose the healthier of two similar products and justify the choice

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: DNA & Genes
topics.description: Describe the double helix structure of DNA (base pairs, complementarity), explain how genes are sections of DNA that code for proteins, introduce the central dogma (DNA → mRNA → protein) conceptually, and discuss the ethical implications of CRISPR gene editing — including potential benefits (genetic disease treatment) and concerns (germline editing, 'designer babies')
evidence: Describes DNA as a double helix with four bases (A, T, C, G) where A pairs with T and C pairs with G
Explains that a gene is a section of DNA that codes for a specific protein, and that proteins carry out most of the body's functions
Describes CRISPR as a molecular tool that can cut and edit DNA sequences, and raises at least two distinct ethical considerations about its use in humans

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: How the Body Stays in Balance
topics.description: Explain homeostasis as the process of maintaining a stable internal environment; describe the main feedback loop systems (negative feedback) using blood glucose regulation (insulin/glucagon) and body temperature as concrete examples; and connect the endocrine system (hormone-secreting glands) to the nervous system as two complementary communication systems with different speeds and durations
evidence: Defines homeostasis and explains why maintaining a stable internal environment is essential for survival
Describes the blood glucose negative feedback loop: glucose rises → pancreas releases insulin → cells take up glucose → glucose falls → insulin release stops
Compares the nervous system (fast, electrical, short-duration signals) with the endocrine system (slower, chemical, longer-duration signals) and gives an example where each is more appropriate

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Cancer & Stem Cells
topics.description: Explain that cancer occurs when mutations in DNA disable normal cell-cycle controls, causing uncontrolled cell division and tumour formation; describe how stem cells differ from specialised cells and their potential for regenerative medicine; and evaluate the ethical debates around embryonic stem cell research and genetic testing
evidence: Explains cancer as the result of DNA mutations that disable tumour suppressor genes or activate oncogenes, causing unchecked mitosis
Distinguishes stem cells (unspecialised, can differentiate) from specialised cells (fixed function) and explains why stem cells are medically valuable
Presents the embryonic stem cell debate with at least two specific scientific arguments in favour and two ethical objections against, without simply asserting one side is correct

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Earth Is Made of Rock
topics.description: Understand that Earth is made of rock and other solid materials
evidence: State that the ground beneath us is made of rock
Identify rocks and stones as pieces of the Earth
Explain that Earth is solid and made of natural materials

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Earthquake Safety
topics.description: Know basic earthquake safety: drop, cover, and hold on; move away from windows; tell a trusted adult
evidence: Demonstrate the drop, cover, and hold on procedure
Explain why to move away from windows and shelves during shaking
Name a trusted adult to tell if they feel an earthquake

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Fast & Slow Earth Changes
topics.description: Understand that Earth's surface changes: some changes are quick (eruptions, earthquakes) and some are slow (wind, water wearing away rock)
evidence: Give an example of a quick change to Earth's surface like a volcanic eruption
Give an example of a slow change to Earth's surface like erosion by wind or water
Compare quick and slow changes and explain the difference

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Power of Eruptions
topics.description: Appreciate that volcanic eruptions are powerful events that can change the landscape
evidence: Describe an eruption as a powerful, dramatic event
Give examples of how an eruption changes the area around a volcano
Compare the landscape before and after an eruption using pictures

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: What Is an Earthquake
topics.description: Know what an earthquake is: a sudden shaking of the ground that can be strong or weak
evidence: Describe an earthquake as the ground shaking suddenly
Explain that earthquakes vary in strength from barely noticeable to very strong
Describe what it might feel like during an earthquake

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: What Is a Volcano
topics.description: Know what a volcano is: an opening in Earth's surface where hot melted rock (lava) comes out
evidence: Describe a volcano as a place where hot material comes out of the Earth
Explain that lava is rock so hot it has melted
Point to a volcano in a picture and describe what is happening

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Active, Dormant & Extinct
topics.description: Classify volcanoes as active (could erupt any time), dormant (sleeping but could wake up), or extinct (will not erupt again)
evidence: Define active, dormant, and extinct volcanoes
Explain that a dormant volcano is not safe just because it has not erupted recently
Classify a given volcano based on its eruption history

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Earth's Layers
topics.description: Know that Earth has layers — a thin outer crust, a thick hot mantle, and a core at the centre — and that the inside of the Earth is extremely hot
evidence: Name Earth's three main layers: crust, mantle, and core
Explain that the crust is thin compared to the other layers
State that Earth's interior is extremely hot — hot enough to melt rock

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Inside a Volcano
topics.description: Understand the inside of a volcano: magma is hot melted rock underground, lava is the same material after it reaches the surface, and volcanoes have a magma chamber, vent, and crater
evidence: Explain that magma is melted rock underground and lava is the same material above ground
Label a magma chamber, vent, and crater on a volcano cross-section
Describe the path magma takes from underground to the surface during an eruption

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Pompeii & Vesuvius
topics.description: Know the story of Pompeii: a Roman city buried by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD, preserved under volcanic ash, and rediscovered by archaeologists centuries later
evidence: Retell the key events: Vesuvius erupted, Pompeii was buried under ash
Explain that the ash preserved the city, its buildings, and even people's shapes
Describe how archaeologists uncovered the city and what we can learn from it

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Ring of Fire
topics.description: Recognise that volcanoes and earthquakes tend to happen in certain places — especially around the edges of the Pacific Ocean (Ring of Fire) — not randomly across the Earth
evidence: Describe the pattern that volcanoes and earthquakes cluster in certain zones
Locate the Ring of Fire on a world map
Explain that the locations of earthquakes and volcanoes are not random

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Tsunamis
topics.description: Know what a tsunami is: a very large, fast ocean wave caused by an earthquake or volcanic eruption under the sea, which can cause great damage when it reaches land
evidence: Explain that a tsunami is caused by an earthquake or eruption under the sea
State that tsunamis travel very fast across the ocean
Describe the damage a tsunami can cause when it reaches the coast

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Types of Rock
topics.description: Know the three main types of rock — igneous (formed when lava or magma cools), sedimentary (formed from layers pressed together), and metamorphic — and that fossils are found in sedimentary rock
evidence: Name the three main rock types: igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic
Explain that igneous rock forms when lava or magma cools and hardens
State that fossils are preserved in sedimentary rock because it forms in layers

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Why Earthquakes Happen
topics.description: Understand that earthquakes happen when rocks underground suddenly move or break, releasing energy that shakes the ground
evidence: Explain that earthquakes are caused by rocks underground suddenly moving
Describe how this movement sends shaking through the surrounding ground
Distinguish between the underground cause and the surface effects of an earthquake

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Earthquake-Resistant Design
topics.description: Know that buildings can be designed to resist earthquakes, tsunami warning systems alert coastal communities, and communities prepare through evacuation plans and drills
evidence: Describe at least one feature that makes buildings more earthquake-resistant
Explain how tsunami warning systems detect danger and alert communities
Describe how communities prepare for earthquakes and eruptions through drills and evacuation plans

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Eruption Types & Volcano Shape
topics.description: Understand that not all volcanic eruptions are the same: some flow gently (effusive) and some explode violently (explosive), depending on the properties of the magma, and that volcano shape is related to eruption type
evidence: Contrast effusive eruptions (gentle lava flows) with explosive eruptions (violent blasts of ash and rock)
Explain that eruption type depends on properties of the magma such as thickness and gas content
Connect volcano shape to eruption style: shield volcanoes from runny lava, steep cones from thick explosive magma

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Famous Eruptions & Pangaea
topics.description: Know about famous eruptions and their global effects: Mount St Helens (1980), Eyjafjallajökull (2010), and how large eruptions can affect weather and climate worldwide; understand that continents were once joined (Pangaea) and have slowly drifted apart
evidence: Describe at least one famous volcanic eruption and its key effects
Explain how volcanic ash and gases in the atmosphere can cool global temperatures
State that continents were once joined in a supercontinent and have slowly moved apart over millions of years

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Measuring Earthquake Strength
topics.description: Know that scientists measure earthquakes using seismometers, that earthquakes release energy that travels as waves through the ground, and that a magnitude scale describes their strength
evidence: Explain that a seismometer is an instrument that detects and records ground shaking
Describe earthquake energy as waves that travel outward from where rocks broke
Interpret a magnitude number as a measure of an earthquake's strength

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Monitoring Volcanoes
topics.description: Understand how volcanologists monitor volcanoes by looking for warning signs — gas emissions, ground swelling, small earthquakes — and that prediction involves evidence and uncertainty, not certainty
evidence: Name at least two warning signs scientists look for before an eruption
Explain that volcanologists combine multiple types of evidence to assess risk
Discuss why volcanic prediction involves uncertainty and cannot guarantee exact timing

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Natural Disaster Solutions
topics.description: Generate and compare multiple solutions to reduce the impacts of natural Earth processes on humans, such as earthquakes, floods, or volcanic eruptions
evidence: Identify at least two natural hazards and their impacts on human life and property
Generate multiple solutions for reducing impacts (e.g. earthquake-resistant buildings, flood barriers, early warning systems)
Compare solutions based on criteria like effectiveness, cost, and feasibility

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Plate Boundaries
topics.description: Explain how plate boundaries cause earthquakes and volcanoes: plates pushing together, pulling apart, or sliding past each other create the forces that trigger these events, and mountains form where plates collide
evidence: Describe three types of plate boundary movement: convergent, divergent, and transform
Explain that earthquakes occur when plates grind or collide at boundaries
Explain that volcanoes form where plates pull apart or one slides under another, allowing magma to rise

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Tectonic Plates
topics.description: Understand that Earth's crust is broken into large pieces called tectonic plates that float on hotter, softer rock beneath and move very slowly — a few centimetres per year
evidence: Describe Earth's crust as broken into large plates
Explain that the plates float on hotter, partially melted rock underneath
State that plates move very slowly, typically a few centimetres per year

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: The Rock Cycle
topics.description: Understand the rock cycle: rocks slowly change from one type to another over millions of years — igneous rock weathers into sediment, sediment becomes sedimentary rock, heat and pressure create metamorphic rock, and melting starts the cycle again
evidence: Describe the rock cycle as a continuous process with no beginning or end
Trace at least one complete path through the cycle from igneous to sedimentary to metamorphic and back
Explain that the rock cycle operates over millions of years through weathering, pressure, heat, and melting

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: How Tectonic Plates Move
topics.description: Understand that convection currents in the molten mantle drive the movement of rigid tectonic plates; distinguish between convergent (collision/subduction), divergent (spreading ridges), and transform (sliding) plate boundaries; explain why volcanoes, earthquakes, and mountain chains cluster at boundaries; introduce the Wilson cycle of supercontinent assembly and breakup

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Seismic Waves & Earth's Interior
topics.description: Distinguish between P-waves (compression, travel through solids and liquids) and S-waves (shear, cannot pass through liquids); explain why a seismic shadow zone exists on the far side of an earthquake; describe how seismologists use wave refraction and reflection to infer that Earth has a solid inner core, liquid outer core, mantle, and crust

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Hazard Assessment & Evacuation
topics.description: Explain probabilistic hazard assessment using eruption recurrence intervals and fault slip rates; describe how volcano observatories monitor ground deformation, gas emissions, and seismicity to issue alert levels; explore why communities remain near active hazards (fertile volcanic soil, poverty, cultural ties); discuss the ethics and politics of evacuation decisions and the social justice dimensions of disaster risk

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Supervolcanoes & Volcanic Winter
topics.description: Describe calderas such as Yellowstone and Toba as supervolcanoes capable of erupting thousands of cubic kilometres of ash; explain how sulphur dioxide aerosols in the stratosphere scatter sunlight and cause volcanic winter; discuss the Toba catastrophe theory and how giant eruptions have interacted with ice ages; contrast supervolcano eruptions with ordinary eruptions in scale and climate impact

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Volcanoes & Mass Extinctions
topics.description: Explain how large igneous provinces (LIPs) — massive outpourings of lava over millions of years — caused global warming and ocean acidification that drove mass extinctions; connect the Siberian Traps to the end-Permian extinction and the Deccan Traps to the end-Cretaceous event; explore how hydrothermal vents on the early Earth may have been the cradle of life; understand volcanoes as both destroyers and creators in the history of life

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Communication with Light & Sound
topics.description: Design and build a device that uses light or sound to solve the problem of communicating over a distance
evidence: Design a device that uses light or sound to communicate over a distance (e.g. string telephone, torch signals)
Build and test the device, identifying what works and what could be improved
Explain how the device uses properties of light or sound to transmit information

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Light & Seeing in the Dark
topics.description: Observe that objects in darkness can be seen only when illuminated by a light source
evidence: Explain that we need light to see objects — without any light source, it is completely dark
Describe an observation showing objects become visible only when light reaches them
Distinguish between light sources (sun, torch, lamp) and objects that just reflect light

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Light & Sound Vocabulary
topics.description: Name and use vocabulary for how light and sound behave — light source, transparent, translucent, opaque, shadow, reflect, vibration, pitch, volume — and apply these terms correctly when describing observations about how light travels and how sounds are made and changed
evidence: Correctly classify a set of materials as transparent, translucent, or opaque and explain each term
Explain what causes a shadow using the words 'opaque' and 'light source' correctly
Describe what changes the pitch or volume of a sound using vibration vocabulary

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Transparent, Translucent & Opaque
topics.description: Investigate the effect of placing objects made of different materials in the path of a beam of light, discovering transparent, translucent, and opaque materials
evidence: Test at least six materials and classify them as transparent, translucent, or opaque
Define transparent (light passes through clearly), translucent (some light passes, blurry), opaque (no light passes)
Predict whether a given material will let light through based on its appearance

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Vibrations & Sound
topics.description: Understand that vibrating materials can make sound, and that sound can make materials vibrate
evidence: Describe that sounds are made when objects vibrate (move back and forth quickly)
Give at least three examples of vibrating objects making sound (drum skin, guitar string, voice box)
Demonstrate that sound can cause objects to vibrate (e.g. rice on a drum jumps when you shout near it)

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: How Shadows Form
topics.description: Recognise that shadows are formed when light from a source is blocked by an opaque object, and find patterns in how shadow size changes
evidence: Explain that a shadow forms because an opaque object blocks light from reaching a surface
Describe the pattern: shadow gets larger when object moves closer to the light source
Predict the shape and relative size of a shadow given the position of light and object

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Pitch of Sounds
topics.description: Find patterns between the pitch of a sound and features of the object that produced it
evidence: Describe the pattern: shorter/thinner/tighter objects produce higher-pitched sounds
Demonstrate pitch changes using at least one instrument or everyday object
Explain pitch as how high or low a sound is, determined by how fast the object vibrates

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Protecting Eyes from Sunlight
topics.description: Recognise that light from the sun can be dangerous and that there are ways to protect eyes
evidence: State that looking directly at the sun can damage eyes permanently
Name at least two ways to protect eyes from bright sunlight (sunglasses, hat, shade)
Explain that the sun is an extremely bright light source unlike any artificial light

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Reflecting Light
topics.description: Notice that light is reflected from surfaces, and that shiny smooth surfaces reflect light best
evidence: Explain that light bounces off surfaces, which is called reflection
Identify that smooth, shiny surfaces (mirrors, still water) reflect light best
Give everyday examples of reflection: mirror, puddle, polished floor

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Volume & Vibrations
topics.description: Find patterns between the volume of a sound and the strength of the vibrations that produced it
evidence: Describe the pattern: stronger vibrations (larger movements) produce louder sounds
Demonstrate volume changes by varying the force applied to a sound-making object
Explain volume as how loud or quiet a sound is, determined by the size of vibrations

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Patterns & Codes for Information
topics.description: Generate and compare multiple solutions that use patterns to transfer information, such as codes and signals
evidence: Describe at least two systems that use patterns of light or sound to transfer information (e.g. Morse code, semaphore, drum signals)
Design a simple code using light or sound patterns to send a message
Compare the advantages and disadvantages of different information transfer methods

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Sound Fading with Distance
topics.description: Recognise that sounds get fainter as the distance from the sound source increases
evidence: State that sound gets quieter as distance from the source increases
Describe an observation or investigation demonstrating this pattern
Explain that vibrations spread out and get weaker as they travel further from the source

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Sound Travels Through Materials
topics.description: Recognise that vibrations from sounds travel through a medium (solid, liquid, or gas) to the ear
evidence: Explain that sound vibrations need a material (medium) to travel through — they can't travel in a vacuum
Give examples of sound travelling through different media: air, water, solid objects
Describe how a string telephone works: voice vibrates the cup, vibrations travel along the string to the other cup

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: How We See Objects
topics.description: Develop a model to describe that light reflecting from objects and entering the eye allows objects to be seen
evidence: Draw a diagram showing light source → light hits object → reflects into eye
Explain that we see objects because reflected light enters our eyes, not because our eyes send out light
Use this model to explain why we can't see in total darkness (no light to reflect)

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Wave Behaviour Vocabulary
topics.description: Use technical vocabulary for wave behaviour — refraction, absorption, reflection, scattering, amplitude, frequency, wavelength, echo, spectrum, angle of incidence, angle of reflection — and apply these when explaining how light and sound travel and interact with different materials
evidence: Use 'refraction' correctly to explain why a straw appears bent in a glass of water
Distinguish 'reflection' from 'refraction' using the correct definitions
Explain what an echo is using the vocabulary of sound reflection correctly

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Waves & How They Move
topics.description: Develop a model of waves to describe patterns in terms of amplitude and wavelength, and understand that waves can cause objects to move
evidence: Describe a wave using the terms amplitude (height) and wavelength (distance between peaks)
Demonstrate that larger amplitude means more energy (bigger waves move objects more)
Model wave patterns using a slinky, rope, or water and describe what they observe

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Light Travels in Straight Lines
topics.description: Recognise that light appears to travel in straight lines and use this to explain how we see objects and why shadows have the same shape as the objects that cast them
evidence: State and demonstrate that light travels in straight lines (e.g. can't see around corners, laser pointer)
Use straight-line light to explain why shadows have the same outline shape as the object
Draw ray diagrams showing light travelling from source, being blocked by object, creating shadow on screen

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: How Sound Waves Travel
topics.description: Explain that sound is produced by vibrating objects and travels as a longitudinal pressure wave through solids, liquids, and gases; describe reflection of sound (echoes) and absorption; explain why sound cannot travel through a vacuum
evidence: Explains how a vibrating object creates regions of compression and rarefaction in air
Explains why sound travels fastest in solids and cannot travel in a vacuum
Describes how an echo is produced and gives a practical application (sonar, ultrasound)
Explains what sound absorption means and why soft furnishings reduce echoes

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Reflection & Refraction
topics.description: State the law of reflection (angle of incidence = angle of reflection) and explain refraction as the change in speed and direction when light crosses a boundary between two media; apply ray diagrams for plane mirrors and refracting surfaces
evidence: States the law of reflection and applies it to draw a reflected ray correctly
Draws a ray diagram for a plane mirror showing a virtual image
Explains why a pencil looks bent in a glass of water using refraction
Explains qualitatively why light bends towards the normal when entering a denser medium

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Wave Properties & Types
topics.description: Describe waves in terms of amplitude, wavelength, frequency, and wave speed; distinguish transverse waves (oscillation perpendicular to direction of travel) from longitudinal waves (oscillation parallel); and use the wave equation v = fλ
evidence: Labels a wave diagram with amplitude, wavelength, crest, and trough
Distinguishes transverse and longitudinal waves and gives an example of each
Uses v = fλ to calculate wave speed, frequency, or wavelength given the other two
Explains what happens to wavelength if frequency increases while wave speed stays constant

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: White Light & Colour
topics.description: Explain that white light is a mixture of all visible colours (ROYGBIV), describe dispersion through a prism, explain why objects appear coloured (selective reflection and absorption of wavelengths), and describe colour mixing with filters
evidence: Lists the colours of the visible spectrum in order of increasing frequency
Explains why a prism disperses white light into a spectrum
Explains why a red object looks red under white light but black under blue light
Predicts the colour of an object seen through a colour filter

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Drawing Ray Diagrams
topics.description: Draw ray diagrams to show reflection at a plane mirror (angle of incidence = angle of reflection) and refraction at a boundary between media; use ray diagrams to locate images and explain how lenses and mirrors work
evidence: Draw a ray diagram for a plane mirror showing the incident ray, normal, reflected ray, and virtual image
Draw a ray diagram showing a ray bending towards the normal when passing from air into glass
Use a ray diagram to locate the image formed by a convex lens and describe whether it is real or virtual

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Ray Diagrams & Images
topics.description: Construct ray diagrams to show the formation of images by plane mirrors and converging lenses, identifying whether images are real or virtual, magnified or diminished, upright or inverted
evidence: Draws an accurate ray diagram for a plane mirror showing a virtual, upright, same-size image
Draws a ray diagram for a converging lens to show image formation
Uses a ray diagram to determine whether the image is real or virtual and which side of the lens it forms
Applies ray diagram knowledge to explain how glasses, cameras, or projectors work

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: The Electromagnetic Spectrum
topics.description: Describe the full electromagnetic spectrum from radio waves to gamma rays, in order of increasing frequency and energy; explain that all EM waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum; and describe the uses and hazards of different regions
evidence: Lists the seven regions of the EM spectrum in order of increasing frequency
States that all EM waves travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum
Gives at least one use and one hazard for each region of the spectrum
Explains why some EM waves are more dangerous to living tissue than others (linked to frequency/energy)

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Waves & Different Materials
topics.description: Explain how waves can be absorbed, transmitted, or reflected by different materials, and apply these interactions to explain colour perception, sight, communication technologies, and the effects of different surfaces on wave behaviour
evidence: Explains the difference between absorption, transmission, and reflection of waves
Uses the three interactions to explain how we see coloured objects
Explains how radio waves, visible light, and infrared are used in different communication technologies
Describes how the properties of a surface (colour, texture, material) determine how it interacts with radiation

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Dressing for the Weather
topics.description: Choose appropriate clothing and equipment for different weather conditions — coat and umbrella for rain, sun hat and sunscreen for hot sun, warm layers for cold — understanding that weather affects what we do and how we prepare each day
evidence: Select appropriate clothing for at least three different weather conditions
Explain why certain clothes or equipment are needed for specific weather
Describe how weather affects daily activities like playtime, walking to school, or outdoor events

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Rain & Puddles
topics.description: Know that rain falls from clouds in the sky, that puddles disappear because water goes back into the air, and that this is part of how water moves around — up into the sky and back down again
evidence: State that rain falls from clouds
Explain that puddles disappear because the water goes into the air
Describe the basic idea that water goes up and comes back down in a repeating process

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Seasons & Weather Patterns
topics.description: Know that weather changes with the seasons — spring brings rain and new growth, summer is warmest with long days, autumn brings cooling and falling leaves, winter is coldest with short days — and that this pattern repeats every year
evidence: Name the four seasons and describe typical weather for each
Explain that days are longer in summer and shorter in winter
State that the seasonal pattern repeats every year

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Storm Safety
topics.description: Know basic storm safety: during thunder and lightning, go indoors or into a car, stay away from trees and water; understand that storms can be frightening but there are ways to stay safe
evidence: State at least two safety rules for thunderstorms
Explain why going indoors is the safest option during lightning
Describe that storms are natural events and there are ways to stay safe

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Temperature & Thermometers
topics.description: Understand temperature as how hot or cold something is, that a thermometer measures temperature, and use words like hot, warm, cool, and cold to describe how the air feels on different days
evidence: Explain that temperature describes how hot or cold something is
Identify a thermometer as the tool used to measure temperature
Use words like hot, warm, cool, and cold appropriately to describe air temperature

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Types of Weather
topics.description: Identify and describe different types of weather — sunny, rainy, windy, snowy, cloudy, foggy, stormy — and describe what the weather is like today using simple vocabulary
evidence: Name at least five types of weather
Describe today's weather accurately using appropriate vocabulary
Match weather types to simple pictures or symbols

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Weather Forecasting & Safety
topics.description: Ask questions to obtain information about the purpose of weather forecasting and how people prepare for and respond to severe weather
evidence: Explain that weather forecasts help people plan and stay safe
Describe how people prepare for at least two types of severe weather (storm, flood, heat wave, blizzard)
Ask relevant questions about weather hazards and find answers from appropriate sources

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: What Is Wind?
topics.description: Know that wind is moving air, that it can be gentle (a breeze) or very strong (a gale), and that wind can move things like leaves, kites, flags, and even push people
evidence: Define wind as air that is moving
Describe the difference between a gentle breeze and a strong wind
Give examples of things that wind can move or affect

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Cloud Types
topics.description: Identify the three main cloud types — cumulus (fluffy, fair weather), stratus (flat layers, overcast or drizzle), and cirrus (thin wisps, high up) — and understand that clouds form as water vapour in the air cools, forming tiny water droplets or ice crystals
evidence: Name and describe the three main cloud types: cumulus, stratus, cirrus
Explain that clouds form when water vapour cools and condenses
Use cloud type to make a simple prediction about the weather

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Geography & Local Weather
topics.description: Know that places around the world have different typical weather: many lowland tropical places are warm year-round with rainfall that may vary by season; deserts are dry and can be hot or cold; polar regions have long cold winters and short cool summers. Explain how distance from the Equator, altitude and nearness to the sea influence local climate, using these as general patterns rather than rules for every day or place.
evidence: Describe typical weather in at least three different climate types
Explain that places near the equator tend to be hotter
Name at least one factor that affects a place's weather besides latitude

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: The Water Cycle
topics.description: Understand the water cycle: the Sun heats water in oceans and lakes causing it to evaporate into water vapour, the vapour rises and cools to form clouds (condensation), and water falls back to Earth as rain, snow, or hail (precipitation) — then the cycle repeats
evidence: Name the three main stages: evaporation, condensation, precipitation
Explain the Sun's role in driving the water cycle
Describe the water cycle as a continuous loop with no beginning or end

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Thunder & Lightning
topics.description: Know that thunder and lightning happen during thunderstorms: lightning is a giant spark of electricity that forms in clouds, thunder is the sound the lightning makes, and we see lightning before hearing thunder because light travels faster than sound
evidence: Describe lightning as a large electrical discharge in clouds
Explain that thunder is the sound caused by lightning
State that we see lightning before hearing thunder because light travels faster than sound

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Using Weather Instruments
topics.description: Use weather instruments to measure and record weather data: thermometers for temperature in °C, rain gauges for rainfall, wind vanes for direction, and anemometers for wind speed — and keep a weather diary over time
evidence: Name at least three weather instruments and explain what each measures
Read a thermometer and record the temperature in degrees Celsius
Record weather data in a table or diary over several days

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Weather Forecasting
topics.description: Know that meteorologists are scientists who study and forecast the weather using satellites, radar, weather balloons, and computer models, and that weather forecasts help people plan their activities and prepare for dangerous weather
evidence: Define a meteorologist as a scientist who studies and predicts weather
Name at least three tools meteorologists use
Explain why weather forecasting is useful for safety and daily planning

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Weather vs Climate
topics.description: Distinguish between weather and climate: weather is what the atmosphere is doing right now or today (it can change hour to hour), while climate is the typical pattern of weather in a place over many years
evidence: Define weather as short-term atmospheric conditions
Define climate as the long-term pattern of weather in a place
Give an example showing the difference: a cold day doesn't change the overall climate

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: What Causes Wind
topics.description: Understand what causes wind: the Sun heats the Earth's surface unevenly, warm air rises because it is lighter, and cooler air rushes in to take its place — this movement of air is wind
evidence: Explain that the Sun heats Earth's surface unevenly
State that warm air rises and cooler air moves in to replace it
Define this air movement as wind

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Designing for Weather Hazards
topics.description: Make a claim about the merit of a design solution that reduces the impacts of a weather-related hazard such as flooding, wind damage, or extreme temperatures
evidence: Identify a specific weather-related hazard and its impacts on people
Describe at least two design solutions intended to reduce those impacts
Make a claim supported by evidence about which solution is most effective and why

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Climate Change Basics
topics.description: Understand the basics of climate change: Earth’s atmosphere traps some of the Sun's heat (the greenhouse effect), burning fossil fuels adds extra greenhouse gases (especially CO₂), this is making Earth gradually warmer, and this warming changes weather patterns, melts ice, and raises sea levels
evidence: Describe the greenhouse effect: the atmosphere traps heat from the Sun
Explain that burning fossil fuels increases CO₂ in the atmosphere
Name at least two consequences of global warming: changing weather patterns, melting ice, rising seas

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Climate Zones
topics.description: Understand that Earth has distinct climate zones — tropical (hot and wet near the equator), temperate (moderate, with four seasons), polar (freezing cold), arid/desert (very dry), and mountain (cold at high altitude) — and that each zone supports different ecosystems and ways of life
evidence: Name and describe at least four climate zones
Explain what determines which zone a place belongs to (mainly latitude and geography)
Give an example of how a climate zone affects the plants, animals, or people living there

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Extreme Weather Events
topics.description: Know about extreme weather events — hurricanes (spinning storms over warm ocean), tornadoes (violent rotating columns of air), floods, droughts, and blizzards — how they form, where they typically occur, and their effects on people and the environment
evidence: Describe how at least two types of extreme weather form
Explain where hurricanes and tornadoes typically occur and why
Describe the effects of extreme weather on communities and landscapes

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Natural resources
topics.description: Obtain and combine information to describe that energy and fuels are derived from natural resources and that their uses affect the environment
evidence: Name natural resources used for energy and fuels (coal, oil, gas, wind, sun, water)
Describe how extracting and using these resources affects the environment (pollution, habitat loss, climate change)
Distinguish between renewable (wind, solar) and non-renewable (fossil fuels) energy sources

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Reading Weather Maps
topics.description: Read and interpret weather maps, data tables, and graphs — identifying symbols for sun, rain, wind, and temperature; spotting trends and patterns in weather data over weeks, months, or seasons; and using data to make simple predictions
evidence: Interpret common weather map symbols for temperature, precipitation, and wind
Read a data table or graph of weather data and identify patterns
Use weather data to make a simple prediction about upcoming conditions

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Sun-Driven Weather Systems
topics.description: Understand how the Sun drives weather: the Sun heats Earth's surface unevenly (land heats faster than water, equator gets more heat than poles), creating differences in air pressure that cause wind patterns, ocean currents, and large-scale weather systems
evidence: Explain that the Sun heats land and water at different rates
Describe how temperature differences create air pressure differences that drive wind
Connect uneven heating to large-scale weather patterns

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: The Atmosphere
topics.description: Know that Earth is surrounded by a layer of air called the atmosphere, that air has weight and exerts pressure, that the atmosphere protects us from harmful radiation and keeps the planet warm enough for life, and that weather happens in the lowest layer (troposphere)
evidence: Define the atmosphere as the layer of air surrounding Earth
State that air has weight and exerts pressure
Explain that weather occurs in the troposphere, the lowest layer of the atmosphere

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Weather-Resistant Engineering
topics.description: Understand that engineers design buildings, flood defences, and warning systems to protect communities from extreme weather — hurricane-resistant roofs, flood barriers, tornado shelters, and early-warning alert systems — and evaluate the merits of these solutions
evidence: Describe at least two engineering solutions designed to protect against extreme weather
Explain how a specific design feature reduces damage from a weather hazard
Evaluate the advantages and limitations of a weather protection solution

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Global Wind Patterns
topics.description: Explain that unequal solar heating drives large-scale atmospheric circulation: Hadley cells (0-30°), Ferrel cells (30-60°), and polar cells (60-90°) produce the trade winds, westerlies, and polar easterlies; describe how the Coriolis effect from Earth's rotation deflects winds rightward in the Northern Hemisphere; explain the jet stream as a fast high-altitude wind that steers weather systems; connect jet stream waviness and Arctic amplification to prolonged extreme weather

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Greenhouse Gas Science
topics.description: Describe the electromagnetic spectrum and distinguish between short-wave solar radiation and long-wave infrared radiation emitted by Earth; explain how greenhouse gas molecules (CO2, CH4, N2O, H2O) absorb and re-emit infrared through molecular vibration while O2 and N2 do not; distinguish the natural greenhouse effect (which makes Earth habitable) from the enhanced greenhouse effect driven by human emissions; evaluate the relative potency of different greenhouse gases

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Hurricanes, Tornadoes & Monsoons
topics.description: Explain how hurricanes form and intensify over warm ocean water (latent heat release, low-pressure spiral); describe tornado formation within supercell thunderstorms; explain monsoon mechanics driven by temperature differences between land and sea; introduce attribution science — how scientists use climate models to calculate whether and by how much climate change increased the probability or intensity of a specific extreme weather event

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Reading Ancient Climate Records
topics.description: Explain how ice cores preserve ancient air bubbles, isotope ratios, and volcanic markers allowing reconstruction of temperature and CO2 going back 800,000 years; describe tree rings, ocean sediment cores, coral skeletons, and pollen records as additional climate proxies; explain how climate models are built and validated against the palaeoclimate record; describe the IPCC process of synthesising scientific evidence across thousands of studies to produce consensus assessments

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Net Zero & Energy Transition
topics.description: Evaluate the energy transition required to reach net zero: renewable energy scaling, electrification of transport and heat, green hydrogen; describe carbon capture and storage (CCS) and direct air capture (DAC); introduce proposed solar radiation management techniques (stratospheric aerosol injection, marine cloud brightening) and their potential risks and governance challenges; critically evaluate the role of individual behaviour change versus systemic policy in reducing emissions

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Length stays the same when an object is moved or bent
topics.description: Recognise and explain that moving or bending an object preserves its length when it is not stretched, cut or joined to another piece. Distinguish length along a cord or ribbon from the straight-line distance between its ends, and use this reasoning in everyday measurement problems.
evidence: Predict that the same ribbon has the same length when straight, curved or looped; explain why and check by straightening it beside a ruler
Explain why a bent cord can have closer endpoints without becoming a shorter cord, and distinguish bending from stretching or cutting
Decide whether an unchanged ribbon moved around a parcel still has enough length for a planned use, checking the length along the ribbon rather than its apparent endpoint separation

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Liquid volume stays the same during ordinary pouring
topics.description: Recognise and explain that ordinary pouring between containers preserves the volume of the same liquid when none is added, removed or spilled and there are no other changes to the liquid or conditions. Distinguish liquid volume from liquid height and container capacity, and apply this reasoning in everyday pouring problems.
evidence: Predict that juice poured without loss from a wide cup into a tall narrow glass has the same volume despite a higher liquid level, and check with the same measuring jug
Explain that a larger-capacity container does not create more liquid; distinguish an unchanged pour from spilling, adding or removing some
Decide whether pouring the same juice into a differently shaped serving vessel changes the amount available for equal servings, then verify using equal-sized cups

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Development and spread of zero and positional notation
topics.description: Explain a source-supported account of the development of zero and decimal positional notation in India, their transmission through Arabic-writing mathematicians and later European adaptations, and their continuing usefulness for number records and calculation, including modern digital devices. Distinguish a placeholder from zero as a number without attributing the entire development to one inventor.
evidence: Use a supplied evidence sequence to explain India’s major contribution and how arithmetic knowledge travelled through Arabic-writing and Latin-adapting scholars; do not turn the modern term Arabic numerals into an exclusive origin claim
Distinguish an empty place in 302 from zero as the result of 3 minus 3, while recognising that earlier cultures also used placeholder marks
Explain why keeping an empty place matters in a modern number record or a calculator’s decimal display, connecting that usefulness to the historical development of positional notation

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Formulating mathematical problems
topics.description: Formulate a mathematically answerable question from an observed or given situation involving quantities, shapes, positions or measures. Choose what to find out, identify relevant available or needed information, and state a suitable mathematical criterion or method. Express the problem through speech, pointing, drawings or a model.
evidence: From a neutral scene of objects, choose a quantity to find out and formulate a question without the adult supplying the unknown; identify which information is available and which would need to be counted or measured

Distinguish a preference question from one with a mathematical criterion, or refine it into an answerable one; explain when missing information or an unrestricted question prevents an answer from the available situation
Transfer the operation to a shape, fit / position or measurement situation, stating a suitable comparison, model or measure rather than merely repeating a familiar addition question

topics.subject: Art & Design
topics.name: Making and controlling marks
topics.description: Use suitable drawing or painting tools to make marks deliberately, starting, moving and stopping the tool and adjusting movement or pressure for an intended line, area or effect. Explore a different tool or surface and adjust handling to produce a chosen effect. This does not require letter knowledge, recognisable pictures, a particular handedness or a fixed grip shape.
evidence: Make a chosen line, patch or other mark with an appropriate tool, showing purposeful starting, movement and stopping rather than only leaving an accidental trace.
Change movement or pressure to alter a mark in a chosen way, such as its direction, extent or coverage, and indicate the intended change by showing, pointing or ordinary language.
Use another suitable drawing or painting tool or surface and adjust handling to make a chosen effect; comfortable functional handling matters rather than one prescribed body position or hand.

topics.subject: Learning to Learn
topics.name: Remembering visual forms
topics.description: Recognise a previously seen visual symbol or simple representation after its sample has been hidden, distinguishing it from close alternatives using remembered visual features. This concerns remembering forms rather than reading a named script, remembering a fixed number of items or reproducing a timed memory score.
evidence: Inspect a simple unfamiliar form, then recognise it among close alternatives after the sample is hidden; indicate a distinguishing remembered feature by pointing, drawing or describing.
Distinguish a remembered form from a changed orientation, missing part or altered arrangement where that difference is relevant to the displayed forms; do not rely only on naming a familiar object.
Repeat with a different family of symbols or simple picture representations after a suitable intervening activity, without seeing the original sample or receiving hints that identify the answer.

topics.subject: Learning to Learn
topics.name: Noticing present sensations and thoughts
topics.description: Deliberately attend to an ordinary current sensory experience, notice when attention moves to a thought or another sensation, and bring attention back to a chosen focus without needing to judge, suppress or change the experience. This can occur when calm as well as when upset.
evidence: Choose an accessible current focus, such as an ordinary sound, contact sensation or comfortable natural breath, and indicate a specific feature noticed during the activity.
Notice a thought or a change of attention during an ordinary quiet activity and indicate that the focus changed; a learner may report the process without disclosing private thought content.

Return attention to the chosen experience and repeat in a different everyday setting or with another accessible sensory focus, distinguishing noticing an experience from making it stop or feel positive.

topics.subject: Personal & Social Development
topics.name: Social roles and changing responsibilities
topics.description: Describe familiar social roles and relationships, connect them with responsibilities toward other people and the environment, and explain how a setting, event or changing circumstances can alter a role, relationship or duty. Use everyday examples without assuming a particular family structure or requiring private personal disclosure.
evidence: Describe a familiar role, such as pupil, friend, family member or someone helping care for a plant or shared place, and explain a responsibility that comes with it.
Compare one person’s roles, relationships and responsibilities in two settings, explaining why a duty or way of relating to others differs.

Explain how a provided event or change in circumstances alters a responsibility or relationship, including a care duty toward the environment; naming an event or expressing a feeling alone is insufficient.
Apply the role–duty–circumstance relationship to a new supplied scenario, without treating duties as fixed by gender or a single family arrangement.

topics.subject: History
topics.name: Indigenous cultural renewal in Canada
topics.description: Explain in age-appropriate terms how colonial policies in Canada, including residential schooling, disrupted many First Nations, Métis and Inuit family, language and cultural connections. Use attributed contemporary community-led examples to explain cultural renewal and its relationship to identity and belonging, while recognizing distinct peoples and continuing cultures.
evidence: Explain that colonial policies, including residential schools, separated many Indigenous children from their families and suppressed languages and cultural practices; do not imply that every person had the same experience or that cultures disappeared.
Using a named community-authoritative account, identify who leads a contemporary cultural or language renewal initiative and what is being strengthened or reclaimed.
Explain how the example can reconnect people with family, community knowledge or cultural identity, rather than merely say that the project is nice or respectful.
Transfer the historical-disruption, community-action and identity relationship to another attributed example, keeping its people and source distinct.

topics.subject: Geography
topics.name: Traditional and treaty territories in Canada
topics.description: Use attributed, locally verified resources to identify the traditional Indigenous territory or territories and applicable treaty reference for a Canadian place. Distinguish traditional territory, a treaty area or relationship, and a present-day reserve; these references are not interchangeable and may involve more than one people or account.
evidence: Name the peoples and traditional territory or territories identified for a place by the supplied locally verified sources, attributing each account rather than assuming one exclusive owner.
Identify the applicable treaty by its full name or number and regional context when the sources establish one; do not invent a treaty where the verified resources do not establish one.

Explain that traditional territory concerns a people’s enduring connections with lands and waters, a treaty records a particular agreement or relationship, and a present reserve is a particular designated land area rather than the whole traditional territory.

Use a second verified place/resource packet to identify its different territorial and treaty references; explain why the nearest reserve or a municipal boundary alone cannot establish those references.

topics.subject: Performing Arts
topics.name: Matching a sounded pitch
topics.description: Listen to a comfortable reference pitch and intentionally reproduce it with the voice or a suitable pitched instrument, comparing the result with the reference and adjusting higher or lower when needed. Repeat the matching with a new reference. This is relative matching to a heard model, not naming an absolute note or explaining vibration physics.
evidence: Reproduce a comfortable reference pitch after hearing it, rather than only label it high or low or change loudness.
Listen to a comparison between the reference and their attempt and adjust the produced pitch towards the reference; showing the adjustment is sufficient without technical language.
Match a different comfortable reference using the voice or a suitable pitched instrument, without relying on a fixed remembered note.

topics.subject: Performing Arts
topics.name: Creating and shaping musical sound
topics.description: Create or improvise a short piece of musical sound for an intended idea or situation. Choose and organise sounds and silences, listen to the result and deliberately adjust timing, sound quality, loudness or a musical contrast to shape the intended audible effect. Present and adapt the result. Voice, body, suitable instruments or found sounds may be used; a repeating mathematical rule, pitched singing and written notation are not required.
evidence: Create an own short musical sound piece with deliberate sound and silence choices, rather than only copy a model or explain an abstract sequence rule.
Listen to two versions or an attempt and adjust an audible musical feature such as a phrase contrast, timing, loudness, sound quality or ending for an intended effect.
Present the chosen sound piece and adapt it for another idea, situation or available sound source, demonstrating the intended audible difference.

topics.subject: Performing Arts
topics.name: Creating and performing expressive movement sequences
topics.description: Choose, combine and practise a short sequence of body movements to express an everyday action, idea or experience, using movement qualities or spatial choices intentionally. Perform the chosen sequence and vary or adapt it for a different intention or situation. Movement may be seated or standing within safe available access; no fixed dance style, athletic norm, costume or spoken script is required.
evidence: Create and practise a recognisable ordered sequence of own movement choices, rather than only copy isolated teacher actions.
Use a purposeful contrast in movement quality, direction, level, shape or use of space to support the intended action or idea.
Perform the chosen sequence with its intended order and adapt it for a new intention or situation, showing the changed choices.

topics.subject: Art & Design
topics.name: Composing visual artwork
topics.description: Choose and organise visual elements and suitable materials in an artwork to express an observation, idea, experience or feeling. Try an arrangement, make a purposeful change and present the intended effect through the work, demonstration, pointing or ordinary language.
